generated_text: Rather annoying when the midwives say, "Don’t plan for sleep," and it's such good advice. I got nought sleep last night. I’m more exhausted than when I stared death in the face running this marketing gig full-time.      It's the truth. I was in exactly the same mess when  Mikey  was an infant. I reckon sleep is overrated anyway. Though I’ve missed coffee like I’ve missed love in this world. Still, you're used to late nights pulling spreadsheets and collages and whatnot. You're just working in black and white now.      That much I can confirm. I reckon, once the baby’s routine kicks in, I’ll get MySpace levels of sleep back. So, what’s the plot for tonight, then? I was meaning to ask, and I know it's your birthday—Don’t think about arguing with me. You’re coming out for a bit of a night with a bit in it.      No, you didn’t have to think that. I'm determined to be a stay-at-home statue, wrapped around this little one.      You can do both. I’ve seen women who still design bloody websites and walk three miles a day while looking after children. You’re a graduate – surely you can juggle three things and still act natural.      Now don’t go making me feel lazy. I've been out and about with your sister, and the in-laws at the weekend. Honestly, I think my feet are already taped to the pushchair.      So, you can’t be accused of under socialising  now . But there is a birthday about to fall off the calendar. I’m having dinner at  Jamie’s Italian  and a bottle of  Cloudy Bay  to plug the gap. You’re coming, even if I have to chain you to the chair.      Alright, alright. I'm on the case. Let's see, I can get someone to look after him. I reckon your brother-in-law would take over. He’s doing a lot of baby-sitting to keep the peace with your sister.      Perfect, I knew you’d say that. That leaves me go back to my day job if you don’t mind – I have some posters to proof, and that boy's crying means it might be something serious.      If it’s seriously colic, then I think I'm onto a broken baby plot for  Netflix .

Rather annoying, though, innit? You used to just get on a train or a ferry ‘n wander about without a care in the world. Now you've got to sort out this Eurpoean Travel Info System—aint that a belter? I mean, it's not like the EU was in chaos eeny time since Brexit, was it?      Classic government-speak. "European Travel Information and Authorisation System"—ETIAS, if you're keeping track. It's not like it’s a passport or sommat. Still, I suppose it’s better they sort it out now rather than crash headfirst again, eh?      What I don't get is why we had to leave turkey twizzlers and melon to have this added to our lives. We had the safety net of the Schengen in our back pocket. Now you've got to apply online ‘n wait a couple days for approval? I mean, I did it in advance, but I know some of my mates fritzed out near the last minute. One actually missed his train to Paris because it took longer than expected!      I remember when your mate Gareth went to Barcelona and only took two Lidl sandwiches with him and a mini bottle of Ribena. He arrived and said it was like being Baptised in new experiences—aint that what he called it? Bet he had a rough time trying to find turkey twizzlers in a Spanish supermarket!      Hahah, yeah. He sent me a picture of him trying to eat a churro like it was one—piece ‘n fury. Eventually, he worked out it’s better to carry a few snacks in your rucksack when about to cross borders. Still, you can't blame the lads for fritzing out. It's not like it's rocket science or a national service test, but it's that extra hoop, innit?      All I'm saying is that while it's a bit of a shambles, it does give us a chance to be more prepared. My supervisor told me about a time he went to Berlin and ended up trying to find his passport in a Bulgarian bistro. Some people still haven't lost that reckless traveler vibe.      Yeah, go on then. But let's see how it goes next summer when I'm off to Prague. Hopefully, they'll update the app or something soon. ‘Cause I swear to God, if I have to apply and then find it rejected because of some broken upload… I might chuck a right massive wobbly.

Right, who’s up for dessert? I just made some chocolate fudge brownies—the ones with the gooey middle and a splash of sea salt on top. They’re still warm, so we’d best eat them soon before they harden into bricks.       Pause.  Can I have two? Two and a half, maybe?      Oh, come on, Elsie, I said that last time too. And you ended up needing a toothbrush and a calculator. One is enough for you. Two for Freddie, though—only cause he’s a growing boy.      Is it true, Mummy, that you used Monopoly money to pay for the sugar? I overheard you and Daddy yesterday saying something about investing in properties and trading in brownie rights.      Well, not exactly. But it turned into a teaching moment, darling. We were playing a variation. When you land on 'Free Parking,' you get an extra dessert token. And you can trade brownies for property cards if you want to build up to 'Cherry Pie Towers.'      Cherry Pie Towers? Like the one in Wellington with the pink spire and the lemon meringue gargoyle?       Giggling.  That’s what Freddie drew on the Monopoly board with the marker last night, because he’s an artist. And he told me quite seriously that if you own all the desserts, you automatically win the kingdom.      And someone said music and art weren’t useful. He’s a chef-architect-monarch-in-training all in one. Just mind the marshmallows being poured into premium property lots.      Can we do our own version next time? I want to invent the 'Mint Chocolate Property' and charge rent in lollipop coins.      Don’t listen to him, Freddie. My idea is to put the whole board inside a giant fruit tart, with icing roads and marzipan houses. And any player who goes bankrupt gets turned into a lemon meringue pie!       Sighing with a smile.  Well, as long as the chocolate gets used fairly. I’ve got a recipe for Black Forest Gateau with three layers and the kind of acidity that stops it from being too sweet. It’s got real cherry compote, not the fake stuff that tastes like sadness.      Does your recipe accept bartering with Monopoly money? I’ve got a £200 note with a brownie belly on it to pay you in advance for backup help.      Is that a diplomatic currency offer? I call first dibs for the second layer.

Rather annoying this, innit? Traffic’s mental again, even at this time. Should’ve walked, like I said.      I’m more annoyed I agreed to this meeting after work. Had to cancel a few messages to do this, and it’s such a daft reason to make the trip eenyways.      Yeah, but I reckon it’s not all bad. Might be a chance to swap stuff. Got that old box I never used in the garage, you’d get a use for it. You always was the tidy one when it came to tools and stuff.      Aye, even back at uni I was always the one to keep the lab benches clean. You were always the one dragging me off to late-night takeaways. Still do that by the way – I’m starvin’ now and I haven’t even had a chance to grab a snack!      Blimey, I said tea. Not a drive in traffic and a meeting. Go on then, I can pull into that roundabout up ahead. Let you off near the shop and we can grab a bite?      Brilliant! Fries and a coffee would hit the spot. Or maybe a hot dog if they’ve got it. Been craving one all week.      Mate, you say hot dog, I say it’s a chicken wrap. Let’s compromise on fries and two coffees and see who gives in first.      Deal. Now, just someone make the damn traffic budge! God, this is already dragging on.      Just don’t start moaning again about the price of fuel. I’ve had enough of it all day at home about how I’m “a bad citizen” for using the car.      Ronks! That’s your own doing then. Should’ve talked her into sending a teleport to the garage.       laughs  Aye, if only technology worked at her pace. Still, least it was nice of her to come meet me for the drive. I could’ve lost my hearing otherwise.      Nah, you’d’ve sorted a new one with your fancy tech admin gig. Me, I’m still stuck with my 1990s set goin’ on in my place.      True, true. But let’s see who’s sussing out the latest gadgets at your place next week. I’m planning on blowing your mind with a new smart kettle. Boils water by just thinking of tea!      Perks of being best mates and best data holders. Now can I get my damn coffee?

Rather a damp day, isn't it? That’s the weather for you—too much of it in recent weeks, and I’ll not be moping around like a wet sheet. I've been meaning to ask, Ivy, what with all that rain, I was thinking of planting some bulbs in the garden. Got a few left over from last year. Do you think it's still possible?      Oh dear, Alistair, I know that this isn't the best time, but you're quite the reasonable chap. We've had the ground practically like slimy custard, but if you dig deep enough... well, I’ve even seen people do it. Though, mind the spuds—those potatoes are in there well and good, you don’t want to unearth them by accident. What sort of bulbs you talking about, daffodils?      Blimey, planting when the earth is almost breakfast, no doubt. I've been thinking of a bit of repotting myself, ever since Martha gave us that lovely looking geranium last summer. Good for the eyes, like. I do tell you, being stuck in one place doesn't mean you don’t need a spot of greenery. Old George gave me a go on pruning—said it's like rhythm in a way. You cut here, and it flowers there, fairly simple, like.      Aye, somethin’ to do, something to plan. I miss the bridges and the hills—never looked at a trowel in my working days. But you know, a man just needs to keep a bit of structure. Also, I've been meaning to talk to you both—do you remember that curry place in Norwich? I fancied going there again for the Sunday bhangra, you know, the vibes they had. Maybe next weekend? Just for laughs.      Oh, the spices there do something, don’t they? I always tell you, Alistair, that garlic lamb could bring the dead back. But yes, I'd love it. It’s been far too long since we had a good night out. Though I do worry about the stairs with that spicy food and the dancing—my legs do love a challenge, you know.      Blimey, if goin' on a curry night is our new identity, I’ll wear it like a badge of honour. Never could stand tandoori chicken myself, always went for the chicken tikka. Tastes, Ivy, like roles in life—everyone’s got ’em.

Rather annoying when the measurement isn't clear on these product listings. I've had a few customers complain that they ordered a 500ml bottle, only to find it's actually 175ml once it arrived.      I know what you mean. I had a customer in Hitchin—well, actually I don't think they were from Hitchin, just had an accent suggesting it—who said that our listing wasn't specific enough. Honestly, I had to tell them I was terribly sorry and send them a coupon for their next order.      Well, it's not just a language problem. It's also about clarity and expectations. British people are pretty literal when it comes to quantities and measurements.      So what are you saying? That I need to start writing things in centimetres and grams in every description? Half my customers in the Midlands still use imperial.      Not quite. Maybe add a note in parenthesis at the end, like ""—something like that. Might get a few less complaints and more trust in the brand.      It sounds like good advice. I was thinking of launching a new product range in July. You know, something inspired by your holiday in France last summer, maybe with lavender and other natural scents?      Oh, that's a brilliant idea. And we could market it as "handmade in the English Midlands with inspiration from the French countryside." That kind of mix always sells oddly well on social media.      You think I should do an Instagram live session when we launch it? I know I'm not the most photogenic type, but the products speak for themselves.      Yes! You know that your authenticity is a huge part of the Honest Skincare brand. My students always say they admire how you tell your own story and not some polished up version.      Thanks, I do try. My nan always said that being yourself is the best marketing strategy you can ever have. Although she also always called me 'honey' and told me how lovely I looked, no matter how messy I was.      Oh please go easy on the nan-via-the-English-Midlands charm—still makes me miss mine, you know.      Anyway, all joking aside. I really do need someone to help me with the language and tone of the product descriptions. You interested?      Perks?      A few jars of lavender body balm to experiment on your students? Possibly?      You're on. Let me just make a pot of tea and I’ll start looking at the wording.

Rather shocking the news from Scotland last week, isn’t it? That factory closure in Fife — it’s gone and put dozens of folk out of work.      Aye, I read about it in the paper. Poor lads and lasses — some of them were employed there for decades. Do you know anyone from around there who was affected?      Know of a few. Jim Aitken — he worked in that factory since he was twenty-two. Imagine going through thirty years of the same routine and then waking up and finding the whole place shut down. He was one of those who never truly had much in the way of prospects, you see.      It’s tragic what’s been happening with these factories. I left teaching a few years back, but I still catch the news every now and then. A world away from teaching secondary in Brighton — harder to forget the problems when you're practically living them.      Oh aye, you ever looked at that fella down the road — the man who once worked full-time and now sits by the shop, smoking his pipe and watching the world go by? Sometimes I think he’s still waiting for the bus to take him to work.      That’s Tom from the corner is it? – Mate of yours?      No, not really — just a sombre little figure that makes you think. You know what it is? When you get to our age, you just see more people slipping through the net. Like they just don’t have a plan left.      Aye, and I don’t mean to sound like a right old pessimist, but most people about our age never truly saved for retirement. Paid into the system, but never really thought it’d be this difficult.      Doesn’t help when the government cuts to the lot, does it? I’ve been on benefits most of my time after retiring. Not that I’m one to complain — got my sister to look after me, you know.      Well, I’m just as well as can be expected with this job I’ve got at the school. Some mornings, I swear I’m still teaching year sevens. But the kids are brighter now, really. They see things more clearly — global issues, economic changes, even how the world is shaping up.      And your lot at the school — have you noticed the effect of this factory closure in Brighton?

Rather chilly this evening, isn't it? I turned the heating on ages ago, but it's been like a sauna and a shower at the same time today. Blows hot air for ten minutes, then stops and leaves us all shivering.      Yeah, our central heating at home’s not playing ball either. I’ve been reduced to wrapping my thick scarf round me just to heat the desk next to the kettle. It’s starting to feel more like a shed incident than a living space.      Honestly, we had the same problem for weeks. We even had the boiler man in – turns out the thermostat was jacked up. He sorted it, but it cost a fortune. Still, at least now we’re warm when we’re cooking Christmas dinners and whatnot.      I know what you mean, I used to make mulberry jam up to the point it was bearable to leave the house, but then it suddenly started raining. I ended up in my workshop under a blanket and a desktop heater, preserving the last lot. Mulberries aren’t like blackberries, they need proper weather.      Oh, I love that! Jam is a great way to spend early December. What with everything else going on… plus, I tried making it once, but got way too much pectin in it and it was more like glue than fruit.      Same with apple pie – my sister and I attempted a large family one back in Wordsley. It looked great in the pan, but when we opened the oven door, it deflated like a flatulent balloon. Some Christmas memories are better left with the marshmallows and tea.      I’ve found it best to let people make their own dishes. I’m the PhD student, remember? I let my cooking be whatever my failsafe recipes throw up. At least the digestive issues are consistent!      Should we start discussing Christmas stuff? I’m already thinking about presents. I have no idea what to get for any of you scientists and engineers.      I’ll be honest, my present list is mostly Amazon vouchers. It’s always safer with people who keep on changing what interests them.      Still, I did get this new toolkit for the workshop the other day. It came with a torque wrench and a few hex bits I’d been needing. It’s a bit technical but it was worth the wait.      So are you planning to retire to your own tools one day, then?

Rather annoying to be honest, I can't find any of our decent cutlery—the stuff with the penguin etching on it. Have you seen it, Mum?      No darling, I haven’t. We ran out the other day as well. I'll have to make a note on the list to order more from the place you like. I reckon it's about time we sorted out a proper system for all these little things before they vanish again.      Honestly, who needs penguin etching on cutlery? It just makes it harder to clean. I mean, I like to keep things simple these days—straight, no frills.      You like that because you still live with your flatmate and have no sense of style! I’m just saying, if we're having dinner at mum’s, we may as well make it look nice.      I must say this happened when I was growing up too. People’s stuff would always disappear, especially after family gatherings. Used to drive my old man potty.      Nothing like a sturdy wooden spoon and a bit of elbow grease! I’ve still got my old set from when I was a lad—nothing fancy, just workin’ tools. Mind you, most of the stuff we had got chucked in the bin because they thought it was broken.      That’s the trouble with families, love. You’ve got your sets, they’ve got their sets—but in the end, it's all a bit of a jumble.      Also, have we considered just buying more? Even if we don’t use it all, better to have a spare set than to argue about the same pair each week.      Honestly, you could write a research paper on this! I mean it is a classic domestic organisational study. But jolly good point.      Back in my day, we used the same few forks for everything. Barely had a knife, mind. You just sort of got on with it.      Ah, nostalgia with a twist of austerity. But I do like the idea of creating some set rules for where these things are stored and who’s responsible for washing them up.      That might be the way forward. If we all had individual zones in the box, maybe we'd be a lot less likely to lose track of things.      I'm down with that. Just like your university case study on organisational efficiency! Let’s make a start at the next family dinner.

Rather annoying the new barista at work isn't she? I swear she's got it in for me. I got the wrong order yesterday—again. It's not even funny anymore, just tedious. But I suppose it's all par for the course, I suppose?      Mmm. She eeny weeny? I don't like her either. I reckon she's not all that nice with the customers. A lot of people have been moaning about her, Miss Alice said she was quite rude to her once. We don't like her. Isnae called Sophie, or Petra?      It's Petra. I've made a note to talk to the manager, only I’ve been so busy getting the turkey ready for the ski trip. Och, we leave on Wednesday, right? I still can’t believe how fast the week has flown by. I’m looking forward to the fresh air, honestly. Just escaping the cold and this endless drizzle.      Yes, five days! We’re going to do snowball fights and go on the slopes and wear my new red coat, aren’t we?      Aye, your new coat looks lovely. And I've packed your mittens and woolly hat. I reckon we should both try the off-piste skiing too – Mateo showed me a few videos and it looks brilliant. Though I might end up somersaulting into a snowdrift again. Still, better that than not trying, eh?      Oh no, remember when you fell over in the snow and thought it was a trampoline? We all roared with laughter and then helped you up. Can I try the snow ballet, Mummy? I saw some pictures of people doing flips on the slopes.      Oh yes, absolutely. We’ll start you off gently with some instructor time, then maybe we can both take some lessons, see if we can avoid the guesthouse window next time.      You got all snowy on the window! It looked like a mad monster!      Well that’ll be the topic of the next barista’s story, no doubt! Right, enough about snow monsters – you remember to pack your thermals, don’t you? No goody-two-shoes stuff about forgetting.      I packed six of them! And I filled up the box with granola bars and your lucky ski hat. I’m helping you.      That’s my star. I think we’re set then. Now, how about that chocolate cake I made earlier? Or do you fancy another game of 'build the snowman' before bed?

So did you do your maths homework yet? I’ve been staring at the algebra for like, an hour and I’m still confused.      Nope, I haven’t even started it. Why? You doing it now?      Yeah, I’m trying. But it’s so annoying. Like, when are we  ever  going to use this in real life? I mean, most people just use calculators, right?      Fair point. But Miss Thompson says it’s supposed to train our brains or something. Honestly, I just do it so I don’t get a detention... again.      Oh no, me too. I got told off last week for leaving my English homework in a wrinkled bin bag. Fun.      I’m not even going to ask about the bin bag. Do you remember what we did in Food Tech last term? The chocolate breakfast cake incident?      How could I forget? That was the best ever. I thought I ate the cake before the teacher could stop me, but she still took a photo.      Yeah, and the next day there was a rule that no edible crayons. Hilarious. Remind me… are we still doing extra Spanish this term?      I think we are, but I’m still not getting the present perfect tense. I’m mixing it up with French again.      Me too! Like, why isn't it the 'perfect present'? That would make more sense. Anyway, what are you thinking about doing after school? Job-wise, I mean.      I’m not sure yet. Maybe something in admin or stuff at a café. I don’t want to be a teacher though, too many kids.      Same! I was thinking maybe retail or even something techy. My cousin works in IT and says it’s not as boring as it sounds.      That’s actually a good idea. I was thinking about it too. I tried using her for Spanish homework help once and she said “never again.”      She probably didn’t need the emotional whiplash of listening to you over Zoom for an hour.      Haha, yeah. Look, I think I’m going to give up on this maths now. You in? We could go listen to some music and vibe?      Vibe at 8pm? Of a Friday? Absolutely. I’ll bring the speakers. Just don’t play your dad’s old Oasis songs.      They’re  classic . But fair, I’ll make a playlist instead. My new love is this chill lo-fi thing.

Rather good film that The Sound of Music, isn’t it? I still remember watching it on a rainy Sunday when I was a girl. Just about every family had it on their shelves, didn’t they?      Yeah, I’ve seen it a couple of times, but honestly, I prefer newer stuff—like the  Parasite  one, or  Everything Everywhere All at Once . They sort of… mess with your brain but in a good way.      Oh, I’ve not seen those. Too many subtitles, if you ask me! Do they speak too much English in them?      Some, but a lot’s in Korean and Mandarin, yeah. Still, the acting’s brilliant. It’s all about… you know, life’s chaos, and how people react to it.      I think I’d find that rather heavy for a Saturday night. Nothing better than a musical and a cup of tea for me! Haha!      Fair enough! Everyone’s got their own kind of film, I guess. So, what about you—do you have a favorite?      I do, actually. It’s a bit odd, but  E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial . I remember it being such a big deal when it came out. I must’ve been about twelve. My cousin brought the tape round, and my mother nearly had a heart attack watching it! Thought the monsters looked a bit too real.      Haha, yeah, I remember the debate: is E.T. just a oddly dressed kid or what? But the kid who played him was real good. Still,  E.T.  was one of the first films I ever saw at the cinema. My parents took me when I was seven. It terrified me a little, but I loved it.      Well, I suppose it does to most of us. Films like that stick with you. My brother used to play that cassette at least once a week—well, he still does. We haven’t spoken for years, but I could always tell from hearing that tape that he’s doing alright.      That’s actually really sweet. I suppose the best films do more than just entertain. They connect us.      Oh absolutely! They tell stories that stay with you for a lifetime.      I suppose they do. That bloke on the telly recently was talking about how films can make you question your own life, in a way. It’s strange how that works.      Oh, I’m sure the food and the songs helped more than the questioning!

Rather annoying the wet weather isn't it? I was supposed to drive out to Hitchin tomorrow for that teacher’s workshop and I’ll be stuck in this traffic more than I will be on the road.      Aye love, the roads are as bad as motorways in India I’ve heard. That friend of mine from Hinjewadi posted about the traffic this morning on her WhatsApp group — sounded like something out of a Stephen King novel! Why'd you not fly or something?      Please! You know the workshops are for credit and online ones don’t count. And flying from Birmingham is three times more expensive! Not when I’m still learning to budget properly after getting that postgrad in linguistics.      Budgeting is important, I suppose. I had to warn you about your brother last week: spending like the government’s paying him in Manchester while he’s working part-time. He nearly blew his rent money on some cricket tickets for the Ashes.      Oh, not again! Casper and his sports obsession. He’d sell his bones for a game of rugby, I swear.      You laugh now, but grief when he can’t afford to buy his mother dinner for her birthday. Speaking of, are we still on for the family lunch? Bring your friend Clara, I think it's important she sees what the weather is really like in these parts.      Oh, Clara will be delighted, she adores food.      And not to mention a good moan about the weather. Some folks from the law courts moan more than the politicians do. Can’t fault 'em, though — it’s nearly about to fall off the calendar.      Another thing, I meant to ask you about the court usher life. Still enjoying the outings and the formal meetings?      Aye, it’s not for youngbloods, but there's a certain sort of peace in holding the dock as it were. You meet all sorts — barristers, lawyers who lost their hearing, and that one bloke whose dog always comes with lunches for him and wears better shoes than half the lawyers.      So you're like a guardian of law and goody shoes on four legs?      Something like that love. Just don't tell your brother he's not allowed to bring the dog to court.      Alright mum, I won't tell him that. I’ll just make him walk to work on time like the good lad he should be.

Rather annoying that the lecture theatre was booked out last week, isn’t it? I had such a plan to try out the new interactive maps with the geography students.      Yeah, I remember you saying it was going to be a bit of technical mess—some overhead projectors and a few chunky laptops. I thought, honestly, it’s the least you could do.      Oh, you’ve only just remembered? I told you this last Monday, right before you left for your interview in Shanghai. You were so excited, I practically had to fish for your attention.      I like to think of it more as reappreciating the plan the second time round. You know me like that—absent-minded, but fervent once I’m on board. And I’m glad I was, because it sounded very immersive. A world away from your usual whiteboard storytelling!      I suppose immersive is the right word. I did get in touch with the tech department and they agreed to help rewire the spare classroom so that the students could divide into smaller groups. I do like the way it’s shaping up—everyone gets to be hands-on.      And the response from the students? I imagine they were excited.      Absolutely. They seemed much more engaged. I got a few emails afterward, one from a student who’s into urban development saying he thought the model could be used for visualising city planning in real life.      That’s not bad at all. Let me guess, you consider this your finest hour so far?      I would say I’m on a roll recently. I even had a colleague stop me in the corridor about how I’m finally fulfilling the lecture notes from ten years ago. “You’re progressing,” she said. “As are your students.”      You sound like you’re quite smug about that. Maybe you ought to go out and celebrate.      Are you offering to take me out for supper again? I tried to remind myself that I need to stick to my budget as we’re planning to redecorate the flat next month.      Of course, but let’s compromise—how about something around this budget? I found a nice little gochujang-based stir-fry place not far from here, and I heard the dumplings are to die for.      You can say that again. I have been craving some authentic North China cuisine, after all. And with the heat we’ve been experiencing recently, a little bit of spice does seem appropriate.

Rather annoyingly, I haven't worked out who's supposed to do the babysitting this week. The first couple of days are sorted by Anna, but I'm not sure about Thursday or Friday      Can't Uncle Tom do it this week? He says he wants to help out more.      I don't think he can. I think his wife's having her hair done on Thursday. A lot of people seem to have this obsession with haircuts these days. It's quite interesting, really. We've had three different people from this family chase after the same stylist within a month.      I'd rather not talk about hair today. I'm still thinking about Alice and Dan's photoshoot on Saturday. I'm really excited to see the results.      Oliver, you're very lucky. A professional photoshoot with your friends, while I've got to babysit, no doubt nursing a cup of coffee with a lack of sugar and lots of milk.      You always say that, but why don't we just invite Mum over for coffee, maybe book some time with someone for childcare?      I've tried. All the usual options seem to have something on. I tried to get in touch with Clara, she's baking a cake for a friend's birthday, and Sarah's reading group is today. Honestly, everyone's quite busy these days.      Well, what about your weekend? There are people at work who have been asking about your reading recommendations.      Oh, I've been getting very into some historical fiction lately. It's been a great escape from the chaos of parenting and teaching most of the time. I even pulled the kids into the act last night, we had a sort of little family storytime. They were surprisingly engaged.      Maybe we could do something like that for the photoshoot. Turn it into more of a fun experience. Involve stories or something.      That could be something. I'd be more than happy to help with that. I just need to work out how to do lunches and keep the twins from climbing the walls while doing it.      You're a gem, really. Rather annoying the new barista at my local café, right? Always looks like her head’s about to explode when I say “to go” after ordering my flat white. Honestly, what’s the deal with that? I had this incident where my colleague, Laura, spilled a latte on herself while fulfilling the "das man in the office" stereotype. Just made a mental note to not utter go-to phrases on potentially life-and-death breaks. Any plans at the weekend? Thought about going out, but genuinely can’t decide if it’s worth the effort after lectures.      Me neither. Thought about going to that new bar off the town centre, but hearing it’s packed and you have to queue for at least an hour just to order a drink.

Rather annoying the queue at the supermarket, innit? Seems like everything sticks to my trolley like it's got a mind of its own.      Mate, I've been where you are. I was trying to get some fresh coleslaw and it were all like squashed together in the eeny weeny fridge section. Made me twitch, I’ll reckon.      Oh aye, I had a similar experience the other day. I went to this little shop down by the river in Cambridge. Tried to get sommat for the weekend, but when I asked the bloke what meat he had, he said it were  only dead chicken meat . Joked, of course!      My turkey curry was a disaster too. I left it on the stove and then the smoke alarm went berking, and now I think the whole house smells like an explosion in a spice factory.      Buckshee alarm system happened to me once. Pulled a pan out, and it were like, you know, near scalded the clappers off me. I nearly went into the next room for some oxygen, I really did.      Did you manage to salvage anything,Speaker_1?      Eh, I ended up just putting it all in the bin. But while I was, I found these old photos in the back of a drawer. It were my gran and all, trying to make some ‘traditional’ cookin’ which looked more like a chemistry experiment.      That's a good one. I had a recipe book from my uncle once—meant to be a proper German shepherd’s pie, but he’d wrote in the middle, about half way through the recipe: "Add the touch of soul, then mix vibes and hope for the best." Proper cabby.      Aye, I can picture the smell, like burning toast and treacle. But you know what, it were better than me curry. I'm thinking of giving my gran a hand next week, you know, passing on the knowledge.      That’s a proper grand plan, honestly. I think it'd be brilliant if we could capture it, you know, for a scrap or a blog or something. Could go viral, I reckon.      Just don't expect her to follow directions. Last time she tried a box cake, she added what she thought was cinnamon. It were actually fluoxetine tablets. Thought we were in for a tea-time revelation.      Ha, talk about a kick over the line! We’d best get cracking then.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? I was just thinking 'ow nice it'd be to 'ave a proper trip out, maybe 'ead down to London agin.      Now there's an idea. Not since we 'ad that fumble wi' the youth hostel in Cornwall 'ave I been anywhere really  worthwhile . It was 'igh time we fancied up a bit of travel. Did you 'ear, they're actually doing a refurbishment on that old building down by the river there 'as a nice view.      Didn’t it get bought by some big developer? I read about it in one o' the papers. Now, I'm not too 'ungry for London per se—unless it's for one of them new cafés in Soho. I do miss the buzz, though, even if I'm more the teacher type—leading kids 'round museums and such.      Oh 'eck, I did miss the 'ospitality, you know. Me and m'colleague always had a laugh. Good ones, too, like that one time wi' the 'ippos. Y'don't 'ear about many 'ippos in London these days, do you?      Nigh on none in the city centre, no. Back 'ome we 'ave a chap, Horace, 'is 'orse is the pride of the parish. Rude thing it is, but beautiful. ‘Balances on hills like it’s never 'eard of gravity.      You lot are talking 'bout travel, but 'ave you had a look at these prices on real estate these days? Can't even  dream  of buying a property in about half the country. I 'ave a cousin trying to sell 'is place in Birmingham and 'asn't got a look in.      And we're both still hanging on to ‘ouses 'as well. To be honest, I think I 'ate furnishing. No one wants a land ‘ouse wi' a garden no bigger than a waiting room, mind you. It's as if they're being  designed  by firms 'oo 'aven't 'eard of space efficiency.      Mind you, it's not the 'omes as go—'t's the 'orses or the trips or the gossip wi' the in-laws that really keep you goin'. Me and Elaine were watching some election coverage the other day, I must say I'm not quite sure 'oo those folk are supposed to represent, honest to God.      Yeah, the lot o them! It's a circus really. Unless I'm paying attention for the bits about education and school funding, it's all 'igh backs and side 'its for me.

Honestly, I don't know how you do it, Em. Every time you mention the baby, it's either bottles, nappies, or this poor girl isn’t sleeping a wink.      It's chaotic, Steph. Look, I know you're helping with the research for uni or whatever, and I  am  proud of you, but I swear this baby's as complicated as a PhD thesis. A lot worse.      Okay, but you used to be all about 'babies just need to be fed and cuddled,' and now look at you. You're living with the baby 24/7—what happened to that plan to just focus on yourself for a year like you said you'd do after Marco left?      Plans go to hell the second you're suddenly a single mum in a world that acts like you're now responsible for everything at once. I mean, even your sister starts mastering Anglo-Saxon for no reason and I'm out here trying to figure out why the bloody milk is so thick.      Right, right, you're being dramatic—but listen, I dropped in two bottles freshly made as a gift. I only did it because I know you probably didn't have time to run to the shop again today.      You are the best, and I know it’s not much but the baby actually slept past 5am for the first time last night. And guess what? She fed on those two bottles. Who knows, maybe your supermarket-grade formula is a godsend.      Okay, don’t kid yourself. Formula is delicious and comes with no emotional baggage. I bet she'll develop a love for about five different milk brands by the time she's 18. You're looking at a baby who'll grow up into that ‘brand loyal’ type.      Joke all you like. I still wake up screaming if I dream about baby monitors and baby carriers. You know your Aunt Gwen was nice enough to look after her for you for the weekend, right?      Oh yes, she mentioned it. I’ve been a little busy with my research team, but let me be honest—mentally, I’m like 30% away go. But I think it's more of a ‘mum brain’ thing than anything, you know.      You're already your mum. Every time I look at you, I picture you with a stroller and those matching baby shirts people like so much.

Rather chilly this morning, isn't it? I’ve just boiled the kettle and made a brew. Felt it in the bones, same as you, I reckon?      Oh, absolutely! Got me reaching for the extra blanket before the kettle even boiled! Mind you, the forecast says it’s een to clear up later. Might even be nice enough for a short walk later on.      I don’t know if I’d call this clearing up, Dad. If I go out, I might as well just wear a full winter coat and triple layers. But, hey, I’ve got to fetch the laundry from the launderette soon—might as well get it over with.      Oh well, you’ll be warmer for it. I left the kettle on last night, didn’t I? D’you know, I think the world might end if I run out of hot drinks at the moment. Cold tea is an abomination in my house.      I hear you there! No, you didn’t leave the kettle on. Good job, too, or I’d still be looking for the circuit breaker. Though I might have if we’d not both reminded you yesterday!      Aye, and watching the news last night, it feels like the utility companies are at war with us: “power out, water pressure low, broadband down.” Some of us have better things to do than be stuck at home with the kids and the dog!      Like what? Writing client copy for a suspiciously generous budget? Dad, just let it out. You’re jealous you’d rather have a laptop and deadlines than being here at home trying to make your colleague stop crying because their Apple pen broke.      That’s not the point, Jane. I meant cooking or gardening—that kind of thing. Not that I’d know where to start with the fertilisation schedule.      Oh, you’re in luck there, David. I’ve been reading a book on herbs. Turns out, rosemary doesn’t like you if you water it too much. Try that and it’ll just shrivel up and die.      Well, I’ve got the washing schedule sorted, then. I’m doing colours and whites later on—will you go out with me for a bit more of that mulch I mentioned? I think the roses could do with a bit of tending.      Can you pick me up on the way past the garden centre?

Rather annoying this new rat puppet they've got at the village fete, isn’t it, Beryl? It’s got rather too much of a cheeky sort of grin, if you ask me. Keeps leaping about as if it's had too much coffee.      Oh, don’t be silly, George! The children love it—and the way Margaret manipulates it's absolutely charming. Though I must say, I’m starting to wish I’d gone to the optician instead of wandering over to the fair today. My glasses seem to be playing tricks on me. But I’ve been struggling to get the bus to go in on Saturday mornings without getting bumped off for a services worker. They don’t seem to understand that we old chaplies still value culture!      Rise and shine! You'll be amazed at how quickly the world shifts when you stop travelling. I retired two years ago, but now I drive more than I ever did in the office. Had to start a school-run service for the grandchildren—only complicating my life with their bus timetables!      I don’t suppose you ever took the bus, Reg! Being a proprietor and all.
