Rather annoying the queue was, eh? You think they couldn't get a bit more staff in ‘ere on a Saturday?      Well, more people about, innit? I’d have thought they’d be cashing in with all the tourists. But you’re right, the place was crawling when I came in earlier.      Yeah, I reckon it’s not all that different from a decade ago, though. At least the atmosphere. I mean, you can still tell what was once a place of industry and hard work, like the forges and the workshops, but now it's all cafes and frozen yogurt shops, even in the summer.      Oh, don’t get me started about that yogurt shop on the corner! Reckon they put more sugar in that stuff than the Venetians would have mined salt for in the good old days. But I’ll hand it to ‘em, breakfasts are still hearty 'ere.      Oh aye, you ever taste their ciobarine? It’s a bit thick, but I reckon it’s like a proper comfort puddin’. Bet you’d still get the occasional ragoazzo out fishin’ for squid early in the mornin', though. These days, it's more students and backpackers.      Mate, I often wonder what it was like back when the gondoliers weren’t just for show and the place was still a proper trade hub. You ever heard that the city’s foundations were laid with wooden piles driven into the marshlands?      That’s mad, innit? They’d have had to have been real hardy lot. Can you imagine walking over those canals when it was about half submerged?      And talking of which, I had a thought — what if we take a cab tomorrow to see some more parts of the city up close? I heard the northern ‘oods are still treacherous for high water.      Aye, it’d be something fresh, I reckon. I dunno about you, but I could stick out one more gelato if we do. Even if it’s the 'oreo' one with chocolate flakes.      Oh, I’m not fussy. Just so long as it goeth with my cappuccino. If it hits the sugar high, we can go explore that art gallery behind the chapel, the one with the mosaic floor. Been meaning to have a look.      That’d be a good plan. Just like the old days, when we’d have ‘a proper shuffle’ around places and learn something new.

So did I tell you yet how chaotic the gym’s been since that refit last month? I swear half the machines don’t even work properly half the time. But I’ve gotten used to it, gotta stay in shape, right?      Yeah, you mentioned it. Honestly, I’ve been avoiding it like the plague. I’ve got this ridiculous backlog of holiday leave I’m planning to clear next month—figured I’d use that as an excuse to skip the whole gym thing and just travel.      Ooh, where are you going? Anywhere hot or just glorified countryside?      A bit of both, actually. Got a friend in Gran Canaria working on a project and she’s dragging me along for some ‘relaxing week’ of surf, sun, and co-working. But I’m sad to be off for so long, I was about to try something new at breakfasts—smoothie bars!      Oh yeah? I went to one of those hides on the high street near the office—Kalyn’s, or whatever—had one with beetroot and ginger, and it was absolute nectar of the gods.      I’ll have to try that. Honestly, watching you sweat it out at the gym all week has made me miss my nights out with you. I know I’ve been buried in this new campaign at Bupa, but I did have this one at The Reverie the other night with a bunch of old uni friends. You’d have laughed at my ex when he showed up in a tank top.      Ugh, is he still in the world of being ‘prioritised’ but not in a good way? I about blocked mine last week after the hundredth message asking for my birthday present suggestions.      That bad, huh? Poor you. I handle mine by sending him playlists to the bin, quite creatively. Maybe you need a new hobby to replace all this ex energy? Like pottery or something?      Pottery? I once tried a night class, ended up with my thumb in the clay and a constant jabbing comment from the instructor. I think I’m more the “coffee mornings with work colleagues” type, honestly. Speaking of, I’ve been thinking about go back to my parents’ place more often—always feel at home.      I know what you mean, blokes sometimes make the house feel like a museum. I’ve made it to mine this weekend, after two months of ignoring all calls from my nan.

Rather exciting to be called grandaunt, isn’t it? A little bit of a squint when first I got the news, mind you. I’m more used to being asked by my daughter where my contributions are for the childcare grant. But then, I suppose being born in France adds a touch of drama that I simply couldn't refuse!      Born in France! My goodness, that does spice a grandchild up a bit. I must admit, I never thought much about it personally. Yet, interesting as it is, you might be surprised how very foreign the whole of Europe suddenly feels these days.      Oh, I'd venture that it's not the foreignness, precisely, but the administration of that foreignness. I read somewhere that property and enterprise in France are marred by the usual mix of anarchists and bureaucrats, and I think it's little wonder if you're pondering a move there. Still, I heard a number of clever minds are returning after some time abroad, attracted, perhaps, by a sense of reconnection to European culture.      One can only imagine the bureaucracy required if a book is to be published in such a context. A property as beautiful as Chichester Cathedral, with its proud spire… watching it collapse, remembering Mr. Porden who once stood among its stones?      Yes, indeed, quite a pity. I imagine he would have had quite a tale or two at the upcoming open day and photo exhibition at Chichester Cathedral. Our art competition at the local community centre certainly doesn’t reach that level, but one can dream. You've made something of your own mind, though—continuing to write that book!      You know, about the book... while conducting research on Mary Tudor and Philip of Spain, I visited a number of Spanish archives. The way history permeates the archives is something unmatchable in Britain. My, they do preserve the treacherous well!      And have you written about it? I assume you've encountered some very intense histories there, from the ones I've read. Speaking of treacheries, have you seen the recent argument with bollards on the high street? It took the grace out of a perfectly good evening walk.      Oh yes, that argument on the high street is nothing new. Just one of those local housing issues, no doubt. The new landlord, I imagine, has already had some issues with property management. I can hardly blame the residents for feeling exasperated.

So did you lot actually finish your AQA maths revision guide yet or what? I haven’t even started and it feels like my brain is already half-dead.      Don’t even start with me, mate. I only did three chapters and then my little sister wouldn’t stop crying because she lost her shoe. You  know  it’s the middle of the week, and she  still  thinks it’s Friday.      Yeah, I got it worse. My mum started talking about pulling out all the Christmas decorations  this  weekend and dragging me into it, but it's  June . I said to her, “Mum, I don't even know the quadratic equation yet, how can I contemplate  Star Wars inflatables ?”      Honestly, I just pretend to revise for like two hours and then spend the rest of the time playing Fortnite with Ed, my cousin. He’s been bugging me for weeks to show him some tips.      Stop being lazy! You lot will end up looking for a GCSE retake class while I’ll be off doing something  mature  like applied computing or whatever I put on my application.      And what, fail the interview because you didn’t revise? Mate, I saw you fail the mock biology test last week?      That was one test! Besides, my mum said I can join the after-school chess club and that’s  positively  career-oriented! She thinks it’s going to make someone at university go, “Oh! He can checkmate in three moves!”      Mate, your profile just says you can pause games and stare at the board for longer than most people would consider healthy about now…      Anyway, talking of cool stuff, have you seen the new Marvel comic? It’s that one with Eclair and the Spider-Kid superhero team? I just found out that the store in Wembley does pre-orders now. They even have exclusive covers!      Do they have free food with it? Because I’m getting distracted by the spring rolls here.      No, but the lunches we have in school are literally the same as the ones in that bag you opened earlier. You're like a man with a bag of bad memories on your back if you ask me.      Yeah, I’m trying to go on a low-carb diet anyway. Pass the dumplings. I’m only allowed one carbohydrate a day and I think I already cheated with the rice noodles.

Rather annoying this new supermarket’s branding, isn't it, Sarah? I was in there yesterday and it felt like every product had some ridiculous jingle now.      Oh Joan, I know what you mean. Not only that, the shelves are so low — you can barely see what’s at the end. I swear, they’re trying to make us feel short! But at least their prices are a bit better, right?      I don’t see what the big deal is, Gran. My mates at school all use the mobile app now — it scans the stuff you want and you just leave. It’s much faster.      Faster? In my day we just popped into the shop and came back with our basket. No need for all this tapping and scanning.      I used to think the same, Joan. But actually, it’s nice to have something when you can’t be bothered to go out. You know, like when the weather’s wet and you just want to stay in.      Yeah, that’s what I do when I get told off for missing homework — I ask if we can just order in and play games.      Oh Marcus, not again! We’ve been over this. You’ve got exams – no games while you’re supposed to be revising.      Aye, Sarah, you’ve got to be firm with the kids these days. When we were younger, you just helped out in the fields and that was it. No screens, just fresh air.      Fair enough, Ellen, but the world’s changed a bit since then. Though, there is something to be said for simpler times.      Oh, I agree. I remember when we lived in Kendal and the school barely had electricity. The snow could last all winter. My, what a lot of development there has been since.      Speaking of the past, I was thinking about moving again. I’ve rented for so long, I’d like to settle down and buy somewhere. Even though it’s always been with your family, Joan.      Oh no, you don’t serious? You and your silly man with the plans go off on one again and I’ll end up clearing out more stuff.      You’ll be the one arranging the clearance, what your mother-in-law wants.      Oh, leave it out John. I’ve never had a new life to clear out in my day. Unlike some people.      Wait, I thought we were going to celebrate Jonathan’s birthday in the next few weeks, Grandad?

So, have you decided yet what GCSEs you're going to take? I'm still stuck on like... art and geography, but my mum is like, "You can't do art if you want a proper job later!"      I know what you mean. My brother took art and design and then couldn't get into university because he didn’t have enough "academic" subjects. I think I’m going to do media studies and ICT, but I'm not sure. Oh, and I   have   to stick with music 'cause I play the clarinet.      Oh yeah, you're like super good! I couldn’t even play a note without someone laughing. I still can't get over how you did that YouTube cover of that Ed Sheeran song last year. My nan still plays it.      I know! I screamed when it hit ten thousand views. But honestly, it doesn’t pay the bills. I mean, have you noticed how influencers and YouTubers just keep getting famous off the back of nonsense? I follow this one bloke called Mr Waterfall Bloke, and he just falls in bogs and rants about land.      I've watched that! He’s hysterical—it’s basically comedy. But it feels like half of them just copy the same content: binging weird food and fake death challenges. I mean, imagine being 30 and still making videos for Silly Stones or whatever.      True! Honestly, I just don’t get how some people get millions of followers and others struggle. I had a school project where we had to profile a famous person. I did Ariana Grande—I mean, she's a pop star and a flamin’ genius. My mate did a man who lit a fire on the news and said it was “art.” Honestly, that shouldn’t be allowed on the national stage.      Yeah! And then you’ve got GCSEs and all this school stuff. Like, the other day I was stuck in PE trying to do a press-up and waiting till the whistle so I didn't look like I was being lazy. My teacher knows me too well, though. She’s like “Eyes off the clock, Lottie!”      Oh no! My go-to is fake being thirsty if I don’t want to run around. I just head fake to the water bottle like it's a fashion statement.      So, have you ever seriously thought about what you want to do when you finish school?

Rather a lot of changes in the countryside these days, don't you think? When I was a lad, you'd see a fox or a badger nearly every evening. Not now, it's all wind turbines and hedges being cut to bits. Look at the children today — they can't tell a sparrow from a blackbird if their life depended on it!      Aye, that's a truth. A lot o' policy nonsense in this country, if you ask me. It was easier in my youth. We had more time to notice things. Didn’t need no smartphone to tell us what bird it was — just a sound, and we'd know. All this digital age, and still people can't put a pin to a sparrow!      Oh, I agree, love. I used to take the little ones I looked after out for walks. They’d watch rabbits dig and giggle when a pigeon fluttered down. Now they’d rather stare at a screen than look up. Don’t tell me, Ken — do you have one of these smartphones now, or have you kept one of those big heavy phones?      I do — well, I’ve still got my old one, cluttering up the draw… but I’ve got a little flip phone from the utility provider. Fancy – works for calls and texts, no more, thank the Lord! But I’ve seen somethin’ new in the garage — a tablet, or somethin’. Daughter put it in for 'emails'. I don’t get it. Just a fancy photo frame with buttons!      Aye, and now they want you to drive these ‘self-driving’ cars! Can you imagine — you just put your destination in, and away you go. No touch the steering wheel! Madness. I used to enjoy a good mechanics job — changing plug leads, laying it out step by step. Now it’s all ‘software’ and ‘diagnostic tools’ and I can't speak the language!      You know, it sounds dramatic, but there are some benefits. I could see the two of you learning how to use the tablet if you wanted. It’s a new world, I know, but the technology isn't so hard if you take it slowly. I’ve had a few go at teaching my parents, if you'd like to stop by for a session?      Aye, maybe I will. I might give it a go. It'd be handy for me daughter to send messages quicker than she can write a letter!

Rather annoying this new schoolteachers be bringin’ in, if you ask me. Me time they just wanted you to turn up, quiet as a mouse, and not make no trouble. Now it’s all about “confidentiality” and “wellbeing,” and children frightened to say nowt lest it upset some eeny weeny  thing .      Ay, I read all about that on a paper—a transcription from a teacher’s  word for word  to parents. She were goin’ on like it’s a business and not a school for young ones. But, don’t you worry none—we’ve still got jokes, even if the world is goin’ round the bend, don’t we? You like that one about the doorstep?      Well, I do, if you’re tellin’ it properly. I’ll be the judge of that.      Right, here it comes—So I said to Brian, “The only reason delivery boys ever knock on the door is if you didn’t have the decency to answer when they were  calmed down  the first time round.”      Here now, that’s the real  belt and braces , innit? Makes you laugh and it’s about the humble postman. Ha – no, wait, he said  delivery boys , not  postmen —you’re getting your positions wrong again!      Oh, don’t be too hard on her, Ethel. We’re all a bit out of sorts these days. Besides, I had a  tweet  about the deliverymen just yesterday. Some bloke said he got a call  forty-two  times in a week from the same man asking the same question each time.      Honestly, you teachers! Going on about data and technology and worrying if the lad up the street’s got binoculars for show and tell.      Well, I’m told they don’t do show and tell no more. It’s something else now— circle time , I think it’s called. I swear to God, if they start with that, I’m writing to the Health Service myself and going back to bein’ a patient with a diagnosis!      That Health Service is about as reliable as a wheel of cheese made of polystyrene, I’m afraid. But bloomin’ marvellous conversation we’re havin’.      You teachers, you lot start off all proper and intellectual, then end up laughin’ about ‘bottle feeds’ and ‘healthy snacks’ at a teenage party! The last one at the library was a  riot . They were all trying to copy American binge drinking, poor deary.

Rather annoying this lot o’ snow, innit? Me an’ the cat got trapped in ‘ere like yesterday, and I’m not even half-way through tidyin’ up the veg patch      Aye, proper biblical stuff this is. I frightened half the street when me electric fence went on—standing there, surrounded by birds with sore necks and a chicken that's possibly dead      What've you got in that veg patch, then?      Trying to grow carrots and parsnips, but it's looking more like a graveyard with all the snow on top. You remember that lettuce patch I made? Gone, smashed flat the other night by sommat heavy and wild that My turkey, definitely not the melon though. The snow tried to cover it up, but the melon, bless it, just sat there like a green anorak      I've been watching Come Dine With Me with a mug in me hand. It's the worst! That fella ordering puffin and expecting compliments. Good job I don’t like him      Aye, I watched one of them yesterday. Got a bloke trying to impress by serving shepherd's pie in golf balls—it wasn't a work of art, it was suicide. How's the stag do coming along? I know you've been panickin' about the hen party      Honestly, trying to make it less like a funeral and more like a party. They wanted glitter in the speeches and suspiciously strong vodkas. I thought we were doin' a barn dance, not a science experiment      I'm  trying  to make it interactive, about half the people there couldn't tell a man from the caterer. It was like a game of guess the farmer      I've got a plan for the stag do, though. Burgers, bad jokes, and a karaoke machine. The rest? Well, the stag can't complain too much once he's had a few too many      Sounds good as long as they've got a driver. I've 'ad a couple of weddings go sideways because some lad thought he could steer after a lager      Oh, goin' on holiday next month?      Scotland, just for a long weekend. Walkin' the moors, getting lost in some remote village. It's supposed to be romantic but I'm scared we’ll come back with broken boots and bellyache from dodgy stew      Might meet up with them later in the week—got my cousin coming over for a few days.

Rather lovely to have you all under one roof, what with it being the first Sunday in ages. Tea first, or shall I serve the beef?      Not tea, dear. A bit of variety is nice. Though honestly, I have to say—your roast beef is the best I’ve tasted in decades.      It was lovely, Gran. Really. Almost as good as the pudding you’ve made now, if that's possible.      Haha, well, there's no pleasing one’s own flesh and blood, is there? But if I’m bloated by tomorrow, I’ll have you all to blame.      Gran, you only cook like this for company. My turkey on Christmas was… well, it left something to be desired.      Oliver, I was very sad in the world that week. It is not my fault the turkey sprouted a second leg and then suddenly decided it’d like a bit in the oven!      No, you didn’t have to do that. One leg is quite enough—especially when it sings, apparently.      I mean, we all appreciate that creativity is alive and well in your cooking, but there was… a lot of it. I remember when we got home from the funeral and Mateo asked, fairly terrified, “what kind of bird is that?”      Mateo? You mean Silas’ partner? Last I heard, that bird was still chasing him out of the chicken coop.      Children, really, let’s not discuss feathers and flapping at the dinner table. What delicious and sunny day it was, though! We all looked out of our separate flurries of grief and the light just broke through the clouds, didn’t it?      It was beautiful. I barely noticed the cold. There was so much to do with laying out the funeral—had to get the vicar to borrow some sods from the man at the golf club. Billy insisted it had to be a flat grave, bless him.      He always was a tidy one. No space for the rabbit to nest and whack your head with the spade, like you once did.      I never did that!      Oh you did. You buried one of Billy’s line in the garden, and then sowed marrows right on top. Came out with a rabbit at planting time.      Must we rehash those days, Dad?      Just talkin’. It were good times. We had them. It’s a shame I never learned to cook like you, Elsie.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be at my own place eating takeout, but it’s family dinner, and I thought I’d be nice today. Anyway, I need something less heavy. Beans on toast is genius. Not quite gourmet, but I respect what you’re doing. Deer burgundy and all that.  laughs dryly  Not sure   I’d   use cumin in that, but hey, I’m not your average taster! I mean, I love a good stew as much as the next Brit!      Oh, honestly, if I had my way, we’d just order pizza and be done with it. Classic, efficient, and easily taken away if needed. But no, My turkey curry definitely needs cumin. It’s not a proper curry without it. I reckon you're missing out, Elinor.      Forgive me if I’m not breakfast, no doubt. I’ve been doing house calls for work all week. I’m roasted! hides behind wine glass  haha  But the cookies? Divine. The man himself baked them, if you can believe it.      Right! Here to brag about supplying the hobnobs.      Well, I’m not about to start cooking. Let’s just say it: Men are not, and were never, made to cook. Let’s all agree on that and move on. Silly question, Selby!      Honestly, this is why we still exist in the era of stone knives and bearskins.  grins  Some things never change, do they?      Can we all pause for one second and acknowledge how many people are at this table eating the same food but talking about different meals? It’s like a Ronseal failsafe scenario.      And the classic British family dinner has just found its thesis statement. Let’s put it in a museum.      You know, I was thinking about it the other day—the way you boys and girls argue about what the perfect meal is. I swear, it’s worse than trying to find a holiday that works for everyone.      Still, I’m happy with what’s on the table. Meat go bad on my tongue these days, but I’m still here for the brussels sprouts. Always was. And the boxset binging after. Pass the gravy, Selby.      You’re in luck, Derek—there’s even extra, just to spite me.      Only at Mummy and Daddy’s. You can go all week without seeing a tomato, but you get gravy thicker than chartreuse.  grins       It’s not just the food, is it?

So do you think universities are really equipped to handle the way students learn these days? I mean, when I was in uni in New Zealand, it was all lectures and books, but now it's all about engagement and tech.      That's true—especially in the UK now. I’ve seen a lot of my colleagues experimenting with blended learning models, where theory and digital tools are integrated. But most resist change. A lot of them just haven’t had the support to innovate.      Interesting. That’s why we launched the EdSpark project. We're providing tools and training for educators to build interactive assessments, sort of gamified learning—like mini apps that test understanding in real-time. You know, like that MyFitnessPal app, but for education.      Oh, I love the idea of gamification. I’ve used it in my classroom with secondary students, breaking lessons into ‘levels’ and giving badges for participation and quiz scores. They loved it—kept them more focused. But getting buy-in from higher-ups is always a challenge.      It definitely is. One thing we’ve had some success with is using micro-budgets—small grants that let educators pilot low-tech ideas first. Like creating a mini documentary on a topic, or a podcast, without requiring big-tech infrastructure. It works especially well with arts students, and it's really gone viral in a couple of uni communities in Australia.      Viral—now that’s a term we hear a lot in this digital age. But how do you ensure the students stay engaged long-term? I had a group make a series of YouTube vlogs about history topics and it got some great traction, but motivation dipped after the novelty wore off.      Oh, I know the feeling. We’ve had to implement a feedback loop—that constant interaction is key. We use a platform where students can upvote each other’s projects, leave quick feedback, and form peer groups. It mimics the way people interact on social media. It works surprisingly well as a peer mentorship system, too.      That’s such a clever way to use existing behavior patterns to encourage learning. I keep thinking about what we’ve been talking about with our students—how they multitask so easily online but struggle with deep focus in the classroom. It's about aligning the tools they already use.      Exactly. And we’ve seen big interest from educators who are also parents.

: You’re not putting the milk back in the fridge, are you?     : No, I’m not—why would I do that after I’ve already stared death in the face this morning?     : I mean, you picked it up and then put it back on the counter.  On purpose.      : I’m in self-preservation mode. I only buy full-fat because I feel like I need to be rewarded for existing.     : You and the rest of the nation. Do you want me to make you some tea? Or is your mental health system too overstretched for me to offer the simplest of comforts?     : Just water, thanks. The tea left from last week tastes more like wallpaper paste at this point. Speaking of, I think I turned my kettle into an archaeological exhibit by not cleaning it.     : I found some mud in the bottom when I boiled it last night. I thought,  well, I guess the kettle has memories now.      : Hilarious. I’m not even halfway through my shift yet and I’ve already had grief from a student who thought I was going to reject him during circle time.     : Ha – no chance of that. He probably still needs you to confirm his existence.     : Ugh, I will be thrilled to never interact with another human again, which may sound dramatic, but in four-year increments.     : That’s not a life ambition, that’s a profile on a toxic dating app. Anyway, did you hear I got promoted?     : I heard a fly turd the other week and had more of a reaction than what you’re implying. Surprise me.     : No, I’m serious. I got moved up to being the senior project co-ordinator for the London and Kent region.     : Oh my god, that’s massive! You must be doing all the fancy administrative stuff and hoisting champagne flutes in grand halls with lunches delivered by pigeons with mini sandwiches attached to them.     : Pretty much. I told my boss I go to Kent on weekends to be immersed in rural vibes so I can inspire my urban-based, password-hoarding team with a deeper sense of place.     : You made that up on the spot, didn’t you?     : I prefer to call it poetry. Also, I bought food at the market near your place—got my hands near to mucky earth, which I kind of consider sacrilege, but it was worth it.     : That’s the real work, you know?

Rather chilly this morning, isn't it? I needed three cups of tea just to get out of bed. I remember the days when I could dream on a pillow and wake up with sunshine, but no, now it's frosty and quite the dash from the duvet!      Morning, eeny! Yeah, I understand the chill - I had to wrap up like I was going on a polar expedition. A shame, but I needed that adrenaline to get me out of bed and into work, which is quite a trek from here anyway.      It's true, you do have a long way to go. I'd imagine that commute is quite the trial, especially with these frosty mornings. But what's a bit of rain or fog between a good cause? Ten more years and you’ll be home for tea, and I’ll be the proud grandmother with an apron far too big for me.      I can see that alright! The morning rush is usually the part of the day I dread the most. But the work itself isn’t too bad, I mean I do like the satisfaction of knowing I’m keeping things on track in the production department. It might sound a little dry, but today we’ve got a meeting about how we can slash our waste from the production line. Pretty exciting stuff really when you think about it.      Oh, that does sound quite interesting, making things efficient and saving the planet all in one hit! Though, let’s be honest, someone at the top has also got to be looking to save a few quid while we're at it. Also, have you considered studying some more? I know you're interested in environmental science, and you've nearly about got me convinced to take up bridge again from talking about it.      Maybe next year, eeny. For now I’m trying to keep up with my step. My sister’s planning on taking the kids to her parents at the weekend. They want to spend a weekend getaway in a farm nearby, said it’d be a way for them to appreciate nature. We could come along as well if you wanted. It’d be a nice break from all the whirring machinery and concrete jungle.      That does sound like a nice notion. I go stir crazy on my own if I don’t get out at all.

Rather annoying this, innit? I mean, I knew it was snowin’ in France ‘ere first... got us stuck in this tiny b_and’t_ in Grenoble. No signal, no wi-fi, just a chandelier the size o’ a football and a litre of red wine each night. Got eeny ideas on wot we’re gonna do tomorrow?      Honestly, not a clue. I was gonna investigate this research paper I stubbled onto about um, y’know, some new scientific methods in crop growin’, but the internet's as dead as the wi-fi in a pre-Cambridge college. Though I did listen to that new Coldplay album the other night—entirely in French version. It still gives me the shivers though.      Nah, I reckon their French albums sounds more like sad disco. But eh, I’m used to that. Mum put Coldplay on durin’ every therapy session. "It's in his roots." I'm ever so grateful, m’arse. So, when’re we relocating to Nancy for uni?      We need sturdy evidence—some solid data on the best routes. We might need to bike for a bit. I’ve read something on adaptive transportation... something where you adjust travel methods based on weather patters?      Right, so it's a fancy way o’ sayin' don’t get lost and pack thermals. I’m already wearin’ your jumper, which by the way someone said in one of them French books sounds like  "le chandail"  or summin— ch’dalley?  Sounds like you singin’ in solfeggio.      I did translate that bit. It's "le chandail," but I had to double-check with an online translator. Honestly, I think I need to switch to a proper scientific translator to do justice to the complicated methods they’re discussin’. Though I might just stick with audio books—they’re less confusing.      Fair point. I reckon you’ll understand more if you stick to talkin’ like Dr Who’s academicky grandkid with a French accent. So whatcha gonna do when you ain't lost and ain't runnin' errands? Apply to uni goin' on pond life?      Yeah, I'm line in for Cambridge, wanna do plant sciences, bloomin’ marvellous if you ask me. Y’ever seriously think about studying sport roles in France? I heard the setup is like, better than the FA’s in the ‘80s.      I’m more interested in bein' a footballer, but I kind of maxed out at 50 push ups and a sprained ankle when I was 15.

Rather annoying when a spider turns up in the kitchen when you're cooking dinner, isn’t it? The first thing you do is drop the knife and reach for the tea towel! I saw one the other day, probably thought it was £20 under the sofa.      Aye, they’re brave things now, spiders. Mine got bigger and bolder after I put up all them spider plants. Maybe they think it’s an invite! But this one bird, though, it used to come in through the window. We called it the intruder for months until we found out it was nesting under the eaves. It was like it owned the place!      Oh, I’ve had that too. My birds are practically part of the family now. The one that flew into the living room the other week, it landed and just sat there like it hadn’t a care in the world. Made quite an impression, fluttering about mid-air while everyone was watching telly.      Mice, though — that’s a different ball game. I had one that chewed through the bin bags and got into the cat food. I swear if we’d not heard it scratching, we wouldn’t have known. You’ve got to be always watching for them little devils.      Mate, I’ve had them in my office before. Found a huge nest once, buried deep in the wall cavity. Took the building manager ages to get sorted out. And the worst part? Our computers all got full of dust and dropped hair. You’d have thought they thought it was a hotel with all the boxes stacked about.      I still don’t get how they manage to make a home about nowhere. I’ve tried all sorts of the baits and traps, but most of ’em just disappear. Probably gone to live with some mate down the road.      That’s for sure. I once put out one of them humane traps — and it worked. Problem was, I was bloody terrified to go anywhere near it once it clicked. I convinced myself it was already gone, and that I’d just heard the trap trying to catch the wind.      Haha, that sounds like a common one. I reckon if the traps had mirrors in them, it might help if you don’t wanna go looking at what you just caught.      That might be the solution. Though if it’s a particularly healthy mouse, it might just bite the mirror in half.

Rather lovely to finally meet in person, Delyth. I've heard so much about you through the family... Our dear cousin Edith insisted we get together more often. I’ve been meaning to ask — you were telling me earlier over the phone about the family tree?      Aye, it’s beginning to take shape, more or less. I’ve been dusting off some old letters of my mother’s that were tucked under the floorboards in the old house in Bristol. She used to keep meticulous records of births and marriages. Found a few surprises too. Didn’t even know I had a great-uncle who went to India during the war.      Oh, that sounds fascinating. I’ve always been interested in our roots. I did a bit of research on mine back when I was teaching at the high school, actually used it in a lesson plan. Living in Dorchester, there’s something grounding about knowing your history.      A teacher, you said? That’s awfully respectable. I taught, too, many a long year. Primary school, all girls—village girls, mostly—before I retired. Hard graft, but rewarding. You’ve gone to university, I expect?      Yes, I did my postgraduate degree in educational psychology. It was a bit of a stretch financially at the time, but I’ve never regretted it. Though I have to say, nothing quite prepares you for trying to win the attention of a class of 30 ten-year-olds all at once.   [chuckles]   Aye, I know exactly what you mean! Still, mind you, I had a lot fewer children in my classes, those were different times. I did miss teaching, though. After I stopped, it was like losing purpose for a while.      I’m so sorry to hear about your loss, Delyth—your mother, I mean. I read your letter. It must have been terribly hard. I remember her as a sprightly woman, always bringing the very best gingerbread.      We lost her to cancer, endometrial, they said. Took her rather quickly. I was with her the last few weeks. That's where I got the idea for the family tree, really. She wanted me to map out our history before it was all forgotten.      That must have been a bittersweet task. If it helps, I’m more than happy to help you trace more of it. I’ve had experience working with local archives and parish records.

Rather lovely this morning, isn't it? That crisp autumn air and the way the light falls through the trees... It's so peaceful out here compared to London.      Absolutely. It's a shame we don’t get to do this more often. By the way, did you hear about the new hot air balloon festival they’re planning in Norwich next spring?      Is that right? I remember something briefly coming up in one of the local meetings I had to attend last week. It seems interesting—though I can't imagine the council approving it without a few protests, especially with all those power lines running through the countryside.      Oh, goodness—power lines are always such a sticking point. But what’s a bit of risk for an eccentric balloon festival, right? I bet the kids would love it. Speaking of which, what did you think of the new dog we’re fostering? He’s been a proper terror in the house this week!      A bit, yes. Chewing hides, barking at shadows. But I suppose he’s just unsettled—moving from a rescue kennel into our home must be overwhelming. I think with a bit of time and patience, he’ll settle in. At least he’s brilliant for the kids. They adore him.      Definitely. And talking about the kids, I think it's about time we started planning a family camping trip. You know, something low-pressure—just to get them out of the city, connect with nature a bit.      I’d like that. It might give the dog a chance to burn off some energy, too. Just as long as we don't end up in a situation like last time—when we forgot the kettle and ended up eating cold beans for the whole weekend.      True—that was a sorry affair. Still, I think it helped the kids develop resilience! Jokes aside, financially, I think we’re steady enough to spare a few hundred pounds for a decent weekend getaway. Might even stretch the budget and get a glamping site rather than a basic pitch.      I’m all for it—though I do draw the line at spots with "experiences" billed separately. The last glamping place we visited tacked on £40 for go-karts on day three, and I’m not convinced anyone under 50 in the group needed that.      Fair point. But all joking aside, I really do think it's important we manage our finances carefully.

Rather chilly for a midweek afternoon, isn't it? I was half expecting it to be mild when I cycled over.      Aye, I know what ye mean. It’s a proper British spring if ye ask me—two days of sun and seven days of drizzle. Ruins plans for the garden, I tell ye.      True. I’ve been trying to get my students to appreciate British weather—metaphorically, of course. They think it's all grey skies and cloudbanks, but occasionally, when the light hits right, the countryside is beautiful.      Still, I’ll trade it for worse. What with the gym schedule and early mornings like that, you don’t get too many chances to relax. This café’s a real bonus, I must say. Rather glad I’ve been dragged into your class—yoga, was it? Made better sense when I heard the term 'core strength.'      It was, thanks for coming! I told you the lattices here are the best around, didn’t I?      You did, and I’ve got to say, your health tips’ve made me think. I’ve seen more people in my local gym who’ve quit work at fifty then people who actually want to keep moving. I’m at the gym, and I barely remember how to do a proper squat.      That’s the problem with spotting—everyone thinks you need to be lifting 100kg at once. But it’s the consistency that counts. It's like language learning. You can fling yourself at it with a dictionary and a phrasebook, but if you speak a little every day, it builds naturally.      Aye, touché. I’ve had to teach a few new coaches at my gyms how to make classes feel less intimidating. No one wants to feel like a beginner for the rest of their life. I passed on your advice once or twice—those 'beginner exercises' got quite a warm response.      I’m touched. I’ve been reading  The Language of Coaching —a bit heavy but full of insight. If you’ve got time, it’s well worth a read.      I’ll put it in the pile on my bookshelf that's more for decoration than action.      Hopefully, it'll go further than that. By the way, I was in Hitchin visiting my brother last week and found a great little bookshop with a café upstairs—think I'll take you there sometime, if you're into the literary scene.

Rather chilly this morning, ain't it? I’ve just boiled the kettle, Richard—the tea’s in first, like nanna always taught me.      Thanks, Mrs. Redgrave! You’re a legend. We’ve only just finished breakfast—granny wouldn’t let me put sugar in mine! Said it’s bad for the teeth an’ all.      An’ rightly so! A lot o’ folk think they can just spoon it in an’ call it a day! When I were a youngster, we didn’t have no sugary gob, but we had brains an’ a clear head for it.      That’s her, always like that. Me, I preferred my tea strong and left it to cool. Probably why I’ve got the teeth o’ a dog I used to patch up down the docks in Hull!      You always said that Brian! Hiding behind bad jokes when I asked why you never went to the dentist.      Did you really, grandad? Nanna, is it true you used to take care o’ the whole family as a young mum and dad?      Oh, we didn’t have time for nonsense like “care”—just kept the fires lit an’ the pot on. Brian barely had shoes half the time, an’ he was off to the fields with the lads to fetch in the hay!      Aye, but I never let the cows chase my tongue, if you catch my drift. Mary—look at the kid now, sippin’ on tea an’ asking questions! We were too busy surviving to have about with such nattering!      Well, this place is much cosier than your old house in Hull, Brian. I mean it. These windows don’t leak, and there’s central heating—y’expected to use it, not just stare at it like a donkey at a telephone box!      He did once. Tore up the yellow pages to light a fire.      Haha! That’s brilliant! Was he mad for trying to dial a number by touching the paper with a finger goin’ on fire?      Not much sanity in me in them days, I’ll admit it.      Now, you two—let’s get the china down and set the table. We’ve got a proper cuppa, scones, and some poetry from over the road. Mavis from next door swore up and down she’s got a rhyme scheme for today.      Poetry, from her? I hope it isn’t about onions or resurrected pigeons again.      Oh, it’s always the onions, love.

Rather annoying this new satnav eh, love? Thought mebbe we’d know this road by now, like it’s the seventh time we’ve passed this field with the red tractor in it.      I know, it’s like they specifically programme it to lead us the long way round just for fun. Right, now  this  bit I remember, just past that old church on the hill.      Aye, that one that’s all wrapped up in ivy. It was a dump back in the day when we was lads and lasses chase through the graveyard.      Right, but enough of nostalgia. I’ve got a gig in half an hour and if we don’t stop at the roundabout, I swear I’m just gonna jump in the back and pretend to play the fiddle on the way there.      Haha, you’re a laugh. You remember when you sprained your wrist at that ceilidh in Keswick and tried to play the tin whistle instead? Half the wedding group had to shout the tune over you.      Come off it, I’d say it was poetic falsetto if it wasn’t for the grief I got from old Mrs. Drummond.      Still, that ceilidh was a cracker. Real community spirit. I’d still swear that the parsnip scone recipe you pinched off Mrs. Grey was the reason half the crowd got the hiccups for three days.      That’s a suspicious claim. You just didn’t like them scones because they made you nostalgic for your mum’s kitchen.      Aye, and she made better ones too. I daresay though, the real story of the gig is how we get there. I’ve been wondering if you know that new plug-in they’re trying out near the lake.      Which one? There’s that new high-tech one by the bird hides? The one the RSPB mentioned was all about sustainable energy.      Aye, that. Mebbe stop and top up as well as getting some supplies? I do need new wool for my jumper I’m knitting. Got far too much green in it.      Don’t go wasting money on that moss-and-ivy look again – give it some navy line in, luv. It’d go with your eyes.      Arrr, you only say that to get kitted out in wool every night so you don’t have to wear your dad’s old tie for soundcheck.      Is that a yes to the shop then?

Rather annoying that the client kept changing their mind about the number of rooms they wanted. We spent two hours on that site and another half an hour bickering over whether we needed a gym or a shared kitchen.      You wouldn’t have said that as a student, now would you? Back when I started, we designed theoretical buildings on napkins and handed them to people with a cup of lukewarm tea. A university project brief tends to have too much detail, but at least they don’t waver like that. What’s the final word on the communal living layout?      Honestly? I like the idea of blending flexibility with character. I think communal spaces are the way forward, especially for young professionals and students. Just wish I had met someone who could actually draw what I visualise.      Roxy used to do that for me. She’d sketch out my ideas and sometimes better. I still miss her when I’m stuck. Speaking of — how’s she doing, by the way?      She's still working the night shift, and that solicitor is still driving her mad. She can’t focus at work because she puts in a 14-hour day only for her boss to assign her tasks at three in the morning. She says it’s emotional suicide. I suggested she find something new, but she keeps saying, “I'll sort it out soon.”      Ugh, that’s her old script. You know how she sets goals and then just disappears. I remember one time she said she’d read War and Peace and then oddly left it on the table for six months.      Exactly! I offered to speak to her manager, but she said no, she needs to walk away herself. I just wish the office had more female vibes. I’ve been trying to push her to explore architecture or interiors, but she says she’s not creative. Honestly, I think she just needs confidence boosting.      A bit of me says she would make a great project manager. If only someone tried to mentor her.      Speaking of mentoring and creativity — what are you getting to eat? I’m craving the avocado on rye today, but I feel like I’m repeating the same breakfast three times a week.      I usually go for the smoked haddock and poached eggs, but I’ll switch it up. How about a bagel with lox and some of that smoothie you like?

So, I’ve been doing a fair bit of thinking, Sarah. I know it's been a while since I got out of university, but I really think it’s time I take the plunge into something new. If this works out, maybe we take a break from the big-city hustle. I’ve been thinking… maybe set up a little stall at a local market, get to know the community more, maybe even help you out more with work. I could mentor some of the students occasionally if they’re interested in business or sustainability.

Gives the place a bit of spice in my opinion, but goodness knows the council might disagree.      [Burps loudly, then giggles and claps his hands]      Ewan, you’ll be in for a swirl of complaints when you start school!

Rather annoying this, innit? I’ve been at this Spanish malarkey for months now an' I still got the gist of it no clearer than fog on Blundells Bank on a winter morning! Oh, alright then, John, let’s hear how  you’re  doin’ then. Off the top of yer head — what’s Spanish for 'Tomorrow I’m going to the market'? Now that’s like tryin' to build a shed with no screwdriver — muddled bits, no sense of structure!      I’ve been doin’ those book courses — listenin,’ written notes, repeat after me. Or Castilian and Catalan — they live side by side, in the same village most times, an’ people switch back an’ forward the same week.      Aye, that’s right. Proper got to be more instinct than textbook. No wonder I got the lot, ‘cos every book sez things different. One says “Hasta luego”, another says “Hasta pronto” — bloody give me a clue!      I reckon the best way to learn is immerse yer in it. Y’know, proper live a little bit of the culture. Some people, like, set off for a year with tuppence an’ a backpack goin' on ‘how I learned seven languages in monasteries and libraries’. I, on the other hand, go three bloomin’ minutes in a foreign town and I’m missing a fluency in fish and chips!      I think I’m goin to give online talk sessions a go over this next month. Or them language exchange sites. S’all so confusing I got to do sommat drastic — I can’t keep accidentally askin’ for the loo instead of the bill when I eat!

Rather annoying this, isn't it, Dad? I mean, everything's on computers these days, but we still got to go through this lot. You take it too seriously, James. Remember when breakfasts were mostly toast and this happened all over the kitchen in a dramatic sort of way? Cooking was as messy then as looking for a will in the sock drawer now.      Yeah, but Kelly Brook can’t scan the documents for me — even if I did once vote for her for something. Look, there was a time when I would have rhythmically explained all this to you about how –?      How grammar, verbs, and letters come together into a sort of magic? You know what? I'm just glad you're helping me with it — although I miss the days when your biggest concern was whether you had mastered the past tense or whether you topped the lunches with a little chocolate from your pocket.      Still, I’m around. This way you can get the documents go.sorted rather than being buried under your antiques or – God forbid – my childhood football shirts. I suppose it could be a blooming disaster if the house went up in smoke with all that in it.

You mean, made him even more of a nuisance than he already were, innit?      Exactly! Bit o’ fun to relieve the tedium, though.      Nah, I like it.

You’ve got to admit, breakfasts are perfect for playing mind games. Honestly, I’ve often thought—what if we could time travel, just for one cup of tea? Mate’s tea, the real stuff. I mean, Hayek, Churchill, Gandhi—imagine having that hypothetical conversation. Imagine getting your IT skills to 1847 to help out Ada Lovelace. Or me as a PA to someone like Freud, going over notes for his next essay. You’d be the best analyst of his goings-on on your own timeline.      You’re just trying to outwit your husband with fantasy roles, aren’t you? But yes, you could sum him up in one question. ‘Sigmund, where’s your mother hiding the belly-buttons from your childhood?’.      Only if you promise to raise a cup of tea to all of them at the imaginary party.

We've had several sickness claims, and I’ve been pulling my hair out trying to reassign people. It’s non-stop.      I can't imagine. My job is far more—settle, really. Nothing too dramatic, just spreadsheets and emails most days. But I do worry about how young people, especially, are feeling in society these days. All the violence in the news gives me the jitters. We had to take a first aid class at my last job, just in case. Funny thing was, the best part about it was the stories the instructors told. One of them had to clear a choking child at a graveyard—can you believe it? I nearly spilled my coffee when he told the story.      Graveyards? Now that makes me think of the old cemetery in Boston that’s just a bit over the border. My grandmother used to go there to visit her parents’ graves. She would always say something about the tombstones being different from the ones in your part of the world. She didn't like that they were all written in Latin or some weird old language.      That's interesting. Graveyards here are a bit more modern. I think it's because of the war cemeteries nearby. They’re so neat and uniform, like in the movies. I don’t know, I can see why people would get stereotyping in their heads about places and people based on that kind of thing.

Haha, and you think you’re so posh talking with that East London toot?      Look, I’m just trying to        Arry, c’mon. Just ‘cuz you’re from London, it don’t make yeh classier alright!      Says you-INNER.      Says I, you  trouble . But seriously, me n Mia were on the student shop line this morning and it took 45 minutes just to buy a packet of rice.

Rather than share a text-based conversation, I request a more interactive approach. Allow me to engage with you like a real conversation rather than responding with a static script. Is that acceptable to you? Wait — if you   specifically need   the full generated conversation with the agreed speakers, topics, and format, I will provide it now. Let me know how to proceed! ---      Right, well, the bus back to the guest house is always late in the summer, so we should probably walk back sooner rather than later. I don’t fancy standing at this bus stop for an hour in these heels.      Oh, don’t listen to the news, Emily. We’ve had worse summers than this, haven’t we, David?      Aye, it might be early, but we’ll still make it in good time. I reckon we should finish our espressos first. My back does ache a bit after walking with that moped all morning, though.      Uncle David, you couldn’t even ride the moped straight! Auntie Fiona’s chasing you down that hill in one of those supermarkets was not my idea of fun.      Come on, Tom, your gran nearly lost her beanie in that chase. I was laughing so hard I couldn’t even take a photo.      She’s got a mind to document it on Facebook and make us all look like absolute clowns.      That’s just her ‘record every day like it’s a holiday’ thing, isn’t it? Honestly, the woman is a content machine.      I miss waiting for the bus with the dogs back home. I swear the dog at our local hospital with the golden retriever spots me before the nurses do.      You’re not in hospital! You’re at school goin’ on about dogs?      Well, I do spend a lot of time there. The hospital visits are part of the biology project. It’s all about caring for pets and stuff.      That’s right. You’ll be a vet next, won’t you?      If you end up as a vet like that, at least they pay the rent. I remember you, Em, getting your tattoo done right after uni. Was that the Manchester one?      Yeah, it’s a small one, near campus. I had the whole design planned out before I even walked in. It’s just birds and stars.      I saw it when you were on Facebook, you know. Looked lovely, but never say you won’t be sorry when you need a plaster for work.

Rather a lot of ground covered in Cornwall, I’d say. A few nice photos, I expect?      Oh yes, plenty! Especially down by that lighthouse.      Aye, we had a bit o' cycle race on the clifftops too. I'm still out o' breath thinkin' 'bout it.      Oh Graham, that was brilliant, but I must've lost my spectacles again.      You did. We had to stop twice to find 'em. Nothing like the days when we could see a fiver from thirty paces.      What I found strange was volunteering at the YHA.      Oh, you were a proper team! I didn't know you'd worked with kids before.      It's not about the kids — it's more about the old folks needin’ some company. I suppose it’s a bit like the school again, makin’ sure everyone's looked after.      Ah yes, school, I remember them days. Used to be in Costessey, as it is. I only made it to secondary, though.      Well, that’s got to be more than some people.      And it's interesting to see how the world's changed. All these technologies and things now. Still, I blame the crabs more than anything.      Oh, the crabs at St Agnes! Trying to get a decent picture with you had the patience of a saint, Harold.      I did alright, didn't I? I just stood there while he waded knee-deep into the sea after them.      Going to that place like ‘Yorkshire in a day’? You're quite something, Lucy.      Oh, I did it once and thought, well, it's a land of beauty and beer. I tried to do Cornwall in a day too once.      That’s a bit grand! I’ve never been more than a few dozen miles from home.      Then perhaps it's time you all came away. We could do another trip if you'd like. Just don't expect me to run after crabs again.      Aye, and forget the cycle race. I might be past it, though I still think I can sprint a bit.      I say, let's not get too ambitious, eh? One lighthouse at a time. I'm quite happy with our little trip and these fine photos of it.      And the relationships, of course — they’re the best part of any journey.      Quite right, quite right. I would've missed out on a lot without you all about.      Aye, and I for one don’t know where I'd be now without you lot.

Rather skip the newfit sludge, innit? Eh, Aimee, thou ‘ave any pints of lard or summat?      Mate, I've been on a proper diet for two weeks now. I even gave up fags! Gotta keep the bod buff if I want to impress at the site hens night next week.      Oh, come on, James. A little carbs won’t kill you! I mean, unless you eat ALL of it, which you probably will! I brought some pasta from outside the diet store.      Right, that’s sorted! All we need is a drink, and we’re sorted fer the turkey!      Terry left the wine in the boot of the car for two DAMN HOURS and I think it turned into something else. I’m about 80% sure I smelt bile when I opened it. Not a wine person, but even I know that ain’t right.      Ugh, why do we let that man choose the vino, eh? Last year he tried to sneak in two different kinds of cough syrup and called it a "fusion cocktail.''      Bloke tried to get a taste of the sauce. Not takin' it personal, just not takin' it!      Yeah, but don’t get me started on Terry’s attempt at relationship advice. Last week he told me to “put a ring on her and then also sort out a way to get her to pay half the rent.” Some guy’s best mate.      Ugh, romantic and pragmatic! Don’t know that I can fix the wine, but if we run out, I do have some strong feelings about treacle waters.      Treacle? Like, the brown stuff you give to kids to drink with their gingerbread? I am NOT getting drunk on crack water tonight, lass.      Git with 'im! It’s better than the “cough syrup cocktail,” innit? Mind you, best err on the side of caution goin' on dates these days. Me nan said to me, "Lizzie, if they don’t like your mud, they probably ain’t the one." Reckon she meant shoes, but mebbe it works gen’rally.      That’s beautiful. Is it in a book? Should I Instagram it and charge $5 for a quote?      Always the insta queen, ain’t you, Aimee? Right, unless we’re getting a second opinion, I’m moving to the pasta and before I accidentally poison myself again, can someone pass the cheese?

Rather lovely to sit out here on such a peaceful Sunday morning. I confess, it's been a while since I got to enjoy some quiet with a proper cup of tea. Not much peace left after twenty years of primary school teaching. Do you often travel this far from London?      Honestly, not usually—this place is more of a treat for me. I spend most of my time in Zone 1 with spreadsheets and pitches. Not the best place if you’re looking for a calm morning. But I like to get away when I can. So, what made you decide to be a teacher?      It was rather accidental, to be honest. I went to university thinking I’d do something in publishing, but I took an education module for a laugh and fell in love with working with children. I’m from Dorchester, and I think there’s something about growing up in a slower place that made me appreciate when someone really cares about learning. How about you? I imagine running a business isn’t the path you thought you'd be on when you left uni.      You could say it grew on me. I studied business—everyone I knew in my family said I was made for it. For a while, I worked in marketing, stable, decent work, but then I got this idea about selling eco-friendly office supplies, and I just had to take the leap. It’s not easy—long hours, funding issues—but it’s exciting. I love solving problems and seeing that spark when a client finally gets someone who truly understands their needs. Did you ever consider a different career?      Only in the dream where I have more money and less weekend work! I’ve had a colleague, though, who nearly did make the jump—started a catering business from scratch, catered weddings and things. To be fair, she ran it for about two years before the pressures got too much. It’s quite something, juggling passion with the practical side. Would you ever consider diversifying?      Possibly. I’ve been thinking about expanding into corporate sustainability training. You know, helping businesses not only buy eco-friendly products but also adopt greener practices. Do you think a teacher like you would have patience for the chaos of that?      I like a bit of chaos—classrooms are my bread and butter! Honestly, if you wanted a mentor, you’d go far with someone like me on your team.

Rather annoying me a bit, eh? Our new housemate. I mean, it's not like 'e's got to be 'ere all the time, but it's like 'e've found a new hobby where it's just lurkin’ about the place like as if 'e owns the place already. Keep it simple. ‘E'll probably get disappointed if we don’t bless 'im with a cake or something, but I dunno. Websites mentioned it’s a 'ritual' or sommat.      Oh, aye, ‘vibes man’. I might’ve been obsessed with one after seeing that viral video of a cupcake artist from Denmark or sommat.      C’mon! Really? That’s your go-to for solving problems? Rather a lot, didn't we?      Aye, it's been a busy afternoon. What with the cold snap, I was glad to find a few fresh veg left in the market.      You do know the butcher fancies you, don't you?      Oh, William? He's just friendly, that's all.      Nay, you’ve been coming by his stall every week this month, and every time he gives you a better cut or two. Knows how to charm a lady when he wants to, don't he?      You're being silly. I've no time for men like him, not these days.      Just saying. Still, enough talk of the butcher. What did you get from the greengrocer?      Some leeks, a couple of parsnips, and a nice bunch of chard. Should be enough for a stew if it snows again tonight.      You always say that, and yet I still end up taking the bones.      That’s because you fancy it! You always said as much. Hot soup by the fire with a book in hand… Sounds like the life!      Sounds like it, does it? Well, I’m not young enough for all that jiggery-pokery anymore. All that bending and lifting?      You don’t seem to mind when the telly’s on. That fishing programme you watch every week—count me out.      You don’t understand it, but you don’t have to. Not all of us need ballet and poetry, eh?      No, I suppose not. But you lot do have a habit of watching things that make you grumpy.      And you lot run about like you're still twenty chasing after someone else's children. All that shouting about nappies and porridge!      At least I used to earn something, unlike you!      Aye, that’s what you say every time. And what of it? At least I’ve got the TV remote in my hands and a warm fire.      Don’t go getting too smug, old man. If it wasn’t for me, you’d still be living off tinned spaghetti with string!      Now you mention it, I might just make that tonight. With a bit of those leeks?      Only if you promise not to overcook them. We can’t all like stringy vegetables, you know.      Fair enough. I’ll make it the way you like it. Deal?      Deal. But only if I can have first taste. I’ve been on my feet all day, you know.

Rather chilly this morning, ain't it? That’s me remembering to draw the curtains in time ‘fore they all got nippy with draft.      I prefer it warm, gran. Keeps the radiators on full blast all day. Look, I’ve unpacked my things in the spare room. I left the folder with the mock papers on the bed. I reckon I’ll try to get that next round of practice done before tea.      Ah, mocks, you used to dread those when you were a lad, didn’t you, love? Didn’t your mum nearly pull her hair out over those exam books?      Aye, she were the real terror when marks weren’t up to scratch. One time, I dropped my best O-levels in ‘whatr, Arithmetic – I nearly got barred from the kitchen for a week!      That’s a bit harsh! Why doesn’t no one teach that anymore?      Oh, GCSEs and all that lot, you can’t blame the kids. They’ve got more complicated methods now. I do tell the lads, though, practice takes time. You don’t just learn to solve an equation by reading a textbook. You’ve got to work it through.      Tell him that, Brenda – he’s been at the same paper for two days now, and asks me the same question every time.      Aye, “What’s two times seven” – and he thinks I know the answer just for looking ancient!      That’s not fair, Granda! You’d better not be skiving either. I’m supposed to revise geometry today – come and help when you’re about!      Right, the thing is, love, mind you don’t be too hard on yourself. I was like you once, up until unwell with trigonometry. But ‘course, I left school at sixteen and passed maths by the skin of my teeth.      ‘Course you did, Brenda. Ain’t we all passing things by the skin of our teeth in this house!      Oh, leave off, Kenneth – I’ve got the tea going. You two set the table, ‘fore the lot of us starve goin’ on about numbers! Brenda, give him a hand, wi’ the plates, will you?      Time to lay off your badinage for five minutes, Granda!      Well, tea comes first, and then revision. But I expect you’ll have ‘me poorer at the end o’ this session than a beggar on Humbleton Bridge!      Oh, let’s not frighten the lad.

‘Ey lads, anyone got that MultiSport tablet stuff? My mam was on at me ‘bout gettin’ more vitamins ‘cause she says I’m runnin’ on fumes like a ‘eavier than lead.’      No way—get a grip. You’re twenty-three, eeny weeny, and we’ve got you down as the heaviest bloke in the group on a table. A vitamin tablet ain’t gonna fix this.      Nah, nan’s like that. She worries more than me when I’m late home by five minutes. Still, I got these new smartwatch things. Lakelands did a sale, and the thing’s only twenty quid anditunes music My nan still thinks I’ve invented jetpacks or summat.      D’you know how I feel? I’m just spendin’ too much time waitin’ for breakfast, nothin’ more than a coffee with a bit of sugar and a biscuit. I’m tryin’ to do this vegan thing, but I’m starvin’ by mid-day and just feelin’ like I’ve got the Ibbitts out of me.      Honestly, I’ve been on a mini cleanse for two days and then I got cravings so bad I ate three pieces of cake. I’m still smarter because I watched a documentary while chompin’. It was called “Jimmy Doherty’s Gut Feelings.”      Honestly, this all reminds me of my aunt. She’s got this thing with juice cleanses and talks about ‘detoxin’ like it’s the way of livin’. Can’t even make a curry without addin’ a flamin’ kale.      She’s not wrong tho. I mean, you ain’t gone anywhere if you plug in a detox series, watch  The Crown , and bin a whole crate of baked beans.      Hey, speaking of, I’ve bin watchin’ this one programme on iPlayer—the one about uni life. I envied the bloke who had that sprite of academicky space in London.      That’s not the one I like. I prefer the one with the course on the history of fashion goin’ on in Manchester. It’s weird, but I wanna know why brogues suddenly became the go-to in the 90’s.      Y’know, me mum was like that in the 90’s. Just belly-laughin’ on the phone, ‘cause this one’s new pair of jeans went up to the knees and all I did was crouch at the bus.      That’s probably ‘cos yeh didn’t fold ‘em right. They’re just slim-fits no wossname, but if you go in them anywhere, you’ve had it.

Right, I’m just scribbling down what we need for tomorrow’s shop. We need bread, pints of milk, some apples—oh, and more anti-itch cream, probably. That mosquito or whatever it was finally left Tom alone last night, but now it looks like it’s back for a second bite!      Aye, I know what you mean. Tom’s been grizzle enough without that lot too. If I had me way, I’d bin out with the bug zapper or something. We’ve had wasps in the garden again, even though I thought I squashed the last lot three weeks back.      Mozzies are no’ fair. I managed to get one of ’em with my phone light though last night. I turned the torch on and watched it crash into the wall and fall down. Pretty much worth it if it was the last one.      You need to be careful with that stuff in your room, Tom. Don’t want you felling dizzy or nothin’. I’ll get some citronella candles tomorrow—might help if we light one in the garden and one in the kitchen.      Actually, on that note, there was something I read the other day about natural remedies. Tea tree oil, baking soda—sounds a bit odd, but apparently, it works for some people. Though I reckon the best way to deal with the whole problem is to not let the bugs reproduce in the first place. Like, someone check the gutters and the bins. Rotting fruit and stagnant water is a magnet.      Aye, I’ll be sure to add some antibacterial soap to the list as well. I did a bit of a skim through a module on pest ecology at uni—mainly about what attracts them. Lights are a big one. I reckon if we unplug the outside lights, bin them up for the summer, we might survive the next few weeks.      As long as it don’t mean no lights at all, I’ll be fine with it. Not sure how you lads sleep in the pitch black, Tom.      I’ve got glow-in-the-dark stars on my ceiling, so it’s like a night sky. Helps go to sleep on a humid night like this. Any chance of a cold drink to go with all that bug stuff?      Go on then. Add some limes and cucumbers to the shop list too, love. Make it feel like we’re doing something more than just surviving the weekend over this lot.

Rather annoying this cold, innit? I've been grumpy as a badger in a public library. I got the lot—headache, sneezing, that bunged-up nose. Livin’ it up, really.      Aw, take care love. You’ve had eeny weeny sleep, haven’t ye? I saw ye at the kitchen counter snorin’ on the kettle last night. Slap-up way to greet the day.      Hilarious. Know what's the worst? Tryin’ to do Zoom interviews with blokes like Lloyd Grossman, sounding like a Disney villain. "Ahem, er... I, uh, think the biggest issue is the turkey!"      I’d throw the lot of ’em out if they’d used that excuse again. Last week I had food poisoning after a dodgy salmon burger breakfast, and I was up half the night with a doc in my head. I swear the NHS desktop hides my files whenever I try to prescribe me own diarrhoea tablets.      You know what I heard? They're trialling some AI health system now. Uses cameras in hospitals to read body language—like if you’re lying or in pain or about to faint. Imagine that at the dental surgery: “Ah, no, doc, really, I'm fine. The chair's quite soft.” And then the AI’s like, “Yup, definitely fainted.”      Spooky, innit? Like they’ve got algorithm eyes everywhere now. I dunno if I’d trust it. Or if I’d be accused of faking migraines to get away from my parents’ chatter.      That's the litmus test for vaccination vibes these days. Everyone and their sister are suddenly health experts. "Stop me if you’ve heard this one," My aunt texted me the other day: “The hospital called me. They want to scan my aura. It's probably got vitamins in it." I tried to tell her it’s a scam but the bloke down the pub reckons it’s funded by Elon Musk.      They're doin' it for you, innit? Surveillance and snack boxes the same. Honestly, the world's run by about seven blokes with spreadsheets and microwave dinners.      And the telly doesn't help. Last night’s doco was all about flu strains and why koi carp are now walking the earth, apparently. You'd think after three vaccinations and one hospital trip over a dodgy kebab, they'd   tell the truth so we could all rest easier.      Maybe they’re just saving it for the next season of Body Language: The Musical.

Rather annoying this gridlock at the shopping centre. I couldn't get the sausages for tea. We had to rely on cold beans again.      That's the third time this week. I've started queueing for the butcher's shop as soon as the doors open. You'd think they'd clear out the traffic more regularly.      My goodness, I remember when a shopping centre was a place to enjoy, not a battlefield. Still,.Gridlock aside, what did you think of the new music magazine, Edith?      Oh, I didn’t get round to it yet. I've been so wrapped up with transcribing the interview with that jazz producer. But everyone at work keeps saying it's full of eccentric left-field reviews.      You're missing out, Elinor. They managed to get an exclusive with that young folk band from Cumbria—very promising. I happened to read a bit in the café the other day.      You both are so cultured. I'm more of a classic rock fan myself—still play Led Zeppelin on the weekend. I even posted about it on Facebook last week and got ten likes. Rather proud of myself, to be honest.      You should consider joining the local music society, Martin. They still value live performances and have some great discussions.      Speaking of which, I've been meaning to ask you both—do you fancy coming over for dinner this weekend? I'll try not to burn the sausages.      That'd be a delight, Elinor. I still have a few recipes from when I ran the school about forty years ago—mostly for fund-raisers, of course.      Another failsafe is that shepherd's pie I made recently. Rather classic, but it went down a storm with the kids.      Excellent. A bit of scrabble as well, perhaps? I've been trying to improve my tile management. You mustn't stick to two-letter words like I do.      Oh, I stick to them all the time! It's no fun for anyone else. Then again, Martin always claims he's got go-to words on standby.      I have "quay" and "joule" in my bag of tricks. Lift your game, you two!      Oh, I think I'm quite comfortable with my limited repertoire, thank you very much. I have a higher chance of winning if I keep it simple.      That's exactly how I was in my sixth form class, David.

Rather a lot of memories floating about today, isn’t it? This working party brings it all back — like when I was younger, often popping about the West Country and beyond, setting up exhibitions. It’s a mad thought, really, to think I spent so much of my life with ink and presses instead of brushes and canvas.      It certainly is. I reckon it must’ve been invigorating, though. A lot of people would swap their right arm to have had your sort of path. Marketing printing systems sounds as dry as dust to me, and yet you made it look like art.      Well, truth be told, I did throw a bit of the real thing into it. I wasn’t always the businesswoman, you know — I had a gallery in Taunton, albeit a small one, tucked into a converted stables. But when I started thinking of printing systems, I saw it almost as a new medium. I wanted the prints to last — inks that wouldn’t fade, presses that didn’t budge, systems that could churn out consistent, vivid work that spoke of craftsmanship.      I can imagine the German exhibitions were quite the scene. They still are, of course, with all that precision and order. But how did you manage in such a structured environment — negotiating with engineers?      Oh, heavens, they were a marvel. So meticulous! Nothing was left to chance. I remember one afternoon in Munich, we were testing a new offset printing plate, and someone at the last minute wanted the contrast tweaked. The German gentlemen just looked at me as if I had asked the moon to be red and then recalculated their entire process in five minutes flat. They never missed a beat about it. I admired that — you could argue it was robotic, but it was efficient.      And that was you, out there, explaining the English eccentric side to the system, I suppose. I wonder if they even respected eccentricity.      They did — grudgingly. I always tried to remind them that not everything could be measured to the millimetre. The soul of the print comes with a bit of magic. At one exhibition, I brought a framed print of a Somerset landscape — not by machine, but by hand — as a gesture. They didn’t get it at first, but after a while, one of the younger engineers cornered me with tears in his eyes. He’d never seen anything like it — something that moved him, despite the precision of everything else around it.

Rather annoying when the satnav goes mental on us, innit? I was just reading ‘Bolton’ got its name from some old Celtic word for river or summat. Bet you didn’t know that, Dad.      Oh I did, love — well, the general gist. Got eeny weeny bit of geography at school, didn’t I? Bet you’re all into that sort a thing now with yer English course. Got that etymology module, yeah?      Yeah, it’s actually quite interesting. I did this essay on words that look odd but make sense when you break ‘em down. Like quinoa — everyone says it wrong. Me mates at school still go "kwin-wah". Just wish I didn’t get so squeamish when I read about the etymology of words for, y’know, body parts and stuff. It gets a bit icky sometimes.      Fair enough. Like when ye told me in the car boot shop about the history of lightning, you remember? I was so gobsmacked I nearly knocked the wheels off the kerb, trying to follow what yer sayin’. Bet if yer did a philosophy course alongside yer English, that’d suit yer — go on, be honest.      Nah, I think English is enough for now. Though I’m not sure what course to do next. Some of my friends are talkin’ about combining it with something like cultural studies or language and education. What d’you reckon?      Well, I’d say do whichever gets yer animated when you talk about it. Just don’t weigh yourself down with too much theory — I still don’t get half the stuff yer come out with about universities. But while we’re on the topic — the farmer’s market in St Ives is where we should stock up for the week. I reckon it starts at ten, but if the satnav ‘asn’t gone treble by then, we’ll be there on the dot.      If we don’t hit a service station before then, we’ll need a pit stop to clear our heads. Though I’ve seen enough of ‘em recently to last a lifetime — all the same chips and plastic cups of water. But I say this and then I queue up for a go at the map room again if we get lost.      Yeah, I’m just figuring out the spelling of all the counties we’re passing through. It’s all so confusing — like Corn-welly? Corn-wall-ee?

Rather do a bit o’ dinner, innit? Me an’ the lads 'ave ‘ad a few pints an’ me belly’s cryin’ out fer summat tasty.      Aye, we do need ter sort summat out. Got any ingredients lef’ in een? I ain't been inta the shops 'cos I reckon me mummy dunn’t know I’ve been ‘ere.      I’ve brought me mam’s stew over, dump it in the oven an’ it'll be grand. Didn’t fancy eatin’ it on me own... needs to sort it out!      That's real nice of you, speaker_3. My turkey curry's not bin disturbed an’ left it in the back o’ the freezer for safety, in case I was sad in the morn.      Mm, we’re talkin’ prime Curry here, innit? I reckon me basmati rice needs to be boiled, though. Still got the kettle?      Aye, it's 'ere under the sink. Yer always askin’ about the kettle innit, like I'd chuck it out or summat!      Well then, got a cuppa while the stew’s warmin’ up, least way it won’t be throwin’ a tantrum in the oven later.      ‘Balderdash’, as me auntie 'ud say — but I’m also suspicious o’ my own ability to not poison everyone.
