I once tried hotter sauce than this an’ nearly lost me tongue.      Don’t be exaggeratin’, I about did that meself once — brought a man down the street to taste it an’ 'e ended up hospitalised. Properly scorched 'im up.      My, ‘e must’ve treasured that man if 'e took 'im up on me curry. I'm a culinarian at heart, I am — I just haven’t got the stickin’ power as some.      Aye 'eck, speaking of ‘sticking’ — whose turn's it been to clear up after t’last place? Don’t go lettin’ me see if it's me again or I’ll go into a right strop.      Nah, it were your mam’s turn. I said as much when we all came in, mind yer.      It's alright for yer talkin'. ‘Tis your turn next, innit? I’m not makin’ sweeps tomes or nothin' — I ain’t got all the limbs, 'opefully.      So we’re stuck with each other, innit? A proper pinnacle in life, me friend, meself last seen with a tea towel.      Shy! But I mean, it is summat to be proud o’, ain’t it? I once tried to wipe down the countertops an’ ended up with more mess as well as a story for the bed.

Rather annoying driving instructor I've got. You know what they do—drill it in, drill it in... got to go round this corner at twenty because some kid on a scooter stared death into my eyes a week back.      That does happen—some instructors take things a little too seriously. I'm assuming you're doing this because you need to get a job, or are you just trying to expand your horizons now?      Mostly job, yeah. If I'm going to dump someone it's going to be in the car and not the pub when it's raining. You know what I mean. I'm working mostly evenings at the pub, so weekends are the only chance I’ve got for practice.      Makes sense. I left London a few years back, moved back up here, and it's very different in the Midlands compared to Hertfordshire. The roads are better here, but the drivers are... well, everyone has a bit in them at the wheel, don’t they?      Haha, that’s for sure. Last time I went into Brum city centre, I counted five near misses in two streets. What about you? You teaching full-time, then?      Yeah, languages. I teach at the college in Erdington. My especiality is German and Spanish, and I take on a few private tutees as well. It's not quite as lively as a bar, but the satisfaction’s similar—when they finally 'get it', you know?      That's good, sounds oddly satisfying. You ever think about doing more? Like, studying yourself? I mean, you're qualified already.      I did a postgraduate diploma a while back. Now I just pass it on. Honestly, I like where I am. Life’s easier that way. Doesn't sound unambitious, does it?      Nah, not at all. I think it's just more me trying to figure out where I’m going. Job, flat, drinks with mates when I can. That's my grand plan.      Sounds like a solid base to keep on running from. Speaking of, do you play any sports or anything? I’ve heard some good things about the leisure go here.      Not much, but I've been thinking about picking up some classes. Maybe Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu? A bit of something aside from the lager-swillin' and kipper-fryin'.      That's a fantastic idea—like, where does this guy live? Or do they take new people?

Rather annoying when the clock’s gone walkabout, isn’t it? I was just about ready with the first cup of the day, and no sign of poor Elsie. Not that I've much time for a second, mind. Not since I sold the tuppence-wagon.      Oh, don’t be like that, Harold. You know she gets distracted. I found her in the garden a minute ago, listing off which flowers needed more sun and which ones gave her a touch of nostalgia. She's been thinking about her trip to Gambia and how the plants there reminded her.      Right, because of course she'd go and fall in love with the idea of planting another continent's flowers like that. Though, speaking of gardens, I found the most peculiar thing last night, a donation box she'd hidden behind the lavender. She said she'd made it with bits of old biscuit tins and breakfast trays—very artsy!      Aye, she’s always had a bit of a spark to her. Used to make the most fantastic banners for the village fete with just scraps and imagination. I still have one nailed to the garage wall.      And she once tried to hide her diagnosis from us, you know. She thought she was just “imagining” symptoms. I nearly got the phone to ring the hospital myself before she burst out laughing and told me it was all just a bit of Munchausen fancy.      There’s more out of that lass than most. Just wish she’d consider driving once in a while. That’s the other thing — she’s skint these days and she’s still using public transport to get to the village shop.      I’ve offered to give her a hand, but she insists on doing what she can alone. Still, she’s barely left the house. I think she mentioned to me she found a way to keep busy by ringing bells in the parish church. A bit surprising for a woman who used to run off with pottery and flower pots.      I told her the bell-ringing was a lovely thing to do but to make sure she wasn't overworking herself. She just smiled and said it gave her a sense of purpose.      Yeah, go on then. But let’s see about getting her settled at the table before the kettle’s long gone cold. And don’t forget the biscuits from the box under the sink.

Rather annoying when a new app takes up so much space, isn't it? I deleted it like five minutes after downloading and I’m still having to clear cache to make my phone usable again.      I know what you mean. I tried out this fitness app last week. It promised to turn me into a fitness model, but honestly, I was more motivated just watching people panic on TikTok.      Spare me. If you’re too lazy to even finish watching a workout video, what’s the point of using the app anyway? I tried this new cooking app, and the recipes at least don’t lie to your face. Though honestly, I still burned the chicken wings last night.      Burned turkey wings? You must’ve watched horror films while trying to cook. I do the same—end up chopping the wrong hand every single time.      Honestly, I’d rather watch a horror film while cooking than this new Anglo-German docu-series my mum’s into. It's like, why even do it if the subtitles are broken?      I do like the way she speaks though. She doesn’t put on that posh voice to impress people like I do at work. Reminds me of watching German horror films. All the characters speak English but somehow sound like they’re reading from a textbook.      You mean like  The Cube  but in black and white and with subtitles for British people who already speak English? Honestly, I’d rather watch this someone-from-my-ex’s-new-friend trying to explain a time-share holiday.      Just don’t fall for the holiday stories. My cousin recently got talked into something that involved a passport, a boat, and a 5 a.m. wake-up. She’s currently sunbathing and cooking on some Greek island while I’m telling you this over takeout.      Joke all you like. I’ve got a holiday booked next month. Parents were supposed to come with me. But apparently, ‘getaways’ aren’t approved when you’re waiting on a mortgage decision. So it’s just me and this constant fear of being alone with my thoughts.      Relax, you’ll be fine. Alone time isn't so bad. I once met my ex in the most random way—she was trying to get into my flat because her cat had locked herself in between two sofas.      And your cat was the one with the key?

Rather annoying this, having to rely on public transport when you're used to driving. Mind you, it's not got the seats like they used to, has it?      Oh, I know what you mean. Not only that, the bus driver nearly ran over a cow on the way in. I'm telling you, I don't fancy making the journey home if it's anything like that on the way back.      That's a bit dramatic, George. If you watched the road instead of that football match you were muttering about, you'd spot the cows before the driver did.      Easy for you to say, Margaret. Besides, the real problem's not the bus driver or the cows, it's the fact I still don't know how you managed to get the bus back from Darcy’s last week.      Blimey, George, you’re better off asking me how I got up this hill. I had to park two fields over, you know. There’s not a single bloody space anywhere near the front door now.      That’s because half of Norfolk’s population seems to have decided to visit your house as their monthly social event. Honestly, it's like a bloody village meeting.      Be fair, Margaret. It's just Matey from next door, Duckworth, and the Haywards. We were raised on the same road, you know. Silly of me not to foresee the invasion.      You mean the invasion and your refusal to buy a second-hand car off old Thomson last spring. You said it had the 'perks of a real classic'. Sounds more like a museum piece to me.      It did have character, mind you. But Character didn't mean it had to be a mission every time I turned it on.      And now we're all stuck. My ankle’s still playing up from the guest chair incident. I did not expect to have to exhibit the finer points of land navigation all over again.      You're getting distracted again. The point is, how are we getting out of here without a car, a bus pass with a full tank, and a young volunteer?      Pah! I'll tell you goin' on that life if you don’t get real soon, George. Better chuck in a helmet and a siren while we’re at it. Road to recovery’s paved with good planning, or so I'm told.

Rather annoying this new traffic system on the M6, isn't it? I’d think it'd save time, but I've been inching along for nearly two hours now! Mind, the traffic is always a madhouse this time of day with all the flights in and out of Manchester.      Oh dear, yes, we’ve got the same queue here on this side of the bridge. Though I suppose it is logical, with how often flights from the airport are delayed these days. It was easier when you just clattered along and hoped for the best. Didn’t even need indicators.      That’s because it was mostly just lorry drivers and motorbikes out there then, not stressed-out souls like us trying to get home after a family function. I remember when I moved down to Manchester back in the eighties, and I bought a second-hand Ford Capri with a handbrake that worked only when it felt like it. Managed to park it... eventually in a car boot sale.      Ah, those were the days. Good ones, or bad—depending on the puddle of oil you’d left behind. I remember moving with your mother as a child, and the house we moved into had no central heating—it was just a coal range in the kitchen. You had to build the fire every morning before school, or you'd freeze the journey there.      That did seem like something out of a film. And now you can get instant hot water for coffee just by turning the tap. Technology certainly moves on. Though I have to say, I do miss the simplicity of the old things. My nan had a radio she tuned with a crude knob that clunked when it moved about.      Clunky things always had charm, mind. I used to work in the oil fields back in the eighties and it felt like we moved in entirely the wrong direction. Burgers and bad movies, lugging around 50kg tools at 6 a.m. on any bloody day of the week. Guess I’m just waiting for someone to stick me back into that.      Ah, you've always had a flair for the dramatic. Now, the biscuits—would you like a couple more with your tea? The currant ones go well with the scones your mother brought over.      Yes, please, I’ll take two more currant ones if there are any left.

Mum, I just wanted to say sorry again about what happened with your bike. I know it’s been pissing you off for ages.      Oh, it’s fine, love. I’m just glad it’s all worked out in the end. It turned out to be a proper drama, but I saw the police catch the bloke today.      What? Proper? Like, a police chase or something? Like one of those fast and furious scenes?      No, no, not like that. But I got a message from the officer, asking me to check some pictures of the bike from a security camera. Someone apparently saw a suspicious bloke near the bike rack behind the clinic where I work. I recognised the bike immediately—you know how I take care of that thing.      But how’d you find out the police were even looking into it?      I called the station when I noticed it was gone after work last week. Bloke said it looked like a local, maybe someone near the area who’d taken similar bikes before. I posted it on Nextdoor and Facebook, just in case. I put a decent photo.      And did anyone help?      A few people tagged it in their groups. One local lad even showed me where he often saw bikes with similar locks hanging around. Funny thing is, his mate was picked up that very next day trying to sell the handlebars online.      Honestly, what someone sees in bikes, I’ll never know. I mean, your bike’s not exactly the James Bond gadget.      I know it’s not flashy, but I put time and money into it. I even customised the back rack so I can cycle into college without needing to carry my stuff. It was like part of me.      You're going back to college, Mum?      Yes, part-time. I did a BTEC in management a few years back, but never finished. I feel like I need to keep learning, you know. It gives me something to aim for. And also, it helps me not dwell on stuff from my younger years.      That’s serious. You're like my hero or something.      Ha! Don’t be silly. But it makes me feel better, doing that. And with the bike back, I can at least get there on time without pestering you for lifts.      Well, I can never choose not to give you a lift. But maybe you can bribe me with food from that bag I smelt coming up the stairs earlier.

Rather annoying that the train’s delay’s messed up our plan. I was just about to ask if anyone wanted to grab the parcels from the shops before the 16:30 train back      Aye, we wouldn’t have even got back at a decent hour if it was on time een! I thought I’d lost the lot when the signal went out on the 12:45      Fair dos - this lot got here so late we were stewing in the rain for nigh on an hour. They really need to run a service that doesn’t plod along like a cow with a jammy doughnut stuck to its hoof      You know the system well My turkey curry will be stone cold by the time I get back to Cilmyrfa now, and Ro is used to eating it piping hot. Blimey, Cardiff’s a giggle of breakfasts and bone-achy legs by 7am in the week      That’s the downside of working the qmk. One time I sat in a Waterstones for four-quarters of the morning and ended up gluing myself to the floor to read a few of those deadly non-fiction bookshops in-country      Well, from what I’ve seen at the station it’s mostly fairly motley and/or motley      Would ye look at that? Letterbox! Should’ve known. Last mail truck at ten fifty, and the rest just wandered      Just trying to keep a sense of normalcy. Funny thing, normalcy, is it not? You can’t be abnormal in a normal way but you can be normal in an abnormal way      Right, the problem here is that this place is meant for four, and not five. Any plans to fix the situation?      Not sure, but for the time being, guest speaker will have to sleep with his feet at the door as it is a democratic principle      Ah, scheming again I see We knew you had a bit of a player in you      I think it was my turn to do the meats. Defrosting a couple of turkeys like it's the early go's really on your nerve if you've not got a proper microwave      Hopefully between us we can box one up properly and get your lot back on track.      Oh, one of them is for your mother-in-law, isn’t it? She made you promise she’d be asked why not to them?

Rather annoying that the beer’s all gone.      That's it, is it? I suppose I'll have to go downstairs and see what your parents have in their wine cellar.      Not quite a wine cellar, more like a sideboard with a couple of bottles that might have seen the  80s .      I’m all for trying a vintage.      That one from your nan’s was absolutely dreadful. It was like drinking treacle.      Ah yes, the port, or the glorified syrup as you like to call it.      Look, the real debate here is why some people like that sweet turkey wine. I’ve met enough people in London who spend ridiculous money on everyday reds and whites. But pick them a fortified wine and suddenly they’re making rules for themselves.      Maybe it’s just about habit. They grew up in a drinking culture where you knock back spirits as if you were puffing on a cigarette.      I get it, but it’s so different here. Norfolk people don’t sip strong ales from hip bars and expect to get by. We go for something lighter, maybe a local cider or a perry.      But that’s changing, isn’t it? You go to a village pub and there’s a proper craft beer menu now. I remember the last time we went to the King’s Arms in Holt.      Yes, they had a plum beer. I had a sip— horrible , but they were trying. It’s like board games: once you break people away from the most popular ones, they try to figure out what else the market can offer.      True. Speaking of which, are you still fond of that cruel carom game we played the other day?      Don’t remind me. You were up at 6 a.m. holding your thumb as if it were broken.      My thumb was sprained, and that was all  your  doing. Do you plan on letting it slide by with no justice?      Perhaps I should retaliate with the next game. I’ve been on the fence about getting our co-op game out, though. Thought it would be a nice break from the usual blooding everyone’s thumb.      I’m seriously tempted. We could rally the kids and start with something simple—like Dominion or Castles of Burgundy or something over-10-year-olds can understand.      I like that idea. My parents love the idea of them all sitting down, casting dice and arguing over game rules for once and not about politics or Brexit again.

Rather annoying the new bins haven't arrived yet. I remember they said they'd be here by Tuesday. We're running out of space in the downstairs one already.      Yeah, I mean, it is a bit chaotic. I was trying to sort things at work, but the timing was off again on the delivery. I've been keeping a very strict system here at home—recyclables over on the table, food waste by the door, and general waste in the bin under the stairs. It's not like it's rocket science.      Didn’t your mum get the new model last week? I went round there for tea and everything was spotless, bins and all. She said her courier turned up well ahead of schedule. You must have an eccentric local agency, this place! I’m from Swansea and things are usually late and sad in the world of local government!      Oh, we’re British—relaxation is in our DNA when it comes to schedules. I remember the time we moved, Ken didn’t have the first clue about white goods, and that man nearly took the fridge apart trying to fit it in the doorway!      Still, I credit you with moving on such short notice. I mean, we didn’t have time to unpack all our furniture. I remember my nan once told me about moving house and how it took  months  back in her day because of the furniture—like you couldn't just buy it already flat-packed at B&Q and build it at someone else's house!      That's the old world for you. Now with IKEA, you just follow the diagrams and… here’s hoping no one does the head ballet when they make a mistake about the screw placements. I once had a man in the office take three days to understand a chair.      Not to mention the time it took him to fold it to take it home. Oh, and while he was at it, he did manage to rewrite the whole VAT policy. Unbelievable how one man can have two worlds colliding!      Speaking of administrative tasks and time wasted, how did your project co-ordination course go last week? I’ve been thinking about going back to learn proper project management. You know, with the proper qualifications and go-to-meetings-via-Zoom kind of work.      It was really brutal. I had three assignments in the first week and all of them demanded at least three servings of craft activities—sticky notes, timelines, those plastic bits that connect triangles, and circles like we were in a design workshop.

Rather annoying this traffic, isn't it? I mean, do we need this many cranes and roadworks in North London in 2025?      I've been over this with you, hun. Construction doesn't know the meaning of "get out of my way". Happens every decade—someone always wants to fix the road they didn't design.      Yeah, but you’ve only moved back to North London last summer. I thought you'd prefer being closer to your grandparents and that TLS thing you're invited to occasionally?      Well, it's not just the TLS, love—it's also  closer . I've missed the chaos, honestly. You know I like that My Fair Lady bit with cabs and double deckers. But back to the car—how are you with these push-button handbrakes?      Please, I've been better at breakfasts—this is easy. Dad’s still scared of parking his old Saab, and it doesn’t even have keys anymore. You think I should tell him?      Oh, don’t start. Your dad is proudly average in his own way.      And you, by the way—why did you bring the car? We’re only getting you a present from that pretentious bookshop in Finchley, and I know you  hate  choosing gifts.      Very observant. I brought the car because you needed to drive, and yes, I hate choosing gifts. But also, I wanted to pick a copy of Simone de Beauvoir while out and about—there's a TLS review I want to look up before I comment on your grandmother’s latest France holiday email about her misadventures with "the wrong map".      Ugh, don’t even remind me. She still calls the Eiffel Tower  Eiffel  something, like she's trying to pronounce it in her sleep.      Oh, she was bloody sure it was Eele-far too for a week. Honestly, the French are as mysterious as they come. And don’t get me wrong, I miss print—you can’t beat the feeling of turning pages for a good essay. But the TLS app on my iPad is go-to when I'm editing from bed or on a train.      Right, that’s your job—editing blokes who still think your comma placement is "feminine nonsense". While I'm stuck trying to avoid road rage with the people in that red van tailgating us like it's 1939 and they're racers.      Calm down.

Rather skip to the part where you two tried to build a tent in the hurly-burly of pheasants and ended up with a bonfire more than a campsite, eh? That holiday story's got more twists than a snooker pool table!      Aye, it een't the holidays  not  to remember, 'course! Ay, Lucy's dad helped us with a map that was from the 1890s, and Tim reckoned we were going to Somerset or something. We ended up in the middle of a field called Blackmoor.      Oh, I nearly wet mesel when we saw a man in the field, only he was wearing a turban 'cause his head was boiling! He said he’s a farmer and told us to move on or he’d phone the cops!      Blimey, that’s bonkers! Wait, does he still live up that way? I did a work placement at a farm near Leeds owt once, and the farmer’s brother was a proper grumpy old moorhen.      We were meant to be glamping! Bah, ended up as camp and panic. And then, when the tent wouldn’t go up, we tried to use a brolly as a shelter — and Matey here got a sneeze, it blew sideways and burst like a balloon! We had pine needles all over the place for a week.      And let’s not 'member someone got chickenpox and ended up not even climbing a hill once. I had a blister on my toe the size of a skittle.      Aye, but it een't all bad, about half the group ended up in the belfry of a church once during a thundery downpour! Proper old building, you barely noticed the thunder it were so echoey.      Oh, you mean that time you passed out after eating that weird stew with a red bean in it? ‘Bout thought you’d meet St. Cuthbert or whoever’s the local saint up there!      Heh, 've been on a trip to the Lake District once, and there was this guy who looked like a legend with his beard and hiking goonie on — ended up being our taxi driver and got us lost in the fens for an hour. He were a bloke who'd read your soul with a map.      You know what’s the weirdest? On that road trip to Scotland, we kept on talkin' ‘bout this restaurant we passed and thought it were a Burger King...

Rather unusual to go camping in the winter months, ay? I mean, you’d think it'd be like... sleeping in a cold bin with a blanket and a lantern. Not a bad idea if you're a student, mind you. Charming sort of thing, as long as you’re prepared.      Aye, I used to take some of my patients out on the odd winter walk up on the hills. A lot of healing happens in the quiet and cold, you know? Out of the city’s noise, the mind can settle. I heard once that wild winter camping can be like meditation under the stars... frozen, but still deeply grounding.      That's not too far off. I've led a few of these trips for outdoor education—you get left with no distractions. People talk to each other, or they talk to themselves, but it's real. Living with no electricity, no hot showers, it doesn’t take long before you notice the small things... the crunch of snow underfoot, the silence when the wind dies down. I once spent a night in the Cairngorms when the weather turned, and we were just surrounded by absolute stillness and darkness. Brilliant.      Hah! Tell that to my joints—it wasn't so brilliant waking up then. I went once in the –6°C with a fairly decent tent and thermals, but I'm not the young'un anymore. All that exposed skin and the wind... I tell you, you don’t appreciate central heating until you’ve gone forty-eight hours without it. But God, there's something to it.      I’d be a bit skint to give it a try, but I’d be lying if I said it didn’t appeal. My partner once went on a New Year’s Eve trip up in the Highlands and came back with the idea that that was the happiest she'd felt in a long time. Just the smell, the silence, the sheer scale of it all. Said it made her feel small in a comforting kind of way. Not all scientists would agree, but there’s a sort of primal peace in being out there, unconnected.      Precisely. I think it's partly the psychological release from our overstimulated lives. You come back feeling like you’ve been given a go at a map that wasn't your own. You're not trying to fix anything in the world, you're just existing with it.

Rather than going out for dinner again, innit, have you considered making something at home? I know a few proper nosh places in town, but I’d fancy a bit o’ cooking after a long day adminin’ that corpus.      Yeah, well, the timing’s iffy on that. I’ve got a deadline with the engineering firm on Monday, and I’ve been cranking on that report all week. Honestly, the last thing I feel like doin’ is stewin’ or noddles and cheese.      Right, right. But even a stir-fry needs prior prep, innit. Unless you fancy me chuckin’ somethin’ quick on the pan? My turkey and spinach stir-fry’s solid. I’ve been rallyin’ to get back into the kitchen, properly. I mean, the food’s all part of the storytelling, really — it’s breakfast, no doubt about it, but it still tells a tale if you ask me.      Nah, I say go ahead. I’m starvin’. Just try not to tell me it’s healthy, eh? I might falter — quite a few meals I’ve had of late, since I been on site, are not what I'd call a balanced diet. So what's the plan?      Right, I’ve just got to throw together the chilli oil and black bean sauce. You want me to make it spicy or stick with your medium, innit? I mean, Spicy is also part of the experience, a rush, a bit of a kick — you know, like a film scene with real tension. The heat builds up, but it’s controlled — like a good climax.      Make the spice decent — don’t be soft on it. And while you're stir-fryin’, I might have a listen to one of those old books you like. You know, the ones with high-quality narratives, not that modern drivel. You said you told me ‘The Shadow of the Wind’ was decent — am I getting somewhere with that one?      Yeah, it’s a proper banger, innit! De Falla’s got a voice you remember, even now. It’s like the story is set in your room on a rainy night — or maybe a gothic library somewhere in Barcelona.      Right, I’ll start reading while your food simmers. It’s been a while since I had a quiet night in with a decent book. Just like, hearing your pans on the hob, and me engrossed in a story — it’s a perfect setup.

Right, so today in class we were reading a story about a knight who had to solve riddles to get into a castle. James asks me after, "Why don't they just use a password?" and I was like, well, honestly, he might not have had a spreadsheet to keep track of it. Got me thinking about how different the world is today for you two little tech whizzes.      A knight with a password? That's so funny, isn't it Evie?      Yeah, and you know what? They should have used a typewriter to write it down.      Oh, you've been listening to me talk about the old typewriters again, have you? My gran still has one in her cupboard! She says she used to type letters to the Post Office or something, and now I think Excel could have made her job ten times easier!      What's Excel?      Haha, it’s a program you use to plan lots of things—money, school projects, even birthday party details. It helps you add and subtract, and it can make charts—visual stuff that people like your dad can understand without falling asleep during meetings!      Sounds boring. I’d rather just play PlayStation. We built this massive castle with the Lego last night, and I was trying to programme the robot knight to say the Brownie Promise when you press a button. But the codes kept glitching, and it just kept saying “Be nice to girls.”      It did not! I definitely told it to say “Be loyal and true”!      Oh no! Look at you two, trying to out-code each other. I think you picked the right bedtime topic tonight—games and Lego and what you found out at your Brownie meeting! I’m so proud of how you both came up with that whole Burglar Alarm Idea for guest speaker night. I know you were up at 10pm testing it with the wooden spoons and the torch!      Yeah, the light sensor was over-sensitive. Spoon 3 set it off with his breath! It was hilarious.      I think you set it off more with your snack! The Smarties must go in a separate room next time.      Well, bedtime is almost here. Story time, then? Want to try to retell the knight and the riddle to your brother? Maybe we’ll mix in your Lego castle and the new password to get into it.

Rather do I abandon me slippers for a swanky pair o’ shoes, dontcha think? These puggles and my wellies are makin’ more sense than me trousers anyway.      Aye, we do spread the word that we live in a dip in the road. Got eeny mess o’ slippers runner tris and spots on me socks. Almost as messy as the kitchen table. A lot o’ jam and more stubby fingers, I’d say.      Well, we might be having a slap-up breakfast served in elevenses pot likker style. Get the spread out of habit mostly. Last remnants o’ ANON's fridge supply still hanging in there like stubborn posh turkey.      Speaking o’ ANON, I heard the house is set for sale. Anyone sad about it? Me ‘Oildom’ neighbour’s cat would have been breakfast, no doubt. But this happened. They bought some derelict spot, planting fruit and root hides, you know, near a village that went to die since plague days—village with a name like Witchergate or Boggerton.      Could be grief. ANON always fancying a life on a fruit farm, trotting about with a humble bunch o’ herb – rocket, coriander, stuff like that – slap in a huge field. More somethin’ to grow than sprout. If I weren’t stuck with roadworks on the motorway, I'd visit. That is, if me car didn't consider the A1 trunk road a point-to-point drag strip.      Any tea? Can’t drink coffee with those desert tales o’ Appleby and medesham villages. I prefer the touch of my cups and the vibes from a pot of boiled. Going old doesn’t mean I need to handle the unboiled bits to the brim.      Aye, I did cut me hand on me new toaster. Unread any manual, I relied solely on yesterday’s jam schematics. Ended up stickin’ thumb as tight as a cherry. Even worse, me phone’s delivered a flood of junk mail. Now I can’t reach far for sugar, junk bills shoot up like weeds.      I pond life about that. If I was building a new house line in, I’d include a separate conduit box for postman’s poison. Me mobile’s latest sum-up o’ lives feels more like a roles in potholes with broken pipes and bellyache from toffee slots. But that is overkill, anyway.      S’all so busy I forget to feel old. Again, mornings like this, sittin’ in Bradford backs, coatless and slipping, and the conversation’s flaked into jest and before no time, we’ll be off to freshen up those sandals on the tips and tea on.

Rather annoying I had to take my paracetamol earlier. My back's playing up again since that first snow last weekend. Never thought I'd miss the rain after a bit of sunshine, but here we are!      I know, I saw the weather on my phone—it’s gonna get worse on Tuesday. Hope you’ve got the heating on, Mummy?      Oh, I’ve got the oil one blasting! Got that from my nan, bless her. Still works as well as it did. We’ve been lucky she left so much good stuff when she passed.      Right, I’ve just taken the beef out the oven, and the spuds are likeminutes from needing boiling. Smells good enough to make you forget the cold, doesn't it, luv?      Easier to forget the cold when your tummy’s about to be full! Wait, did you remember to buy brussels sprouts? I promised Jo she could cook them roasted with balsamic, didn’t I?      Yeah, that’s right! She texted me on Facebook saying she’d send the recipe if we needed it. We still got a few sprouts in the garden from last year—Elizabeth grabbed them when it started to freeze.      Mate, I got the sprouts and some scallops for tonight. Thought we could have a little Christmas in January feel? Silly really, it’s only the 12th, but it feels like it in here!      That sounds good to me. I do miss going out for the real lot mind. What with work being what it is—I’ve had to cancel a few trips abroad.      I know what you mean! I’m waiting on an email from a client in Spain. Going there would be brilliant, but I haven't managed to book my own holiday since graduating. Work first, holidays later!      Well, when you do go, I’ll expect any stories you can share. I always wanted to go when I was your age. As a nurse, I’m always doing work trips, but they're not holiday material.      We should all do a proper trip after Christmas. Elizabeth, you can pick the place. You're the youngest and know more about social media and what's "on trend."      Who, me? You sure? I’m more of a copywriter than a tour planner!      Well start with something simple—like directions to your dad’s place in Ashford over New Year’s.

So, I heard you've been living in London for a few months now? How's it treating you? I remember the first time I came here for uni, I got lost in King's Cross for about an hour.      Haha, that sounds so familiar. I actually haven’t been lost yet, but I  am  still figuring out the best routes to get places without dying on the Tube. I’ve only moved here halfway through the academic year, so it’s been a bit of a whirlwind. Still, it’s amazing to be here for this postgrad course, don’t you think?      Totally. I mean, London’s a bit of a beast, but you do get used to it. I still live here part-time—you know, I work from home a couple of days a week as a copywriter and I do some remote client meetings. It’s not as intense as working full-on in the office every day.      That sounds like a dream, being able to work flexibly, even if it's still in the publishing world. I’ve been doing part-time survey programming—personally, it's less glamorous than it sounds, but it pays the bills and gives me something to do between lectures. Still, I’ve been scraping by on toast and humble takeaways most nights.      I know the feeling. I swear I’ve lived on pasta and flat white coffee for longer than I care to admit. Although, I’ve been meaning to cook more. Family’s starting to give me the “you’re not a teenager anymore” treatment. I had a proper roast last week—peppered in the way only mums can be.      Ooh, I about had that conversation with my dad last weekend. He still can’t quite fathom why I’m doing this postgrad instead of heading straight into a proper job. I mean, I understand the pressure, but for me, it’s about taking my time and figuring out what I really want to do. It’s not just about money.      I get that. My brother just started at a big marketing agency as well, and he’s the 'responsible' one while I do copywriting and creative work. Still, I’m happy with it. I think the key is not wasting too much time chasing someone else's idea of success.      Absolutely. I suppose it helps that we’re both in our 20s and still have the luxury of learning as we go.

Rather annoying isn't it, how hard it is to find time to get any proper exercise these days? With all the deadlines and transcription work I’ve got piling up. I swear, I haven’t had a proper walk in weeks.      Honestly, I wouldn't know where to start with exercise! I spend most of my time either twitching about on the computer or wrestling with self-doubt while writing. But I think I  ought  to at least be going for a run now and then.      I take mine when I chase the dog round the garden. You'd think he was intent on chewing up half the garden before I manage to clip him back on the lead. It’s not what you'd call a structured routine, though.      You should at least consider a proper push, I think. A little discipline goes a long way. My hips are killing me from too much sitting these days.      Oh don’t remind me of your desktop hides, you poor soul. Have you been taking breaks at least? Because I know I haven’t, and it is doing nothing for my posture. Anyway, speaking of which, how's the house hunt going for you two?      We've been out looking round places. Nothing at the moment though. The prices are absolutely ridiculous, aren’t they? It’s like every decent flat in London has already been snapped up by someone with three times our income!      I know what you mean. I saw a listing the other day for just outside the Zone 2—looked lovely, but at the price, I might as well rent a museum! We’ve been thinking of moving further out, but then the travel time becomes a real problem.      Honestly, you could write a tragedy about the current housing market. People are being priced out of their own lives, quite frankly. I’ve got friends in my age group who are still renting at 60. Unbelievable. Do either of you cook anything other than toast or macaroni cheese these days?      Macaroni cheese with a twist! I’ve tried to do various pasta sauces, but honestly, after a long day with headsets on, the idea of goosing up my routine is about as appealing as a monsoon in Salford in July.      I can relate. I tend to raid the freezer at 8pm and call it a night.

Rather a nice day for a wander through the Gardens, ain't it?      Oh, yeah, it's one of those days where the weather decides it wants to be decent. Thought I'd make a day of it after finally getting some time off work. How about you?      Same, really. Just got back from a bit of a dusty week in the library sorting a corpus—a transcription project for Early Northumbrian dialect stuff. Still, easier than drilling into concrete, I 'spose!      Haha, considerably, yeah. Still working on that site in Huntingdon, even since the new budget came through, we’ve been told to slow down on the expansion plans.      Oh, the Budget, right. I heard the news about the infrastructure cuts, but thought I'd be the government playing with housing again, not the roads.      Yeah, this time it's a bit of both. They’s pulling back from some of the green building incentives for the moment, which is driving me mad, really. I mean, if we had better funding, we'd be using more recycled materials and not just sticking to the old ways.      Sounds like the usual trot through the same problems. You ever think about moving?      Nah, I mean, I've got my mum and her flat in Pembury, and the whole German side of the family back in Berlin. But, no, I like it here in Kent. Although I do miss my Berlin uni days, you know. Funny thing—job as a civil engineer and still can’t sing a note in tune.      You and me both. I'm worse at it! But the other week my cousin dragged me to see "Hamilton" and I nearly cried—I was like, "This is it, this is my soul’s calling, I realized I was hiding from musicals my whole life!"      No way! You? Crying at a musical? That's new. You must've been deep.      I know, right? It were weird. I walked out whistling “My Shot” all the way home, even though I’m like 30 years away from that kind of audacity if I ever had it. But it made me think how, yeah, I might be crunching data by day, but your soul still needs to be fed sometimes.      Fair enough. Maybe I should’ve grabbed that ticket from you. Just been watching too many over-engineered spreadsheets and not enough theatre.      You’d like it, honestly.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh, Tony? Thought we’d get a bit of a break ‘fore pittin’ on with this job. Still, more time to chat, I suppose. How’s the old cab business? Not too many tourists this time o’ year?      Aye, it’s been a bit dry lately, if you’ll excuse the pun. Lotta rain, not a lot o’ custom. Some days I barely fill the tank, so I’ve been doin’ a bit o’ handiwork round me place and this when I can get the chance. You know I can’t sit idle like you, eh, Mark?      Aye, well, I like a bit o’ stimulation, that’s for sure. Can’t spend all day talkin’ about Chaucer and Austen and not get me hands dirty once in a while. This old place o’ mine, though—could do with a bit more sprucing up. Me gutter’s cracked again, and that’s the third time this year.      That’s a bodge job, if I know anything about gutters. I can sort that out for you if you’re up for it, for a fiver. Me and me nephew, we’ve been doin’ a few jobs round the block. Bring in a bit extra cash, you know?      Would ye? That’d be grand. Silly me, I could try and do it meself, but I’ve got enough to worry about with lecturers’ meetings and marking essays. Ever been to a school open day? A nightmare.      Aye, heard enough about education from me niece’s primary teacher. I daresay you’d have given her the talking to she needed. Still, I like what you said earlier about acting and films. I’ve always fancied a bit o’ that. My sister’s got a mate in Liverpool who’s in the film biz. Ever think o’ auditioning?      I once had a go at it for a bit, back in Manchester. Got as far as a stage play at the Royal Exchange. Course, I’m more of a supporting role type, not no leading man. But I find it interesting. I sometimes get my students goin’ on about their dream roles or wanting to go into film.      That’s a good lark, storytelling films and whatnot. Reckon I’d like watchin’ more, though I’ve got my hours to drive. Tell me, do you like the older pictures or the blockbusters?

Rather lovely this stretch, isn't it? That little village back there with the red-roofed farm—what was the name of it again?      Not sure, probably one of those tiny Polish places that only appear on maps as a cluster of dots! But yes, the scenery’s been pretty peaceful all the way out of Białka. Not as dramatic as the mountains, mind you, but it’s got that quiet charm.      I must say, this is one of the cheaper trips I’ve had in terms of transport. The campervan’s a bit of a glorified car, but at least it saves me from campsite fees. Though goodness knows the fridge’s only holding up on bits of fate at this point.      Yeah, it’s economical by comparison to flights back home, at least. And I think the food budget’s holding up okay too—so long as we aren’t fancy-dancy about what we eat. Honestly, I’m just looking for any Polish pierogi these days, even if they are the frozen kind!      Oh, I do like the pierogi, though I’ve still got that hesitation with anything bearing mushrooms. But enough grief—I must say, I’m enjoying this slower pace. Doesn’t feel quite like when I used to holiday with the kids about. All planned to the last minute, swamped with friends, and the like.      Yeah, I find I’m enjoying the solitude a bit more. Travelling alone is different. Takes some getting used to. But not everyone wants a chaotic crew around when you’re trying to think about the next step in life, you know?      Absolutely. Clutter’s not just in your home, is it? Minds can be just as full of old stuff you need to clear out. I’ve been giving that some thought—maybe staying on the road a while more to do just that. No burden of bills, no rent, no clutter.      Sounds like it’s working for you. I mean, I tried something similar for a few months before I started my TEFL course. Though being academically-trailed with lunches of sandwiches and coffee from bognor regis is no picnic either.      Bognor Regis? I bet it had its own charm! Not everyone drifts through hitchhiking stops in the Tatra Mountains. Although I did pick up a hitchhiker near Zakopane—somewhat fluently asked why I was going to Tarnów with a strange sense of urgency.

‘Mum, am I goin’ to get lost on me way to her nan’s ‘ouse if I got to go to Preston by m’self yet? I’ve asked loads ‘o times but I never propper remember it.’      ‘Lottie, you’ll be fine. I’ve shown you a few times on the map and you know if you use the sat nav on your phone you should be alright. An’ if in doubt, ring me. Oh, and don’t go near that road near the old train station, the engineers keep messin’ about wi’ it. Had to fetch my boss from a lay-by last week ‘cuz he got stuck out there.’      My voice came in over the crackle of the car radio. ‘Aye, I know what you mean, Laura. I used to work round that area an’ it’s a nightmare at the best o’ times. You need to take the A6 off the coast road and then you’ll pick up the shopping centre on your left. There’s the usual traffic, mind, but you’ll know when you get there, it’s not really subtle.’      ‘Right, so off the St Annes Road, turn left, then it’s straight on then right again? And then Preston – Mate, I got a test in like, two days, an’ I’ve barely revised. It’s that History one ‘bout the Empire and all ‘at jazz. I swear, they should just give someone who knows nothin’ abeout it an A just to be nice sometimes.’      ‘Oh, you’ll get it through. You did all right last time, didn’t you? I mean, I know it’s not quite the Hay Festival of your dreams but it’s a start. Oh! Did you hear that they’re having the writer of that new superhero book there next month, ‘Atom Ace’? My sister’s been going since she was your age.’      ‘That’s a grand idea, but I don’t understand half them fancy words. Me and queens and that. Let’s not go there. I’ve no need to learn whisht happened in the 50s or somethin’. Enough to feed the kids an’ go to the shop without gettin’ confused by them supermarket promotions, innit?’      ‘Haha, gran, I’ve seen some of them. It’s like flu or somethin’. Everything’s out o’ stock, or half price, or both. Is it ‘cause o’ the strikes again or what?

Rather annoying this newfit lot o’ toys, Christopher. I tried to email Peggy last week ‘n couldn’t get the thing to work nohow. It just blinked at me like it was jest having a laugh.      Naa, Gran, it’s easy, really. Just tap the screen een time an’ select the app. It’s like Pokémon on the phone. Almost as easy.      Some days I wonder if I’m the one backward one, not you two. Christopher taught me to use the mobile when the class started, but the new model came out... like three times already. I’m still using the same charger from the last one.      It’s a good job I’ve you lot to tide me through this madness! I’m clearing the attic out next week, and I think I found your uncle’s old cricket bat and a box of VHS tapes, Christopher. You need to see some of the videos in there — his first stag do looked like a comedy, even back then.      What’s a VHS? Naa, don’t tell me, it’s one of them old telly things from before Sky and Netflix?      Aye, it’s proper ancient, lad. You got to put the tape in and wait ages for the programmes, and sometimes it wouldn’t even play if the weather was too damp!      Clearing the attic will be a job, though. I helped your gran last time and found a filing cabinet full of letters and receipts from thirty years ago — made for the most interesting bedtime reading!      That’s where I saw those letters from when your granddad was at university. I think you’d find it interesting, Christopher. It was a whole different world back then — no technology to plug into, and if someone didn’t write back to you within a fortnight, you thought they were dead!      Gran, you used to say you sent him a Christmas card once with a stone inside it for waiting till January!      Oh ho, well, I did not! He’d written a complete whopper of a poem, and I just wanted to set him straight — with a bit o’ flair!      It wasn’t all antiques and poetry, though. I remember how hard it was to cope with the loneliness when gran lost her husband. It was like the house just... emptied.      It did feel diferrent, love. I had nobody to talk to fer weeks at a time, and that’s when the thoughts... they start to creep in.

Right, lads, here we go — I’ve just bought this brand new laptop, and I thought I’d got the lot, but no luck. It won’t connect to Wi-Fi or charge properly. You’re both technically minded, so I thought you could take a look for me.      Right, let me take a look. So, first off, have you tried all the basic stuff? Like checking the power cable, or resetting the network settings?      Yeah, I’ve done the obvious — no luck. Tried booting it in safe mode too. Still nothing. It’s like it’s dead even when it’s supposedly on.      That sounds dodgy. Did you buy it from a proper place? I got mine off one of them bargain sites and had to return it after a week. Battery lights up for a minute and then it’s off.      Bucks Electronic Store in town. They said it was brand new. I even got it desktop delivered, thinking maybe the delivery got it bashed.      Let me plug mine into the same socket and see if it works there — just to rule out power issues. And then we’ll check the Wi-Fi on both devices to see if it’s a network issue.      Speaking of power, I still use that old laptop I got back in sixth form — don’t even know what it runs on. Still uses Windows 7!      Haha, yeah, my grandad still uses a Commodore 64 oddly. He says it’s faster than this lot.      Okay, so mine’s working in the socket, so it’s probably the laptop. Let’s try a software reset. Reinstall the drivers first. I’ve got a bootable USB that I use for these things.      That be awesome. I’ve just been watching YouTube videos trying to fix it. Banging my head off the wall.      Same with fixing bikes. I watched hours of videos on YouTube to fix my bike. Took me 3 weeks to figure out how to fix the chain with just the spanner and a screwdriver.      Sometimes it's good to see go-to tutorials on stuff, if you've got patience. But personally, I just chuck in a new part. Quick fix, long-term pain.      I’m not big on patience. Thought this laptop would be my cheap fix, but maybe not. If this still doesn’t work, I might be down the shop again.

Rather lovely place, isn't it? You know, for a brand-new bistro in Tarnow. I haven’t been here often enough to be snobby about it, but I've got to say, this is a cut above the usual chains you find in places like this.      Oh, I agree! I’ve been here a couple of times already and it just feels like… well, a proper place to sit, think, and talk. I mean, it's not just the food, which is actually pretty good—though the pierogi here might just chase the ones in Zielona Góra off the throne.      Haha, now there's a debate only another Pole would understand. But what’s on your mind, love? You left your last sentence hanging more than the chandeliers in here, if you don’t mind me saying.      Oh, it's nothing. Just—well, I've been thinking a lot about… you know, dreams. And not in the, you know, kind of starry-eyed way. I mean, like, the dream of who we are, or who we want to be. Sometimes it leaves as quick as it came. Kind of like how we go in and out of addiction, or rhythm in our lives.      Mate, you got a gift, you really do. You say something like that and you pin me right to my chair. I've been wandering through my own dreams for years, like they're just a someone else's coat I forgot to return. You know? It's one thing to dream, but it's another to find your legs and start running with it.      Yeah, that's it exactly. It's about identity, isn’t it? And the courage to keep fumbling forward even when you stumble. I know that better than I’d like to. These days, I try not to chain myself to the past. My friends, my work, they all help. I'm trying to stay fit too. It's surprising how working out clears your mind.      I envy you that. I used to run, but now it's lunches like this and long afternoons with tea and a book. Still, I’m around. Popping into the shops, chatting up the owner on the corner about the best tomatoes or sourcing odd spices.      And you're always the one blooming in the gray. It’s inspiring. I have to say, I’ve never known someone who could turn hours of sitting into periods of deep thinking—and still come back with poetry.

Rather skip the queue and just get us online tickets for the Dorset Steam Fair, then we can save a few quid and not hang about in the heat. D'you need help with the ticket site, Dad?      No, I got me Grandson sorted me out with a tablet and eeny weeny fonts, but the print on 'ere is still too dusty for me old bones. I reckon I'd prefer to save me money and go somewhere I can sit easier instead.      Oh, now don't be like that, love. The disabled facilities are brilliant these days – specially at fairs like that. Mary just made sure I got a wheelchair and a supply of wet wipes for the hot day last Saturday, bless her.      It’s rally well done, actually. You can even hire pushchairs in the parking lot now if you're coming by car and forget yours. I brought mine even though I've got no kids... for no reason at all, really!      Ah, spare the blushes. You just fancied walking around with one and pretending you're being proper responsible. Cheeky rascal!      Well, I did, didn’t I? But anyway, we can circle back to silliness after we decide if we wanna come?      Listen – I know the tickets are a bit of a hit on the wallet these days, what with property prices up the wazoo in Bournemouth, and all. But someone said there are free viewing areas near the entrance for a rush of steam.      Free viewing is a fine idea if you want a view and no fun. I’d sooner spend the dosh and about enjoy me kettle walk properly. I remember the good old days when this place was just a patch of fields! Proper fields with cows and everything!      Maybe we’re all just a bit over the top about prices. Dad, passed me your phone – I’ll just sort the tickets before they sell out. We can get two adult, one concession and one chair access?      Oh, and don't forget to add the 'accessible route' message to the ticket notes – it helps the ticket seller know where to direct you.      D’you need snacks or drinks added or does everyone wanna bring their own? I’ve got no issue with a sarnie and cuppa.      So long as it’s not a dodgy Hazelnut muffin like last time I had from that cafe!

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh, love? Thought we’d get a bit of a break ‘ere. I got the seats all out for the visit today, and I’ve had to wrestle with a bunch of hangers full of coats and wet umbrellas.      Aye, it’s been a proper drizzle all week. Not the sort of weather for dusty bookshelves and clean carpets. I hope yer not too put out, Jean. I’ve brought the kids over with me, and they tend to track in the mud like the hares that chase through the garden.      Is it true you’re moving soon, Grans? Mum said something about a small flat in York and that you’re selling the old house in Kendal. Is it cos you don’t want to look after the garden anymore?      Aye, lad, I’m about to downsize. Not cos I can’t tend the garden—though my legs aren’t what they used to be—but it’s just not practical anymore. I’ve got a nephew lending me a hand with the move, and Mr Wilkinson—my old vicar—has written me two or three letters about whether I should move to be near church more often.      You remember Mr Wilkinson, Jean? Man had a personality the size of a bale of hay and twice as awkward. Good man, though. Would’ve had a heart attack if you started listening to his sermons online.      Precisely. I miss the routine of church services. But unfortunately, they’ve started streaming it on some app, and the buttons are too small for these old fingers!      Technology’s a bugger at times, isn’t it? My students are always texting in the hall, but mind ye, I’ve switched my Twitter off because half the school followed me and it got a bit too much to handle.      I’ve got 12 followers, but that’s only me mates. I used to tweet ‘at times', cos I dunno what else to say. My favourite is to post pictures of my art GCSE work and wait for the likes to add up.      Arts, eh? Still remember delivering newspapers around Darlington back in the '60s and seeing the pond life from the bus window. Art appreciated in those days was in the countryside, not on a screen, I can tell ye.      I’ve been doing some writing on the side, mind ye.

Rather annoyingly, I've got to take both of you to the dentist this week—the schedule they sent couldn't be clearer. James has his check-up on Wednesday and I assume you, Sophie, want me to take you at the same time?      Yeah, please. But it was my tooth on Tuesday that went wobbly last night, so maybe I can go earlier?      That might be complicating things. I've also got a hearing test booked for Thursday. It's not as if you haven't heard the buzzer for breakfast most mornings when it's still miles away.      That's mostly because you play that Minecraft music at the volume of an aeroplane taking off.      James! The ear test’s a health checkup, not a competition.      I think Ashaad might be coming with us for his hearing test too. His breakfasts are mostly cereal and sugar, so no shortage of alertness at his house.      Actually, speaking of Ashaad—his birthday is the same day as his sister’s, which is always a mad rush. I might ask if we can host both their birthday parties at the same time. Have you thought of something to bring? You remember last year when we got those Monet-style cupcakes?      Yeah, those swan ones! But I thought his family prefers apple pie to cupcakes?      Right, we’ll bring that. James, what's going on at your school for the Easter school trip? I heard they might be going to a farm—radishes, specifically.      Ugh, no vegetables again! We did potatoes last term and I about cried at seeing the smelliest radish the world has seen.      Well, your Maths teacher is doing data collection and they’re counting how long each radish grows. My, you are quite the budding statistician.      Can I have my Easter chocolate then before we talk about vegetables?      Only if you promise me your best effort to clear your plate. Though I’ve seen your grandpa with lunches that looked like they tried to do the heist of the condiment station.      That man could derail a go-kart on pond life if you hand him a sauce.      Right, that’s enough. Who remembers last Time we went to your Grandma’s and we all had that flu? 30% of us had high fevers, two had bellyache trips to the farm and one, unfortunately, was bedridden.      That’s bleak! I remember needing cold compresses while watching My chemical romance videos on YouTube.

Rather skip the queue at the café, I've rustled up a few snacks. Felt like a bit of a domestic goddess today, honestly. Nothing like a good scone with jam and a cup of proper tea to knock the cobwebs out. Look at this—some fresh scones from the oven and a bit of clotted cream we bought on the way back from the market last week.      Oh, love, this smells brilliant! Honestly, I’ve had so much takeaways lately, I think it’s nice to have something decent. You always know how to look after me. You know what I like to add on top, don’t you?      Of course, raspberry jam and clotted cream, no messing. Still love it though. Remember when we used to go to the café in Dorking and used to make a game out of who could make the messiest scone first?      Oh lord yes! Mum always used to throw a hissy fit about it when we got back to the hotel. Still, we were kids, right? I mean, it was the 90s, nothing too bad. Anyway, thanks for this. I’ve had the most hectic week. Work’s going mental—it always does before the financial quarter starts. You known what it’s like?      Yeah, I know the drill. Honestly, the only thing keeping me sane these days is the dog. If I weren’t doing this every Thursday, I wouldn’t even know someone was in the house. Let me tell you, Walker is absolute chaos when left on his own for too long. Chews the leg off the sofa, spills wine all over the floor, and stares at me like I’m his personal trainer.      Sounds typical. I had to leave my house for a weekend once because I was losing it with the cat. You know, I still have that photo of us dressed up like zombies at Dad’s garden party, with that cat wearing a bowtie. Unforgettable. What about you, how’s work?      Honestly? Not bad. Just had that agency propose doing a brand revamp with this tech client. They’re based in Manchester, but it’s exciting for once. You know I’m sick of the usual domestic stuff. Though I do miss designing about food or interiors every so often—it made me feel grounded, you know?      Well, if what your career is going to be is planning big corporate makeovers, then I think I’m going to need to invest in new life insurance policy.

Rather do a long cycle ride as a child, I remember going from Almondsbury to Bristol with my uncle when I was about eleven or so. He said it would do me good, and I’d have a “proper sense of achievement” when I got back. By the time we reached the top of Coombe Hill, my legs were spinning like wheels on a bus!      Oh, I remember that hill all too well! I used to cycle past it every Sunday with my father as a boy. We lived in Ramsgate, so it's quite a distance, but the Middlesbrough Flat was far more of a beast. Those early years riding with no seat, no reflectors, no lights... It was a gritty affair. Still, best to think of the glory of reaching the top.      Qualitatively speaking, the hills up here in Manchester were far harder. Sod’s breakfast, no doubt about it. But perhaps not quite as rugged as a career in dentistry?      You have no idea! As a newly minted dentist in the 1980s, I got all sorts of perks with the NHS. I was once invited to a sailing trip by a patient—absolute nonsense, of course, but it was all compliments. “Lectures at sea with your Royal College chap, and dinner beneath the starry sky.” One time, the tide came in and washed the whole marina up. Ended up with a room full of dentists in pyjamas in an upturned yachting boat.      Oh, now  that’s  an anecdote worth retelling. But what about now, Jim? We’ve been talking about a jive event at Steve’s converted barn. I do believe the hall is finally back in use.      Definitely. Andy’s converted the old Carter barn near the lake. It’s just been restored with acoustic boards and proper guest toilets. Plans are afoot for themed nights—60s, 70s, and maybe even a rare 1950s one. We had a planning vote last night. The solar panels proposal? Passed by a narrow margin, I must admit.      Marvelous news. Rebranding our little town has been in the works for years. I’ve seen it drift into disrepair—factories closing, no shops, and then the council blokes coming through with these soulless facades. If only we’d had conservation guidelines like they do in France. I know a chap who bought a cottage by simply waving in the village square—called the notaire and said, “I’ll have the one near the mairie,” and that was it.

So do you reckon an online learning platform focused specifically on rural education would work? I mean, with so much reliance on the internet these days, there’s definitely a gap we could fill, especially after everything with the lockdowns.      That's a solid angle. People like us who’ve worked in or around education know exactly what’s missing out there. Schools in smaller towns often lack the resources they need. Online case studies and multimedia learning would be so valuable if designed right. But how are we going to market it?      I was thinking about using social media, but with a twist. Not just generic content—maybe short-form videos—those mini case studies we’ve been talking about. You know, like how MyGradeMaths does it with mini tutorials. The idea is to make learning bites digestible and relatable, especially for secondary school teachers and parents.      Yeah, but how do we make sure the content is actually useful and not just another shiny distraction? People’s attention spans are short, especially on platforms like TikTok or YouTube. We need to back it up with proper educational frameworks, maybe even PDHPE—Professional Development for teachers. Like a Continuing Professional Development credit angle?      Exactly. If we can partner with local education authorities, even just one per state at first, we could get the ball rolling. And it doesn’t have to be big. Start with maybe a few model case studies—let’s say film-based case studies on critical social principles—like conflict resolution, climate change in rural areas, maybe even mental health? It could be oddly therapeutic for some students.      That’s interesting. Mental health in schools is huge right now. But how do we ensure we’re actually reaching the teachers? I can vouch for that side of things. Maybe a free sample unit as part of an e-mail newsletter? Send it out once a month to educators. Let them see for themselves the kind of stuff we can offer.      Love that. And if we build a nice brand around it—“Mindspark Education”—something that suggests a spark of inspiration, learning that lights up. Websites and socials with that kind of vibe. You could do the content creation, I’d handle the tech and logistics.      Yeah, go on then. But let’s make sure there’s real substance in those case studies. I’m thinking documentaries, behind-the-scenes footage—educational, but also visually engaging.

Rather lovely to be out here, isn’t it? The sea’s promising to clear up tomorrow if the weather holds.      Yes, it’s peaceful. I’ve missed this. A proper walk by the coast. Not running late or punctual for anything at all.      Got a bit of that  post-lecture  twitch, didn’t you this morning? You were scribbling in that coffee shop by 7:30.      I was half-dead, to be honest. Kept me up for hours last night when Alice called.      Oh, how is she?      All right. Still in Brighton, working on that Masters in marine conservation. She said Marco’s still eccentric.      I’m not surprised. D’you remember when I met them the first time—Marco in his dress boots and Alice trying not to laugh?      He still insists on walking barefoot on the sand, as if that’s some deep ecological statement. And then he chucked his pyjamas in the sea.      Oh, he always had flair, even if it was a bit  ecowhatever .      Doesn’t bother me. He’s got passion. Passion counts for something. I often wonder if Alice still needs that support.      She does. All that bureaucracy and funding nonsense. If she weren’t so driven, I’d say she should give up. But she keeps going—despite everything.      I envie her ambition, in a way. After a while, all these lectures and essays… it  can  feel endless, can’t it?      Don’t know. I’m watching mine finish first year and they’re all very fired up. Not like when I was their age. At least they’re not just rebelling for the sake of it.      Parents were just worried about us turning into hippies. ‘Rebellious’ is just a word for waiting till 3 a.m. to study.      Ah, yes. 'Civilised youth,' that’s the phrase I love. My parents still remember delivering newspapers around this coast. I sometimes think I should go back to delivering them myself if this academic life ever hits rock bottom.      Hopefully it won’t come to that. You’ve already had some of the latest grant news, I suppose.      I did. It’s never straightforward, is it? Still, we carry on.      Exactly. We carry on. Like Marco and all his pyjamas. At least he knew what he wanted.      And now we’re walking by the sea, not throwing pyjamas, but at least wondering about what we’ll throw next.

Rather annoying this new season’s trends, innit? Seems like everything looks like it's been designed in a bin liddit!      Blimey, I've been over this with my flatmate. She only wants to wear those kind of low-rise jeans now—Deffo not een inveseement, more like a one-off purchase.      Yeah, don’t get me started on fast fashion. I tried this eco brand last week; it was alright, but twice as expensive. Know what I was doing instead of wearing new clothes? Teaching the kids how to make patchwork bags to reuse old fabric!      That's real supply-side thinking, innit? It’s a good idea, but you still get left with nothin’ new to wear if you’re not careful! I used to shop at the same place—Doncaster, you’ve got to have character when it comes to shopping. Now it’s like H&M in every high street, you know?      I mean, I still like to dress nicely, but I feel like it's a constant cycle of buying and regretting it two weeks later. I’ve taken to choosing only neutral pieces that I can mix in and out. Doesn’t feel quite as guilty.      Mate, I got a real shout-out from one of my students today because the pattern on my jumper matched their craft project. Silly little things, innit? Still, if we carry on in this way, we're bound to influence the next generation to consider fashion not just flashy, but thoughtful—piece by piece, if you get my drift.      I hadn't looked at it quite like that. I mean, I don’t quite know where the line is between faddy and fashionable. Maybe I should start wearing that vintage scarf I've got. It does up decent-like to most things, ‘cos it’s like 20 years passed since it was active.      That's got potential! Vintage is always in, you know. I reckon your scarf could be the queens and kings of this year’s autumn look!      If we do ever do an event in Cambridge where we showcase sustainable fashion with our students, I'll be sure go talk to my uni crowd about getting some pieces for display. Education and empowerment all in one go, innit?      Proper proper, that’s what I’m talkin’ about. We should rally up some folks for that, maybe even make it a proper event.

So do you remember that time I got lost in Hastings old town and came home with like, ten awesome photos of those old cobblestone streets?      Oh yes, you nearly gave me a heart attack! But I have to admit, those photos turned out really well. You've got such an eye for detail now, more than even when you were younger.      Thanks! I’m thinking of applying for a photography course at college next year. They said it covers digital editing as well, which sounds exciting. I'm just worried I won’t be good enough, or that it's not what I like after all.      I get that. It’s scary choosing such a big step like that. But look, I’ve seen you grow up with a camera in your hands. You’re creative, focused, and very passionate. That’s more than most people have, at your age especially.      You always know just what to say. I think part of me is also scared of what my mates will think. Like, maybe college isn’t the ‘cool’ thing? Although, if I book the course, I’ll be in Hastings anyway, not as far as some places. Plus, it frees me from staying at home for the holidays!      You’re bound to see your mates at university fairly often, and college is really about trying new things. I remember applying for a job as a receptionist here because I thought ‘why not?’, and look where I am now. Life full of variety!      I wish I had that confidence when I was you. Also, have you seen the new stand-up from Paul Merton? I saw him at the Hastings festival last year and I laughed until I cried! He's such a legend, I think.      Yes, he’s got that calm, self-deprecating style that I adore. My laughers are usually the kind who tell observational jokes. I actually read his latest book too — the one about his time on the road. It’s funny, but also very thoughtful. Makes me crack up and sit and think about being 40-something with a camera bag and big dreams.      That's so true, I find comedians like that the best. Anyway, Maman, what do you do after work again? Not that I'm planning on interrupting anything important...      Oh, what your mother does after work is have tea, and perhaps help her clever daughter think out her next step, maybe even take photos of her to practice her skills for college!

Rather annoying this new application form they've sent us, isn't it?      Oh, I don’t know, Harold. At least it’s neater than the previous one. I’ve been doing mine all morning.      Neater, yes, but much too fiddly if you ask me. Boxes everywhere you can’t see if you’ve ticked them or not.      Fair dos, Harold. I’ve had enough trouble seeing what was in my coffee let alone a form.      Right, right, but what about the cockerel, Harold dear? Mary’s still dead set on chucking the fence, and that bird is beginning to come into our garden. I swear it watched me last week like it was judging my dinner.      Easier to chuck the bird than the fence in my opinion. Cats would have been breakfast, no doubt about that.      Oh don’t, you’ll make Mavis fidget even more than she already is. Good grief, I thought I was over it when the baby birds fell out of the nest last spring!      Did I tell you, by the way, that I’ve been using my 3D printer again? It's so much prettier than those new plastic shelves, and none of the shabby workmanship the shops have been selling these days.      Bless you, Mavis. What’d you make? A frame?      No, just a flower holder for the window. Mary’s been chucking out some of the houseplants and being ‘artsy’ again!      I did something like that after a bad night’s sleep. Printed a spoon because I couldn’t find one. Not very good, mind. Still barely holds the custard.      Well, for what it’s worth, I’d much rather sleep with that cockerel than the football racket going on at my nephew’s house. He’s been restricting himself to 3-4 games a night and that’s being generous.      I heard football was banned in half the town. Too many arguments and parking problems around matches.      Actually, I get most of the problems from the parents – shouting louder than the kids in the stands, if you can believe it.      Reckon I’m planning to go to his birthday though, mind.      You will? But you said it was going to be this mad ‘street football’ party.      I did, and they changed the plans. Now it’s potluck and a talent show. They’ve got someone in from the town hall doing the announcements.

Rather annoying this, having to bring my daughter over from Australia. I've had her on my mind so much lately, and I've been speaking to you because I thought I'd need someone like you by my side to make sense of it all.      It must be quite the logistical challenge. She's all the way over there, isn’t she? I know you’ve kept in touch, of course. She always was a good communicator—much more so than I ever was in my school records.      Oh yes, she's quite the chatterbox. But, don't forget, I was a teacher, dear. Still, it's not like I've got the energy I once had. I've made a few calls, sorted the visa—a standard process for family reunion, they assured me. But I'm not getting any younger and I do fret about how I'm managing it all by myself.      Well, if I may say, you've taken on more than a teacher would ever advise! No, you didn’t spare the effort, and I'm proud of that—after all, she's your child, and it's the right thing to do. What about childcare once she's here?      Her mother is not involved, and it’s only the two of us. My partner passed away a while ago, and I've been on my own these years. I have some family in Scotland, but they don't know what to make of everything anymore.      I understand. It must be overwhelming. And you know, I'm here for you. I can help you make the arrangements—pick up the child from the airport perhaps, or even house-sit when you need a bit of space. I know I'm not quite the reliable one you had in mind, but I'm willing and not entirely useless when it comes to organizing things.      That’s very kind of you. I've always appreciated your ability to keep your head on straight, even when the world is going mad. Do you think there’s a way you can accompany me on the trip to collect her?      I’d like that. Family is a rare and precious thing. I do miss our daughter's sister sometimes, even though she made her own life in the north. But really, your life matters more. If I can give you some peace of mind, I’m happy to be of use.

Rather annoying to be honest, the Scottish referendum. I mean, talk about a distraction in the middle of preparing for semester exams and job interviews. You would think more people could focus on their actual livelihoods than a political show.      Look, I get it — you’re busy with your lectures and I'm dealing with my own paperwork. But you can't blame people for wanting to decide their own future. I’ve taught in Brighton for nearly forty years now and I’ve seen plenty of political changes come through.      Maybe, but the timing doesn't help when people like me are trying to hold interviews for part-time lecturers who can actually fill our gaps. I had a colleague only last week stressed about whether their kids’s university grants would be affected. My own daughter is off to uni this autumn and I’m already dreading the thought of what tuition fees might be if independence goes ahead.      I see your point. Look, while everyone’s obsessed with politics, don’t forget you’ve got an interview on Monday — the one at the University of Sussex. I told that new assistant over the coffee, yes, we’d be supporting you. I think we all appreciate that kind of ambition and experience.      Thanks, John. I really appreciate it. It’s just one of those things – trying to balance everything. I wouldn’t mind it if the political noise was just a bit less. But to be honest, I haven’t been this nervous about an interview since the first one I had out of university. That felt like yesterday.      You did well back then. Some of us are lucky enough to have experienced that and still be standing. I remember when your colleague, Neil, applied for promotion last year. That was a stressful round of talking points and presentation skills. But he made it through and now he’s doing better work than before.      True, and I wish I could be as composed as he was under pressure. Still, I think I’ve got a solid CV and something fresh to offer. At least Brighton knows how to appreciate good lecturing material. As long as I can keep explaining clearly what I want to do with the students and the university’s values, I think I’ll be okay.      That’s the spirit. And go easy on the jargon if you can — not everyone appreciated it when I tried to go all academic at my last staff meeting.

Rather annoying when the box won't shut properly, isn't it? I've made it worse since I first saw one in my father's shed when I was a child. This one's got a spring that's slightly out of kilter.      It's been like that with most kits I've ever bought.
