I remember once trying one for my son when he was fascinated with all things mechanical — a mousetrap car, if you will — and I spent an hour under a table just to get the axle right.      Honestly, I don't get the obsession with mousetraps. It's like trying to fix a toaster with a cookbook. What’s the point?      It’s fun! I did one once for a school project. We put skewers and wheels on them, and then I made it race down a ramp with everyone shouting about collisions and physics. It was, like, epic.      Exactly! That was the idea. I remember we used to have them for school projects in the 80s. You learn practical skills, problem-solving — all that.      Aha! But let's not forget the American stories. My cousin went out there for a year and came back swearing all the children had mousetrap rocket cars in their playgrounds, and none of the teachers blinked an eye.      That’s not true. If I had done that in London, the teachers would have called the Ministry of Education and my parents.      That's oddly British. We worry about something as simple as a mousetrap and they send their children out with chemicals to make volcanoes in the school garden.      I'll tell you what, I had a trip out to New York not long after university. I barely noticed the children, but the Americans mentioned to me how, ‘you lot just don’t seem to have much imagination about playthings’. They expected us all to be inventing things with pottery and woodworking.      I don't know, I think we’re just more cautious.      Cautious or traditional. I do wonder, though, if we are losing something. My library’s started a ‘Make It or Break It’ kids’ group — and it’s wildly popular.      You're just saying that because you're trying to get people to come in at the weekends.      Still, it's good to foster creativity. It's just a shame we don't embrace the American enthusiasm for ambitious, chaotic projects like that.

Rather annoyingly, I've bought us a whole bunch of new pyjamas.      What, another matching set? You've already got six sets!      I know, it's absurd. But they're so lovely—sort of bamboo things with a funny little frog on them.      Frog? Are they Chinese frogs or British frogs?      Chinese, but they look more like toads to be honest. The woman in the shop said it was good luck to have frogs in the house.      Chinese superstition... Right, because of course you'd believe that.      I don't know, they felt nice and light. I also bought you a couple of new shirts.      D'you pick them out in the dark? Half my shirts in the drawer look like they've been breakfasted on by something...      They're just a bit different from what you usually wear, that’s all. One is kind of a dusky blue—very grown-up, if you know what I mean—      What did it cost, grief?      It was on sale—and it looked quite good, from what I can see. You should wear it with the new trousers I bought you too.      Now don't go making me into some sort of fashion experiment again. Last time that happened, I spent a week dressing like a cricket.      That was just one jumper. And you looked hotter than the summer sun.      I looked like a walking jelly bean, thank you very much.      You look the same every day, though. White shirt, dark trousers—that fails to excite me. I mean, it is a bit predictable.      And it certainly kills less than your experiments with floral patterns.      Those were for events, love.      You chose them.      I know. But I also always picked the lunches we had on our first date. Now do be a good sport and try the clothes on. We're in the middle of China go—least I could do was make our boring British clothing more continental.      You're making it sound like an invasion plan. Pass me the blue one at least. I might manage that.      Good, I’ll take that as a win. Oh, and I might be trying on the pyjamas while I’m at it—I feel like toads and evenings often go hand in hand.      Right, you're declaring yourself a toad again, are you?      Only until we find out if they really bring good luck. I mean, we could do with a bit on this overseas posting.

Rather good match today, wasn't it? That try in the last five minutes was cracker. The Munster lads are coming back from the dead more often than I'd like, sure!      Yeah, we watched it in school. It was on the big screen in the common room during lunch. I liked the lineout moves they did. I reckon if I had a rugby ball, I could do that too.      I’m sorry love but I watched a comedy instead. Rugby is just meanness in a field for me! But when Oisin wants to watch it, I usually sit down with him, just to be fair.      That’s very kind of you Myra, but I must say, it’s better on the pitch! I had the lads in for training this morning, and the lad from Tipperary is a pure brute with the ball.      Now Michael, please don't be hard on the lad. Everyone is better at something, even if it's not running into people. Speaking of which—did I forget to tell you both, I’m turning 71 in a fortnight.      That’s amazing, Grandma! I’ll write you a card. Do you want me to draw stars on it?      That would be lovely, love. And if the weather is kind, maybe we can go stargazing on the night of the party? I always loved those quiet moments out there with the skyline.      That could work. I can ask Mary—she’s the one with the telescope—and see if she’s up for it. I heard she’s into astrophotography now. She might even bring her gear.      I can take photos too! My teacher is doing a school project on stars and galaxies. We had to make a model of the solar system. I made Saturn out of papier-mâché and glitter.      That’s brilliant. You could show Mary how to make one. She’s always taking photos of clouds that look like dragons or something.      Well, while the boys are out there stargazing, I’m going to make a card for you Eileen. I’m thinking of using some photos of Oisin sleeping. He looks very peaceful in the morning, don’t you think?      Yeah, but only if you take the photo before he starts snoring again.      Oh, very funny! Just because you have sound sleep doesn’t give you the right to mock others. You’ll go to bed early yourself if you don’t stop talking so much!

Rather annoying that the new house doesn't even have a spare room. I was hoping it would be easier once... you know, with a child coming. It's not that we need a specific nursery, but a little more floor space would be nice!      I agree. We moved last year and I'm still hunting for the perfect place for the baby stuff. My sister sent over all her old gear—it’s great, but I swear I’ve got a changing mat hidden behind the fridge. It was easier when we shared clothes and shared the nursery between us and her.      Oh yes, I saw the spread when you came over. I can't believe how much the baby supply companies have upped the game. My friend Justine, who's an eccentric lefty lawyer, says you need to buy the co-op branded onesie and hand-me-downs aren't even an option now.      I'm more old-fashioned that way. My Mum always said, "If it’s clean and it fits, wear it!" Still, the fabric isn't always the best on shared items. I do worry about infections being passed on. My brother laughed when I told him.      It’s funny how as we gear up for parenthood, we start second-guessing our parents. I remember my nan would have given a lecture, and now I just sigh and throw something into the dryer. It’s exhausting.      I understand completely. And with your postgrad background in linguistics, I'm always amazed how you seem to read books like they're bedtime stories. I can barely string a sentence together half the time.      That’s where I lean on you! You’ve got about five siblings, after all. You picked the right one to listen to—Tom and I were doing some Danish yesterday. I’m trying to expand the lullaby repertoire for my child. My sister-in-law is Scandinavian and she guest lullabies are supposed to be international experiences, apparently.      Do I want to know what your Danish is like?      Probably not. I’ll stick to nursery rhymes in the lunches we keep meaning to do—my team and yours. My boss keeps asking when the “baby and language integration group” is happening. I really need to figure out how to co-ordinate two teams.      How about we team up with Justine? She might have some ideas.

Rather annoying when people can't get my accent right, innit. I was in Cambridge the other week and someone got all confused with me saying "paddock" instead of "path."      Yeah, it probably sounds quite distinct to people outside the Eastern English region. I remember when I was in Ireland, and my accent gave me a hard time with the locals—they kept mishearing "flattery" as "flattery too."      I’ve had easier time with accents as a gardener—I do a lot of temp jobs. But when I worked in Lefkosia a few years ago, people literally had trouble understanding half my words. I ended up speaking slower, and still had to repeat things like "planting" and "edging" left and right.      I play the guitar, by the way. A bit heavy metal—Donington, you know? Got into it when I was 16. Mate’s uncle bought me a Fender Twin Reverb and I was hooked.      Nice! I once had a pygmy marmoset, but it loved tearing up my crop beds. Poor thing ended up as someone else's pet. Never got into guitars, though. Too loud for the garden work rhythm I do. I listen to lo-fi – keeps me chill while I pot herbs and stuff.      I’m actually an English teacher, as you all know. I've been looking into dialects more for curriculum purposes. Our students here at the language centre also find Eastern English tough to decode. Trying to get some local speakers to film short clips to help pronunciation.      What’s the point in talking posh anyway? Sounds like bollocks. My granddad talked gold standard, and still got treated like an idiot at a posh restaurant. Going in there telling you I’m an artworker does nothing for my social status.      I always tell clients if they’re going to sod up my soil with a bulldozer, I’ll move. Land’s personal, you know. I sort of freelance. Got good at self-protection as well—carrying pepper spray 'cause I once got threatened by someone who took the wrong meaning of "weed."      That's a bit extreme, but I get your point about personal space. Any plans to travel? I just came back from Cyprus, and I'm planning a trip to Barcelona soon.      I’ve made it to North Wales and the Isle of Wight so far. Just like to explore to fuel my art.

Rather annoying that the bus got stuck in traffic again, isn't it?      Yeah, honestly, I'm fed up of this whole commuting routine. I need something that I can rely on.      No argument there. It's just been so tough saving up for a car, though. I mean, even with the ridiculous cost of everything else, cars are still not cheap.      I know! I've got my eye on a used Ford Fiesta, not too old, and the monthly servicing seems manageable. But the deposit is killing me.      You're right. I've been saving for a while now and I'm only halfway there for something like that.      So what are you doing this weekend? I heard you were working from home again.      Yeah, most of it at least. I better start breakfast, though—maybe I'll throw some eggs on for you while I'm at it.      That’s the spirit! As long as you don’t burn them like last time, I’m happy.      Oh come on, it wasn’t  that  bad. I might’ve fried something else, but it wasn’t a crime.      Mate, you turned the bacon into charcoal, it was a masterpiece of destruction.      Fair enough. Silly question, then: ever thought about getting your license? I mean, someone has to teach me how to cook properly.      Actually, I did my lessons a while back. Never finished them all because money got tight, but I'm in the ballpark of passing. I just need to get a car first.      Could I maybe take you up on that idea of practicing driving with you once you have the car up and running? I need to improve for the day I finally get mine sorted.      Of course, it’d be something to do together. Driving’s always way better with someone else there. We could make good time and maybe even figure out a way to save more by carpooling or something.      That sounds like a plan. Just don’t forget the coffee when we go out. I am not about to risk my life on tired, hungry, and inattentive driving.      A promise fulfilled, Speaker_1. Coffee, plenty of snacks, and a strategy to avoid every pothole known to man.      Perfect. Now, if we could just avoid burning the dinner this time...      Only you would say that after making charred toast your life's work. Let me help.

Rather chilly this morning, ain't it? I’ve just boiled the kettle and made us a pot o’ tea. You lot fancy one?      I fancy a cup, thank ye, Auntie Jan. Mummy said I could have one with milk and a sugar. Is it gonna be that eeny kind or the normal kind?      Ay, it's all the same these days—just water from the tap and a bag from the shed, but we stretch it far as it’s supposed to. We’ve got three sugars left and a spoon chase in, but we’ll manage.      Oh, you mean like we used t’die for back in the war? Jan, you always ration turkey like it’s rationed still! Ten more years and you’ll be using a pastry tin for a hat again!      Well, there’s no better way when you’ve got four mouths to feed. Less a’th four at the table, mind, but we fergit not for a second that we’re lucky.      Nonsense, woman. You’d ration a spoonful o’ butter longer than both o’ us put together.      Who’s watching Doctor Who later? I saw it on the TV earlier. It’s about aliens with hats and a wibbly-wobbly thing. Is that somethin’ to do with maths?      No, no—it's a drama. Like a story with music and dress-ups. But you know what? It does have some tricky bits. Some o’ the spaceships look a bit like pyramids—ain't that geometry?      Kinda, like the ones we did in maths last week! Only different because it had wings and a police box and everything inside was bigger.      Aye, space-like that. My, time for dinner yet?      Jan, you were supposed to open the freezer door before you mentioned ‘dinner’. We ain't got no idea what’s in there past the sprouts and mystery stew.      Nor do I, Jane. I told Jan the last time the meats were there for  weeks , not  weeks ! The chicken was more goon than gourmet.      Roast potatoes, sprouts, and goon-chicken. Sounds like a bloomin’ knight feast!      Well, I’ll manage. We’ve got the kettle goin’ and I’ll stir up a casserole from the bottom o’ the shelf. We’ll call it ‘Wartime Wednesday’ all over again.      Can I add some of Grandad’s stories too? Uncle Terry told me ‘bout the Hull Blitz last week.

Right, luv, we’ve got a request for a pirate talk today, right? What do you think, lads and lass? Pirates, Shakespeare, and even a bit of magic if we have time. I’m thinking we can do a bit of stop motion animation later with your Easter pictures for fun. Has anyone ever made a movie with a toy camera?      I wanted to be a pirate once. A real one. With a cutlass and a parrot on my shoulder. But I couldn’t find a parrot.      Didn’t your mum get cross with you when you tried to paint your face with make-up and pretend to be a pirate at nursery?      She said it was messy, not that I wasn’t a good pirate. I told her I was the Black Dandelion, and I had a patch over my eye!      Oh, I love it—creative pirates need clever names. Maybe after this talk, we can cook you some proper pirate food, like rum sauce spare ribs or treasure chest cookies. Or we can go to the real circus if we book a day out—there’s that workshop with the clowns!      What’s the circus got to do with pirates? Pirates swim, clowns laugh.      Mate, pirates often had circus-like shows on their ships—dagger throwing, sword duels, rope tricks. Very theatrical! You know what else is full of drama and swords? Shakespeare!      Oh, remember when you took us to Stratford-upon-Avon on school trip? They’d dress up and do the plays and it was like a real-life movie.      Exactly, doll. We’re doing Shakespeare week next month, so we’ll pair it with pirates and magic. How about you research pirate toys you can make and we’ll combine them with bits of the Bard?      What about the bit where they fight with flashlights? Like sword fights in the dark? That was cool.      Flashlight fights, swordplay, parrots, and maybe even a ransom written in invisible ink with lemon juice. And speaking of magic—you ever do the card trick where you pull a card from behind your ear?      Mummy, can we use your camera for stop motion first? I want to make pirate characters that move like in the box set!      Of course. We’ll take photos of pirate characters and then animate them against a background of the real circus tents or the bard’s statue we saw in Stratford.

Rather do share a drink and bring us all up to speed. I confess I’d forgotten about that escapade... What was it, Jim? You tried to sail from Jeddah to Cyprus without a permit?      No, no, I had a permit — well, at least I thought I did! I was returning from a lecture on modern dentistry over there, and I wanted to make a quick trip. A friend had this dinghy in Jeddah, so we said, “What the hell?” We sailed three days out, hit a sandstorm the fourth, and when we returned under the radar... the navy was waiting. I mean, imagine being arrested with 20 dental magazines!      My word, you could’ve sent them to the tide! But back in Saudi Arabia, I remember the cultural shock of not being allowed to drink alcohol. Living with rules was far harder than working with students. I often wondered if I’d been naive to accept the contract.      I agree — especially with the contrast between the West and the East. I taught in Riyadh for over a decade, and it was fascinating. Though I never touched alcohol — quite a different world. Did you tell the story about the time they banned foreign newspapers for a week? We were all reading the local papers, and –?      And you found it all in Arabic! I remember that. Now don’t tell me you all spoke fluent Arabic after six months?      We did in fact. The students were patient with us. Of course, the real struggle was the food at first — all the spicing and spices. I can’t say I miss it, but I did come away with a most interesting palate!      I prefer the English fare myself, though I must admit I’ve enjoyed this very wine you’ve got open! I only have it once a week now to treat myself, but for the story’s sake, well...      And I remember when the school in Manchester was giving all those charity toothbrush sets to Saudi schools. I convinced the supply shop to include dental floss — as though they’d use it with lunches of bread and dates!      Oh, that’s true, you always had a way with the system! But go on with the arrest, if you don’t mind – I think I missed the part where they released you. After the three blokes in headscarves told you you could forget the boat, and to leave the magazines?      Exactly!

Rather annoying this new toilet seat we've had to get, Sarah. The one for the bathroom emergency when Hal... Well, you know what happens when he has more than one glass of squash.      Oh, I remember the time he tried to sit down after that birthday party and ended up in a right pickle. Still, I suppose it’s an improvement. At least it’s not all over the floor like last year.      Yeah, I got covered in it. I was going to dump the waste and—well, anyway, I had to change trousers when I went out with my mates.      Still, it made me think, with Hal at that age now, do you think about how kids our age get into relationships? I mean, I remember you boys were always off with the girls, Tony, but now I think he needs more supervision—proper rules, you know?      Absolutely. You need to set boundaries, or you'll end up with the same mess as when we used to go out for the day and he’d just stay on the phone for hours.      Yeah, but he’s not even with anyone yet. He still spends all his time on YouTube. I’ve got a mate who’s got work experience in a café. You ever think about getting Hal something like that?      That’s not a bad idea. Would he want to do that? He might find it helpful to get some real-life experience. It’s all very well someone telling you how to get ready for work, but a bit of doing it yourself definitely helps.      It's the way of being, isn't it? I did ballet as a kid and nearly flunked school. My dad used to say, “You don’t get far standing on one leg.” That’s why I got into sales—you learn to talk fast, bend quickly to the customer, and for heaven’s sake, always smile.      I’m trying to get my GCSEs out the way. I don’t want to be waiting on tables forever. I’m into sports and I might try doing a bit of refereeing. My mate Louis does that—says it’s the best work experience you can get.      Oh, I remember goin' on that holiday to Spain with my brother once. Gave me a real sense of opportunity. We saw the explorer museum in Madrid—it really opened our eyes.

Rather annoying driving up here in this traffic, innit? But I reckon it's worth it for truffle hunting tomorrow, yeah? I’ve never tried one yet, but I’ve heard they're daft expensive and daft fancy. Chuffed they have a truffle farm nearby.      Oh een, dear, they’re more than just ‘daft fancy’! My cousin in London told me a chef in Ayrton once used truffles from Istria to make a thousand-pound dish. They’re like little clots of gold, if you ask me.      Mummy, what’s a truffle again? Is it like a chocolate pudding? Cos the name sounds like that.      No, love, they’re a type of fungus, like mushrooms but underground. They’re daft hard to pick and you need a dog to find ’em, proper trained ones. They’re white here, and black in Italy, depending where you are.      And the chefs! I saw this documentary last week. One chef in America actually sold truffle oil for over twenty quid a bottle, and it was basically olive oil with a trace of truffle essence. Peculiar, innit?      Overcharged nonsense if you ask me. You can’t bottle the earthy aroma of a real truffle, it just don’t work. Though I reckon the Americans love to spend silly money on daft things. Last week, I saw a firm in the City investing someone forty grand in a TV show about people who brew their own beer. Blokey stuff.      I saw a truffle on  Blue Peter  once. They showed a man in France digging one about daft big. My mates kept laughing but it looked daft shiny.       Blue Peter ? Not sure I’d trust it as a truffle guide, son. But I suppose it’s good for sparking curiosity.      Speaking of daft shiny things, where's your cigarettes, Terry? I tried to stop for a week but I'm crackin' again.      Gone, love. Lost the packet on the motorway. Not daft going back for it. But I daft mind stopping altogether, really I don’t.      Why don’t you go for that stem cell treatment in Manchester they’re talking about on the telly? I read it can help with cravings. It’s all over the uni campus, though I think it’s a bit expensive.      I’ll talk to the doctor over this, anyway. Or them! It's a midwives’ conference I'm going to next week.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun is making everything feel a bit more bearable in this concrete jungle. I've been meaning to visit that new café on Trumpington Street anyway.      Yeah, honestly, I haven't had a proper break since Monday morning. My team’s been running on caffeine and willpower. It was either coffee or collapse. But I’ve been thinking — I’ve been tracking some pretty interesting brand engagement stats this week. The data is actually staggering.      Interesting… nothing like diving into numbers when you're literally surrounded by the past. You'd think the printing house would be mostly ghosts and dead trees, but no — it’s still printing webinars and PDFs at breakneck speed.      It is fascinating, though, the way spoken language survives and transforms. I was just reading about how even in Cambridge, generational shifts are starting to blur traditional dialects. I've noticed some students dropping certain vowel shifts entirely. It’s like they’re unconsciously re-inventing articulation to suit the digital environment.      That's deep. I’d say marketing takes advantage of that — quite a lot. Younger demographics expect real-time interaction, minimal formality… it's less about "proper" speech and more about being instantly understandable.      So you're saying the way we speak is now a product of screens and timelines?      Absolutely. The milliseconds it takes for a message to be read, reacted to, or scrolled past — it's reshaping the way we phrase things. Gone are the days of letters with footnotes and asides. Now it's:  Dot your i, cross your t, and make it snappy.       It's quite an irony really — language research and digital communication are converging. I've been trying to map how these changes are reflected in regional variation. Turns out, even here in the South East, there's a surprising amount of variance. Provincial terms surfacing in city conversations, and vice versa.      Interesting from such a data-driven angle. But what about space? Do people still  speak  to each other?      Oh, they do, but it's context-dependent now. In a room like this, you'd probably get a more traditional form of linearity, but outside — on the go, in the park, at your local pub — it's more about fluency and rhythm, less about structure.      You could say we’ve moved from linguistic poetry to linguistic performance.      I’m not entirely sure I follow that, but I like the ring of it.

Rather annoying this new European traffic system, isn't it? I swear they've made it more complicated than it needs to be. But at least the campervan handles it all well, I think.      Yeah, I know what you mean—some of the signs are a bit confusing when you're used to UK English. But honestly, I'm just glad we're not in the main roads. The last A-road we hit was backed up from somewhere, and I swear it was because of some catering van that broke down and nobody was moving quickly.      Oh well, not too many people wander this way. Lakelands and forests, you know the sort of place. Our friend in Tarnow’s a bit of a recluse though not in a bad way. I think she just likes the peace, away from the cities.      For sure, and it’s been a nice quiet drive so far. Just us, a bit of bad radio reception, and the odd cow wondering onto the road looking for somewhere to graze. I hope we’ll get to her place by dinner—personally I’m not up for cooking in the campervan again.      Tell me about it! That mini microwave decided to stop working when we got to Poland. I tried using it once, and it just made noise without heating anything. Honestly, the cheapest microwave in Boots would be better than this one.      We could always just carry some food out with us when we get there. I brought a few bread rolls just in case. And Mary—our friend—mentioned she had a couple of smoked cheeses she wanted to share. Maybe we can persuade her into making a proper meal.      Now that sounds like a plan. I'm not sure how much else I can take of driving and provision food. The last sandwich I had was dry enough to satisfy the Queen’s treacle waters.      I’m with you there. Let’s assume she’ll be cooking something, but just in case, I’ll pop a few ready-made meals in the cool box. Even if they are a bit overpriced in the roadside shops, it's better than nothing.      That’s the spirit. Just go with it on this trip, you know? Life’s too short to fuss about the little things, especially when we’re doing all this driving through what one could call the scenic parts.

Rather annoying this, innit? They’ve got the telly on but it’s muted, an' it’s got the football on. Just keeps showing these highlights and I can’t even hear the commentators!      Aw, don’t worry, we can watch properly once the ads go. Got eeny time.  Looks over at the screen.  See that player? He's dancin’ round with that McGoat logo on his side! I swear, McDonald's is on every strip in the league now.      Aye, it’s gettin’ a bit much. I like football, but even united used to have no sponsors, y’know, back in the eighties an' nineties. Now it’s everywhere. Even got logos on the back o’ the shirts an' the socks!      I mean, you can't blame the clubs, can you? The money they get from this stuff’s massive. I reckon McDonald’s must be planting the idea in every team’s head, persuadin' ‘em to bleed red and yellow like their own restaurants. Might get a free burger out o’ it if you support the right team.      Honestly, I’ve seen a three-year-old in a Man U shirt with the “Big Mac” – no, wait, it was the chekin’ logo – on the back. I reckon the parents thought they were gettin’ a better deal or summat. Still, the strip’s lookin’ alright though. That new one with the chequest design? It’s classy, innit? Bit hotter than the old one mind.      Can’t argue with that. They’re startin’ to make ‘em like art sometimes. I watched a match where the whole team was in a gradient black and gold. Looked smooth as anything. Doesn’t hurt the game, but I do miss the ‘ol basic look. Just a simple red or blue shirt with maybe one small sponsor logo.      I know what you mean. I miss when players ran out an' you didn’t have to parse through 12 sponsor logos just to figure out the team name!  Laughs.  Was it Manchester United you said earlier?      Yeah, yeah go on then. But let’s see who wins this game first, innit? Finally, they’re showin’ the scores now. Go on, your team.  Leans in to watch the match.       Aye, don’t bellyache now, you had a bet with ‘em yesterday, didn’t you?  Pauses to watch the screen.  Arrgh, they’re takin’ another corner! That's the fifth one in ten minutes!

Rather annoying I had to take the train to London again this week. The one with the broken air con. I got home and told Mum about it, and she said I should’ve stared the driver down and told him it was unsafe. You wouldn’t have said that, would you?      Probably een beginning to say  anythin’  if I saw a Union Jack embroidered on the inside of a man with a beard and a flat cap walk past me and I thought he was a terrorist. Last week, someone said “you’ve got somethin’ on your trousers” out of the blue. I thought it was a Russian, turns out it was a bloke from Bristol.      That’s like that My turkey shop doorstep bit, you know, the one on India Street. I had to warn you, I thought he was a black man the other day. It was just a white bloke with skin that’s slightly darker than yours thanks to some holiday sunburn in his youth. I said sorry and he thought I was ordering puff pastry. Worst part was he actually sold me that.      You know what I’m tryin’ to sort out now? Job seekers allowance. I’ve sent three applications today, but they want three references, and the last job was ten years ago. I remember the name of the bisto I worked in, but the manager? Long gone. I reckon the benefits system has got tighter than Sillet Stones after Brexit.      At least you’re tryin’. Dad still spends on the flat. He just inherited quite a bit from Auntie Mary— you’d think he’d spend it on the central heating , but no, he insists on a second TV for the spare room. I told him the kids can just share the one, but now I’m cooking on the George Forman because that’s the only appliance that works properly.      My sister’s got the same George Forman. Says it’s养生. I asked her what that meant and she told me ‘it’s Chinese for eating healthy’. I told her I’d rather stick to my beans and toast. Anyway, I did buy a new microwave off eBay a couple of days ago. It took five days to arrive and it’s got a ‘vintage’ sticker on the back. Doesn’t work for life if you ask me.      You sure? I ordered a kettle from the same bloke on eBay and it came with a rabbit inside.

Rather annoying warts I've got on my thumb, Joan. I've had it for ages. Tried pumicing and everything, but no luck. It just won’t budge.      Oh, don’t be daft, Karen. You should get that sorted. We’ve got a good eeny at the chemist’s. It was on offer last week.      Oh aye, I had one once on the side of my nail, gave me a right old time. I put Vicks VapoRub on it for weeks. My daughter says I’m a real old-fashioned person, but I don’t see the point in buying a big meal when I can zip to Tesco and grab something ready made.      That’s where you and I differ, Lucy. So nurseries, right? My teacher was saying they used to be all run by nuns when she was a kid. I thought she was joking, but my gran said it was true.      Oh, that's right. Back in the day, a lot of nurseries and schools were run by the nuns. Especially the Catholic ones. But I reckon it depends where you're from. I didn’t grow up with that—more of a state school upbringing.      Interesting. I do find religion weird, though. Like, how do you know which one's right? I saw a documentary about the Matrix once. It made me think, is the real world even real?      Oh, I’ve seen The Matrix too. It does make you question things, right? Darcy, pick your peas up off the floor. Come on, darling.      Hmmph.      Haha, he’s being dramatic. Go on, we can talk to him about the Matrix too. One day, when he’s bigger and into sci-fi—personally, I think religion and philosophy are kind of the same thing. Both human attempts to make sense of life.      [incomprehensible]      Maybe, but I heard some people actually act like other religions are stupid. I reckon that’s not nice.      Absolutely not. Science tells us one thing, religion tells us someone else. But both should be given a fair chance. It just depends on what a person believes in. Also, some people get really into strange stuff—like Scientology.      Sci-what?      Scientology. It's a kind of belief system. It started in the States, I think. Not sure if I should even mention it, it's kind of... weird.      Is it like a cult? My mate at school says a lot of people join things just to escape being boring.      Well, being boring is as boring as being interesting. It all depends on the people involved. I mean, I’ve got friends who believe in weird things, but they’re nice and happy people.      I suppose it matters more how people treat each other than what they believe in, yeah? I don’t think God cares if we're believers or not.      That's a deep thought for a teenager. Maybe you should write that down, publish a manifesto on it.      Haha, no. I’m not that kind of deep. Just found it interesting.      And always remember, being kind is the most important part of any faith or belief system.

Rather annoying driving up here, eh? You know, me n’ the lassies ‘ad a dance class last weekend an’ I still ain't got the grip on it. I've been humming that song “Wobble Wobble” all week, I swear!      Haha, I saw that on  Strictly Come Dancing  once. I reckon it's not easy, especially if you're not used to it. I tried one too back at uni, but I was far too coordinationally challenged to keep up with the pairs.      It's the blokes that make it look so easy, innit? I can't get over how the pro dancers still smile like that in the middle of a twirl. I’m still wondering whether I could do belly dancing or something – I reckon I’d feel more at home in a skirt!      Maybe try something a bit more, um… British? I mean, folk dancing? I once did a bit of Morris as part of a uni project looking at traditional folk costume. Good fun, but that’s not for the faint-hearted—personally I’d rather shuffle about in Wellington boots somewhere muddy than do that in public.      Oh yeah, Morris dancing, I’ve been curious about the history. Does it come from Old English stuff? I’ve read some papers on linguistic shifts in Northern English and Old English before—always fascinated me.      You're not wrong. It’s kind of a relic of the language. Although the dancing itself is more a mix of ritual and display. You ever think about looking at some of the folk songs and how their words match up to the older dialects? I reckon it’d make a great conversation for the coffee nights the charity has.      That'd be good. Sarah at the charity told me they're trying to bring in more cultural events. I ‘eard someone talking about guest speaker thing at the uni with a bloke from Cambridge on language preservation.      I wonder if you’d be able to get a crack at that as your project for the corpus work? Something bridging modern dialects and older English—might be a fresh angle.      You're not wrong, love. I go on about it to my mates sometimes. If I can crack it, I reckon it’ll outshine some of those celebrity boxset binges I’ve ‘eard you gripe about!      Yeah, I'm not one for celebrities anyway—though I'll admit, I've binged  LoveFilm’s  series of  Peaky Blinders  so much I probably know half the lyrics.

Rather annoying this GPS, innit? It's going round in circles again. I swear it thinks it's in Bolton and not Croatia or whatever.      Relax, love. It’ll sort itself out in a minute. You’ve seen those fella round these parts—market stalls pop up out een nowhere and there’s more olive oil on the side of the road than there is in the shops. I reckon that caravanser just off that next roundabout might be easier. We can pick up a local map.      Is this the bit where we get lost and then find some secret cave to go camping in? In the TV show  Sons of Anarchy , they do that sort of thing all the time. You know, big motorcycles and bursts of ultra-quiet, loads of brooding.      Fair enough, but we ain't got no bikes and you’re not brolly enough to brood properly. Besides, I reckon there’s more festivals happening than caves. That fella down near Motovun? They’ve got some real good music nights over there, if I remember rightly.      Funnily enough, I’ve got a contact at one of the bigger ones near Pula. You'd be surprised how many consultants get invited to bottle – er, I mean bottle-opener – events these days. Good networking, the odd sommelier demo and bottles of wine that will knock the wind out o’ya.      Ooh, and they also sell proper wine from these local chaps who run vineyards. Some hotter stuff than your average supermarket red, let me tell you. Can I pick up a bottle while we’re at it? My patient’s partner sent a bottle round the other week and it were fookin’ terrible.      Speaking of which, have we managed to book in to the recommended places yet? I mean, if it’s anything like Manchester, you gotta get in early to the finer spots.      I tried to ring up that place in Rovinj, you know the one with the view and the fancy tapas? I think it's closed now, but the lady who answered said they still got a few tables if you queue up early.      I vote queueing.      I vote no queueing. I know a bloke who’s at one of them big corporate parks just north of here. They’ve got a private dining area for guests, maybe even a couple of caravans for the weekends.

Rather annoying I’ve just lost me wi-fi, innit. Was tryin’ to stream that new  Call of Duty  beta with Anna. Otherwise I’d be playin’ by now      Aye, we tried too, but it kept laggin’ like mad. Is it me PC or someone uploading a tiddy pic in the background?      Oh, I just invested in like three decent webcams and downloaded everything so I can do live streams. Proper setup, innit? Though my MySpace still looks like it was made in 2003.      Aww, and I bought a whole little mic to make it all fancy, and it still sounds like I’m speaking into a bucket.      No wonder, you’re shouting into a fag packet, for heaven’s sake. You need like a proper stand and maybe a green screen—personally I’ve just been dabbing in the corners a bit to make it look artsy.      Sounds like fun, though. Have you all got plans for the upcoming – Mate, have you heard about the new game that just dropped?      What game? We’ve all been trying to survive the beta and don’t even know what’s out there this week      Just a new indie thing, it's oddly chill. You can play as a kid with a cat and explore a sunny forest. Not like all the headshots and blood stuff most people about.      Sounds far better than what I’m used to. I’ve been trying not to play that aggressive shooter stuff because me dad keeps unpluggin’ me.      Aye, well if you’re all interested maybe we could do a weekend session—no recording, just chill. We could meet up, play something together, maybe bring the cat kid game and that sprite game we all mentioned.      Aye! That sounds doable. Me and Anna could bring the snacks. Pizzas and the lot.      If I can convince my brother to give me his gaming chair for the day, I might be in. Just let me know what your address is and what PSU you’ve got for me PC, and I’ll be sorted.      True to say, we can have a proper gaming day. Maybe even film a little bit for the fun of it. Least we can get our heads stopped from being yanked off.

Rather nippy today, ain't it? That wind off the river sticks to yer bones, ‘as it.      Yeah, I’m more than grateful for this coffee. I’d have frozen off me fingers if I hadn’t grabbed this before we came in. Got any plans after work, Mark?      Might chuck a few sausages on the barbie later. Nell’s making that nutmeg mash she’s got in the oven at the mo. She reckons it’ll dump the lot if I don’t come home before six. Didn’t ask, but I reckon I’d rather fetch chips than lose a baked potato.      That the spud and custard mix? I had it once when I was living up near Stockport. It was either that or the shepherd’s pie, and I’d had enough of redcurrant jelly to last a lifetime by then.      Oh yeah, I’ve been wanting to try some of that. People’s got the oddest combinations, though — I had a client in the north who insists on hot dogs with baked beans and apple sauce. I’d rather eat the side of the plate.      I tell ya, when I were a nipper in Pelaw, we didn’t have all these fancy combinations. It were toast, boiled eggs, and, if we were really lucky, some tinned mince and apple pie.      Still, I suppose we’ve come on. I mean, supermarkets these days — chicken curry, sushi, pho… it's like the world came to the tills.      Or the world and a tea towel. I mean, when I’m in, most nights I just make a bit of a stir-fry. Quick, easy, and I can be in bed by ten if I’m not working weekends. Doesn’t sound too glamorous, but it’s better than delivery for the tenth time in a row.      I reckon you’re the only one holding any self-control, Sarah. I tried cutting down on takeaway once, but I crack after about three days. Mainly of guilt and hunger.      Aye, I’m with Lee. My knees start calling for something greasy by Tuesday if the weather’s bad. Mince pies usually see me through.      You’re all hopeless, but I suppose it’s the same for us all when the days get short and the light goes early. Speaking of, anyone fancy a pizza next week? I know a place near Salford Quays that does a ‘techy discount’ on Fridays.

Rather annoying when a researcher turns up with a request and expects us to know the internet inside out. Mind you, got to admire some of them—unlike my cousin Tony, who stared at a Google search for three minutes before finally typing 'hello' in the search bar.      That’s a classic. I told one bloke once he was basically speaking to the spider on a web. A web by the web, so to speak. Still, easier than explaining what a search engine is to a pensioner. Wait, did you get that chase from Salford Library about the update?      Yeah, I did. Bit of a hassle, but only because we’re trying to track what’s useful. You know, who actually uses Facebook for academic stuff anymore, or if they’re just on it for cat videos. A world of nonsense if you ask me.      You British folk and your cricket... I used to live in Wellington, and we treated Facebook like, well, spare time—and a place to find out who won the lottery over the weekend, maybe. But here, I’ve seen PhD students struggle with LinkedIn as if it were a foreign language. Honestly, we’ve got a generation who can’t work without a little digital hand-holding.      I agree, and sometimes it feels like we’re back in the 90s with encyclopaedias and book indexes. These days it's, "Can you just someone on there?" as if social media is a magic answer machine.      Some students still ask, "Is Twitter like real life?"—as if social media  isn’t  life at this point. I mean, I use it for the weather, my missus’ cat and a bit of cricket. But it’s not like I’m building a research paper on it.      Oh, I’ve got one for you. I had a chap in at the library the other day holding up a phone and saying, "This bloody Facebook is waiting for me to post. It’s holding its breath." I asked what he meant, and he said, "I told it I’m going on a date, and it’s been frozen with anticipation like it's watching the end go off."      That's genius. I’ll remember that the next time someone asks me how to use the ‘business’ version. It’s LinkedIn, for heaven’s sake—it’s not Tinder with a Ctrl+Alt+Del!      And that's the problem, really—everyone wants everything fast.

Rather than share a text-based version of the request, would you like to schedule a time for a visual presentation? It might be more effective for the group to see the materials directly.      That sounds like a good idea. When would you be available? I'll need to check my schedule and ensure all the relevant parties can attend.      I'm quite flexible, but next Thursday afternoon should be free if that works for you. I can block off the time and make sure all the necessary documents and visuals are ready to present.      Thursday afternoon it is. I'll clear the meeting room and make sure the presentation tools are set up beforehand. In the meantime, can you send over the initial summary or key points you'd like to highlight in the presentation? It'll help the committee come prepared and pose questions.      Absolutely, I'll compile a document with an outline, main objectives, and some initial data highlighting areas for improvement within our current processes. I can send that over by the end of the day.      Perfect. I do appreciate you taking the lead on this—these presentations can be quite lengthy if not well structured. Your experience in coordinating such details is a real asset to the team.      Thank you. I'm just trying to ensure the proposal is as comprehensive as possible. There's a fair amount of ground to cover, including potential locations, feasibility studies, budget breakdowns, and our long-term plans for expansion.      Yes, and it's a delicate balance between ambition and realism. Some members of the committee have expressed concerns about overextension being their top priority. I think your key will be to justify the rationale without over-reassuring them about our ability to deliver. We want to be ambitious but grounded.      That makes sense. I'll be sure to weave that through the narrative. Also, I've been thinking about how to involve local stakeholders—maybe inviting representatives from the local business associations? It might help the community feel more connected to the project.      That's a positive move. It also shows we've considered the environmental and social impact of the project, which is often underappreciated in these discussions but very important for proposal approval. Let's include it in your summary and I'll follow up with the committee to line it up.      Excellent. I'll finish your summary shortly and add all the planning notes for Thursday.

‘So I just rented this film called  The Nun , innit? Me an’ me mates seen  The Conjuring  lot an’ we all said, “Aye, let’s see where this story starts.” But… fair to say, it sort uv winds us up, eh?’      ‘Oh, I’ve seen that one! It’s mad, innit? Like they try a bit too hard to scare you. All that swooping camera an’ the creepy music. It’s not like it’s a classic or sommat. But what’s the point, really? Still, I gotta admit, the jump scares are mostly  bollocks .’      ‘I know, right? It’s like, ye expect them! The lighting left a bit to be desired, to be honest. D’you know, I think I turned round at one point in the dark, thinking something was lurking behind me—turns out me dog’s still asleep on the sofa. Silly me!’      ‘Haha, that happens to me too. Last week I watched  Hereditary , tryin’ to be proper scary. Bah, quite a different vibe. It’s more real, innit? Less jump scares, more… proper unease. Be warned, though. It’s a bit of a banger. Left me rattled for a few days after.’      ‘Oh, I’ve heard that film is proper dark! I been meaning to watch it, someone at sixth form said it’s got a proper twist. It just sounds like it’s not what you’d watch at half ten in the evening and be lookin’ for a laugh, innit?’      ‘That’s the thing, the good ones leave you thinking for days. I remember watching  The Babadook  with me nan and it just stuck in our heads for ages. It’s not like the usual stuff that’s all about blood an’ ghosts. It’s deeper. Thought provoking, innit?’      ‘Sounds mad! I stick to my good old  Five Nights at Freddy’s  game or the  Amityville  lot—course, if the jump scares don’t set my heart runnin’. But I’ll try  The Babadook —just if you promise not to shout at me when I duck in the middle of it!’      ‘Aye, fair enough. I won’t laugh too much neither, though I won’t pretend it won’t be funny when your face goes like a startled rabbit! ‘      ‘You’re a laugh—right enough. I reckon we should hold our own fright nights next week, queue it all up on the telly. Just make a night of it, binch of popcorn, and slap on them films we used to see as kids.

Rather annoying when the tablet won't play music to sleep to. I've had it for ages — it's practically got more dents than a banger at a car boot sale. I've been thinking about getting a new one. Do you think they're worth it?      Aye, they’re handy if you know how to use them. Me son tried to explain it all to me once — a grand old racket listing by rooms or kitchens in this and that place. Oh but I'm not techy like that. What's wrong with the present one?      Oh it's not too bad, but it's just . . . so slow. Like when the fridge freezer only turns on when it feels like it. Just unreliable. I did read about a good one this morning over the laptop, the kind you can write on and everything. A bit heavy for my taste, but at least you can prop it up on the old Winnie chair while you read.      Winnie chair is a good fella — still solid after the twins treated it like a wrestling ring twenty years ago.      I know, really special in a sort of creaky, mournful way. But anyway, I’ve been thinking of ordering it online. I saw a few good reviews. Though I'm still trying to decide whether I want Apple, Samsung, or something unnamed but cheaper.      Aye, Apple’s a sure thing if you don’t fancy the homework. Me old daughter says anything with an Android in the system is like climbing a ladder backwards. But I do wonder what you’ll do with it when it arrives. Chained to the wall like all the best things are?      Not quite. I’ll be using the touch-up tools to mark up contracts for a friend who's renting out her place via that new Airbnb type platform. You remember? The one the twins stayed in for their gap year. They came back with sunburn and a story about porridge the size of a wheelie bin lid.      Aye, I did wonder about that one. All that zooming in and out — trying to find a holiday home by watching a stranger video their living room. Reminds me of something from one of those silly soaps the channels go on about on a Sunday afternoon.      True, but some of the houses are brilliant. Anyway, while I'm on the site, I’m going to add the new iPad and perhaps a new set of cushions for the lounge.

So, I just wanted to go through the application with you. I’m a bit worried about the personal statement... What do you think?      Of course, love, show me where you are. I’m not an expert like you, but I’ve read a few things in my time. Got eeny bit more common sense than most, if I do say so.      It’s with that new firm by the South Bank. They focus a lot on sustainable building and community projects, which is right up my alley. The problem is, when I start talking about myself, it all sounds too... generic.      Oh, don’t listen to the doubting Thomas in your head. You always think you're saying nothing, love. You got so much to offer. I remember you at school, always drawing up these little plans for the community garden. It used to make the old school better for breakfast, no doubt about that!      That’s kind of the point, yes! I want to show them I have the vision and heart for community-based design—especially for places like Hounslow or Croydon where regeneration can be tricky.      And you do, love. You’ve got that passion. Just say it. Maybe write from the heart a bit more – no one wants to read a textbook version, least of all an employer. Let them see the  you  behind the CV.      You're right. I just keep comparing myself to someone who sounds like they’ve already built a cathedral or a museum.      Oh, ignore the noise. You’re just starting out and look at you – all education under your belt, and most people about half your age are still trying to decide whether they fancy building or just fancies. You’ve already got the inside lane.      Thanks, Mum. Maybe I’ll start with a personal story from when I worked at that community housing project last year. It shows me engaging on the ground – something technical qualifications can’t fully express.      There you go. That’s you being smart and being  you . Just add a couple of specifics and maybe what you noticed happened as a result. Even if it was something as simple as helping a man pick the right gothic details on his own improvements.      True, I remember that—so funny, but it taught me a lot about listening and design from the resident’s point of view.

Rather a lot’s happened in the last few weeks, hasn’t it?      Oh aye, I’ll say. Prices are rising more than I can afford, and I’d say a lot of us are £20 or so out of pocket a month with things gone up so high again.      It’s simply ridiculous. I reckon it’s not all government making choices—it’s the oil men, the supermarkets, the landowners. They’ve got a stranglehold on everything.      I heard on the telly the other day the cost of housing specially is like three times more than it was when I was a lad. What’s gone on there?      Just speculation, that’s what it is. Families like us can’t get anywhere near buying a house anymore. I’ve been thinking the government should take housing back, make it public again.      I agree with you, love. The other week my niece said the deposit for a little bungalow near London is the cost of a second car for her—can you imagine?      Cheeky young luv, but I’ve seen similar grief when I was working as an engineer. The country wasn't so wide then, was it? You could get anywhere for about £5,000 and now it's £500,000.      You know what I blame? The education system. People don’t get what’s going on in the world. They chase after jobs in cities and pay sky-high rents while the countryside’s all but forgotten.      I had a luvly colleague when I was a childminder who always said: the same story, different money. We were flogging off stuff like housing and not building anywhere near enough. Now the only housing is unaffordable.      And the cars! I had my Mini back in the '70s—£600 was bloody pricey at the time, but now you can’t buy a proper one for less than twice what I paid.      '70s were better in so many ways. Not just the money—people had a sense of community. Still do, in goode parts, but it’s getting swallowed up by the nation’s cities.      It always puzzles me how the government’s allowed one part of the country to have all the wealth and the others to rot. We live hours from the capital and not much better than we did back in the ‘80s.      That’s bleak, luv. But maybe they think we're too soft to make a row?

Rather annoying that the fire escape still needs attention, isn't it? I was just in the old studio and it feels like a cold draft is coming through from somewhere down that corridor. I've mentioned it a couple of times in meetings, but I don't suppose anyone's got round to sorting it yet?      Yeah, I've heard about it, but haven't had the chance to have a proper look myself. A lot of the tenants have been raising concerns, especially those in rehearsals. It's not just the cold—there's the risk of tripping over boxes when people come and go late at night. Not to mention the sound carry. Last week, I overheard the fire department giving another warning during training about that old turkey on floor two creaking its hinges. It’s ridiculous.      D’you think we should make it a priority? I know assembling for the upcoming bookings is a bit tight, but we can't ignore basic safety. I was in discussion with the marketing team about getting some photos of the building’s new look ready—those escalations would give the space character, but not if it’s inappropriate or dangerous. What I don’t get is why we’ve still got boxes of old brochures in there. It’s not like we have storage in surplus.      Oh, they were supposed to deal with that before the renovations started, but I imagine that didn't quite happen. We’ve also got a new tenant coming in next week for that weekend workshop—art in public spaces—but the room isn't ready yet. I had a word with them, so we're rolling out the holiday cover plan early. I can’t be here next week—I’ve got a colleague, Neil, who’s about to finish his apprenticeship. I’m having such confidence in him finally stepping up.      Goodness, that's barely a week away. I remember when he started. My, time flies. I wonder if they've updated the maintenance schedule. The birds have been a bit of a problem too, nesting in the windows again. I tried to get a bird pro in while you were off over Easter. They gave me a quote, but frankly, I think it was absurd. I took the liberty of advising Tom from maintenance to source another provider.      Tom's a good man, if a bit slow on sourcing.

Rather lovely to be here in Hereford, isn’t it? A bit of peace and quiet away from the classroom, and the cold has been mellowed by this fire! Roast chicken was just perfect, by the way. Not quite as scrumptious as what you serve at home, Rob, but it’ll do.      Thanks, Rachel. I reckon it’s not easy being British with a South African background and still managing to love one too many spoonfuls of gravy. It was easier pulling it off as a chef-in-training than it is now that I’ve become a full-time history teacher.      Still, I made sure it wasn’t short of rosemary and thyme — and that gravy? A little bit of home for me, left over from the pot I made on the bus into Hereford earlier this morning. If it turned out a shade thicker than usual, let’s call it character. Or call it Bristolian brashness returning after all these years.   Spekaer_4:   You, ordering your own ingredients en route? That’s news to me—thought you were just the one who loved taking credit for the occasional smoothie or stir.      And yet, he still remembers the best local butcher for the chicken. I give him credit where it is most certainly due.      Rimming, that was a fine bit of cooking. But seriously, after moving to Wales through Singapore for work—and then never back—food has been a big part of how someone like me keeps rooted in the community. A crispy breaded cod at the local pub can outshine any five-star meal when it’s Friday and it’s washed down with a pint.      I do miss the diversity of eating in South Africa, though. It’s chaotic but brilliant—there’s always something smoky, spicy, or sweet happening. But this roast, paired with that potato dauphinoise baked by Enid, will have to do for now.      Don’t give him too much credit, Rachel. I did the waiting on the oven while the sprouts boiled and the carrots roasted. And if it’s the lunches we’ve shared during the week that you’re missing, I’d be surprised if you’re not growing a second stomach.      I think it was more of a shared work of art—collaboration, not competition. And we were all involved in different ways. Pass the gravy, Enid, will you? I’ve had enough roles in the kitchen for one evening.

Rather annoying advert just popped up on my phone ‘ere, tellin’ me abou’ ‘travel like a local’ an’ all. As if I ain’t already travelled enough by bus every day!      Charming as the bus is, you could take things a little more leisurly if you liked. I’m just sayin’. Still, I reckon that ad’s trying to sell you something only a millionaire could afford.      Oh aye, I know! Look it, why don’t  we  decide what “local” really means? Like, not just fetchin’ a coffee from Lakelands and calling it a short holiday. Proper city sommat? Somewhere that ain’t just another bit o’ concrete and left-lane drivers.      D’you mean like Bristol? Fair enough, I suppose. It’s got a nice balance o’ old and new. You’d like the docklands there — artsy and posh, but not too posh, even if I say so meself.      Naa, you know I loved York too. Got some decent pubs, quite a few historic bits. And the welcome, it still felt like they cared about tourists, proper ones, not just people who left litter.      York, yeah. And it’s not like we’ve had a proper break in ages, have we? Maybe we could make it a weekend away? Thursday night, back by Sunday? Book a place online, get us a cottage or sommat.      That’d be nice, yeah. Cos I’m gettin’ bored at home all week, in and out o’ the same five places. Tyne and Wear’s the place for me, but even I can take only so much o’ it. Not that I’d live anywher’ else, mind. My grandma ‘ud have me treed.      Aye, me mam’s the same. She’d give me the talking to if I tried to move further than London. Not that I’d  want  to. Even if it’s London proper, I miss the quieter bits. Not sayin’ Manchester’s too loud, mind — nice enough.      Mancunian life? Nah. If I go north, I’m going in the other direction entirely. Somewhere with beaches an’ cafes what stay open past five. Maybe even somewhere I can manage a day without a coat on.      It’s a plan, then. Choose a city, book the tickets, and try not to bungle it all up. You know what they say — “two can cook, two can clean, two can holiday.”      Two can  dream  at least. Should I check the weather in Bristol or York first?

Rather annoying the queue at the surgery this morning, wasn't it? I had to get my blood pressure checked before the scan. Never mind, at least they sorted it out quickly. I've been dreading this whole thing.      That's awful—get through it now and it's behind you. My dear mum, bless her soul, was gone just over a year ago now. It's still a bit raw, but I think I'm handling it better. The funeral was a comfort, terribly sad, of course. We had to keep it small for the pandemic, but it was touching how many came through for her.      Oh, I'm so sorry to hear that. That must have been difficult. My brother had a bit of meltdowns around the house when Dad passed, to be honest. Darcy, he was—just sat in his room for days, wouldn’t eat. Made quite an impression on the rest of us to see him like that.      You ever notice how we never really prepare for those sorts of things? One minute, your bloke’s alive and tellin' tales, and the next he’s gone. It’s a rude shock. Did grief support help you deal with it? I didn't have the nerve to go myself, but Darcy said it was a bit of help, just knowing he wasn't the only one trying to cope.      A little, yes. You know what it's like—some people find it helpful, others just want to get on with it. I suppose everyone has a different way. I had a proper cry in the bath one night and then just worked through it slowly. Not that I’m over it, mind you. I do miss him.      No need to be over it—just be there for each other. Going back to the topic of the week, if you're having scans and appointments, are they keeping you on tight for that blood pressure? I did cut sods of weight off last year after a few heart scare comments from my doc.      I did stick to my good friend, Dr. Spooner, and cut out the lunches of sandwiches and chips with tea. Now I meal plan like mad—grilled fish, salads, boiled eggs the kids hate. Actually, my youngest son started losing weight after seeing me go at it.      Oh, they always notice, blokes like that. My daughter’s at the gym twice a week now, ever since I started doing yoga.

Rather skip ahead a bit here. So I sat at my desk glueing wires for hours, real string and... What was I doing? Oh yes, I was proofreading! That's my livelihood, after all. I help small businesses get their marketing right before it goes live — brochures, websites, that sort of thing. Keeps the mind ticking over.      I read your last newsletter on a train. A lot of people would think that sounds dull, but I quite enjoyed seeing how things get polished like that. We've been removing errors at work this week — when it's the formulae not the grammar, but it's much the same idea.      I found it easier working on the website that Myra redesigned. I liked how she changed the photo sizes. They were all skewey before.      I think the world is crying out for rules for imagery as much as it does for spelling. I’ve spent this past week returning a dozen emails replying to the same five questions again — mostly, "Does this button size work on a phone?" or, "Can I do this if I change the font?" It takes forever.      We had to redesign the welcome page for the school newsletter in Word. I tried to make it look like the old one so no one else had to bother with formatting, but still, it took all day. I wish I'd known about proofreaders like you, Aunty.      And let’s not even talk about skiing in the Alps last week. That was real chaos. Trying to run a trip on snow and getting emails at 2 a.m. from a client asking whether the lift cable cars worked as "live interactive displays about sustainability." I told them the cable cars just went up and down.      You and your projects are brutal, Martin! I’m jealous. I’d be in tears. My idea of complicated is reformatting guest speaker bios at the last minute — and I remember once a client sent a pic of their kid instead of their portrait!      My ski lessons were good, though. My instructor said I looked like a goat on ice a couple of times, but I took the snow plow route and got the hang of it.      goats on ice — well, that's not a description I've heard before. I’ll remember that when someone asks me how I’m coping with the client from hell.

Rather skip ahead a bit, eh? You remember when we did that photography trip in Norfolk, back when we... got the camera from your aunt?      Oh, I remember! That camera was ancient, wasn’t it? I’m surprised it even worked after all those years in a shed. Got one photo and it liked the idea of badgers, didn’t he?      Oh aye. A real life-changing moment, that was. I had no idea you could take a picture without someone screaming. We ended up with six shots and a very surprised-looking badger.      Right, because of course you  had  to go silent when the thing emerged only feet away from us like that. I still can’t believe you remembered to switch the camera off automatic! I’m terrified I’d end up with a dozen sad blur lights.      Well, I try to make something out of myself every now and then. Anyway, after that little badger incident, you ever considered taking photos seriously, even back then?      I mean, I adored it, yes—there was something about capturing the world in short bursts, not as it is, but as it  could  be. It gave me a bit of a rhythm in teaching. You know how most kids just look at things with sheer boredom, and sometimes it feels like trying to teach the weather.      Fair enough. You know what struck me about our trip? It was the simplest of things. The way the light hit the meadow, or the rush of excitement when we spotted the fox in the long grass. It reminded me why I still travel. Not for all the big things, but because sometimes it’s the little ones—like badgers standing on their hind legs—that keep you going.      Going back to Japan then—ah, that was a  very  different kind of photo trip for you. I still get a bit jealous of your friend Aiko’s photos. You looked like a scholar holding all those scrolls in Kyoto.      I did not. I looked like I was about to trip over every damn stone with a scroll in hand and ruin Japanese history.      Still, I’m happy you went. I mean, I can go for weeks on pond life if you like.      I do. Just no badger photos anymore—please, let them live in your head alone. I’ve had enough nightmares.      Fair enough. But one day I’ll publish that badger book.

Rather annoying when a barista takes 10 minutes to do a coffee, dontcha think?      Never had no luck with baristas. I prefer a good ol’ cup of tea first thing in the morn'. No messing about.      Haber lech een? That’s  not  a bad one.      Lmao, don’t start that again, I still can’t laugh too much or my ribs hurt from last time.      You remember the time us and Alex tried to skinny dip in the River Tore? Only like three decent onions.      Oh God the cold, I can still feel it like yesterday.      The chill left my bones for about a week. I reckon the Dandelions pick and choose what they want to talk about most of the time. Cats are better company.      Well, not all of us can live off gingerbread and milk!      Milk helps a lot, actually, for bloating. I do tell you—personally I think Claudia Roden put in a lot of heart to her writing and food. Recipe for today? Try this honey on pitta, extra rhythm in it.      Mate, I got fairly radical with my photo app the other day. I had a sombrero on a fried chicken and it looked  amazing .      Like those fake filters? Nah, full on. Strictly for laughs.      I do wonder what you’d all do if a zombie apocalypse started and it poured non-stop rain for  weeks . Stuck in your bungalow with no milk.      I’d take the lino off and fold it into a cap. Proper survival skills.      Maybe I'd do something like read some poetry. There’s something about expressing oneself clearly, even if no one else is listening.      If there’s no one about, you just sort of stick out to the side and sing a joke. Even if it’s not funny. Classic Jewish style.      My grandad used to tell these jokes and say things like 'it's goin' on your slab!' If he had a go at me now, I’d say 'well it's goin' on yours!'      So how have things been at the café, Haz?      Quiet weekend, but I’ve been trying new recipes for latkes—trying to get that perfect texture. I’m not entirely there yet.      My kind of thing, all the gnashin' and dashin' done for me and the dirty oven’s got to do it before midnight.      I reckon if you're lucky, you'll still have a few sweet treats on the shelf when the lights inevitably go out.

Rather annoying when a bar of peanuts finds its way into a slot of a handheld console, innit? Mind you, I've done it once after a trip to Blenheim Palace with me mate. Fancied ourselves doing a fancy £20 meal, and then we were picking our teeth in a carpark at half two in the morning playing  The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild .      Oh, I've had worse! One too many at Alton Towers, and I ended up pulling someone else’s USB drive out the back of me laptop instead of me own. Let's just say I saw some very personal Star Citizen builds. Bit harsh when you've got the security guard giving you a hard time about that one, eh?      Yeah, security—what a mess. I reckon theme parks should have their own little customs or something? Half the time I’m at a park, it’s like, “Do you need to go through here or can I just hug the wall for five miles and get told off by a man in a costume?” One time, I was taking me younger cousin to Legoland, and I swear, the guy in the T-rex suit was muttering in Polish.      Sounds like watching a bit of a classic West End film got you rattled at the park. Speaking of films, last night, I watched  Blade Runner 2049  and just couldn’t stop thinking about what it said about borders—real and metaphorical. Like, someone who looks human but isn’t given a nationality—count em as one or not at all?      Aye, real thought provokin’, innit? I did a bit of reading at uni about how national borders are often the same as the ones that separate different regions in games. You’ve got this invisible barrier you can’t cross until you get the key or whatever. It’s the same nonsense in real life—just no developer’s note at the end giving explanation.      Exactly. You know, I once tried to hack a game just to remove a wall so the protagonist didn’t have to do the same old fetch quest. Instead of playing a role-playing game, I ended up doing a role-playing exercise on a forum saying I’d like a passport with an extra go at life on it.      You mean like a  Diablo  password that transfers to a new box?

Rather skip the mushy peas today, love. Just give me a sprig of it, if it's not too much trouble. And maybe a bit more vinegar than I'd usually say, if you don't mind.      No worries at all—get the extra dip on me. Been good on your feet since that last bout of flu, I see. Ay, I read your cousin Nell has been in hospital? I hope it's nothing too serious.      It was, for a little while. Put her in the hospital for a few weeks when it hit the worst. But she’s on the mend now. Lakelands is still a mess, the last I heard, but she managed to get the turkey shop sorted before it all went to left field. Remember when we used to sneak off to Dorest and pick blackberries in the patch by her aunt's barn?      Good times, good times. I've been thinking about Lakelands ever since my brother showed up out of the blue, unannounced. We hadn't seen one another since Dad's funeral over three years ago—personally, it was the last thing I expected. What did he say, grief bridged something old?      Bloke's got rhythm in him. Was it awkward?      Only initially. But I think it's important to mend broken things, you know? Like when you started learning to row. I remember you told me it was the first time you'd ever sat in a boat without floundering. You had a time of it, souring on what you were doing at first.      Still do most days. I'm alright when there's a steady current helping me along—like the Cam here—but when the wind's contrary, I'm a mess. My colleague at the school got me into kayaking up near Grantchester last spring; said something about ‘stability and syncing’ or other fancy schmancy words. I nearly ended up in the river a few too many times.      A little splash never did anyone any harm. At least that's what I told my grandkid when she wanted a new waterproof jacket—didn't do the smart thing and invest in a serious one. Now she's the one who's go-to when it's mud-and-squirtle weekend at the camping club.      Never could go wrong with the right gear. Pass me that salt shaker, will you? Ay, and speaking of squelching—did I tell you about that time I walked into the sermon at aunt Evelyne’s wake and slipped on the floor?

Rather annoying when the phone’s on 1%. Thought me Mam’s promising me her tablet ‘til tomorrow. I got to text Gran she’s coming now.      Don’t ye best use yer phone in full signal area then lass? Be as if I wouldn’t be getting a proper phone on Vodafone if I didn’t take one for meself. Ay, I read all them texts on a paper. A lot too slow for me old brain.      Grandad would know that it’s called Morse code, like the old radio signals. But he messes with me phone too much. Said I should learn it.      What’s that now?      It’s like sending messages with dots and dashes. Like this…  long pause  I dunno. He says it’s good for the brain. Or something like that.      Hmm, old-fashioned I’d say. Less interruptions for ye then at least, eh? Listen, we best get to the shop. We got the food shopping to do for tomorrow’s dinner with the aunties.      I’m not going without shoes to be honest Pa. Gave me fancy shoes from eBay… Delivery was Amazon, so it was quick. Look, they’re real – no fake ones this time!      Good thing. Let’s have a glance. Aye, they look grand. Bit brighter ‘n what I’d expect, but fair play. Who said anything about dress-uping for a simple family dinner?      Some things matter, Pa. It’s like money and being proper. Can I borrow more from Student Finance for stuff? I did get me results finally!      Well, I had to wait a week for my payslip to be processed. Supposed to handle it fast, Vodafone to the bank, but that lot’s like waiting for mail in the 50s. Signals dawdled. Let me see those results.      You’ll see when we get to the uni. I’m going to live there. Garden with glass water bottles and big stationery. Not just the plastic ones from the chemist. Proper recycled glass. Eco-friendly, Pa!      Haha. If it survives one week wi’ me in, I’d be surprised. Who lives in gardens now?      It’s about memories, Pa. Like how ye told me when you were a lad ye used to go to Bolton on the bus for ‘a proper pen’ from Woolworths.      Aye, and they were the days. Lot of loafing, but things were cheaper. Still, I suppose now it’s all about surviving the real world, and before that, surviving the text messages with those bloody emojis!

Yo, mate, haven't seen you in what feels like ages. You just get back from uni or...?      Yeah, just finished my last term at the uni in St Pancras. How about you? Still working on that dissertation?      Nah, I handed that in a week ago. Finally free! I haven't celebrated properly yet—been stuck on my laptop writing up references for days. Got side-tracked by a YouTube rabbit hole about Japan last week, honestly. Ended up downloading three documentaries and a manga series.      Oh yeah? I like to think of it as  productive procrastination . Besides, Japan’s wild, right? I've been doing some research on Tokyo for my exchange application—it could actually work this time! I’m applying for the winter semester next year and I think I finally got all my docs in order.      No way! You've been trying for like... three years, at least. And the uni in Tokyo, you remember that one time when I came to your house and you told me you got rejected because your essay was about anime and the impacts of short attention spans on youth culture?         Wasn't  that  bad... Well, maybe just a little. Point is, I’m taking it more seriously now. I’ve even been learning Japanese online, using some of those new AI tools—makes it easier to understand grammar and stuff.      That’s cool. I tried a language app a while back, but I gave up because I got bored with the same questions about my cat and my morning routine. What’s the university like over in Japan?      From what I’ve read, the structure is different—less emphasis on exams and more on research. I know that sounds like a dream, but it does mean you have to do your own time management. I’ve got friends who went over there last year—they said the food’s insane. You could probably eat all day and still find another ramen place.      You know what that makes me think of? That Indian-inspired lunches we used to have at your mum’s? Remember when we tried to recreate a  ramen burger  with the kebab shop gochujang? It was a catastrophe.      Oh yeah! We were eating bean sprouts with what can only be described as  clash-of-the-continents  sauce. Still, those afternoons had to count for something right? I mean, where were we if not ambitious?

Rather annoying Facebook keeps deleting my photos. You know when you do that thing where you post it public so they stop removing them?      It's not public by default these days, is it? You've got to be quite careful. That said, what photos were you trying to post?      Some from last weekend at Buckfast Abbey. I reckon it's about time we all went on a day trip like that. The walk around the abbey, the gardens, and the views from the top were spot on.      Oh aye, I remember the last time I went there like it was yesterday.
