Mary climbed the tower like a young lass, and I was stuck on the ground floor catching my breath. You’ve still got my left leg in storage, by the way.      [Laughing] A bit of a hill for dear old David, perhaps. But honestly, it was lovely. I've been thinking, maybe for our next trip we could try the coast. Maybe Bude or even take a little short cruise from Plymouth?      A cruise, eh? Sounds like a good idea. I never did quite get on to the boat early in the morning with the coffee in hand and watching the sun rise over the water. Mind you, I’m not denying that it looked nice on the brochure!      Honestly, the weather is getting quite odd these days. Seems like it was meant to be lovely this weekend and we had rain all day. Who knows what it will be like next. At least a cruise would give us some shelter from the floring!      I've been looking at a few websites for future getaways. You know, about travel packages and insurance? With everything that's going on with David Cameron and tax avoidance stuff, you never know what is coming next.      Tax avoidance? Come to think of it, that reminds me. My sister had an interesting tale about her tax return at her age. Thought they sent something wrong, it turned out it was accurate. Not unlike my GP visit last week, had me in for a full check-up and it turned out I just need more vitamins and less steak.      Still, I did run into a bit of trouble with my car goin' on the blink about a week ago. Just wouldn't start at all. Had to get it towed in, bloke said it might be some dodgy battery or something.

Rather annoying driving up from Kent last Sunday — sat nav decided to send us down this winding little B road and I got turned around half a dozen times before I found the hotel! How on earth did you two manage to make it all the way to Belgium?      Oh, well, I’ve always een good with my wits and a good map,   love  . My George — bless his stubborn soul — just wanted to rely entirely on the sat nav and insisted on taking the most scenic of scenic routes! We ended up in some wine-growing village where the woman at the gas station gave me a map and wrote instructions in three languages! Still couldn’t read half of it, mind.      Oh, that  does  sound typical George! I swear, he’s one of those people who thinks if the sat nav says “drive for two hours,” the car’s got an inbuilt helicopter just waitin’. But breakfasts in Belgium, that was a treat! Haha, ever had those thick-crusted milk chocolates that melt on your tongue before they get to the wrapper?      I know the ones! We had them in Brussels — I think the baron said it was made in Wallonia or something. Everything we tried was so much richer than back home. And then all the fruit markets! You remember?      Oh aye, the fresh strawberries! I had a whole punnet every mornin’ with tea. Bit of a luxury, eh? And the woman at the market spoke not a jot of English. Just grinned and pointed a lot, bless her.      Also, have you seen the way the fruit is displayed? Rows and  rows  of strawberries, raspberries, and those big Belgian tomatoes — you could spoon them into a bowl and call it a cooking lesson.      Honestly, I considered staying for the summer! Maybe rent a bike and cycle up to the coast. Enid, you passed on cycling with me and George, but the cycleroute was bloody nice! There were flat paths, bikes for hire everywhere...      Oh, I know, love, but with me back and knees? No thank you! I’m happy with a stroller for now, after a day or two! Still, the weather go bad on you two?      Just one day of rain, but the innkeeper had a spare set of boots by the door. Very thoughtful. George made me tea with this honey from the region and said it was the start of something romantic.

Rather do this than watch telly, innit? Bit easier than the hurly-burly in town... What d'you think of the fire today, love? Not too much smoke, is it?      No, seems fine. Just as long as the things in it don't catch on flame and we end up with a trisht      kitchen all over again. I remember that pan from when we first moved in—do you?           Oh aye, that was the one that nearly met its maker, or the fire extinguisher did... Right, let's get these courgettes ready before the pot's out of the oven. I've made that new turkey stock you said you love. Hope you’re not allergic to turmeric this time!      Turmeric in the turkey? Is that an Edinbugh thing you’re trying out, or are you just pulling my leg again?           Neither—and don't flatter yourself too much—this one’s just for us tonight, not a dinner party. I thought we could keep it to ourselves. Invite only real friends... Like Alice from Facebook, whom we haven’t met but nonetheless claim to know.      Alice from Facebook’s not even in our group, Hayley. She keeps commenting on photos of yours and calling you ‘Jayne’! She probably thinks you’re your sister, and then thinks this is a full-blown reunion. Just ignore her.      Oh aye—  ignore her?       Says you. You're the one who thought it was romantic to have about forty friends from your marketing days you've never even e-mailed back. Not much of a friend circle if you ask me.           Well, for heaven’s sake, not every bit of friendship is based on dinner parties and candlelit dinners. Some of ‘em are just there, like a Facebook frie...      Like a  friend sprite  or something?   .   Well, I do have proper ones. Like that Tom from the hairdresser who always chats about his cat as if it’s on the Royal Thai Railway or something.      Tom in the gel nails green coat?      Aye, him. Every time I go in I get 30 minutes of his cat's tea preferences, never mind the new cut!      Perks of being the only one who listens. I tell you, my lot of friends are all into perfumes and chemical ingredients. Always asking me to smell something or other...      Like the roses used in real perfume, you mean?      Not as hassle-free as this lot, though.

Rather unusual to find oneself in a room full of utter strangers, isn't it? Though I've lived in Bristol all my life, I rarely meet folk from so far afield. Sheffield, Manchester, and a retired EFL teacher from Gloucestershire… I declare, it's quite like a cross-section of old England! I've met more Australians in my time, though. Funny thing is, they tend not to dress like bankers—they prefer a bit more casual in this heat, wouldn't you say?      Oh aye, nothing like the business men's style back in Manchester or London. When I was a director, I had to make sure I looked sharp regardless of the weather, but when I went to visit Queensland on business, I noticed folks dressing more loosely. The sun is brutal there! I had to pick up a few shirts and sandals just to blend in properly. Living in Manchester, you’ve got to have something a bit more formal if you want to be taken seriously.      Aye, we're not all stuck in suits and ties up in Sheffield. We’ve got a dialect that’s just as loud as our personality. Though I have to say, Southerners do seem to take the whole "business as usual" thing much more seriously. I remember one of my students told me she was confused when I said "Cheers" meaning thank you, because down South it means something totally different! Now don’t get me wrong, I still know what to say in a proper room full of bankers.      That reminds me of my teaching days in Bristol. Trying to explain to a group of students from all over the world the difference between "cheers," "thank you," and "well done" in context about as exciting as watching paint dry! But the thing that fascinated them the most was the whole business of accents. Going to Australia was like watching a linguistic switch flipped—the English turned into something quite recognisable but with such a warm, laid-back ring to it.      I’ve done business in both Bristol and Sydney. Interesting how Australia took what we had and sort of tamed it into their own. Though being from a business background, I’ve to mention the whole bank loans situation—Down Under, it's easier to get something approved with a bit of charm and a good go-to-meeting man.

Rather annoying, the amount of time people spend swiping on that phone thing, dontcha think? I was sat next to a couple at the local dining hall, and I swear neither of them looked up once! It is as if they cannot speak without the blinking thing being involved.      Oh, I hear you, Mum. It is very annoying. But if you think about it, they might be missing something—they might not have seen the best episode of  The Crown  since Queen Elizabeth was in a horse race. We’ve been bingeing the latest series. It is brilliant, the drama. You'd probably like it more than some of that old soaps you used to watch on ITV.      My soaps? Oh, you mean  Coronation Street , back in the day. I still catch a bit of it sometimes. A good little hour to take in the problems of old Mrs. McDonald breakfast, no doubt. But this  Crown  business—sounds a bit posh for me! No, you know what I have been enjoying? One of those  Sounds  ones—about true crime and detectives, I listen to it while I’m baking cookies.      Oh,  Crime Junkie , is that it? I tried that one a little while back. Gripping, but very dark. I prefer my podcasts cheery—like  How I Built This  or some of those TED Talks. You should try one, it is a good way to wind down and still feel like someone is talking to you without you needing to read or type. Besides, I can do the dishes while I listen!      Oh, well I suppose I could make time for it! You know I do enjoy a bit of a story, just the right length to match a cuppa and a biscuit. Speaking of which, do you think they serve digestive biscuits here, or are we just getting some ‘vegan baked treacle waters’? I tried one once on holiday, and well, it was a bit too wooden for my taste.      Haha, I hope not! They do have a nice selection of cakes here, though. Try the chocolate avocado mud cake—it is surprisingly good. I’d steer clear of the digestive ‘vstamp’ they have on the go—unless you fancy it tasting like a slightly broken pencil. But really, do you think they’d serve us with mud cake and then say it is your fault we didn’t like it?

Rather annoyingly, I haven't been able to get anyone to talk about this internet mystery yet. Have  either  of you heard of it?      Not really, Mrs. Reddie! What is it? A new video or something?      Nooo, it’s that Chinese thing about eating  old eggs  with rice and vegetables and stuff.      Oh aye! A lot of people have been discussing this on social media. It’s called  pidan , or hundred-year eggs. It was originally a version of Chinese preserved egg, but the process has changed over time. It's more of a  60-day egg  now.      That  sounds  delicious, honestly. I’ve never eaten it before. It doesn't actually taste like old eggs, though?      Fair enough! But here's the thing — the old methods involved burying the eggs in mud and ash for months, which made them hard and sort of black and looked like they'd been cooked in tar. Modern methods still use similar processes, but with chemicals and shortcuts.      Who eats it, though? Is it a snack or is it like food for grandmas?      Good question, Jamie! Well, it’s more of a side – normally it's served sliced with rice and/or pickles. It’s popular in parts of southern China and has made its way into high-end Chinese restaurants in the West as well. It’s kind of like someone took a fertilised ostrich egg and made it a delicacy.      Ugh, is it  smelly  then? Like stinky tofu?      A little, about as bad as your brother's socks. But it still tastes like egg, just… a  bit more intense .      Doesn't sound uncool, but I'm not sure I'd like it. What do you think passedover?      Honestly, it sounds a bit too adventurous for me. I tried squid once and that was enough!      Fair. Jamie’s clearly out for it too with that face. It’s one of those things that's more interesting when you  hear  about it than when you  try  it. But really, pond life, it's not about the taste alone.      What  is  it about, then?      It's about fermentation, tradition, and conservation. Back in the old days, when fresh food was scarce, this was a way to keep eggs without overcooking them or losing them to spoilage. It’s kind of like pickling, but with a completely different ingredient.      So, it’s like a taste of history and the dirty places it’s been?

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know, me an’ Jake had this kinda thing ‘appen like... every weekend. But lately, it’s like he don’t fancy it no more. It’s not like we don’t wanna, it’s more like... he says he  wanna , but then it don’t... y’know. Work out.      Oh no! That  is  awkward. A lot o’ blokes get this stuff, though. You said he was stressed, or summat?      That’s what he said when I asked him. Told me it’s pressure from work. But  Mate , I’ve seen him play video games and laugh like mad in the pub an’ still get it up! So I think it’s more about him, not the situation.      I think he migh’ be gettin’ a bit nervous ‘bout performin’. A lot of blokes worry about not... y’know... being any good. It’s weird, innit? Cos they think that the more they stress ‘bout it, the more it should get fixed, but it just makes it worse.      Could be grief. He  has  been goin' on about how tired he is. He’s got this job at the uni library part-time, an’ he’s doin’ his A levels. Maybe his body just don’t wanna cope with all that pressure? I dunno.      There’s also this thing called erectile dysfunction. I read summat abou' it once. It can happen when someone’s had stress, or anxiety, or even if they’re unwell. Doesn’t mean it’s permanent, most o’ the time. But he does need to talk to someone professional, not just vibes off a friend.      I know! I tried suggestin’ we went to see the doc, but he said no way. Said he’d “wait a few weeks and see.” An’ it’s been three bloody weeks already.      Blokes are rubbish at admitin’ they’re not 100%, innit? I’ve got a cousin whos been doin’ the same thing. Still laughin’, still nice t’her, but when it go’ serious it just... stopped. It wasn’t realtil much later she figured out he’d had some kidney stuff goin’ on.      Shaw. I just wish I didn’t feel like we was stuck in a loop. I don’t like worryin’ like this. I want ‘im to be happy, and I want  us  to... go back to bein' how we was.      And you  will , but you’ve got to be alright ‘bout talkin’ to him, and maybe even pushin’ ‘im a bit gently.

Rather annoying I can't take any of the sw01 syns sticks on my own, they’re like... What's the word? Like balsa wood, not even wood at all.      Yeah, honestly, I feel like I've been gymplying them all week trying to get soft enough to bite, I gave up today and just ate one of the midget Gems in my bag.      Fair enough! Honestly I don’t care about the syns anymore, I just want soft food.      Didn’t you get the pot of vegan pesto I frozen to add to baked potato?      No, I only grabbed the double peas from the freezer turkey, I haven’t even made my left over roast this week! I’m going back to the supermarket tomorrow, and I think I'll just buy the most expensive kale they’ve got to make me breakfast, no doubt it’s covered in some fancy preservatives in there.      No, you can’t buy kale tomorrow, we need to divide your budget with me and do shop together otherwise we will spend too much and I can't keep splitting your tax to cover your grief.      Oh please, we’ve known each other for six months and you still call it my “grief”. I’m not in denial, just in a bit of a deep fryer phase.      If I could blame the fryer for the fact that I've gained ten pounds in four months, I wouldn’t even be a carer, I’d definitely buy out the fryer and weigh my legs and call it being “prioritised”.      Not nearly about to fall off the wagon for you, but talking of which, I had to delete Siri on my phone because it keeps answering my questions and I end up not doing any exercise.      Trust me, if you had my calendar full of sundowners and exercise, you wouldn’t delete anything.      Guess I will just have to sort out a reward Saturday, as long as we can both agree to not break the 'no syns' regime!      Defo, I’m bringing my best spice mix, and we can go for a walk before we order something or cook up a proper pre made ready meal in the oven, I don’t want to be binging on what your scale tells you. It said I was 20 kgs last week and that can’t possibly be right because I still fit into my tight jeans from two years ago.

Rather than going the usual route of booking a swanky resort for our holiday this year, I've been thinking... What if we try something different? Like road-tripping through France? I've always wanted to take in the countryside at a slower pace. What do you think?      Road-tripping? That sounds like a nice change of pace, but I haven't driven on the continent in years. I remember that A360 tends to get a bit dodgy in the rain. Imagine me swerving like it’s a go-kart race. Still, the idea of getting off the beaten track isn’t a bad one.      I was hoping you'd like it, actually. You know I like that sort of thing. I’ve already sketched out a basic route from Calais to the southwest—maybe even up through the Loire Valley. I’ve even thought of making a short documentary of it. I've been feeling more motivated to write and create lately.      And what exactly would that documentary look like? Are we expecting a critical analysis of regional architecture, or will it be more of a 'Here I am, slightly sunburned, eating a croissant' flick?      A bit of both, maybe. I'd love to write from the road. It's just such a freeing environment. I can imagine writing postcards from every town we pass through—real ones, not just emails. Silly, I know, but it feels meaningful in a strange kind of way.      Let me guess—this is the same woman who left a detailed note in each of our suitcases in Florence last year. Still, I like the idea. If you’re writing, I suppose I could try to figure out what our perfect day would be while we're there. I’ve been wondering about that for a while.      Our perfect day? Well, for me, it would be waking up late, curling up by the window with a book, a pot of tea, and you bringing me something warm to eat. Not much else, honestly. Not even the Eiffel Tower.      And what about a hypothetical perfect day related to politics? Since you've been so passionate about it lately.      Oh, go on then. A perfect day politically would be one where I see real, active progress—maybe a green hydrogen plant in Northamptonshire, or Kettering with a proper cycle track system. I’ve been writing to the council more than usual, honestly.

Rather lovely to have you here for dinner, old chap. I do confess, it's been a string of rainy afternoons, and having you over has put some colour in the week.      I must say, the roast was spot on. You've picked up Martha’s recipe well. She always said the key was the horseradish and thyme variation.      Oh aye, I had notes. Not that one reads cookbooks, but Martha had a habit of scribbling little reminders in her own hand. "Second time lucky," she’d always say. Tore her recipe books to bits, really.      All the better to cook by heart. On the note of what’s coming up, I did get the postcard from you about Scotland, didn’t I? Dazzling hills and all. A world away from the usual drizzle about Crickhowell, I imagine.      Ah, aye, it’s been a charmer of a holiday, though not without its controversies. I still don’t see why the independence debate won’t just die a quiet death. These places aren’t built in a day.      It’s not for the faint-hearted, that’s for sure. But it does make for good postcard subjects at least. Should have got a few more in, because tomorrow’s Jim’s birthday. You remember the gathering at that little pub near Silke?      Silke? The one by the canal? Yes, yes. He always does his best to draw the old lot out. I assume it’s still the usual lot: Terry and his wife being their usual curious selves, and that new chap Neil, still trying to make sense of the local ale?      Oh, Neil’s progressing — or so he claims. Drink-wise, at least. But it is a reminder, isn’t it, that time hasn’t just left us behind. All passed 50, and some of us older. Still holding on to the traditions.      Aye, I’d say. As long as we can still walk the walk and talk the talk. Speaking of which, what are the plans for the weekend? You set anything in the Midlands with the lads?      Work on Saturday morning, then a meet-up at the technical conference in Leicester in the afternoon. You know how it is — the Midlands love a proper opportunity to talk specs at tea time. But perhaps we can manage a drive out your way after that?      Do come over. I’ve been meaning to give you a look at the new extension.

Rather than just a chair, Arabella, can I see what you've drawn for the Syrian refugees? We were talking in class about how art can help make a difference. I asked the kids to think creatively about how they can support people who are far away and in need.      I drew a chair, and on the seat I put a smiley face and some stars. I wanted them to feel a bit happier when they sit on it.      Miss, I drew a bed, not just a chair! My teacher was saying the children might need more than just a seat. I thought they’d like to lie down and rest too.      That’s lovely, Oliver. It shows you were thinking of their comfort. Now, who can tell me what sort of chair they think is best for someone who’s tired and sad?      Maybe a soft one, like the one we have on the sofa?      Hmmm, a recliner, you mean?      Or maybe a throne? They might like to feel important like a king or queen, even for a little bit.      A throne! Now that's a grand idea, Oliver. Imagine designing a special chair for someone who’s been through a difficult time. It's not just about comfort but also dignity and hope. And that's what your drawings are doing.      Miss, do you think the Syrian kids can see our pictures? Like, maybe the grown-up someone sends our drawings to them?      Oh, Arabella, I do hope so. Sometimes letters and artworks get sent to refugee camps through charities. I actually had a colleague who taught in a school about forty miles from the border with Syria. He used to collect kids' drawings and they said they gave them out to young people in the camps. It sounds cruel, but it can also be something beautiful they hang on the wall or put in a notebook.      Miss, will it help them pass their tests?      Well, not passing a math test, maybe, but learning that they are not forgotten can always help with their confidence. And speaking of tests—you both took your recent class tests last week, right?      Mmm, go me! I got a 10 out of 10.      I had a 9, but I lost a mark because I forgot to add all the commas in the question.      Well done to both of you. It's important to keep practising, and over time, the commas and the spelling will get easier.

Rather annoyingly, I haven't seen anything from the old history group yet this term. They've been so busy with the conference, I suppose. Remember how they used to meet up every Sunday after lectures?      Yeah, I know what you mean—somehow, things just haven't been the same without them. I remember we used to sit in that little café on the high street, making fun of everyone’s A-level notes. Do you ever wonder what they’re all up to now?      Honestly? I'm just grateful my students this term aren't quite as chaotic as ours were back then. It's enough of a challenge when you're dealing with 20-somethings trying to figure out what lectures are for. Still, I suppose it’s fitting—our group was the real wild card in the department, wasn’t it?      Definitely, definitely. Catsfield definitely had a way of finding us late at night. Reminds me—before she went back to the States last year, she gave us those adorable baby clothes. Good thing, too, I think the weather here is a bit too cold for tiny cotton onesies.      Oh, I love those, by the way—every time I see the elephant onesie in the drawer, I grin. Poor thing was almost completely outgrown by last week, though. You'd think we were raising an elephant by the way he kept growing! Honestly, what amazes me is how quickly the days fly by. Last week at the park, someone dropped him off and just a few minutes later came to collect him—looked like he aged ten years while I was being left alone with him!      You're not about to fall off the wagon with the “how fast the baby is growing” vibes, are you? We're not old yet!      Touch wood, but I'd have to say time has never passed so fast. Although I will admit, when I'm at work, the day feels long. It's just the moment I start thinking about him waiting at home, all the time just... compresses itself.      Yeah, I keep meaning to message James about the weekend tour. I think he's delivering something around this area. Last time he came up, he really wanted to see if we'd kept up with our prehistoric posters on the walls.      That bloke never stopped being your biggest fan. So, have you made the call?

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? I needed this walk. The university has been such a whirlwind with all the publicity from our new program launch last week. I can't say I'm entirely enthusiastic about being suddenly thrown into the spotlight.      It's well worth the chaos, if it's all going to plan. I heard one of the students saying he watched the announcement on their morning commute—it’s that kind of stuff which tends to catch on. I, on the other hand, was quite entertained by that journey! You remember the ridiculous number of red lights we hit, don't you? I swear I felt like every policeman around united just to give us a hard time.      Oh yes, that was a journey! I was half-expecting someone’s cow to start walking down the middle of the马路. But I digress. Do you remember that comedy festival in Norfolk about a year ago? I must've laughed until tears came out just watching those street performers in the pouring rain, planting five oversized daffodils to “lure the sun” because of some superstition about planting in odd numbers?      Of course I remember! And the one about the baker trying to tell jokes with flour as a prop. The only thing funnier than his jokes was the audience sneezing at the end of every one. I think I actually made myself a superstition back then. I pinched a leaf from one of their daffodils and stuck it in my wallet, claiming it's what helped me win the best lecturer award the next term.      How very you—superstitious and a bit mad at the same time. I still carry that leaf, in fact! You know, about the publicity... I've been thinking quite a bit lately about how we present our institution. We need to make it more relatable. I've got this idea about sending lecturers to do guest performances at local comedy nights. Envision it: A maths professor with a script full of equations as one-liners. It's either going to be a hit or a complete disaster!      Now  that  sounds like a holiday project! Imagine us taking a sabbatical next summer to do the whole country tour—Norfolk to London with our academic-inspired comedy. I can go as a pretend police officer if you promise not to go over your notes! What do you think, will they clap along with our bad puns or just throw virtual tomatoes?

Rather annoying this new phone of mine. You know, dad, everything's just an app now. Even remembering to update them is a full-time job on its own. I can't even call you sometimes unless I open it first. Not like your landline, which just works — well, when it's not broken anyway!      Aye, I know what you mean. It’s not for a man of my age, this modern lot. Why'd I need a phone that does everything? I just want to ring and chat to you like a proper telephone. The other day I tried using that mobile you bought me to take a photo, and IManaged to delete my addressbook by mistake.      My word, did I not show you how to photo one properly? Probably need to show you again, dad, properly and slowly. A bit like how I did with the steam fair tickets — online booking doesn’t come easy if you've never done it before. The Great Dorset’s next weekend, remember? You said you wanted to go see that old tractor they brought back from the fifties.      Aye, I do — quite a marvel to see those old machines working, like they were just yesterday. You reckon the bus'll take a van from here? I’m thinking of trying to get that old fishing gear shifted, it's taking up too much space in your mum’s attic.      A van hire might be the way to go, yeah. I've got some apps for that. Just need to check a few places for good deals. You’d be surprised, some of these places can be really cheap if you book early — but don't mention it to your mum about the van. She'll have a fit if she knows you're moving things without her consent.      Noted! I'll handle it unobtrusively. My, you've made me sound sneaky. All right, what's that new game you're so fond of these days? Do I have to grow another head or something to play with you?      Haha, not quite, dad. It’s a new one with strategy and adventure — but let’s face it, I'll probably have to play it on my own because go back to my pond life if you ever had to fight monsters in there! Still, I’m thinking of coming down the boxset weekend to show you your way around.

Rather annoying this, isn't it? The council wants to knock down the library. I would've thought they’d be more sensible with heritage sites. I mean, it's not like it's a Victorian eyesore that's in the way of some shiny new development. It's just a quiet place where people can read and catch up on the papers.      I agree. My mum used to read most of her newspaper there before she moved to the village. I don’t get why they don’t just give it a bit of a spruce-up instead. You can't chase away people's memories with a wrecking ball like that.      I know, it's the same with the shops on the high street that look like they haven’t changed since the 70s. They keep the old façade but what goes on behind it is just a chippy serving dodgy chips for far too much. It’s all window-dressing if you ask me. They should either give it a full renovation or knock it down and build something useful.      That’s true. It’s like patching up the skin but leaving the inside rotting. I suppose with the council as tight as ever, they probably can’t afford to fix properly. I reckon the only ones who will profit from this “new development” – if it even happens – are the contractors, because they'll get huge fees just for presenting proposals.      Ugh, I can already foresee the shiny blueprint with glossy renderings of what someone  could  build on the site. A “community hub,” they’ll call it. Some flimsy café with a community noticeboard and a meeting room no one will use because it’s fully booked most of the time. I’m not even sure why the area still needs another “hub.”      Maybe part of that is why I've been thinking about the new upholstery I need. My lounge is falling apart, and I was wondering if I should go with that dark grey fabric I found or something a bit bolder. I’ve been browsing online for ideas.      Dark grey would be safe but also very versatile. If you want something bolder, maybe a deep terracotta red. That’d be warm and rich. You could balance it with neutral cushions or go for a contrasting patterned throw. It’d definitely work with your existing furniture.

Rather annoying this new Spotify algorithm, isn't it? Seems to think I like pop songs by people I've never heard of. Never mind, I'll stick to my old playlists. Still, I saw a classic album in the bargain bin the other day,  Dark Side of the Moon —Deezer it is, if you ask me.      I reckon it's not all that bad, Graham. I mean, I use Spotify and it helps me find new artists. Like this girl I found who's huge in Portugal—she's decent. But yeah, nothing beats your playlists.      Oh, I prefer Apple Music. They've got a much better editorial section, and I do some bits of music editing, so I appreciate curation. Fun fact—I recently found out that I’m part of their Duet micro-features!      Blimey, aren’t you working better than I am now then? I've been thinking of changing jobs in fact. Blooming bosses and all. But, you know, I've still got the clippings from that time I went to Glastonbury in '88. I mean, that’s a hobby to itself, choosing the tent, what to bring, where to be.      Ah yes, Glastonbury – memories. I got fairly tipsy and ended up on the comedy tent’s stage once. Still don’t know how. Anyway, for a hobby, I’m into birdwatching, which may sound a bit strange, but it's meditative. You just sit and wait for the birds. Mary—Speaker_2’s mum—used to call it being ‘snoozey’.      Not a fan of meditative things, but I do love going to markets and buying vintage vibes for my salon. Got some cool retro pickups that plug into a cassette player. Real classic for my clients. My sister Lucy—Speaker_3—she’s got more taste, though. She curates a vintage music blog alongside editing videos all day.      It's not that bad, really. I edit and I DJ occasionally. Websites and mixtapes. I keep meaning to do a collaboration with some local bands in Bournemouth. But I run into scheduling issues.      You really need to share if you ever do get something going, Lucy. I’d love to see it. And speaking of presents—what’s the one gift you’d like at Christmas that’s completely unreasonable? For me, it’d be those vintage speakers I saw in that shop in Portsmouth. They look like they were used in the 60s jazz scene.

Rather annoying this new car tax eh, lad? Thought me old Escort would've lasted another few years 'fore I got to splash out agin.      Nah, I think it might be worth it in the long run. My mate said electric cars cost less to run in the end. Got eeny weeny bills and no road tax an’ noVed.      Oh aye? A lot o’ folk in this neck o’ woods still stick wi’ diesel though, specially fer the journey t’ work and back. You get that run when yi' live miles out o’ town like.      I kno, but the thing is, wi' GCSEs and all, I’ve bin doin’ some thinkin’ aboot the future. I reckon electric or hybrid cars might be the way forward. Less emissions an’ all, an’ eventually cars won’t be allowed to run on petrol much longer.      That’s true enuff. I’ve seen the changes happening. Fer a start, the insurance on these new ones is still jolly steep for younger folk. Yer not in full-time work yet, so yer credit rating won’t help much.      I kno, it was a bit of a shock when my Mate Mikey got a quote last week.£900 a year just for somethin’ that’s like a phone app an’ looks like a spaceship!      Aye, but it’s also got to do wi’ yer experience and yer age. I remember what it were like at yer age, and let’s be honest, premium prices were  hillum . Insurers still have about as much respect for us young drivers as the council has for old bin lids.      So are there any sorts o’ things I can do to bring it down a bit, like for when I’m eligible? Maybe if I do a basic driving course?      Aye, defo. I’ve seen them black-box ones too. They crack down on yer speedin’ and things, but if yer drive proper, keep the big one out the way, an’ no hopin’ in the ditch wi' a tank o’ petrol, goin' on them can help your rate. Mind you, it depends on the company, but that’s a start.      That sounds doable. I don’t really want to jump straight into a bike wi’ those motorways everywhere. Unless it’s to York on a Friday for a laugh, o’course.      Aye, I ken. Always best to take it slow an’ steady, lad. Cars 're a right plunge these days, but if yer want somethin’ safe an’ no slippin’ off the side o’ them roundabouts on the A59, keep us updated on yer plans – I've a cousin in Harrogate that once sold

Rather than share a recording of this conversation, I'll provide a detailed written account for accuracy and comprehension. Let's proceed with the conversation script. ---      Right, what've we got here then? Another chicken curry with the chicken texture like I've been eating cardboard with some sauce squeezed on top again?      Maybe the takeaway was out of stock of chicken? I dunno. It's not that bad though, is it? Some places just use processed meat anyway.      Honestly, if I had to eat another dry chicken curry, I might just get the windpipe out too... like, literally, if you'd tracked me down and done the honours, I’d have said thanks.      You're being dramatic, Maureen. But fair play, the chicken here in Cork can be hit and miss. A good takeaway down in Shannon is miles better, mind you. Why doesn’t everyone just go up to Limerick for dinner in these cases?      Maybe, but ordering online’s lazy and I still might end up with that rubbery chicken.      I listen to podcasts sometimes to pass the time while I do dishes. Do you know, one of them was on workplace stress. They mentioned something about blood pressure and heart rates. How else can you measure stress at work, Gearóid?      Oh aye, don’t get me started. Stress levels? I could probably mail you a list of KPIs, missed deadlines, hardware breakdowns and suspicious system activity. Stress is just part of the job. You can’t ignore it, it's in your blood and bones by Friday lunchtime.      That sounds really about you, Dad. I don’t even know what KPI is... but I can tell you when your face becomes a brick wall.      You sound like my stepmum, Lucy. She says "your face is expressing more than your words ever could."      And it bloody well bloody does. I tried smiling once for a meeting, accidently crack my jaw as tight as a safety lock. Next thing you know, I was on the floor with the tech team scrambling. That's how you know something's wrong.      Dad, you really need to see if you can pronounce your words better in meetings. You started tripping over your own grammar the other day.      It’s because I’m thinking in code 30% of the time. And 50% of the time I'm trying to remember that ‘frequency of words on Google’ matters more than string parameters.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh gran?      Aye, it’s been pissing down since Wednesday, same as it was at my mother-in-law’s funeral.      Can we stop the car and have a snack now?      Hang on een minute Harry, we’ve got a few miles to go yet before we reach Ulverton.      I don’t like that place. I heard there are nudists there.      Nudes? I don’t recollect that when I was a kid. You must’ve been to one of them alternative fairs.      Aye, people change and places do too. Just keep your eyes to yourself and you’ll be fine.      D’you know, I think the whole EU Referendum did more for breaking up old habits than anything. More people are thinking for themselves now.      That’s true. I remember Terry Wogan didn’t want us to vote for Brexit, but we did anyway.      Speaking of thinking for ourselves, I’m seriously thinking about doing a law conversion course. I’ve seen more people go in that direction.      That’s a good call if you’re thinking of becoming a solicitor. I know quite a few who’ve done that and set up their own firm.      And while you’re thinking about degrees and all that, someone at the supermarket told me the other day they’d converted the scale from grams to kilograms. Some nut had been measuring a ten-kilo bag of potatoes in grams!      Oy gran, I don’t care about scales. I just want to know what birds we’re going to see on the hill!      I reckon we’ll see a few buzzards. My mate Matt said they’ve been hangin’ out near the old wind turbines up there.      Oh, I love those old stone villages you find up on the hilltop. There’s a kind of magic to them, especially when you drive through the narrow lanes.      Magic? You call it magic, I call it a muddy place with lots of goosieholes for your car.      You’re just not into the vibe, gran.      Vibes are fine, but I’d rather have a vibe with a good parking spot and a tea shop nearby.      Tell me about it. Parked at the top and walked a mile to find the car again. I swear, if they don’t sort out their car parking, people’ll stop visiting altogether.      What’s the point of going on holiday if you can’t explore properly then?

Rather annoying I find having meat substitutes. You know what grinds my gears? When it’s designed to  look  and  taste  like chicken, yet it’s still a processed blob. It’s not like suddenly we’re gonna stop being responsible for the environment and start pretending this is the solution.      I  get  that, but I mean, if it’s lab-grown meat? I’ve been following some stuff on synthetic meat in the news. They say it uses way less land, way less water. We can still have the taste and texture of beef without killing a single cow. You don’t like the idea of it?      Honestly, the idea of lab-grown meat kind of freaks me out. I’ve met enough eccentric rich people in this city who talk to me like their money can  fix  the moral issues of meat. Like, assembling meat in a Petri dish makes breakfast guilt-free? To me, it’s still a band-aid on a bleeding leg. The root problem is, humans love eating dead animals.      It’s not just about the environment—personally, I’ve seen some of the conditions in the abattoirs. I’ve delivered medicines for cows in the past… watching how they’re treated is a little too much. I’m not denying that hunting is often fairly considered, but industrial farming is  horrific . I’ve been trying to go more plant-based, but I  do  miss the protein.      I get that. That’s also why I take my vitamin B12 tablets like it's an ambition in itself—there's a science behind making sure it stays in your blood. I don't want to make it sound about oppression, but there are intersections you can't ignore. When you consider the lives of farm workers, and the workers in the meat processing plants, and even the scarcity of land in developing nations... It’s complicated. I’ve been writing about it more.      Honestly, the most glorious thing is being able to cook something intense without using meat. You know that recipe I told you about—tomato-based stew with lentils, topped with a homemade cashew “cheese”? It took an hour but tasted like luxury. You’re not into that kind of cooking, Sarah go?      It sounds  okay , but personally, I just can’t commit fully to being vegetarian. That bloke on  Curb Your Enthusiasm  once tried to make a dinner and everyone’s in culture shock.

Rather annoying this new phone, eh? Constantly wants updating. I've had it 'bout a year and it's already starting to lag when I try and run them new games.      Nah, it's £600 worth o' tech at the end o' the day. Got eeny use outta mine 'fore it was 'ad ta be replaced. I've been relying on a cousin’s eBay listing too. Fair dos, this stuff don’t last.      Honestly, you’re both daft. I seen laptops last years when bought second-hand. You just gotta fetch the right one. Still, I reckon I'll go with Netflix and chill, not another web shop for now. My turkey came doorstep-free last week an’ left a mess. Ten minutes I had it an’ already bin too late. I think the courier screamed at it an’ it’s still tryin’ to breakfast me.      Haha, no wonder ya ordered gingerbread and not a chicken, then. Still, Christmas is a tough'un. I reckon I'll try and do a few more games, though. Gotta be in the mood. Got that new action flick coming out in two days. Heard it's got a bit o' everything: blood, explosions, and sarcastic sidekicks.      Yeah, slap a gun in someone's hand and set 'em to run and it's a guaranteed win. Last flick I saw was about a woman chasing ghosts in someone's mansion. Tales of the dead: my man's already got one o' those on his Christmas list—complete with a red and gold trim. Still, at least it's cheaper in the online deals. I about got one off Argos for half the price.      And I suppose you found the ghost of Christmas toys past and gave you a discount too, didn’t you. Honestly, I've thought about packing up and going somewhere. Just for a week. Not too far, Whitehaven's not got all that many places to go, but maybe a road trip up past the Lake District?      Sounds grand. I’ve not been on one of those in ages. Was going to drop by university, but they’ve told me I best wait ’til go back in January for term if I want a place. Not much else I can do, really, between studies and the boxset binges.      I envy ya, seriously. Being able to go where yer want, study, maybe even make a life outta it.

Rather annoying the queue took so long, isn't it? I was practically ready for tea by the time they’d got to our building maps.      I know, I was nearly over by the old library entrance. Not quite sure they timed the queue system right — far too many people for such a narrow corridor.      It was ridiculous. I reckon half the people in that queue were a bit confused — not sure if they were doing this for social credit points or just seeing what was on.      Oh, I heard from someone that the law lectures today are well under wraps — supposed to be some top barristers giving talks. I reckon they’re the real reason people came.      Honestly, I’d probably skip an Alumni Day if it weren’t for the dinner afterwards. You know my brother is one of the caterers? Half the dishes are for family connections and friends first. I still managed to sneak an invite in. Mum was threatening to repack my bag for the train again — not sure how old I am but I still pack like I’m twelve.      You know, I visited Spain last month for research — quite a contrast to this. I tell you, Cambridge today is a far cry from municipal courts in Seville. Have you ever been down there?      I’ve done a bit of travel in Spain, but the south is quite different from the north. I spent a summer in Oviedo once with my sister, and the people just couldn’t get over my accent. They said my pronunciation of 'granada' left a lot to be desired.      I can believe it. You know I had to get a passport because most people I meet at work now are EU nationals. Interesting talking to different people, mind. I met one guy from Hungary yesterday — his university training barely mentioned British legal culture. Makes you wonder if the system should be overhauled to be less idiosyncratic.      You say that like it was all set in stone. I mean, we did just sort out a law to make queens and commoners have the same rights to property. It’s a slow process, but the law is fairly adaptable in that way.      That’s the spirit. Anyway, shall we get some tea from that stand there? Just don’t expect me to drink the stuff that came out of the box this morning — I’ve had some dodgy coffee at events before.

Rather annoying me a bit, eh? You know how me lectures start ages before they’re supposed to? Like... got to be there by ten past one because the uni thinks we need an hour to find a seat and make tea? Not to mention they’ve got us doin’ this bloody new online system for registration eeny every single module. I’m startin’ to feel like me brain's all digital now!      Aye, I've heard all about it. You're tellin' me you ain't had one of them Leeds University "light touch supervision" myths yet? Me mate at the uni says he went in one morning, sat in the wrong seat, and the proffessor marked him as missin'. My word, I’d bin melonin' if I'd paid over the odds for them fees, only to get no lecture in me head for it.      Mm! And I've no doubt if I said anythin', I’d be told to sort me awl out! No, you didn’t have lectures this week, why? Or were you taking me for a massage, maybe? You gone off to the hot tub in the land of Nod and back?      Aye, I did have a proper workin' out from the massage. Gone to see Matey Dave at the same place me mam swears by. Sorted me out after all the hours I did at them lectures last week. Bit stiff after that, but now I’m good as new. Who’d have thought my back could talk?      That’s so weird! I’ve had one at uni once, and I swear it’s like a bloody conversation! The massee’s like "Ooh, that’s a pain in!" and the toucher’s like “So let’s see what we can do about it.” Not that I’d tell me lecturer if  he  started doin’ ‘em. I’d rather do the coursework passed out on the floor.      Aye, but you can’t get a good massage for nothin’ unless your mate’s runnin’ a charity. Let me know if you fancy one. I can tell them what I do for a living, and they’ll let us in for nothin’! Just say I’m goin’ on for a research seminar or summat.      Oh, no, I don’t want to be binnin’ your research cause you took me for a chi! Besides, I’ve got my next lecture startin’ in ten mins, and I’ve got to be there ‘fore they shuffle the chairs and lock the door again.

Rather lovely to have you both over for lunch. Thought we could talk about a few things, like the family picnic next weekend and, well… the news has been fairly brutal lately with what’s going on in Calais.      That’s a kind thought of you, James. And yes, it’s all quite disturbing, isn’t it? I read about the camp being dismantled and the kids who are missing. A lot of my students come from refugee families, and it breaks my heart. It’s easy to forget they’re human lives, not just headlines.      Oh, I agree. I’ve actually volunteered with a school project that supports refugee kids learning English. It’s heartbreaking how many have survived poverty and violence, only to be stuck in limbo here. It makes me think, do we even have the systems in place to support them properly?      That’s a very good point. I, um… actually spent much of my career in management in the food industry, you know, logistics and team coordination. If I had the energy these days, I’d love to try and do something, maybe work with refugee families—perhaps connect them with support groups.      That sounds like such a compassionate idea, James. You’ve got a lot of experience from your work. Maybe there’s a way to volunteer your skills, like organisational support or mentoring?      It would be amazing if you did. If we could get you involved with that, we could all help out. As for lunch, I brought over a few pastries from the bakery I passed on the way in. Also, I thought we could try and make something ourselves next time—like a curry, or even a risotto. I’m finally feeling confident about trying the recipes I found online.      Now that sounds like another plan to consider! I’m no great cook, but I can rustle up a decent stew if it comes to it. As for future plans, I was actually wondering if the three of us could meet once a month, maybe at someone’s place, just to keep the family connected and talk about things like this. Life always seems to get in the way.      I’d like that. It would be a nice way to ensure the family still stays in touch rather than just life drifting along. And maybe we can discuss practical ways to support causes like the migrant crisis.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun is just beginning to shine through the office window. Mind you, I rather prefer a bit of rain for painting the garden, but today’s a good day for tea, wouldn’t you say?      Aye, can't argue with sunshine when it’s kind enough to show its face. Not like it listens to me when I curse it over a wet paper day. Mind if I pour a bit more?      Please, by all means. Oh, and congratulations on the promotion to Senior Lecturer — when was that? Still buzzing about it?      Thanks! Last month. Bit of a whirlwind, truth be told. You know how it is when you've been working at the same university for twenty years. I half expected the committee to forget they’d promised me a raise the other week. But enough of that — how’s the new breakfast nook coming along? I happened to pass a kitchen in your driveway the other day.      Ah, yes. We’re in the early stages still. I’ve decided to do the majority of the design myself, but I’m short on enthusiasm for plumbing. Found a few tradesmen, mind, but they’re all so… unpredictable. One quoted me then vanished. You ever had trouble with that?      Horrible, really. I’ve learned the hard way to vet people twice as thoroughly as their CV promises. I got Mark to do our kitchen, and he's a workhorse — no complaints. Let me give you his details if you’d like.      That'd be a great help. Mind you, I still prefer to make a bit of fuss about it in public. Nothing brings conversation quite like mentioning a dodgy handyman or two. Not much else like sharing your fails at DIY with friends.      Aye, I've heard your tales. That time you tried to hang your own chandelier and nearly tiled the floor with it. Still, you mentioned you were bringing Sarah to the Christmas drinks, right? I haven’t seen her since our trip to Aberystwyth a few years back.      Yes! Sarah’s coming, and James, too. I believe they’ve moved back from the continent now. Bit cooler up here for their children, or so they say. Still, I do miss the Italian coffee — harder to find a decent espresso than a decent tradesman these days.      Tell me about it.

Rather than share a text-based conversation, I request a more interactive approach. Allow me to pose a question first... What particular aspects of this scenario interest you most—the generational exchange, superstitions, or perhaps the culinary inquiry? Share with me your preference, and I shall proceed accordingly.      Actually, I would like to try to continue with the dinner-party conversation if possible. Maybe something light like discussing a recent book I read, but I'm open to other ideas.      Splendid! Shall we journey together into the realm of the "fascinating tales" or perhaps delve into the "explorations of truth and superstition"? A choice is yours!      Let's explore the "fascinating tales" first! I found the stories in the science book I read quite interesting.      I'm pleased to hear that! So, which tale among them intrigued you the most, and why?      Hmmm... there was this one about the Great Wall hides, which were allegedly used to transport goods. I found it fascinating that such a monumental structure had secret passageways and ways of keeping people out while also facilitating trade. It made me think of other historic structures as well.      You have quite a curious mind indeed. Excellent observation! Have you read of any other examples, and what made the Great Wall stand out?      Not yet, but I will look into it. The Great Wall stood out because it was such a visual example of secrecy and complexity. I wonder why people are drawn to stories like that. They give you something to think about.      Ah yes, the human mind is forever fascinated by the hidden and the hidden histories. Do you think you prefer the tales of real history over fantasy or superstition?      I do enjoy fantasy, but it is the real stories that make the most sense. They show the development of people and how they interacted with technology and each other.      That's an astute view. Indeed, history can be a curious blend. As such, perhaps next time we can explore a bit of the 'Horrible History' angle—my favorite chapter is about the ghastly experiments of the past.      That sounds exciting! I'm curious about that now too. Maybe we can find out some of the interesting science experiments they tried in the past?      Outstanding! So, shall we agree that perhaps we begin with one genuine historical tale and one historical experiment in the new week to contrast?

Rather a lot’s happened in the last few weeks, hasn’t it? That Storm Fergus battered the place when I was out with one of the ponies at the stables. I've been meaning to ask you, Lucy, how did your granddaughter like school this week?      Oh, it’s beginning to sink in, I think. She was   quite   cross yesterday when they had that Halloween assembly—said the costumes were “not scary enough.” I told her, love, if she’d seen a horse properly spooked, she’d quickly forget about vampires and gobble-up.      I went horse-riding! Not at Grans’ stables but out at Roberts’ farm near the village. My teacher took us for outdoor education. Funnest day ever. The boy I sit with, Freddie, shouted at the horse I was on the whole time—Don’t watch the bear, don’t watch the bear—like it was some kind of cricket match.      And what did you lot get up to for Halloween? We took the whole class to the park—set up a bonfire and told some spooky stories. Got one lad in a cow costume as a last-minute decision. Hilarious. Reminded me of watching  Beetlejuice  with my cousin back in ‘88.      My costume was a witch! I had a broomstick and everything. We carved pumpkins at school. Mine looked a bit more like a mouse than a face. Miss Spilsbury said it was “imaginative” but I thought it was a bit outlandish.      Aye, ‘course imaginative is good! We carved potatoes when I was a lad—nothing fancy. Just dug up a field and lit them with candles. Not much cop compared to your lot now, but better than watching the telly, I suppose.      You lot must’ve trekked about quite a bit, with that horse-riding and all. Any plans for a weekend away soon? I hear there’s a little country fair up in Milton, good for handmade crafts and whatnot.      Actually, I’ve been toying with the idea of a day trip to Stratford-upon-Avon next weekend—bit away from the usual routes for you, Lucy and Alan, but I think it might be a nice change. You know, Shakespeare, traditional market, cafes. Bring some of you along?      I’d like that! We could dress up as characters and take photos. Or maybe dress as ghosts for a laugh—spook the places tourists tend to go.

Rather annoying this, isn't it? You think they'd have decent roads by now in such a busy area... What's the hold-up?      I can't say I'm surprised, love. I've driven along this road since the '70s and nothing much changes. Same potholes, same single file of traffic. It was like this on the way to the fair last year too. You'd think the council would prioritise this.      If only they had money for reasonable road repairs! Instead, they're handing out houses to people who can't afford them. I heard a fiver on the radio last week—apparently, there's this new policy where first-time buyers in poverty get free council housing. I don't mind helping people who are struggling, but I do worry about what happens next, especially for the elderly.      I was about to say something similar. I've heard horror stories about this new housing policy... I mean, don't get me wrong, I'm not saying the elderly should be left out in the cold, but it feels like the system is being stretched too thin. These new housing developments don't seem to consider mobility or accessibility. I only saw on the news that there was a protest last week because a new flat was being leased to a young couple who weren't disabled, but it was originally reserved for someone with limited mobility.      That's not uncommon. Silly really, building one-size-fits-all homes when they should be investing in proper elderly and disabled housing. I had my own house until just a couple of years ago—piece of toast is a struggle now with these aching legs. Can't even make it up the stairs by myself.      That's why I do what I do, Charlie. I work in care, and I see it all the time. People get housing that doesn't meet their needs. My sister had to move four times in two years before she found a flat that had at least a ground-floor bathroom. But you know what the worst bit is? The council waiting lists. My brother-in-law had to wait 18 months for a space in a proper elderly home.      That's shocking. I think part of the problem is that these schemes aren’t co-ordinated. They need to work together more. If housing policy doesn't account for the needs of older people, they'll just box themselves in—and it might exclude people who actually need it the most.

Rather annoying the frost sticking around this late in the year, isn’t it? Still, it’s not like we got the allotment fixed up yet, has it?      Oh, absolutely! It is a bit worrying to be honest, I mean, you can't really start planting much if it’s still freezing at dawn. But then again, we’ve got time.      Oh aye. A lot of people would’ve got a head start, but we're not backward in coming forwards. Right, now you said you’ve got the plot sorted? Just need to clear it now?      That’s mostly it, yes. I did check the council supply list, and they have some well-loved spades and rakes. I left a message this morning – I’m picking them up tomorrow. But I was thinking, before the heavy work starts, maybe we could do a gentle bit of breakfast planning—like, what do you want to grow?      Oh, I love that idea, to be truthful. I was thinking of trying some broad beans—early maturing, you know? And I’ve always fancied getting some decent land for asparagus. It’s a real treat when you can buy in local produce for the kids. We do little healthy eating exercises in the school – saves us a bob or two, and the kids really get involved.      That’s brilliant, and asparagus will be perfect. I’m going for zucchinis and salads this year—easy and productive. And maybe a few strawberries? It just feels oddly satisfying when you can pop them in your morning cereal without having to drive to the supermarket at the crack of dawn.      I daresay we’ll need to make the area pest-proof, though. I read a little bit about using mesh for that sort of thing. Doesn’t sound too expensive, but I do need to check for local recommendations. Got a man in the parish hall who did something similar with raised beds. He told me he nearly gave up halfway through but then found some grant money from the gardeners' trust.      That’s always a good idea to keep the budget in line. I do wonder, maybe there’s a chance of a shared compost system too? That way we goenvironmental on the back of it.      You’re on a roll today, aren’t you? That might be something to chip in to with the other plot holders.

Rather annoying I know, innit? You’d think me parents would get that I’m not a primary school kid no more an’ need me own space like a proper adult!      Aw, I hear you. Chuffed they’re bemused as you’re spending more time with us. Got eeny plans for the weekend yet?      Nawh not yet… been stuck in the house A lot, to be fair. Proper cabin fever, innit? Miss goin’ out like it’s a whole different galaxy.      S’all the same ’ere too... like, I’ve even brooked me little bro out to the park just to feel human. On the other hand, me mates an’ I did get to plan a bit of a picnic this Saturday if you fancy taggin’ along. I’ll be the one bringin’ the kale sandwiches, obviously.      Wah? I’m Anglo-Saxon for a reason lass, you know I’m a felling-in-the-straight-and-narrow type. But yeah, I’d fancy it, if it’s not too fruity. Got any actual crisps in your plans?      Laid-out crisps… plus mini quiches, a little charcuterie board, and – cheeky kiss – a sneaky bottle of cheap red. Sounds like a proper Saturday sorted to me!      If I weren’t already in tune with the principles of the White Rose Movement I might just ask what the hell a White Rose Movement is, innit. But yeah, floring’d to come. Should I bring a bottle of lager or does that break the vibe?      Bring what you like! I'll bring the chilli oil an’ thyme twists for the failsafe vibe. Not that I need the chilli oil, mind. I do just like ‘avin’ an excuse for it.      Aye, well as it so happens, I’ve just bought a pack of Strongbow for when I fancy feeling all Casey Clum as and that. Let’s say we go halfsies on a couple of whiskeys if we fancy it later? Still got a couple of them tinnies the bloke gave go me on my birthday. Expensive stuff, innit.      Sounds like a dream team of tinnies and Strongbow. Me brother’s in at the uni sports centre all Saturday, so I won’t have to wrestle anyone for the bean bag to myself. Can I bring ‘im too? Only he fancies fitting in a bit more... so he wants to make friends.      Sure, bring him, as long as he doesn't make a pass at me.

Rather annoying me, this tutorial. D’ya think anyone actually knows what they’re doin’? We’re all just clickin’ randomly and盼in’ for it t’be over      Aye, honestly I’ve seen better tutorials on YouTube. Just skip through it an’ hope y’get a decent placement. I got one with   5 v 12   last time, aye. A real laugh.      Y’all are making it sound   worse   than it is. It was just a bit chaotic the first time, but once y’got the hang of it, it wasn’t  too  bad. Besides, the real fun only starts   after   you get your turkey placement. You’ve gotta queue though. I waited like三十 minutes, mate.      Eww, no chance of playing with you lot again then. Thirty minutes! Why doesn’t it just give you a match straight away? Game design these days is mental.      Nah, I mean the queue’s not  that  bad if you get into a queue with other people in your place. I mean if we all queue as a group, it only took us like ten minutes max.      Oh right, of course. I forgot you can queue as a squad. I didn’t think it mattered, but yeah, the time cuts down quite a bit.      Oi, you lot fancy watching a film after? I just got back and my TV’s on. There was a new action one I wanted to check out.      What’s it called? I’ve been watching  too  many action films at home about geopolitics lately. I swear half of the films now are just “crisis in a made-up Middle Eastern country” with guns and barely any plot.      Aye, I’m with mate. Unless it’s got some proper explosions and a bit of me fighting a tank, I probably won’t be watching. I dunno about y’all, but I stick to my comfort films and that’s it.      Fair enough. I’m more the “feel-good” cinema type anyway. I did a shoot ‘em up the other day with go-karts on fire and I sufficed, but real talk, I prefer watching something where no one dies.      Aww your soul’s too pure for this world, Leah. But kudos for trying out every genre.      Thanks, thanks. I’ve got over thirty films queued on my list alone. I’m not entirely sure what I’m gonna do with them all, though. They just seemed like a good idea at the time.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun is doin' wonders for the garden. Mind if I put the seats out on the patio while I'm at it?      That's a brilliant idea, Nan. I'll grab the cushions as well — wouldn't want it to be too uncomfortable for the film night!      Oh, film night! Almost forgot. What are we watching again?      We're going back to one of Dad’s old favourites,  The Full Monty . Remember, you helped him set up the projector when I was about twelve.      Oh yes!  Right ... That was the summer I accidentally left my knitting on the deck and Mycroft, bless him, tried to use it for a dog collar! I still laugh at the look on his face when I walked out the back door with the shears about to trim the rose bushes.      I happened to like the dog collar — at least until you trimmed it again that evening, didn’t you say so?      It was a practical collar, if a bit inappropriate for a spaniel!      Still, you were grief when it came to that garden. I mean, how did you remember where everything was without a map? I remember – twice I borrowed your trowel and ended up with a broken thing because the handles were all hidden in clumps of foxglove or something.      And you never said sorry, did you? No, just blundered around like a prat and thought I wouldn’t notice what you had done!      Hey, you repurposed all the trowels into pegs in about five minutes. That’s not my fault the garden wall needed something to hang things off.      Oh, I know! I’m not cruel. Still, I expect an apology.      Only if you promise to stop knitting cat slippers at 6 a.m. on any bloody weekend I might have.      You’re lucky I don’t knit you socks that pinch!      Nan… we need to finish the preparations. I’ve invited some friends from work — a couple of them are stopping by the next train in. Moya said she'd bring the crisps.      Is it? I’d hoped for a bit more peace this week.      You can have peace after the 3rd reel, after I'm asleep with popcorn everywhere and not replying to your unsolicited life advice.      That wouldn’t be  unsolicited , my dear. That’d be  family duty .      You spoil me, Nan. Likewise, I shall spoil you slightly back by not reminding you how you got that sliver in your thumb by trying to weed out those thorns  on a tea towel  one day.

Rather annoying the new DVD player we got isn't working, isn't it? I mean, it's like... barely a month old and already it won’t load any discs! Honestly, you think you’d get better tech in 2024.      Ugh, it was probably that dodgy shop we got it from in Cardiff. I   told   you not to trust that stall on the market—they had prizes for spelling your name! I mean, come on. Should’ve bought it online like normal folk!      Oh, don't get me started. You know I can't shop without touching it!  Totally  irrational, I know, but still. Anyway, moving on. My turkey friend Elise asked me to interview her for a project about... I think it's called  The Undateables: Friends Edition ? Or was that another one?      I watched the old  Undateables  with my Nan in the early noughties. It was hides, you know, those Casio watches and clodhopper shoes—vintage horrors.      Oh, I laughed so hard at the one with the guy from Surrey who thought "vintage" meant fabric condition. Anyway, it's quite a task. She said she's penned some cheeky ones about her ex, and needs it for a comedy blog. You'd have fun with it, Em. You always find the killer quotes.      I dunno, feels a bit full-on. But if you're doing it, maybe I'll give it a bash— if  you promise me a marshmallow and a tea at the end.      You’re having such a typical London rift—DVD player and  undateables  alike. Honestly, I've only survived mine by sending people to that secret spa in Berkshire. You know the one with the high tea and free wifi?      Oh, you mentioned that before! Was it the one near Aylesbury? I could see us dragging our queens over there for a  proper  catch-up with lunches and a little retail therapy?      That’d be  heaven . Just not like this place— this gothic room with creaking floorboards and a cat that hates me . Honestly, I’m living it up like a boxset baddie. Pass the mags. I’m planning my next fictional murder.      Murder with a side of belly laughs and dodgy DVDs—what a weekend! I mean, honestly, who even needs a man when you’ve got friends like us and board games?  Unless  you want to romanticize it in a Welsh-based serial?

Rather annoying this new washing machine eh? It's done more smashes than washes in the first week. I swear it's trying to announce it's from Cambridge by being all posh and faddy with settings.      Haha, I know what you mean. I tried putting in my muddy hiking boots and now I’ve got a warning screen about   "unbalanced load"   like it's a nuclear reactor. What’s next, a side of philosophical musings on clean garments and moral fibres?      Oh, I got that when I washed your football socks the other day – it said something about   "balance, nature, and the pursuit of static-free equilibrium."   Honestly, I miss the old one. Just chuck it in, whiz it for an hour and there you go – back to basics.      Fair enough. But it's probably for the best eventually. The last one, remember when it tried to pool-test for HGV in the spin cycle and ended up flooding the kitchen? That was a near-death experience in sock fluff.      Nostalgia for disasters though, eh? I mean, we did make that beautiful lasagna and watched that  Eyes Wide Shut  marathon on the couch that night while it was all gurgling away in the background. Remember how the water mixed with the sauce and Hayley used her bath towel as an apron?      Oh, I could still chew on that lasagna memory. Our food game back then was strong—your mum’s jam sponge, my nan’s oddly sour stew. Some things were best left in the past though. Like that weekend I tried to make  kimchi  and it fermented in about five minutes.      Oh right, that had to be removed from a sealed box and given to the bin man. I think the housing officer threatened to evict us. My sister texted me just the other day. Says she saw your face on the news with a toaster. She sent it to all our cousins with a question:   "Is he getting a PhD or is he looking for fire sprite?"      Oh great, add that to the list. Now I’ve got demonic appliances and cousins delivering news around my head like gossiping crows. I bet your cousin Marta mentioned that our  Criterion Channel  marathon made her rethink Netflix forever.      That bloke on Criterion, your dodgy VHS restoration tutorials—you made it to the conference seminar last month, didn’t you? I watched the recording from work.

Rather annoying this VW business isn't it? I suppose anyone with a car these days is affected in some way... What with the emissions scandal and all that.      It does seem shocking, honestly. I read that they fixed millions of cars without telling anyone. Just like the banks, really. I'm surprised more people didn't notice.      My cousin had one of those Golf TDI models from a few years back. He said he felt like he’d been robbed when it came out. Ended up taking it to the dealership and swapping it for a hybrid. Funny how things work — now he’s buying a brand new electric car. Can you believe it?      Well, that’s the direction we have to go. No point in getting angry about the past. I’d rather argue with the housing prices I’m seeing up here. Living in Cumbria is nice — better than when I was in Dublin — but the prices here are getting out of hand.      Oh, absolutely. I’ve looked into the area over the last year or so for a new place. We used to rent in the Midlands, and we thought moving up to Cumbria would be a smart move — nature, lower crime, less pollution. But it feels like the only people who can actually live here are retired couples with pensions and savings.      That’s because of the chain, love. Silly people hanging on to houses for years and not selling up. Our parents wanted to downsize to a retirement flat in Walsall, but every time they look there’s a six-month wait. It's the same all over the North. The prices are climbing fast, but it doesn't compare to the South.      Exactly my point. The South is a whole different world. Going into London is like entering a different country. Prices up there are just astronomy. I read that the average price for a flat in London is now over £500k. I’d sooner give up my pottery again than spend that much for a little box with a garden.      I’ve seen figures like that as well. I think it's partly the influx of foreign investment. The housing market in the South is being driven by the wealthy from countries like Russia or China — it's more of a status game than a practical decision.      And the further North you go, the fewer people with that kind of disposable income.

Rather annoying when a new housing estate goes up right on the edge of the village, if you ask me. Ruins the view, and no local consultation at all. I’ve asked the council, but they seem to think we’re all quite alright with the view of a concrete jungle.      Aye, I agree, old friend. It was all open fields out there when I was young. Now it’s just concrete and chaos. Not that I blame the lads much; young people need a place to live. But why can’t they put the developments somewhere else? Costessey still looks lovely.      Honestly, I’m more annoyed about me pension. It’s taken nearly six months to sort out that MyHMRC nonsense. I sent an e-mail and got back some automated blither from the government website. Couldn’t even get in touch with someone. Living in a B&B now and they won’t breakfast me unless I apply earlier than the chapel bells.      I hear you, love. I tried to do it all online too. One time, I thought I was filing for a state pension but ended up on some form about fishing rights. A bit rude to be honest when the system can’t even tell the difference between a pension number and a cod liver count.      My Mate Harry at the local pub, he tried it all once and gave up. Now he walks into the job centre like it’s a place to go for a morning stroll. He says they never help, just scare people off. Honestly, they treat everyone like a problem to be sorted, not an old citizen who’d rather have a decent breakfast than a spreadsheet filled in at 9 o’clock in the morning.      That’s the thing, the B&B’s breakfast is the most cheerful part of my day! Proper tea, not that cold brew they have at the cafes these days. But I say ‘proper’—I mean it’s just toast and a pot of tea at 8 a.m., but it bloody well tastes better than I’ve eaten for weeks.      As long as we’re on the topic of breakfast, I've been dreaming of the big English breakfast. Not since the 50s really, after I moved from Norwich. The sausages go bad quick on your own if you don’t get up at the crack of dawn. I’m still wondering why we can’t all stay in B&Bs all the time.

So, I just read this article about evolution in biology class. My teacher was explaining it, but it felt... off, you know? Like, is it even true? I mean, sure, we humans are probably descended from apes or something, but I kind of wish there was another explanation.      Bro,  what ? It’s like science has evidence! Like, all the bones, the DNA stuff—they all match up! I mean, I don’t get why anyone would even debate it. But it’s one of those things that makes me think deeper. Like, if we all evolved from the same place, does that even make  race  real, or is it just made up?      My uncle still says evolution is just a theory made up by scientists to throw religion out the window. Dudes, this is sad. Like, religion and science aren’t always at war. They’re both humans trying to explain the universe!      Yeah, but what’s the deal with people thinking being part of a group is so important? Like, my friend shared this video online about feminism, and it immediately got comments from people saying it’s a "hate movement." It’s exhausting.      Honestly, watching how people react to stuff online feels like watching a trainwreck. Mate shared a joke the other day and it went viral—hundreds of likes, but nearly as many people calling him out for being sexist. I don’t even know how we assess what’s “okay” anymore.      That’s just a reflection of how we interact. You can’t make everyone happy. But the internet also gives a voice to people who’ve  actually  been excluded because of their gender, race, or sexuality. I just watched this documentary about how Black women in the 70s had to fight for both feminism and racial equality. It’s  deep .      True. But it still gets personal. I had this argument with my mate over the weekend—well, he called it an argument, but I just felt attacked. He was like, “You’re overreacting to equality stuff.” Then he said feminism is a new phase and women just want attention.      That’s so reductive. Like, no, it's not about attention—it's about  systemic  change. But how do you explain that without sounding like you’re dragging politics into the conversation? I mean, isn’t school supposed to focus on learning, not this?      It’s not even ignoring it.

Rather annoying to be honest, I had to cancel a few meetings. But they said it’s minor keyhole surgery, and I’ll be back on my feet in no time.      That's probably for the best. When I had the cough that wouldn’t go away, the doctor was on about infections all the time. I ended up with some tablets and a week on the sofa.      Oh, love, if only I had a week on the sofa these days. It was easier when you were young! My back was playing up for months last year. Finally tried the acupuncture at the community centre, and I’ve not felt so good in years.      That’s a change from my time. I had a bit of everything on the lorry—back pain, blisters, the lot. A few years ago I had a dodgy hip. It was all about the tablets for me back then, no time for fancy therapy.      I don’t mind the tablets as long as they work. Still, the operation is the main event for me. I’ve been getting jitters—personally, I’d rather have a full Saturday watching a rugby match with my dad than be on an operation table.
