You'd love it then. I don’t know much about rugby, but I do know my way round a clean room! Bet you’ll be back in time for that winter sale at the shops. Speaking of, we need new tyres on the car. Our MOT date is in two weeks!      Oh, aren’t we lucky we can afford all that! When I was young, money didn’t stretch as far as it does for you. Still, it’s about friends, isn’t it? I wouldn’t touch the shops without Jane [Speaker_2] by my side—you know that.      And I’d be lost without the lot of you! Family and good friends are what make life bearable. Though I have been thinking about skiing again. My brother insisted I go with him last year, but I said no. We had to clear snow off the path to the car every morning! Freezing.      That’s the life, isn’t it? I did a bit of skiing in the '70s—ran my own lorry across the border to France. Fun times, even in the snow and cold. But I’ve long since retired from the slopes.

Okay, luv, bedtime's almost here, and I just wanted to have a little chat with you both... What do you know about how people lived a very long time ago?      I know that people were owned like things before, like in America! My friend Martha told me about it at school.      Yeah, they didn’t get to go free! It was like a really bad game.      That's a very good start, but let me explain it a bit carefully. A long time ago, people from Africa were taken from their homes and forced to work in faraway places without being paid, just because some powerful people wanted their help. This was called slavery, and it happened mostly before the 1900s.      But why was it allowed? It sounds so unfair!      It was very, very wrong and very unfair. Some people thought they had the right to own other people for money or power. It took many years and lots of brave people speaking out and fighting to stop it. In some countries like the UK and the US, it was officially ended, but impacts of it still exist.      And then, what happened?      Well, after slavery was banned, there were still lots of problems between people of different races and backgrounds. And because of these unfair ideas, there were sometimes wars. Like, in the US, there was a war called the American Civil War, which was partly because of someone not wanting to end slavery.      Oh, wow. So slavery led to wars?      In some places and times, yes. People had different ideas, and when they disagreed about something as big as human rights, it can lead to terrible things like war.      That sounds scary. Did people fix it?      It took a lot of time for people to learn and do better. Today, we try to make sure no one is treated unfairly just because of their skin colour or where they come from. But it's still a big topic we as people need to think about and talk about.      So what can  we  do about it?      Good question. We can try to treat everybody with kindness and respect, no matter who they are or where they're from. We can also learn more about these histories, and teach others when we can. That’s what I’m trying to do with you both tonight.      I think I’m going to tell Martha about it tomorrow, and maybe she’ll tell her mummy!

Rather annoying the new dramas on the iPlayer, aren't they? I was watching one the other week—basically the same plot as some old one from the 80s, if you ask me! Got me checking my programme guide more than the telly!      Aye, it's all recycled now, isn't it? Not like the days of Coronation Street or EastEnders. Used to be real life up there, more or less. Still, easier watching telly than reading a book, if you ask me!      Oh, I don't know. I'd rather curl up with a novel! Just finished "Where the Crawdads Sing"—you haven't read it yet? My book group all raved about it! It’s one of those books that makes you obsessed.      I’ll be the first to say most of the books I've read are for breakfast, bedtime and then... well, coffee table after I've finished them! I'm more of a telly person myself, I'm afraid.      It's all I do when I get home, really. Switch the telly on, pop a pot of tea and zone out for two hours. At least it switches my brain off.      Tell me about it! My days are long enough. I start early, work till the evening, and the last thing I want is to be stressed out at home. I just sit back with the dog, a cup of coffee, and enjoy the skyline for a bit.      That's the spirit. When I was still working, I'd get home and want to be out with the lads for a pint or a curry. Always something going on. Nowadays it’s just the wife, the telly, and whatever cooking I can rustle up without burning anything.      You're not still trying to be a ‘masterchef’ like you used to, are you, Grandad?      Ahh, I give it a shot, lass. Not all my efforts are edible, mind you—tomato soup once turned out more like tomato paste. But I stick to what I do well, innit?      Right, but enough about the telly and goings on on the plate! How's everyone else been? Did you hear about Jackie? She’s had a little health scare, poor lass. She went into hospital with chest pains, big scare all round.      Och, that’s not good hearing. I expect it was a bit over the top, but better them checking it out than not, eh?

Right, who’s up for helping me unload the dishwasher first? I need one of you to take the plates...    ...and the other can do the forks and knives. Deal?      Can I do the plates? The big ones?      Of course, you can do the bigger ones. But be careful with the cups, they're a bit fragile. Harry always knocks one over when he’s excited.      I’ll do the forks and knives! Can I carry the spoon tray too?      You can hold it like a knight holding his sword. Just don’t go galloping off with it!      My teacher told me George Stephenson invented the train. Is that true?      Yes, he did! He’s often called the ‘Father of Railways’. He built one of the first steam locomotives that helped people travel faster.      So, like, he made the first train puff puff?      Exactly! It wasn’t just puffing, though—it was a proper steam engine powered by fire and coal.      But how did he come up with the idea?      Well, from what I remember, he was a really clever lad who loved machines and engines. He started out as a simple colliery manager but did a lot of experimenting. One of the big ones he did was the Rocket—this engine was super fast for its time!      Were they like the Hogwarts Express then? With windows and all?         Not quite like the  Hogwarts Express , but nearly about as exciting! The first railways were quite rough—more like sticks on wheels than the shiny trains you see today. But they got better and better over time, just like the Hogwarts Express.      I wish I could visit the train tracks. Can we go on a weekend?      We can look it up later. I remember passing a small heritage railway near Peterborough once. They have steam trains there that you can ride.      Can I dress up like a driver?      Course you can! They even have goody bags with whistles if you ask nicely.      Is George Stephenson in Harry Potter?      Not in the actual books, no. But sometimes real-life history mixes with magical ones in fanfiction. Some writers even imagine what Harry Potter would’ve been like if he’d ridden a Stephenson-engine steam train to Hogwarts!      I like that idea! My Hogwarts Express would be powered by steam, like a dragon and a train mixed together.      That’s a brilliant imagination you’ve got there, Harry!

Rather annoying when the Wi-Fi drops while I’m in a Words With Friends game. Someone always takes advantage and racks up the points with some mad s    like " zyzzyva ."      Honestly, who writes words like that? I bet you half a croissant it was my mum playing last time. She likes to say she’s 'on a roll' and then drops a " quixotic ." I swear, she got a dictionary app to play fair but used it as a cheat session.      That’s what you get when your mum still thinks being a retired librarian gives her some sort of linguistic  edge . I reckon she'd start a debate on Oxford vs. Cambridge like it was a pub quiz round.      Honestly, I need to play my cousin Oliver next, he used to make me look like a fool with his obscure German loanwords. He’s got, like, a PhD in something Anglo-Saxon or whatever.      Oliver hides behind his degree, but the rest of us just play to pass the time. I do like the satisfaction of blocking someone’s turn with a ruddy  thunk  from a high-scoring word, though.      I tried installing it a little while ago, but I found the whole thing too intense. I’d rather just watch cookery shows and pretend I’m sommat of a chef.      Oi, don’t talk like that—this is your kitchen and your business. If you say you can't make a soufflé, I buy it.      Alright, but it stays in this room. I did alright when I started out, about five years back. Just a coffee stall to begin with.      And now you're rolling in that East London café game. People actually queue up for your toffee apple brownies.      I passed one last week on my way into work. Thought they were closing ‘cause it looked dead, but then I saw your name on the window.      Nup, just a bit of a slow Monday. I tried running a supper club last week but, you know, East London’s full of supper clubs. Half the goers were my cousins and I had to pretend to like my own cooking.      That’s the thing, though. You’ve got to be careful. I heard about this girl who opened a supper club in Shoreditch and ended up with all sorts of legal issues—health and safety inspections, contracts, the lot.      I read up on it for a uni project.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? I’ve been meaning to go for a walk after work, if it stays this nice. I’ve been working from my computer since before ten, and I’d say I could do with some fresh air.      Yeah, it is a bit of a bright one! I went out for a bit this morning and just tried to get some air in. Honestly, I’ve been working from my flat for the past two weeks, so I’m aching for a break in someone else’s atmosphere.      Oh, working from home too much can really get to you. It makes it even harder to separate work from personal life. What’s your day typically like?      Just messing around with printers, scanners, and computers—what you’d expect from an IT admin. But I also get to help the teachers make posters and assembling course handouts. It’s not too bad—relatively boring, but everyone here is friendly enough.      Sounds like you’re pretty hands-on. I was a waitress once, full-time, so I get the ‘always on your toes’ vibe. I’m in charge of the canteen staff here now. Cover supervisor by trade, but in this role, I help run the catering when the staff are off. Keeps my mind busy at least!      That’s interesting! I imagine that must be quite a switch from what you were doing before.      It was, but I suppose I just enjoy working with people—whether they're students or staff. Besides, I can brag that I made the best scones in the county once. Still do, if I might say so myself.      I’m Russian by birth, so the English scone is quite an acquired taste for me—but I do like it. Bread with butter and jam is still a classic for my family. My grandma always makes the baked apples, you know, with cinnamon?      Oh aye, I’ve had those! Very traditional, but I suppose I haven’t had a good one since I was over in Moscow as a student. Heavens, that was twenty years ago! My daughter took the pictures—it's hard trying to get around with three kids in the back of the car.      Three kids? That’s quite a few! Is it just you and your husband?      Aye, well, my husband works in London, so I’m the one who does most of the juggling.

‘Mum, am I gettin’ confused or is tha’s the third time we’ve ‘ad to stop ‘cause o’ traffic?’      ‘I think you’re right, darling. I was wondering that myself.’      ‘Blimey, it’s rush een! I thought we’d get to the next shop by now. Hold on a minute, lads. I’ve ‘ad enough of this.’      ‘Even tha’ wasp-stung road sign wasn’t ‘elpful. Is this the one where we get the new blankets? Tha’s shop near the college, innit? I promised Lucy we’d get ‘er somethin’ like that one you’ve got, Gran.’      ‘Oh, the one with the Darcy fox print and the hemstitch? That’s the one, yes. But do we really need two new sets of blankets this week? I bought some in last week!’      ‘Eh, spare never ‘urts. I reckon we’ll need more when we move, luv. Y’know, I don’t fancy sleepin’ on a cold floor when we start redecoratin’.’      ‘Do we all know what we’re gonna do about the new house? I mean, who’s stayin’ in which room durin’ the renovation? I want the smallest one so I can ‘ave a proper room for college applications. Like, someone said full house survey and I was like, “count me in!”’      ‘Well, you’re gettin’ it ‘alf way – no promises when the builders arrive, eh? I’ll ‘ave to take the largest room to supervise the lot o’ them. Tha’s where the ladders are safest.’      ‘And I thought I was the organized one! I just hope the waters in the new house work. The last place we looked at looked glorious on paper but the pipes were older than Bolton, I swear.’      ‘Gran, that’s what they all say. I mean, we’ve ‘ad better plumbing in our last flat. That thing where you opened the tap and it went muddy pink—bad memories go there!’       Laughs  ‘Aye, an’ don’t forget the time we ‘ad to boil the kettle thirty times to get rid o’ the taste. Still, we kent laugh about it now, eh?’      ‘Only because we’re not over thirty any more. Or younger! It’s a big move for all of us. I think it’s about time we started acting less like teenagers and more like grown-ups. Just a thought.’       Laughs  ‘You mean, until we’ve finished renovatin’ them floors and the whole lot?

So do you think I should accept that online request? It's from the people who made that  apex legends update  I told you about. I’m just not sure if it's safe      Aye, we’ve had the same kind of things on our email in Liverpool. Be careful een, if it doesn't seem right, it's best just to ignore it.      I mean, I delete them before they even show up on my main folder. It's easier not to waste the time clicking on something that sounds dodgy.      But how do I even know what's real and what's not? I've been stuck on that mental loop for hours and now I'm just moody because I’m overthinking it.      Oh luv, don’t let the internet make you feel like that. It gets too much sometimes doesn’t it? I see you college kids always online these days. You should be thinking about GCSE stuff and not these emails, ha!      Fair point, Sam, but it's not just the emails. I applied to start up work in London next year and I’ve still got grief from uni, like, modules aren’t even finished and I’m already second-guessing every decision.      True. I’m still figuring it all out too. I want to study psychology because I love how the mind works, but what if I’m not good enough?      Well, I think you are! That’s just a classic case of the mind doubting what you know is right. It's like painting a picture—sometimes you see all the brushstrokes, and it seems about wrong, but walk back a few steps, and the beauty makes sense.      That’s poetic for someone with barely a GCSE, Sam! Maybe I’ll start writing a ‘how to manage your brain' guide if I ever figure it out.      That's actually quite sweet. I don't think you should underestimate anyone based on what they’ve got on paper. You've got a lot to offer with your stories and insight.      And no, you don't even need to travel to London, love. There's so much on your own doorstep here in Surrey. Just don't forget to take in the beauty that's right behind the boxset binges and the gaming sessions.      Speaking of which, have you checked out that new game, Cosmic Horizons?

Right, so today in class we were talking about different metals and fabrics, and it made me think — let’s chat about it over dinner. You both like Minecraft, yes?      Yes! I like building houses with iron and stone.      Me too! And I also found some redstone! But I don’t know what it does yet.      That’s a good start! Redstone is like the electricity of Minecraft. In real life, metals like iron, copper, and gold have uses too. Iron makes strong tools and weapons, copper is used in wires, and gold is mostly for decoration or jewelry. Do you know much about fabrics?      I know about cotton. It’s soft and you make clothes out of it.      I like wool, it’s warm and you can shear the sheep!      Exactly! Cotton is soft and grown in warm places, while wool comes from sheep — in real life and in Minecraft. But there’s also silk, which is super soft and used to make fancy clothes, like robes and hats.      Oh, I have silk in my game! I didn’t know it was real!      It is! People used to make it from silkworms. Pretty amazing stuff. Speaking of amazing, have you heard the story about the Comberton knight?      No! Is it a new legend?      It’s kind of a funny invention. Some friends and I used to tell stories about a knight who lived near the village with a cloak made out of spider silk and a sword made of meteorite metal. No one really knows how it started, but now even your grandpa Swears he remembers it.      That sounds like you made it up!      Guilty as charged! Maybe we’ll have to write it down before someone claims it as real history. Anyway, after that story, remember to take your vitamins. You know vitamins help your bones grow strong, just like your character gets stronger in the game when you eat food.      Do they taste like mushrooms and steak?      Not quite, but they do help you be strong like a Minecraft warrior. So go get your orange juice and your pill — and maybe go trade some copper for some better armor in your game. Battle the creepers!      Can you teach me how to make silk from silkworms in Minecraft?      I’ll find a silkworm in the game!      Silkworms aren’t in the game yet, but if they were, you’d probably need them to spin silk in a furnace.

Rather annoying this new bar ain't it?      Aye, it's not like the old one in town centre no more is it? Blows its cobblers.      Aye, we used to hang out in there wi’ them daft lads from uni eeny every single week. Now it's just some posh arseholes in here.      Y'know what tho? At least it's quieter now. Gave me chance to think properly. We arn't doing much once this term finishes though, are we?      Nah, I dunno. I were gonna start learnin’ guitar again lik' I did when I was turkey. Oi, you still got that old one you left lyin’ around the flat, don’t pick it up no more.      Yeah, it’s still upstairs. Felt old when I tried it. Not a bad thing tho. Blokes, ever looked into that new band down the road? They’re pretty decent.      Naa, who are they? Any good? I mean, we used to go to loads of grief when we were younger. Rememb’er watching that local lass rhythm section when we got way too drunk at the park pop-up?      That’s riot! I thought I were gonna end up in hospital after that one. Still, it were a good tune.      Who’d have thought us daft ones would end up a bit more responsible now. I dunno, still got plenty of moan and gin and being an unhelpful prat when it come to people.      That aint changed a bit! But yeah, I mean, th’ old ones arn’t gone yet are they? I mean, Steve does Facebook gigs still, doin’ ‘Rise Like A Phoenix’ every Friday.      Aye, it's a laugh. Do you think we could meet up them boys when they’re doing one?      Let’s do it. Git the lunches sorted and the whiskeys in.      Gob Iron! You're like a man with a plan goin' on! But if you start talkin’ about preppy college line in, I’m out.      Aye aye, you'll be the only one who hears it and then proceeds to karaoke it with earnest tears in your eyes.      Perfed! That’s the plan them! It's a shame I can't sit here for ever talking music.      And alcohol, clearly.      To be fair, I'd rather talk about that before I talk about what's happening with some of them paedo cadre on the news evernight. Makes me sick.

So did you guys hear about the new exhibit at the Saatchi Gallery? They’re doing that Montenegro photography show again. I’m thinking of checking it out after I finish my EPQ draft. It's been doing my head in honestly.      Yeah, I saw the poster in my mum’s office. She liked the last one with the coastal stuff. I might come with you. What’s your EPQ on? I still can’t get mine off the ground. My teacher says it's too vague.      Wait, are you going to the Montenegro one? I went last year and the photos of the mountains were  insane . I wish we could just go there for a holiday. But anyway—Speaker_1, my EPQ is on vegetarianism in schools. I’m interviewing teachers and kids. It's kind of hitting a nerve though. Some people actually think it’s a ‘middle-class problem’.      That’s so annoying. My grandpa says people in places like Africa don’t even have the luxury of being picky. I don’t know—sure, there are issues with poverty, but vegetarianism doesn’t mean you don’t eat. It’s about human rights and environmental stuff as well.      You’re overthinking it. Look, I’m lactose intolerant anyway, so I’m like, half vegetarian by accident. Also, my aunt cooks this amazing lentil dahl. You should come to hers for dinner on Thursday. She’s trying to convert someone into full vegetarian. Maybe you can audition my defence? It's bad.      Oh, is it a family thing? I’ve got a sister who does juggling in the evenings because she says school isn’t doing it for her. “Finding personal fulfillment” or whatever. Honestly, I just wish teachers could teach without stressing us out so much.      I wish. My EPQ tutor is just like, “you can do it, you can do it,” but the deadline is still in two weeks and I’ve only done half the bibliograp...      Why not take a walk or something? Breaks help. We can juggle while we do it? My cousin taught me how once, after a day of arguing with the dinner table about govt funding on humanitarian work. It's weird, but it worked.      I’d like to go to university somewhere with cafes and libraries all over. So I’m planning to look at conservation and nutrition roles after sixth form.

Rather annoying this new sock tax eh?      Aye, it's mental. £200 to live in this dump. I’m more than happy to murder someone for a toastie.      Chut, you guys are being such typical Northerners. I mean seriously, £200 for a kitchen with one splitter and a toaster that catches on fire every other week?      Like, I've seen my nan's caravan and it's got more tech in it than this! My brother was like "are you sure you're not joining the army?" cos they get like three-star hotels for lodgings.      What’s worse is that we can't even cook anything decent. I tried boiling some pasta and left it on for三十 seconds, came back and it looked like it’d been through a war. I mean, you’d think they’ve got at least enough breakfasts to feed us.      I’m just sat here, using the phone desktop as my chopping board cos I can’t even find a cutting board.      My auntie sent me this wooden board the last time I went home. It’s still in my drawer for "emergencies". Honestly, watching you two try to cook in here without burns is like national treasure – Mate, have you tried Tesco Extra value swede?      No, don’t go there. I have a feeling that the reason we don’t get fed, is cos people just aren’t full in this house. I haven’t seen a full stomach since we left school.      I just wish my nan and grandad weren't so proud of me living away from home. I about blocked them off after they said "at least it's different to this place" and showed them photos of the inside of their caravan.      My mam says I need to be grateful for the 'experience' of it. I told her about the cockroaches in the toaster. She sent me a nice microwave.      Experience? I think your experience is to just sit and wait for the microwave to go off.      At least your nan doesn’t send you food packages every week, I got this entire tin of baked beans sent to go with my map of life improvements.      I swear my nan is trying to build a food hoard box in my room.      So how have you made it to six-form without burning it all down?      It's survival of the fittest, and overcooked swedes.

Rather lovely to be here at the Seven Stars, isn't it? I was just telling my students that Totnes feels like a slice of old England now they're all overseas! How's Wales treating you this time of year?      Oh, it's such a treat to be out of Cardiff for a bit. Snowed last week, so I thought I'd come down for a bit of sun and a break. A lot of work tends to happen this time of year, you know, what with all the training sessions. But you, what's the plan this Christmas?      Well, I’ve just finished wrapping up some school-year-end admin. I've got the whole of December off. Alice and I are thinking of visiting my parents in Torquay. The children love the sea, and I reckon they'd enjoy some of the little shops opening up for the festive season.      Oh, I envy you that. I've been wanting to take some time off and do something different ever since I started my consultancy full-time. Have you got the kids over to visit that family friend of yours, the one who used to run that glamping site in the Cotswolds?      Yes! James and Susan. They’ve always been lovely. Their place was such a hit with the kids – all the fairy lights and fire pits and stuff. Though James gave up the glamping last year. Now he runs some kind of tea-tasting business out of an old barn. Susan says he's just someone who can't stay still for long. Ever had a chaotic work week like that?      Oh, absolutely. I worked with a client recently who changed the entire project mid-meeting because he saw about five new trends while eating his sandwich. But it can be exciting too. I'm starting to think about maybe taking some clients to Torquay next spring. There's a lot to do with sustainability and education projects, you know?      Well, if you ever want a local guide for any events, I'd be thrilled to help. I’ve done a fair bit of event organisation as part of TEFL academies before. And with the kids a little older now, the opportunities do seem more… accessible.      That would be brilliant. I can go over details on the train if you'd like. Just don't expect me to not interrupt you every five minutes with a question while you're explaining what your actual job is.

: You lot never answer your phones these days, Dad. I rang ages ago. Is it that new number you got?     : It is, I got a new one after the last phone was stolen in the queue at the supermarket, I swear things were picked up like in a film. Got a fiver out, and poof—gone!      Almost as bad as the time you left your phone by the barbecue and got a call from it halfway through a pizza.     : That’s classic, I still remember that! But seriously, the area's changed a fair bit since I was last around, isn’t that new store where the Boots used to be?     : Oh aye, that place now does everything—haircuts, food, even has an optician. But the good news is the speed cameras up here are actually working now. Cats are better behaved when they know the camera’s watching.     : Speaking of, you ever get caught by one of them flash things?     : One bloke nearly took it out, yes! Nearly got a fine too. I was with your mother, to be fair, and she was having a bad day. The camera flashed just as we came out of the newsagents. She thought it was targeting her, fairly dramatic, mind you.     : You lot in customer service deal with dramas all day, I imagine. How’s work at your place, still chasing people out of the call centre for coughing?     : That’s not a thing—though yes, people have been getting sick left and right. Made me think about taking your sister up on her invite to move to Brighton. Less coughing, more sun.     : Brighton? I’ve been! Going there with the school trip to Tanzania next year. We went to Zanzibar once for a break. Got put on weight like I was stuffed into a balloon with curry and chapati.     : You always did stuff your face. I hope they don’t have as many racists as they did before. There were some right shots back in the day.     : Still some, I’m afraid. But it's mostly the older goers really. They see a white or black or brown kid and expect trouble.     : Sad times, bloke. You’ve your mother’s way with people, though. You’ll handle it better than I did when those lads gave me the evils at work once. I nearly took a swing.     : Don’t tell the health and safety folks that.

Rather annoying day today, wasn't it? That meeting about public relations for the new module schedule — it felt like we were talking circles round the same point for two hours. I swear, someone needs to start categorising these things alphabetically to make it half-decent.     Deer, it's beginning to sound like the kind of nonsense they'd write on satire TV. I wanted to suggest introducing a PR consultant, but I think they think that's extravagance. Still, you did make a good point about student engagement. You might be the only one who remembers that when it's time to promote the final syllabus.     Oh, I wouldn’t say the only one, but yes — most of them think promoting a syllabus is just printing it and sticking it on a noticeboard. I reckon if we branded it properly and put in a bit of music to make promotional videos — maybe something chill with an upbeat, modern vibe — students might actually remember to attend.     Now you’re speaking my language, indulging both your academic ambitions and my pop culture obsessions. I overheard one of the other lecturers say they'd be happy if we just played Ed Sheeran and called it a day. Imagine that: Ed watching us lecture.     Laugh out loud. Ed – dead serious in front of a class of 200 students, while the lecturers dance in the background? Honestly, I’d consider that promotion. Speaking of which, we should go out for food. I'm beyond my usual lecturers’ meal of a sandwich and bad coffee.     Agreed. After this week, I say we find something decent — nothing too posh, because most of us are still earning while eating the same brie and pesto sticks as everyone else. Let’s walk into town and see what we can find. Shopping for dinner does sound oddly domestic to do on a Thursday evening, doesn’t it?     It does. Invites a certain kind of normalcy, which I think we could all do with right now. I could stick to my budget as long as we avoid the wine shop. They've recently started a new brand with "lecturer discount" — no, you don't even want to know.     Can't really get much more British than trying new wine and lamenting over college lineups, can we?     Very British, yes — and utterly typical. Alright, let’s get moving. I'd quite like to pretend for one evening that we're not two overpaid academics arguing about syllabi over cold chicken.

Rather annoying this, really. I've been at it for ages. I thought it would be a doddle, making a shower curtain with the material I had leftover from the blind cover.      A doddle indeed. Look at the fraying on the edges—it’s hardly coordinates with the rest of the bathroom décor. You think you'd get a holiday from all this domestic self-sufficiency once in a while, but no, one's always knitting bean bags or making curtains.      Well, nothing was quite the colour when I popped into the craft shop last week. I saw everything but what I needed! And I can't seem to get the pen to work on my sewing machine now. My hands are definitely not as steady as they used to be. Ten more years and I’ll be using a pastry brush and string in lieu of thread.      Cats would definitely prefer breakfasts made from string and bread crumbs. Less effort for me, at least, planting the odd bit of feline indulgence near the laptop. As for the bean bag, I was going to tell you—personally I think it takes three left turns and land on one’s nose. But tell me, what exactly did you knit it out of?      That left-over wool scarf – very chunky, fairly motley in style, really. It’s a bit like somethin’ that would be found at a jumble sale held in a disused chapel, which may in fact have been full of derelict bean bags to begin with. But it oddly gives a certain charm to the room, if you ask me. It’s got character.      Character is most certainly about thriving on chaos. Just don’t try to knit the next lot of curtains from thimbles and elastic bands—you know that would be barely wearable and even less washable.      Oh, I’ve got guest towels in the spare room with that same sort of logic. I used a few dockers jackets and some old hens’ eggs waiting to be tossed out. It turned out like something off of  The Good Life , with lunches delivered in satchels made from various doilies.      Then again, if you started with the curtains goin' on your own improvements, I’d probably go straight for loosened dentures, no constriction of any kind, and let the shower curtain zip gently with the breeze at its whim.      That’d make for one very atmospheric dry shampoo, wouldn’t it?

Rather chilly this morning, isn't it? I needed six cups of tea just to get out o' bed.      Six cups? My, you must have had something specific to toast with that lot, Harry. Not to worry—I’ve got the kettle on for fresh. We’ll make a proper eeny weeny breakfast of it if you like.      Aye, that’s a grand idea, love. An egg and one too, if it’s easier. I’ve had some interesting news to pass along, and it needs the company of a decent breakfast, don’t you think?      Oh really? Spill it before I forget the toast, deary!      My word, you two are still at it like I’ve not been in the room half the time, haven’t I? I’ll get the toast done if you lot keep chattering and forget yourselves. breakfast, no doubt about it!      Aye, Alan’s right. Good morning to you, lad. I was just telling Janet here I heard from that solicitor over in Norwich, and it seems there’s some business about that plot we all said we’d buy back and turn into a proper wild garden—y'know, the one by the river, just off Bedale Road.      Oh! That old bit of land? Good grief, the council almost turned it into a car park for that new retail park. And we were all so cross, weren’t we? Who said anything about buying it back?      That plot’s not exactly buyable, Harry—unless it’s in the way of being split up between all of us. Unless, of course, we’ve got binding shares or a type of standing to do that.      I suppose you’re not suggesting we suddenly go crowding up and trying to unbuild a development that’s already been planned for years?      Aye, but that’s just it. The solicitor told me the company that bought it fell into some legal difficulty and the plot’s come back to the estate. So they’re listing it for sale by the bundle of a couple of lots—might still be fairly priced.      Then this is news worth the six cups of tea, Harry. But let me warn you—if we go at this, I shall not let it go without a proper valuation, a structural survey, and due process. No more romantic planting without real groundwork.      Well, you heard the man—or the solicitor—and I expect we can have a proper morning shuffle up about it, can’t we?

Rather annoying the queue at the supermarket today, wasn’t it? I was trying to get home ‘fore it got dark and pick up some of that chicken for dinner. I’ve asked Jane [Speaker_4] to make her famous cranberry and sage stuffing for Christmas as well — wouldn’t you two agree it’s eeny better than shop-bought?      Oh totally, Jane — your stuffing is a masterpiece. A real Christmas treat! I mean, I’m not much of a cook, but I know good food when I taste it. I got so busy last week when I was out with some friends in Oxford that I hardly had time to finish my shopping. I ended up rushing it at the last minute — and let’s just say, I’m living with some questionable left-overs this week.      Oliver, I feel for you — I turned up at the car park for my uni alumni gig yesterday and breakfast still in my bag. I mean, I didn’t  plan  to miss the start, but we got caught in the traffic. Still, the chaps were glad to see me, and we had a laugh over it. They’ve got these two young ones now as well, and I tell you, it still astonishes me how fast time goes.      That’s so true, Steve. I remember being fairly young, and now I’ve got a whole schedule of shifts and study sessions every week as a trainee nurse. It’s a bit much at times — especially when the budget feels tighter than ever. But I’m glad I made the change. I thought I’d definitely be out of my depth, but my sisters and I all being healthcare workers now — it’s a bit of a family legacy.      That does sound quite the thing, Jane. I had my thirtieth and even my fortieth with barely a blink, if I’m honest. I do miss a bit of the simplicity though. Like cooking for oneself — or not cooking at all, to be totally honest. But being part of the family, I reckon you’ve all got a recipe for being happy. Even when shopping’s a nightmare or the bank statements take a hit.      I do love our little Christmas set-up, honestly. We travel a fair bit for the holidays, so it’s lovely to be together like this. Just chilling, telling stories, and, yeah, figuring out what the box contents will be when the parcels are opened.

Rather lovely to sit out here on Sunday mornings, isn't it? The sun's just easing through the pines, and the coffee here is something else—way better than most places I've found in this part of the world. So, Mr. Bushey, what brought you to Northern Cyprus?      Call me William, if you like—and well done on the coffee remark. It’s not often a Brit notices coffee these days. As to Northern Cyprus, I’ve spent quite a few winters here, pulling out of a long stretch of not doing much back at home. Retired suddenly after a big redundancy package... didn’t seem right filling my days with telly and crossword puzzles the whole way through.      My, I can understand that. I've left London for this place more or less permanently, yes. A fresh start and all that. I’m a teacher by trade, but the schools here have been a bit—how do I put it? Less... routinised than what I'm used to. No tests, no Ofsted, just a small village school full of kids who treat me like a character from a fairytale because I have curly hair and a British accent.      Good on you—curly hair and rhythm in the classroom gives you a national treasure vibe about you. But I’m curious, what made you  leave  England? More tea or less tests?      A bit of both, honestly. The whole system’s become such a numbers game. I felt more like a filing clerk than a teacher half the time. I wanted out, something slower, something with a bit of sea and hill views. I missed  time  as much as a new place. I’m from Dorchester originally—Dorset’s green hills are part of my blood—but this place has its charm.      And does it? I’ll have to say I prefer the baked sunshine rather than the perpetual overcast of the South. But I'll admit it's a land of contrasts—pretty villages, stone walls, people waiting on the tour groups. There are days when I swear the place is bursting with English retirees but no students.      Some of the young people you do meet are amazing. Picked up the odd local kid go-karting in the afternoon and trying to get them to respect Newton’s laws in physics. Gets rocky. But the box of chalk on the blackboard still makes me feel at home, I must say.

Rather annoying isn't it, how thick the smog is today. I had to close my window when I got in from my shower this morning. I’m so used to Norwich being clean, but this just adds to it.      Yeah, it’s getting more frequent. We haven’t had it quite this bad since last year, but today was ridiculous. I reckon it depends on the wind. If it’s still, all the pollution just lingers.      I don’t know, there's something different about this. The air tastes and smells chemical. I was walking past the school car park earlier, and I saw one of the teachers coughing violently, and the kids were still out there playing in the sandbox.      I saw that too. It makes me wonder how much the school authorities are aware, or how much they care. I mean, most of the parents are expats or diplomats. I suppose they send their kids to Anglo-Chinese schools in Beijing and not out here where it's rough.      That could be why. I don’t like thinking that the local families—those who can’t afford the fancy international schools—get stuck with the consequences. I’ve started telling my students to buy air purifiers for home, and I give out tips on how to wash them – even though I know they can be expensive.      I’ve done the same. But did you know the other problem? The dust is so fine it passes through standard masks. Our colleague Mark at the language institute also got a bad chest infection a few weeks back.      That’s scary. It shouldn’t be this bad, even for a developing country. I spoke to my parents in about pollution at home—well, you can imagine their reply: “It’s worse than a fog, and not nearly as romantic!”      Maybe they’re not wrong, but for us, it’s not even weather anymore. It's a health crisis. I don’t mind working any longer, but the thought of being indoors for ten hours a day just to breathe clean air... it's soul-sucking.      I keep thinking maybe one day the government will do something. The road here near the flats is lined with trees, but I can go days without seeing them green if the smog is thick.      Well, that green bench we were sitting on last week when the weather broke was nice.

Rather annoying the new oven’s taking so long to preheat. I’d have thought it would be up to temperature by now. Never mind, it’s not like we’re in a rush.      I don’t mind waiting a bit, I had a long day at the office today. Papers stacked up like the Tower of London. Kept twitching at me every time I turned a page.      Honestly, if I saw one more project plan, I’d scream. It was bad enough as it was! My day was alright—sat at the desk in my PJs most of the morning, like I always do. Though I made sure to go for a walk after lunch to feel like I was contributing to the planet a bit.      That’s the spirit! I had to visit two home patients, both very sad in their own little ways. It gets to you a bit sometimes. But breakfast was good—muesli and coffee, which I suppose is a bit of a non-event compared to what you two do for food.      I thought I’d give it a go today—chicken, roasties, that sort of thing.      And did you look up a recipe on your phone, or are we trusting in your culinary genius?      I looked at a few, and then decided to go with my gut. Binary choice really: follow the instructions or do it badly. I’m picking the former every time. Pop those roast potatoes in someone?      Just a second, I need to adjust the sourdough—don’t want it going too golden while we talk here!      Look, are we even going to do something exciting this weekend? I’ve just watched the last episode of this show and I officially need new content! Going stir-crazy with barely a cat video to watch.      What was the show called?       Homes of the Invincible —it was a re-make, I know, but it was decently spooky. I could see us visiting such a mysterious place over the weekend.      That sounds more like your line than mine, love. I’d be terrified in something like that!      Then go for it on your own if you like! Any chance of a camping trip? Finally, some fresh air instead of the box room!      Can you see me hiking with a tent and a bag? I live out of a backpack, not a belly bag!      Oh, very funny.

Rather annoying this new bus route, innit? Thought it’d make it easier to get ‘ere from Sunderland, but nay, they’ve stuck us on some new detour. I've nearly missed me stop twice already.      Look, I get it — changes can be a pain. But apparently, the new route avoids the inner city rush and cuts down traffic overall. Plus, it goes straight past the Cambridge University Press bookshop now, so  we  can kill two birds with one stone, yeah? Might as well stretch out the trip a bit when you're in the mood.      Right, but it adds twenty bloody minutes to the journey, and the bins are still out for hours in the mornings. It’s not just me — heard the same from a few uni folk I works with who moan on the Slack channel about it every mornin’. It’s like they’ve never ‘ad to get somewhere on time before.      Well, if they don’t like it, maybe they should follow the example of that student protester the papers were full o’— you remember the one, lugging a whiteboard around the station with “Bus Route Nazi” writ on it and refusing to board any bus that didn’t adhere to the old route? Absolutely surreal, but got national attention. Made the buses re-consider their plan, leastways.      Aye, saw that on Twitter. Fair play to ‘im, I suppose — don’t know if it’s fair for just someone at the uni to get their way. You’d reckon they’d listen to folks who  live  ‘ere, not just the students. Mind you, I still like where I live in Cambridge better than most places about. Not like Sunderland, but then again, it’s different — more space.      Yeah, it’s got charm and the uni gives it a real buzz. I do miss, like, the transport system in Manchester though — much better for getting into the city. But the student vibe here suits you, I reckon. You always say you miss the “local feel” while you were at university. Though Cambridge academically always topped the tables, right?      Some do, but there you go, I come from a course that placed higher than even govt stats on most years if you ask me. Just depends what you’re comparing it to. I suppose it always helps ‘aving the press and whatnot close by. So at least I can get me classics and linguistics books delivered every week with a proper cuppa in me hand now we’re passing that ‘ole bookshop.      Exactly.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? I suppose it's a shame we can't take a walk first, but the lunch appointment is in a bit more of a rush, ay?      Oh, don't worry, Julia. Look at it as a treat—no kids, no responsibilities, just good food and better company. I've been craving proper English roast chicken for ages.      I agree with Nicola. Not often we get to meet up like this. The last time, Liam brought the kids and we ended up having to order pizza because we didn't think.      Right, right! Still, it's precious when you get time to just talk and not have to explain why you shouldn’t be eating the cheese with jelly—it tends to draw the wrong kind of attention from the kids, doesn’t it?      That’s an understatement! My son once tried to breakfast on margarine and tomato sauce. Brian still laughs about it, though he’s the one who let it happen, to be fair.      So, Julia—your son’s bringing the new girlfriend, I hear? Is she finally the one?       laughs  Let’s not get ahead of ourselves, Azalee. She’s lovely from what I’ve seen—he’s very taken with her. He brought her to the funeral for his grandmother last week, and she was just so sweet and respectful. You know what it’s like with young people—never know what's going to stick, but for now, they're happy.      That's the main thing. Also, it's a relief to finally be able to see the grandkids properly in a few weeks. I about lost my voice trying to type everything out the last time we had a call.      Speaking of calls—I was wondering if you'd like me to arrange for my stepdad to come up for the weekend. He mentioned he’d like to visit. Since I’m working remotely, it’d be no problem sorting it.      Oh bless you, Azalee, that would be lovely. Let me know once it’s sorted. I keep meaning to learn to do video calls but, well, you remember my relationship with technology.      Don’t worry about it. If you want, I can sit with you and walk you through it. I know it’s a bit blokey sometimes, what with all the icons and buttons, but I promise it's not rocket science.

Rather lovely this time of day, isn't it? The light’s casting a golden sheen over the water... What do you think? Just the two of us and the river. No car fumes, no noise, just… peace.      It truly is. We haven’t done this in ages. I liked walking from Woolwich, didn’t feel like getting the bus all the way from home. I only just remembered this area before the O2 got built. Oh, how it changed it! That huge white thing looms over the river like a spaceship.      You’re not the only one who thought that. I remember when I first saw the construction, I was working on a transcript that day and had to look up from my notes to make sure I hadn’t hallucinated from caffeine overload. It’s a bit alien in the middle of all that history, really.      I suppose it’s modern enough in its own way. The concerts at the O2 draw so many people, you’d think it's the new Tower Bridge. Speaking of which—haven’t we passed the old bridge yet?      We’re just about to come to it. You can see the ferries going past—it always reminds me of Venice in little moments like that. Though I much prefer it here with no tourist crush and no need for a car. I’ve given up on owning one, honestly. The whole idea of driving through London leaves me wanting to scream, and the cost feels someone else’s problem.      I know what you mean. I gave up my car years ago—only complicates life and comes with so many hidden prices. We’ve been better off cycling or walking. Especially with the kids. Last summer, we went to Cornwall for a holiday and didn’t rent a vehicle at all. Biking and the local buses were fine, really. The children surprised me—they actually liked the treks.      That’s surprising, to say the least. But I suppose it does teach them something about patience. You know, speaking of the children, I was talking to Sarah the other day, trying to help her with her math homework—measurement conversions, the whole American cup thing. I swear, trying to understand that the Americans still use gothic symbols on measuring cups is like trying to read hieroglyphs!      It always puzzles me how they jump from cups to pints and don’t have a logical scale to speak of.

Rather annoying this wet weather isn't it? I mean, I love the occasional rain, but it's like it's never going to stop now. I’m so ready for summer proper, you know?      Oh, honestly love, the weather in England is a bit of a joke half the time. My dear, I’ve been drenched twice this week just walking the bins out! Though I suppose a bit of water is better than sweltering too much, eh?      Honestly, someone should invent a magical umbrella just for us Kent folk! But when it's not raining, I'm usually too busy keeping up with the little one. She's learning to potty train now, and it's like a full-time job. I swear she thinks the potty is a dangerous animal or something.      Oh no! That’s the same with my cousin back in Gillingham. He had a meltdown when we suggested swapping his dinosaur-themed potty for a rocket one. It was like announcing a total revamp to his entire identity!      Kids and their strong opinions, eh? Nothing like when I was raised up in Harlow — potty as it is, and that’s final! Tell me though, how are the children getting on at school then?      Oh Matey, we had sports day last week, and Haylie burst into tears when her ‘animal socks’ got muddy. Silly little thing. But oh, the pride on her face when she managed to run full circle without falling over! That made up for the sock mess.      That’d be adorable. Haylie sounds brilliant. Any plans for a ‘Build a Bear’ or something? I did that with my wee cousin — you can imagine the litany of complaints when she didn’t get the exact unicorn he imagined.      Aaah, cuddly toys. My sister had that little Pooh bear since her youth passed on to me. Still have it on the side table. Proper heirloom it is. I always say you can judge a person by what cuddly toys they had as a kid.      Oh, I think it's more the mums and their obsession with kitchen appliances, honestly. You know, the best adjective is ‘multi-functional’. I tried to use our blender once, and it sounded like a jet engine in the living room. Sue me, I’m a full-time mum, not a appliances expert.      Oh gosh, I'm scared to touch my mum’s new toaster.

So, I’ve been doing a bit of thinking, love. We need to set some personal goals before we dive too deep into this new chapter. I’m feeling ready to commit to something long-term, but I want it to be with a plan. What do you think?      I’ve been thinking along the same lines, actually. It’s easy to get swept up in the easy rhythm of life, you know? But I think now’s the perfect time to step back and really think about what matters. What did you have in mind?      Let me get this out first. I’ve had a few offers back in New Zealand—expanding my business there. It’s still got potential, and I think Myra, my sister, could really use the help running the team over there. I’d be willing to cut back and hand over more of the leadership if you’re up for a move.      That’s a big shift. I’ve been in teaching in the U.K. for 15 years now, but I think I could pack up and start fresh—especially if it means being with you. I’ve always wanted to live in a place with that kind of open space. What would that timeline look like?      If we make a few calls and start negotiating, maybe early next year? I’d want to give it a year or two to settle in before making any big decisions like starting a family. I want to ensure we’ve got our foundations right—financially, emotionally, in terms of lifestyle. I don’t just want to move for the sake of it.      That makes sense. I’ve got some friends in Australia I haven’t spoken to in a while about joining up. Maybe a weekend trip here to touch base with old contacts—would you be up for coming with me?      Absolutely. It’s important for both of us to feel like we’ve got support networks here. I can help you with that side of things too. I’ve got some contacts in education and mentorship programs that you might find useful if you decide to re-enter the workforce here.      That would be amazing. I’ve also been thinking—maybe we set aside specific times each week where we check in with our goals, even small ones. Like, lifestyle goals, savings targets, or work progress.

Rather annoying when people can't get through a request without grumbling. I was in Costa the other week and I got the barista to add after-eights to my latte. No need to make a song and dance about it. Charming person would just say "please" properly.      Right? I swear, we’ve got the 'I know what I want’ vibe gone completely mental. I’ve only had to ask someone once in this lot to go to the shop and they’d treat it like it’s a death sentence.      Oh, don't even get me started. I went camping with some mates over Easter and one of them couldn't handle a small flame. Couldn't even light the turkey twizzlers without panicking. Fitbit on the back of their ankle the whole time, if you know what I mean.      That’s a laugh. I remember when I was younger, I hated the cold so much I used to hug my arms around myself and tell myself, “Keep calm and carry on.” As if that would somehow magic me warm. Doesn’t work—personally I still get the chuffers if we’re not in Yorkshire and it’s only ten degrees.      You lot are missing something important, though. You ever try and remember when something happened with your mate, and you’re all “was it last Christmas or the one before?” and end up arguing over who was wearing what? Me and Em had the biggest row trying to remember someone’s birthday.      That's the absolute worst. I swear, with my mate Mark, half my life is either "Was it at Margate or Camp Heysham?" because he nearly flammable his tent once and the other time the tent lit up green because of vibes. Honestly, you’d think he was part of Pokémon or something.      Oh, come on, that's just you. I play Pokémon all the time. The games? The cards? I used to have such a sweet Charizard I tried to bluff people into taking a hit stick.      Right, but you always knew Mark was the wild card in the group. Not just the tent thing, but remember when he tried to travel like a man with a Fitbit and a map? Sat in a service station for an hour trying to read the bloody directions without smoking. Never could go three minutes without a fag.      Honestly, it's why he’s not in accounting.

Rather good to have you all under one roof, what with it being the first Sunday in ages that we've all got the time! I’ve rustled up a bit of bangers and mash, seeing as there's four of us now. Still as hearty as when I was a lad!      Hasn’t it been a proper treat today, love. I reckon it's the sort of evening most folks would’ve spent huddled up on the sofa watching telly, but we're having stew and laughter instead. That’s living!      Funny you should mention telly, Mummy – I saw the new series of  Line of Duty  last night, and the plot twists are getting wilder by the week. It keeps you on your toes. Though I’m starting to feel more like the producers who write the scripts these days than the audience!      I’m far more into documentaries – been binging a few about space this week. They did one on the James Webb Telescope, and it's amazing how much further into the universe we’re seeing. It makes you feel small, in the best way.      You always were full of enthusiasm about those things, darling. Me, I’ll still take a good old country documentary with proper folk music and countryside walks. You can’t beat the view of a Norfolk mist at first light, can you, Alan?      It’s enough to bring a tear to a man’s eye, let me tell you. There’s something about that horizon when it’s low enough to trip over, and the cows are oddly silent. Now, you were saying something about sports, Connor?      Aye! We’ve got a friendly invite to a football match up in Norwich next month. One of the local cups. It’s a bit of a long shot for us, but you don’t get chances like that every day.      Oh, I’d rather not sit in the cold for three hours just to see a team I don't know lose 3-2 in the last minute. You know me!      Now that’s being stubborn, young’un! There’s no better feeling than roaring your head off with the rest of the lot and a pint in your hand.      Let's not get too riled up over a few goals. What about the line-up for the party next weekend? Who’s bringing the chips?

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be hanging about with me mates anyway. Felt like a bit of a waste o’ me time after the first few weeks. Not saying I've given up yet, but it's not really feelin' like the right fit at the minute. Deffo want een job that’s  not  tied to the uni system. Ay, I’m tellin’ you, I’ve only had three clean pairs o’ shoes all term, an’ two are goin’ in the bin. Uni’s a proper mess.      Nah, I reckon you'd get on better if you sorted yer act out. I mean, I’m not sayin’ it's easy, but what’s the plan if you drop out though? I’m not sure I’d be brave enough to just chuck it all and say "nup, I'm out." What about the money you’re squardin'? Actually, I just happened to be born in Liverpool, and my mam’s from there too. She says the name’s a bit shouty, like, real bold—v ery Liverpudlian of her.      Well, your mam’s got good taste. Liverpool sounds proper fancy compared to me tiny little seaside town. Falmouth feels like another universe. I remember – Mate, I got expelled from primary school once because I stole a whole bag of lollies and dressed as a pirate for the first week back. Me mam was proper mortified, but the teacher just laughed at me and said I was a cheeky sod. It stuck.      Mate, you’re a legend. I’d be scared outta me wits if I got excluded for stuff like that. I mean, I was brought up to play the game, keep me head down and be civil. My sister was that compliant you barely noticed she was there. Honestly, if I bin you I’d be lookin’ at somethin’ more creative. I reckon you’d go further in a field where you can just run with ideas instead o’ waiting for someone to grade yer bloody essays.      Nah, you've got to keep the big whines in check if you go freelance, you know? I mean, it's not the system that's goin' on your nerve, it's everyone else – lecturers, mates, the whole vibe. You don’t go from secondary school to uni and suddenly get it. You just have to work it out on yer own, an’ that can be a killer.

So, I heard you've been living in Manchester for a few years now? How's it treating you? I remember the snow falling mid-July the last time I visited!      Ha, it's not that bad anymore—I swear I got used to the cold. But it was pretty wild during the winter holidays, yeah. Work kept me pretty busy. How about you? Still in Oxford? I heard that coffee shop by your office closed down!      Yeah, it did! Honestly, it wasn't the best coffee anyway. Found a new place, but the queue is  always  like three hours. Still, it’s part of the charm, right? Oxford moves slow. On the other hand, you look well. Still working for Pearson?      Yes, I am, and I absolutely love it. A bit stressful at times, but it’s a really exciting team. I've been working on expanding this new marketing campaign into some European markets. It’s different from what we used to do back in London. How about you? I heard you moved up to project co-ordinator—congrats!      Thank you! It wasn’t planned, actually, but I’m loving it. I get to juggle quite a few roles now, which is good for learning. Although, I’m not sure I’ve mastered the art of balancing work and eating properly.      You know what I miss? When we used to live in the city and someone would always bring us a takeaway. Like, once a week, one of us would buy out the takeaway menu and it would feed three people and be gone in under five minutes!      I about cried when I finally remembered the date of the Thai place near campus. It’s been a mission finding good takeout around here. Speaking of which, have you managed to keep in touch with most of the old crew? I feel like I’m missing out on all the fun.      Honestly, not as much as I’d like. A few of us still stick to that monthly catch-up. You should join us next month! We're heading up to Manchester—you can come with me and let Manchester feed you properly for a change.      That sounds brilliant. I’ll see if my workload allows it, but I’d love to. It’s been far too long since we all hung out properly.      Definitely. I’ll send you the details once we confirm.

Rather than going out an' getin’ swamped in tha shops, why dontcha hop online 'n see ifcha can get it delivered straight to th' door? I’ve been doin’ me own shoppin’ online fer ages now. Saves a lotta faff.      Yeah een, I've tried Amazon once or twice, but I ain't too bothered about all them fancy choices. Online shoppin’ just feels a bit... too easy, if yer know wot I mean.      Nonsense, me lad. It’s called convenience, or ‘ave I not taught yer nuttin’ in life!  laughs  I reckon Ebeye's real good fer somethin’ like that old boot yer lookin’ fer. Funniest things turn up on there, I swear I've seen them ads in me head in me sleep now!      What? Real proper boots? Or just old bits 'n pieces everyone's chuckin’ out?      Both, m'boy, both. Fer a grand bargain, too. Last week I picked up a full box of vintage rulers, compasses, an' chalk fer a bob to teach ya grief when ya start exam markin'. Real treasurers, them. Still in their original tin.      Real ones, eh? So like, does it work? Checking online an’ all?      Oh aye. Just gotta ‘ave a good read o' the description 'n maybe check the reviews. If the star ratings are all a bit iffy, best move on—’av’d better things to spend me money on. ‘course, ifcha  really  want it, most people about daft nuff to ship it anyway.      Alright then. I suppose I could check Ebeye an’ see if they've got it. But I still like the smell o’ real shops, like Nuttall’s down the road. There’s somethin’ reassuring about holding it ‘n all.      Aye, I get that. There’s a bit of magic in the old way, ain’t there? I miss the whistles 'n the calls o’ the market square, where yer had t’ bargain fer yer veggies. Bit more of a lifestyle these days, eh?      I reckon. I’m just not sure I’d ‘av’ known where to begin ifcha hadn’t told me about this.      That’s what fam’ly is for, innit? I’ll log in with ya over th’ tea—ain’t nuttin’ funnier than me trying to work out how to collect an item. Trials of old age.      Likewise, whether online or offline, I’m stuck with ya, ain’t I?  laughs  Alright, let’s crack it.

Rather a cold wet morning we’ve had, isn’t it? I blame the damp in this old Cambridge house, got right in my bones.      I know, I was nearly late for work this morning because my train was delayed. And I had to wait for twenty minutes in that soggy rush-hour wind outside King’s Cross. It’s one of those days that makes you wish you were somewhere with a bit of sun.      Aye, sun. Warmth. It was quite a place to be in when I was young. London. Didn’t have elevators in most places back then, everything was stairs, even in the big buildings. I used to walk up and down that many times in a day it’s a wonder I didn’t fall over.      I didn’t know you were from London, Gran. You always spoke about Cambridge like you’d always been here.      Well, I moved here in ’72 for a bit. When I was younger, Mordern, as it’s called now, was a few rows of shops and terraced houses, not all that different from Lewisham I imagine. Back then, as a young man, I thought London would always be there, something eternal. Doesn’t seem quite the same now.      Changes are inevitable, I guess, but sometimes it feels like things move too fast. I’m trying to get promoted next year at work. It’s competitive, you know? Production control is all systems and someone at the top always looking for a new way to crunch the numbers.      Aye, and it’s a wonder you still have time to come and visit me with all that going on. I do miss you, though. You used to bring such good coffee, this place is positively a dump without your lattes.      Don’t listen to him, that’s just sour grapes for cutting the treacle scones. I did bring some tea from Marks & Spencer. It’s not the same as Starbucks, I’ll admit.      That’s my good girl. I’ll have one of those scones and not a word more from you. Now, tell me, when you do get promoted, are you going to stay in the city or move elsewhere?      If I get promoted, I might have to go out to Milton Keynes. The offer might include relocation.      Milton! That’s further west than I ever went, mind you. And with all those roundabouts, I’ve heard.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be flying first thing. But you know how it is — piling off the plane with a hangover and having to find a cab at 7 a.m. isn’t for me. Not to mention Heathrow at that time of year.      Got eeny plans to eat yet? Or are you just gonne sit on the sofa all day stuffing mince pies into your face? I reckon I’ll do a bit of baking; my Nan taught me some interesting recipes that she always called “proper festive.” Sausage rolls in puff pastry with a bit of cinnamon... like, mad, but they worked.      Oh, I’d rather not know about that. My turkey always ends up tasting like sawdust. Honestly, I think I’m cursed in the kitchen. But I’m thinking of serving up little pigs in blankets again for the sides. They’re always a hit, even if I do say so myself.      I pity the poor dears who ate them last year. One of the pigs had a twig in it. I swear, if a fox isn’t behind that — I don’t bloody well know what is. Did I tell you, by the way, that I found a deer by the side of the road the other day? Poor thing?      Yeah, I’ve seen a few of those. Flick of the headlights and they’re through the windscreen like it’s not there. Makes you wonder why the supermarkets just don’t start importing roadkill. Just sayin’.      [laughing] They’d better not. I’d rather not be accused of eating roadkill for dinner in front of my parents.      I think you’d just blame the delivery man. “Not my cooking, thanks.” Speaking of which, are you guys coming over for Christmas lunch? Maybe we could do something, like, put the treacle sponge in the oven and actually serve it?      Doesn’t sound too bad to me. I’ll bring some mulled wine. My Aussie family’s got a  proper  recipe — with cloves, nutmeg, and a little bit of rum. Not the cheap stuff you get in supermarkets, mind.      That actually sounds goon. I’ll see if my parents are up for joining in.      Hopefully, they won’t bring that Time Lord from Dorset again. The one with the scarf made of 3000-year-old curtains.      Oh, that’s right — I heard he’s doing a baking demo at the local café next month.

Rather annoying this new speaker’s voice. You know what grinds me the most? How it’s so flat... got no character, no flavour. Like they switched down a gear in their voice box. An’ where is we off to again?      Cambridge. Just like you to make a day trip out of it, yeah? You got an assignment handed in at 12 – don’t forget. I’ve only got a flat mate's sofa this time, not my house since I’m not back there 'til the weekend.      Oh right, the ancient civilisations coursework. You'd think the uni would build it in with the dead week, but nooo, they’d rather pile it in like that. Anyway, you’d better make sure to left your laptop this time – I ain't backtracking home for it again.      You’re making it sound far harder than it is. I mean, Cambridge ain't that far. Less than an hour if we don’t get stuck in M1 madness, right? I say we make the most of it and hit up Waterstones or one of those bookshops in the city. I’ve been looking for a rare sci-fi collection and I heard something like that might’ve been sighted in the Pendleton store.      Only if we stop for tea first. I refuse to go into the city on an empty stomach. Any chance of a proper scone and clotted cream?      Absolutely not, no chance in this car. We're saving the fuel for the way back. It's bad enough I had to spring for the diesel at half past eight this morning. Any money saved is money well saved.      I about blocked at that news! My car's the reliable old Renault, but yours is practically a motorhome and you're still griping about fuel prices. Don't even get me started on the smell.      What do you mean? I did a quick clean at the start of the week – any ‘smell’ is probably just your mind scheming to blame your car. As for you being broke over fuel, I’d've offered to chip in a couple of quid if you took the bus.      Right, but stopping at the bus stop would go against everything I stand for about getting our own way – plus, I'm an engineer, not a bus commuter. Who lives in the future? Us drivers, that’s who.

So, I just heard this new album by That 1975 band. It’s wild, like... they’re mixing disco with some sort of robot music now. Not sure what they're aiming for, but it's probably “cutting-edge.”      Oh yeah, I skipped that one. I went back and re-listened to some   Frank Ocean   stuff instead. " Blonde" still hits. Man, I think he's one of those artists who’s gonna be studied in music classes in like fifty years.      Frank Ocean? I don’t really get him. I’ve been getting more into   The Smiths   lately. All those weird guitar riffs and Morrissey’s like... MySpace-era poetry vibes? Cuts through the noise, you know?      Aww, cool! The Smiths? Dude, you must watch a lot of   independent movies  , no?      Haha, yeah, he’s into the artsy film stuff, not the blockbusters. I still haven’t seen  Oppenheimer , but I feel like everyone is talking about it. I mean, did you see that  Thor: Love and Thunder  teaser?      Ugh. I saw that. It looked so... cringey. Like, I’m not saying Thor is bad or anything, but the director is making him soft now?      I got you. Still, the visuals looked cool. But someone recently told me to watch   Christopher Nolan  ’s  Tenet . I haven’t even made it past the first ten minutes. It’s like physics meets a dream where I don’t understand anything.      That movie is cursed. I watched the first act once and then gave up. My brain fails at time inversion. Speaking of which, have you all started the physics homework? My equations are like Morse code.      Dude, that relativity question on the worksheet is a landmine. I had to Google what a frame of reference even is. We should’ve gone to the after-school physics club instead of staying here with lunches we can't finish.      I know right? But the food’s bad anyway. The chicken is rubber goop. I tried it again today. Still rubber goop.      I had a sandwich today, but the bread was stale and the filling was like someone had forgotten to fill it. Like... someone lazily filled it with air.      Tell me about it. But hey, while we're stuck here, I’m gonna blast my The Smiths playlist and forget we’re in sixth form. You all in?      Only if there's some Manchester rain and existential vibes involved.

Right, so today at Balanceability, Sophie did a handstand on the balance beam! I think it was a real breakthrough for her—she’s been working so hard on her core strength.      I don’t think I can do a handstand yet! Thomas wouldn’t help me much if I tried, would you, Thomas?!      I reckon it depends on how deep the pool is! If there’s a manmade waterfall in the garden, maybe we can splash around. But Mrs. Taylor said you can’t dive in the community pool cause you might hit your head.      That’s very true. I remember when I was a kid, the school had a pond where some of us tried to jump in, and one of the teachers got really mad. Still, I’m glad I didn’t risk it now and then. A head injury at your age is no joke!      But Thomas said if you do a cannonball into the shallow end at his friend’s house, you won’t get hurt. James is the friend. His mum is renovating the house and there’s even a swimming pool in the plans!      What about cats? Did you know National Cat Day is in Japan in February? My teacher said we should bring in a cat poster. I drew a Shiba Inu because they’re like, kind of adorable and fluffy but not like British cats. We did a conversation topic at school about what cats like.      That’s sweet, Thomas—but in the meantime, maybe you can read up a bit more on good food combinations. Some students had very creative ideas: pizza and chocolate, apple pie and ice cream... I was surprised, but it makes me question how many people have tried all these pairings!      I like burgers with辣椒 and fries. Sarah said that you’re supposed to have assessments soon, Mummy? Are you going to teach us again?      I am, yes. I’ve been thinking it might be time to give homeschooling a bit more structure, just to help with your reading and writing. I know school can’t always give individual space, and I want you both to do your best.      So you’ll help us with our assessments? I want to pass go and collect my pond life if I do well!      Well, if you study hard and we go through your homework properly, I promise we’ll make it fun.

Rather annoying I’ve just got aching knees again, ain't I?      Oh no, what’s it this time—long walk, or one of them gym classes you do online?      Both, actually. Did one of them yoga things on a Sunday, and eeny weeny bit of hill walking with the dog. Still reckon it’s not as good as a good old run, though.      I’ve tried running but I’m not blessed with stamina. My sister’s into jogging clubs—she always says chase the endorphins or something.      Still, I’d trade a painless knee for a decent relationship any day. You single still?      Yeah, left it a bit of a mess to be honest. Ditched the last one I had—fella from Canary Wharf, far too into spreadsheets and breakfast clubs. He’d say I was “unpredictable in his emotional narrative.”      Oh right, those fella’s. Good ones, or blokes? I do like the lads from further south—bit more smooth with words, aye?      Bit more book-smart, maybe. Doesn’t always mean a better bloke. I’m thinking of trying Tinder again, just to tick it off the list really.      It’s not as bad as you’d think if you’re picky. I been on one of them app groups at work—lotta girls with similar views, aye? Had a laugh at one bloke who’d listed his job as “Professional Chisme.” Made no sense to me.      Sounds like nonsense. I’d prefer date a man who can cook, not fancies. I’ve already got my sister’s boyfriend to plug me in with friends.      My sister’s over here—had a guest for Friday night, a friend of hers from uni. You fancy meeting them? Come along, might get a laugh, you know.      Yeah, alright. Though I’m not promising to fall in love over a pot of pesto.      Still, a laugh's nice, and if the bloke can go for a run with you, that's a bonus. Not much else I do in my spare time.      Fair point. Pass on my name to your sister, I’ll see what happens.      Will do. You might find yourself more into it than you think—get out the house and all that.      I'm already bored of this flat, I'll tell you that. Seems like I live alone, apart from the odd visit from the cat.

Rather annoying when a bar won't play anything but Bruno Mars. I mean, it's a real minging chorus if you ask me. Have you tried The Hare and Hounds by the river? Their ales is far more £20 a pint, but the live music is actually live.      Aye, I've been a few times. The band last week was dossin’ a bit but I had a decent pint of best bitter and a plate of steak and kidney pie. To be fair, you can't beat the ambience for a pint 'mongst the punters. You'd fetch frozen to your bones if you tried to play any fiddle in the cold wind round here.      Aye, I’ve noticed. I left my scarf at home again, so I’m as chilly as a pickled egg in a chandelier. Still, I reckon slap some cheese and garlic on a courgette and you've done something with it. Dinna blame the veggies; it's the presentation.      That’s the bluddy truth. I tried to knock up some stir-fry with broccoli and the kid I live with wants to send it back. Can’t fault 'im, though – it looked more about texture than taste. I reckon I bled green into my ladle. He once brought home a rare steak from a Michelin star place and said it was overdone. I asked what he meant by 'done' and he looked at me like I took the kettle to boil water.      Aye, he's got goon written on his forehead if you ask me. Just give the lad a line of quality rasher bacon and he’ll forget all about his rare Doran steak. Now, how aboot we fill up the kettle and boil some decent tea so I don’t bellyache from the cold?

Rather annoying when the buzzer goes off mid-answer, isn't it? I was just about to say  basilica ! Easy for you to say, you've got years of doing this. I’m still trying to remember what a  narthex  is.      Didn’t your church have a narthex? I went to your wedding. I still say the hardest ones are architectural: hemicycle, cloister—Donna, you’ve got to stop waiting for me to explain everything.      I'm just being thorough. Last time we played, you didn’t tell me the answer for why I lost on  rotunda .      I think it was written in the rules somewhere. Probably in tiny font and only in Welsh.      You know, I never liked games like this. All that competitive –  ha!  – verbosity. Why not just take cards and name something you’ve seen today? It would be far more engaging.      And far more fun, wouldn’t it? Who cares about rotundas when you can tell stories?      That’s not the point, Gwen. It’s all in being able to retrieve obscure vocabulary  mithraeum ,  pavilion ...      ...and  amphitheatre  if you're lucky!      I’m still annoyed about  amphitheatre . That time last year, you got that for  Forum  and I was just seconds into  Colosseum  when you said it. I stared at you for five minutes.      You can’t blame me for speed. Nor the fact that I once watched a Roman history documentary and retained some vocabulary.      This is a man with a master's in geography who still forgets that  the  – pause for effect – line in the Welsh mountains between Mynydd Dinas and Mynydd y Garn is actually called  Epynt .      Well, you're all welcome to take over this game while we talk about poetry and stuff. I'm not above changing the subject.
