You mean like how we did about six minutes ago, when the discussion went from  tabernacle  to your adventure on the ridge?      Yeah. That counted as part of the game. I got my last card from a tea leaf.      And yet Carol here lectures about vocabulary as if it matters in real life.

Rather annoying that the Wi-Fi still isn't working, isn't it?      Oh, come on Claire, it's not the end of the world! We haven’t come all this way to scroll on our phones anyway.      I agree with Andrew, actually. Got a pack of cards in the bag if someone fancies a game of rummy or something?      Rummy? Not if I were you. The last time we played, I nearly got banned from the local pub.      Oh, right! That's the one where you accused someone of stacking the deck just because you lost, isn't it?      And that Myfanwy definitely did! I swear to God.      Oh, you're both too silly for me. A good round of canasta is far more refined.      Canasta? Now that’s something I haven’t played in ages. Andromeda, will you deal the cards for once?      It's Myfanwy, Claire—personally I think Myfanwy is short for "My fantasy to be someone else entirely", but who am I to say…      Oh, just shut up and take the cards Richard.      My name is  Rhys —you know that don’t you?      And Rhys you will be if you carry on misbehaving at the table. Strictly no cheek from me, you know. I had a proper job you know—before I retired.      That’s all right, Myfanwy, most people do retire from jobs. Just not you. You retired from  life .      Oh! Going are we? Well I've had enough of ungrateful grandchildren to last me a lifetime!      All right, all right. Let’s just play the game before someone else retires from the table entirely.      Honestly, the two of you are unbelievable. Let’s just settle in. Richard, deal a new deck while I sharpen the knives and forks in case things get a bit tense.      That go straight in my diary—fine dining and card games with my aunt and her friends. Just what I wanted.      And what your mother would've wanted too. She used to say that games bring families closer together.      It's true you know—like when she used to make us play charades every Christmas. Remember the time my cousin dressed like a giraffe using the sofa cushions and a Christmas jumper?      Oh, that's right! And Richard used the baubles as glasses?      Actually that was me. I had  so  much pain.      And yet here we are, still here.

So, I just finished watching this new series everyone’s talking about. I know it's been on for like...ever, but I’m finally catching up. It’s  House of the Dragon , right?      Yeah, that’s the one. It’s a bit intense though. I tried watching it last week but couldn't get into it. Too much politics and people screaming at each other.      Politicking and screaming? Sounds exactly like social media. Oh, don’t get me started. I’ve just been grinding through accounts for work. Didn’t even get to watch Christmas films.      Honestly, who  has  time to watch films at the moment? I’ve been training like mad at boot camp. You know I’m shipping out next week. Ten more days to Christmas, and I’m already away for two weeks. This is going to be rough for my family.      Ugh, I feel for you, Hattie. Me and the shop manager at Tesco have been ordering way more wrapping paper and baubles than we can handle. I swear, if I hear one more person say “changing the world” about a banana tree, I might throw a stock item out the window.      Haha, yeah. That “feel-good” vibe at the shops is a bit much. Anyway, Speaker_1, are you sure you’re going toxford? Your dad always said you're the one who’d bring home the degrees and the coffee mugs with Latin on them.      Yeah, I’m oddly excited. I’m applying for the law program. It’s way more theory than I thought I’d like, but it’s my parents’ dream for me. What about you, Alice?      I’m doing a traineeship at PriceWaterhouseCoopers. I mean, it’s not university, but it’s a foot in the door. My sister’s in accounting too, so she says I'm on the right path.      I don’t know how people your age sort out all the technical stuff. I’m just being asked to fetch tea and take lunches to people on the first floor. Not that I mind—it's experience, I guess.      That's still goenvironmental on your CV if you ever change your mind. What about you, Hattie? You're always off doing big things.      It’s all part of the gig. Being a Combat Systems Engineer is amazing, though. I’ll qualify as a proper naval officer after I finish training over in Portsmouth.

Rather lovely day today, wasn't it? That walk in Grantchester—it was just the ticket. The sun was warming and the birds were singing. I’m more than a bit tired now, though. All that walking is a workout for someone of my age, I can tell you.      Oh, Mummy, I loved it. It was so peaceful just strolling by the river. I don’t get enough of that with working in the shop every day. The only time I get outside is if I cycle to the train station or something like that. Speaking of, when are we planning that cycle trip to Ely again?      I don't know, to be honest. I’ve never really cycled more than a couple of miles, but I’d like to give it a go. I reckon it'd do me the world of good—sitting about all day in the flat is doing my back in. But honestly, if I can't be bothered to drive in the car, I'm not getting on a felling machine looking for punctures and flat tyres.      Nonsense, you don’t need a car for everything. I never did. When I was your age, love, we walked everywhere. There was something to be said for knowing where you were without a map. And if the cycle’s got gears, you can still tackle that hill by Ely. You don’t need to be a professional mountain biker for a gentle ride.      True, I suppose. Though sometimes in the village, the roads can be tricky. It took me ages to get the hang of the one near the sports field—sharp bend and no warning sign. I had to get a good wobble in about five times before I felt confident taking it the right way.      Honestly, you could write a complaint to the council. I mean, if they're not going to do something, they shouldn't just lay the roads out like that and leave people guessing. I remember once driving past there and nearly got my side view mirror taken off by someone else waiting to take the corner. It was a bit of a mess.      Oh, I think it's just the way the roads were built when money was tighter. Then again, if you're all so set on getting about on two wheels, maybe we can get you two together

Rather exciting to be here at Cambridge Law Faculty for Alumni Day, isn't it? I always think it's a fantastic way to meet old friends and, more pressingly, new collaborators.      Oh, absolutely. I quite like these kinds of events—get to mingle with others who might be interested in similar things. I’ve been working with research databases lately, and it's not all that glamorous most days.      If I may chime in, I've had the pleasure of teaching linguistics to law students before. They’re quite curious when it comes to legal semantics.      That’s very interesting. I’m a language research co-ordinator at a policy think tank. We look into how language evolves, particularly in multilingual societies. Speaking of which, I spent some time researching the Basque Country, and it’s quite fascinating the way local languages persist in the face of globalisation.      Oh, I happened to visit Spain for a conference a few years ago and spent a weekend in San Sebastián. The people there were incredibly proud of their language and culture.      I visited Spain too, many years back. What strikes me is how distinct the Basque language is. It doesn’t belong to the Indo-European family, which is rare. It's like a linguistic island in north-west Iberia.      Exactly. And what's quite telling is how strong the sense of identity is. There's a real push for autonomy and bilingual education. It reminds me in some ways of Wales: a vibrant language with political significance.      Indeed, and I've spent considerable time in Welsh hill towns myself. Far more peaceful than London, I can tell you. I always walk through the valleys when the weather is kind. Very reflective.      That sounds lovely. I know barely a word of Welsh, but I can appreciate the effort to preserve it. I’ve always found minority languages quite poignant.      And the initiative is working. Wales has one of the most consistent language revival programs in Europe. Makes me wonder how such strategies could be applied to other regions facing language loss.      A thoughtfully asked question. Earlier in my career, I did a comparative study between Wales and the Basque Country. They’re both remarkable in their own ways.      That would have been fascinating to read. Speaking of differences—what’s your take on language preservation in China, Professor? I’ve been told there’s a push for Mandarin to the point where local languages are at risk of disappearing.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know, how they talk about people as if they're not even... real. Just some weird statistic. Like they're not my family at all.      I know what you mean. It gets tiring sometimes. But you can't let it get to you, Harry. You've got a good one with your mum and dad. They've always been on your side.      Yeah, too much social media anyway. If I watched what people dump on it, I’d never leave the house. Remember when we did the ice bucket challenge at your mum’s like three years back?      That was the summer I accidentally poured my ice on the cat and Myra still hasn’t let me live it down. It was ridiculous! I had half the cousins in on it, and I think Aunty Sharon had an aneurysm when she saw it. She said it was 'the most Anglo-Saxon thing in recent memory'.      That's typical of her. Still, I liked it. Made for a nice cause and it gave you lads something to do—what I don’t get is why it had to be  ice  and not, say, warm honey or something less... destructive to hair.      Ha – Mate, you got a proposal, and now it's  honey ? You were nearly in tears when you fell through the decking at the bbq.      True story. I've got chickenpox on the psyche from that summer. It just goes to show, doesn't it? That kid of yours, Connor—what's he up to at university?      He’s about to finish his geography course. Decided to do some kind of placement in Latin America next year. He says he wants to learn more about climate and housing issues. Sounds idealistic to me, but I suppose it's good he's thinking about the future.      Sounds like it's going to be quite an experience. I tried something like that when I was doing my undergrad, but I had to pull out. It was meant to take place in a flood-affected region in Eastern Europe, but the charity lost their accreditation.      I get the vibe go-do-good on your own if you've got the budget. But kids these days seem to do that without even being asked, don’t they? Anyway, what’s for dinner?      I think there’s some curry left over from last night.

Rather annoying this new coffee machine, isn't it? Seems like everything sticks and it's always coughing up bits of debris. Never had such luck as a teacher with my own mug, mind you. Now I'm retired, I can't even make a decent brew without it grumbling like a student in the exam hall!      It was on sale, Ayda. I wanted to upgrade from the ancient one Aiden left behind. That one was practically a time capsule. But yes, arguably it’s as complicated as one of your algebra classes.      Well, I suppose you paid for the luxury. But even if it made a mile-high espresso, the real debate still is where on earth we’ll put it when we move out of this place. The removal costs alone are enough to make my ears ring. I’d sooner hand in my head for a month's rent again.      You heard the lady at the estate agent, Hattie. Removal costs usually eat five figures these days, even for a spare bedroom full of books. I reckon we’d do better chucking out the coffee machine, the cat tree, and that two-poster bed as it is. Call me sentimental, but I’d hate to part with the books.      You’re all spoilt about it. We could always split and store it ourselves. There’s a unit near Riseholme—cheaper than the removal guys if we do it ourselves. Still, we’d have to get rid of at least half this madness.      Ayda, are we seriously talking about storage costs when half of us can’t even be sure where we’ll live next? Politics are tying everything up in knots. I’m tired of the same arguments from the Labour lot. “Radical change,” they say—that fails to include affordable housing or decent provision for housing support.      That’s for sure. If they were even half the idealists they claim to be, they’d be building homes instead of focusing on fancy speeches and fixing tax for people who don’t need it.      Let’s not go full political with lunches on the table. But hear me out—maybe it’s time for us to pool a bit more. I’ve been looking into govt grants for downsizers if you’re moving to a smaller property. Could line us up for a decent break.      And your source of funding for all this planning, dear?

Rather annoying that the barista at Totnes isn’t grilling the sticks this morning, don’t you think? It used to be one of the highlights for me and my students at the language school. Now it's just a cash register clanking and the smell of lukewarm coffee.      Well dear, I’ve been coming here for decades and I reckon it’s not all that different from a decade ago. They still have decent pie and cider, don’t they? And don’t forget, catering for students’ preferences can be tough. They like their “latte, please,” with vegan foam and a frozen option.      I know, I know, but still, it feels like they’ve lost a bit of the charm. The eccentric barista who used to recite poetry from memory as he made the pasties is long gone.      Ah yes, Gilbert! That was a character. You always said he’d have made for a great ESL character study. Remember when he once told you to “lub the pudden” and you sat in the corner trying to tell the class it was a local joke and not that you had lost your tongue to a dessert?      Good grief… I reckon I owe him a letter then. Tell him I’m still denying that one. But enough about the coffee, I really wanted to talk to you about Christmas. It’s still early, but I want to make some plans and don’t want to let it all slip out again at the last minute.      Oh, well I had a lovely email from Auntie Edith. She wants to come here for the 26th, as she’s moving out of Wales permanently. Her walk-in cupboard has a memory problem, she says.      Another person gone because their house “no longer fits”? The trend is staggering. I do miss her terribly for the baked treacle scones. I think I’m going to open a freezer compartment just for any leftover Christmas pud.      You mustn’t stick too many in at once. You remember what happened to the previous one?      Yes, well the snowball effect of festive treats did come with a bill! But all joking aside, Mummy, I’ve had a few offers about freelancing in TEFL beyond the language school, and I’d love to know what you think about your daughter moving into more self-sufficient work?      Well, you’ve always been ambitious, darling.

Rather annoying when afit’s goin’ to bed an’ someone sticks’un up in ‘eir pints, don’t it? Me minge keeps runnin’! Ee, I dunno what it is wit’ sommat like that, but ee—get me?      Got eenough of that at uni. Me tris-fam were always sleepin’ in the same room. One of ‘em snorin’ so loud I reckoned a kiwi bird was pickin’ a fight. We had to chuck me pillows and stuff out the window, or they’d end up on the fookin’ floor!  laughs       Oh, don’t go on! I had the same wi’ me nan! She’d left ‘er ‘andkerchief on the back of the settee, and I’d be the one sneeze an’ by the time I got back breakfast, it’d gone up me nose!  giggles       Proper laugh that, innit? I remembah the time I went for that visit to Waterfields, the fookin’ balker up near me nan’s land. Left meself high and dry for two ‘ours because they ran out of Richmond sausages!  mock horror face  I’m takin’ it personal, I am, like, it was  me  they were messin’ wi’ that day.      Oi! You should’ve been there! I was just walkin’ in for a pint when you made that dramatic rush to Waterfields. Looked out the window, saw a moose and ran back here ‘neath a fookin’ horse, there you were, flamin’ late and smellin’ like thecontents of a fridge bin had let ‘im out for a weekend.      Ah, it is unbelivable how that lot bin goin’ on. I mean, even if you’re not keen on the Richmond, they’ve bin round for years, innit? Ee, I remember me gran passing on, an’ my grandad had that same fookin’ bag of Richmond lunches delivered every week by the bakers.      Still do, I think. Picked some up for me grannie the other dae. Got a whole pack of sausages wi’ a tick in the corner. Never could tell ‘un apart from a pig one if me life depended on it, I’ll be honest.      Oi, don’t bellyache! I’ve had one in me ‘ands this week, and I wouldn’t give that to the devil ‘isself to save me life!  laughs       You see? Right group of yobs. Laughin’ up our arms about sommat like that before midnight. But what else? Our lives is so dramatic round here, innit?

Rather annoying the new traffic lights on Longmoor Road, aren’t they? I mean, they save like five seconds and waste twenty waiting for the damn thing to change. Not a fan.      Aye, I can see that, love. But at least you can’t parallel park in that eeny weeny drop-off area anymore. Not like I tried to anyway. Almost dinged that poor man’s car last Sunday when I was trying to reverse out. Still gave me a right guilt trip, mind you.      Oh no! That must’ve been awkward. Let’s just hope you didn’t spread your “legendary parking skills” to me, then. I had to ask a teenager in the car park of Morley Caillet to help me park last week. Probably felt like aiding an animal in distress, bless them.      Haha, now that’s a giggle. I still can’t believe you’ve never managed to park on your own at the supermarket. I remember when we used to go to those tiny village shops and you’d just drive round like a proper petrolhead, trying to squeeze in behind老爷车!      I’ve still got grief over that Citroën we tried to squeeze in behind the bus. Still don’t know how you landed that one – magic or sheer madness?      Madness, if you ask me. But fun madness. You know what? Maybe we should make it a weekend thing again. Give me those tiny supermarkets and someone who thinks they're a natural at parallel parking, and I'm there.      Yeah, that’d be a laugh. Maybe we could invite Margot and Pete along too. They’re always up about something weird like vintage tractor shows or biker festivals. Might take the mind off work stuff for a bit.      Aye, it’d be nice for all to catch up, ‘specially with you always buried in your project meetings. Just don’t have me trying the parallel parking again. I think I relied a bit too much on my little “cheat stick” from 1977.      Oh please, I think it was your mustache doing the guiding work there. Alright, serious now – are you in for the weekend thing go? I can get Margot to check there’s a venue that doesn’t have a café with only pasty options.      Fully in, love. So long as it’s somewhere with a decent cake shop after, I’m your man.

Rather annoyingly, I haven't had a request yet for either of the French or Spanish pods. The first couple got taken rather quickly, though. I’m more than a bit disappointed by the lack of interest in language learning at the local library.      It's a pity really, I mean it's all the more reason people should try out one of your little pods. My cousin wanted to learn a bit of Italian before she went to Sicily last summer and she had to search high and low to get a reasonable course. We've been meaning to take some language classes for ages, but with Mummy duties getting in the way...      I know, it's the same for me. Between job and childminding, finding time for anything seems an impossible task. It’s ridiculous! I had the Postgrad degree in Linguistics and I'm now turned into a glorified babysitter by day and part-time language breakfasts by evenings. I've been thinking of making some in-person language play sessions for the mums and mums to be near here.      That actually sounds brilliant! Think of the networking it would give you—mommy-and-me with a linguistic twist. I've enrolled in a few parenting classes, but they're all about how to trot rhythmically in baby carriers and change a bottle – no one's teaching us how to speak to our babies in another language. You'd have an absolute captive audience.      I could start with a small group, just those of you who've been inquiring about the language pods. You know, maybe once a week, preferably on a hotter day, when everyone's in the mood for being indoors and curious – not that your curiosity is ever in doubt.      I'd be there the second the first class is announced. And I might even drag some of the mums from the park with me. There's one in particular, she speaks quite a lot of Spanish, and her twin boys are about six months old now. She might be interested in something like that.      That would be perfect! If we get to such a group of bilingual mums, we can start with some basic phrases and maybe even some lullabies – you know, set the foundations for a trilingual infancy! I owe you one for that idea, by the way.      Well, I just tickled out that idea because I know how much you love getting your little language labs going.

Rather a lot of activity in the garden this morning, old chap. That blue tit's been busy mending its nest again. I swear it went off for more down feathers!      Aye, them birds don’t miss a day, do they? Always at it through rain or shine. I saw the sparrow try to sneak a look earlier. Poor thing looked fascinated but wanted no part of a fight. A savvy bird knows not to mess with a blue tit protecting its young.      Honestly, you two are like the RSPB already when it comes to garden birds. I fetch the cake tray, and you’re still arguing over who’s got the best supply of worms.      Ha! You’ve met enough eccentric bird fanciers in your time, Felicity. You know them, the ones who think every broken branch is an emergency in the treetops. But honestly, it is a marvel how clever they are. You’d be hard-pressed to find a better engineer than a bird building its nest.      That’s where you come into it, Harold. You’d make a fine bird mascot if we ever had one at the senior citizens’ fair. “Meet Harold the Nest Consultant.”      Be a spot of fun. Though – speaking of birds – I’ve not had the chance to check on the puppets. Would you like to go out and see them, Felicity? The garden path’s dry enough, and the old legs aren’t in quite as much protest as they used to be.      Oh yes, the puppets! That little robin and its hillstream companion – where  did  you find them? I about cried when I first saw the goldfinch talking to the sunflowers. It’s a terrible cliché, but it does make you feel a bit like Alice in Wonderland, doesn’t it?      Enid, you passed the Sixthform with honours, and yet here you are, giving all your affection to a stuffed sunflower. You mustn’t let the grandchildren know – they’ll have to call you “Nana the Pantomime Fan.”      Sarcasm lost on a sunflower with tinsel, George. Anyway, Harold, I’ll pop out and check on them – just hold the teapot in, will you? Darjeeling with a touch of cake, your usual.      You’ve been looking after us too long, you know that?      She made a better cook over this lot’s last decade of catering disasters than Churchill’s military planners over the evacuation at Dunkirk.

Rather skip the starters, don't you think? This grilling weather has me just wanting something hearty but light... perhaps the mezze platter?      Splendid idea, Joan. Keeps a body healthy in this heat. I'll have the same—get a bit of everything, make a proper eeny-meeny-miny-moo of it. Still got Bill's hearing aids in my bag? I should pop along to the dispensary in Kyrenia next week; he promised he’d get a new pair. Know how he is—puts it off until the batteries are long gone.      Bill is a gentle soul, but prone to woolgathering at the worst times. You know the story of the turkey on his farm back in Dorset? The one that flew over the fence and landed in Oliver’s garden?      Oh aye, dear, that’s a classic! And when it started waddling toward the cat like a deranged knight at a medieval fair!      Exactly! I told him that bird had destiny written all over it. I swear, if there’s one thing I’ve picked up in my years of teaching, it’s that human—or avian—fate is often… well, messier than it appears. Speak of which… How’s your Mateha journey coming along? Still dabbling with the local wise woman?      Mateha? More like Sila. And I’m not dabbling, I’m… well, just someone who listens. She taught me to read the energy of the earth, oddly enough through dowsing. Also, she says the wind talks and it’s not always logical conversation! Most people are sceptical, I know. But I’ve felt the shift here, in the hills of this place.      That’s quite beautiful, you know. I’ve always thought there was something to the idea that we’re part of something grander. My cousin Mary, who lives up near Exeter, lost her husband to cancer last year. Since then, she’s been into shamanic journeys. She says she’s found peace through dreams and water rituals.      Aye, the human spirit is a strange thing. Grief does strange things to a person, but so can hope. Hope I get to know more of that… or at least find a line in the sand that I don’t go further past.      Now you sound like you’ve been reading too many kabbalah books at the bookshop in Ayia Napa. But I do wonder… have you tried learning any Turkish yet?

Rather annoying the new kitchen isn't even finished yet, is it? I was hoping it would be done by Christmas, and I could at least pretend this place isn’t falling apart in photos.      Oh hun, don’t start grinning like that—get on with things sooner, make complaints later. That builder’s  not  the one you want to nag if his wife's in labour or on a train strike. You've got to know when to fold, love. And besides, what was it worth you said you paid him to do the job?      Blimey, kitchen renovations... like rebuilding a cathedral. I've seen that sort o' thing at the supply farm, where we've had that old turkey oven replaced by one of them new fancy induction things. Ten grand, and half the men in the village thought it was joking. But I tell ya, it was about time. Those old stoves, they'd gone past their sell-by date.      I know, I know, I’m not saying it's not worth it. It’s just that I was over at Emma and Jake’s for dinner last night and I swear if we land a kitchen like their's I'm moving back in. Their bloody toaster even tells them how healthy their toast is, from what I saw. Anyway – speaking of food, I’ve got these leftover scallops from dinner, are we having them tomorrow or not?      If they’re already in the fridge and been touched by air, they’re not having it. Strictly no second helpings of leftovers once they've left the pan—unless you're at a hotel buffet and you want to look chic scanning the cold line.      I did make them Steve though! He brought round the red wine. We were telling vibes and stuff. Maybe he’ll ask me to go to the rugby with him. I haven’t seen that match with England versus New Zealand yet. Got guest tickets from work.      Ah, the rugby—now that was my sport once. I used to play for the Arden RFC in the 70s. Though to be fair, it was more '70s style'—which was largely just going out, getting chucked after a half and stopping play for a ten-minute go at a map of the Thai Empire.      You’re just in love with that past. And the boxset of films where rugby players all wear V-necks and never get seriously injured.

‘Ey lasses, ain't ye seen that new Jeremy Kyle show yet? I saw it on the telly last nigh, an’ it was like more than I could take, innit?’      “Oi! No, I didn’t! What happened? Is it another one of een Catfish types? I swear the lot o’ them is mad! My mam gets so wound up watching them. A lot o’ lies, if ask me.”      “Yeah, I ain't clued in to it much. But when me cousin sent me the clip, I swear I nearly fainted. That one girl who thought she was wi' someone and then found out he was some random like older bloke wi’ a fake profile. Oi, no wonder she was crying!”      “Oi, I think it was worse than that. I think the chap admitted to it and said it was for cluck, just messing with her for fun. Like what’s even the point in that? He didn’t even have the decency to tell her she was being fooled.”      “Eh, I hate people who do that. What’s their problem? Do they live on YouTube clucks or what? I reckon it's just attention-seekers. You want views, don’t you? But mista, least way it's all on the telly and somethin’ to talk about when you're stuck in the queue for the fish and chips.”      “Fair one. Although I reckon Jeremy Kyle shows are just absolute poison. I mean, what about the ones who pretend to have cancer to get sympathy money outta their mates? It's so sad when it’s about people who really suffer, but then you see it’s all a scam an’ they just wanted views and notoriety. Not that I’d watch it if I could help it!”      “You lot are all nosey like me, ain't you? I reckit it's a cautionary tale at the very least. Ain't no blessin’ having a social media life if you can’t tell the difference between what’s real 'n what isn't.”      “Deffo. I got a mate who thought she was in love wi' someone online, an’ then found out he was real and was dating her line in the real world. Total mess-up, bloke had to change ‘is whole identity. It was like The Jeremy Kyle Show, but in real-life nigh!”      “What a laugh! I swear ‘e must’ve been on that show!

Rather annoying my Wi-Fi’s playing up again. Thought it was fixed ages ago. Felt like dragging university work got any easier, at least the internet would be reliable. Not a chance, though.      Augh, those engineers and their "get back to you in two days" nonsense. My dear Margherita used to say they never handed over problems on time in Venice. You should go with her—they’re sorting out some event in Paris and she mentioned needing help with translations.      Margherita? I liked her when she came last summer. She told me some of her bee stories from Italy. I mean—bees and art and the like, seems such a mix. But that My Wi-Fi’s back on! So, what’s in Paris?      D’you know Paris is in the world? Half the time she goes about as if it’s been breakfast, no doubt. It’s a German exhibit she’s helping coordinate at the art gallery near Montmartre, you know the kind. Also, the curator speaks hardly any English—so German’s needed, and she’s scrambling.      Right, as if I’ve got the luxury of reading Goethe in my sleep. But I studied Classics at university, so got some German. Looking back at it now, I feel almost like I never left the lecture halls.      You were quite the bright spark in that subject, Mark. Still, if you go, you could work on your language skills and maybe catch a bite to eat with her brother Giorgio—who’s hotter than the summer sun in Verona.      That  would  be better than most of my days at university. I mean, not the Giorgio part necessarily—mainly cooking lasagna and not staring at that frosty PowerPoint I’m delivering.      My, you've gone soft since your education. All that grammar and philosophy, and now you’re talking about PowerPoints. Remember when I had to teach you your first German word? I told you the word for "tomato" as  Tomate , trying to sound exotic.      And I almost passed out you remember delivering it around bedtime by the window, with the cat goading me on. But if you say there’s work and travel and even some authentic Italian food, I might be convinced.      Good. Now finish your pesto pasta and pack your bag. We leave next week. And don’t even ask me about your French—she’s going to overcorrect you anyway.

Rather annoying driving today, isn't it? That man nearly clipped me the other day in Gillingham. I got so stressed, I nearly went off road.      You're overreacting, dear. I remember when I was young and driving—some people wouldn't even stop for red lights. That was a different time, mind. Not like these days with all the cameras and regulations.      Honestly, I would love to live somewhere a bit quieter. Places like Bournemouth, or even Weymouth—though the traffic there can be a nightmare when people come for the holidays.      Oh yeah, I've driven through Dorset once and it was packed. You can't get anywhere without a Sat Nav anymore, especially if you're not a local. I always use the phone, but my phone is so old it still has Windows 8!      Windows 8? Blimey, that's ancient. I had one in my early days, you couldn’t tell what was going on half the time. But that’s just life now, isn’t it?      I’ve had to learn it for work, a bit. I look up things for patients sometimes. You’ve got to be good with technology these days, even if you’re just a care assistant.      Right? My course required a lot of English and academic studies. It was intimidating at first, but once I got the hang of it, it made sense.      Oh yes, education. I never got past secondary school, thought I’d do manual work, but ended up not working much at all. Still, I’ve had a few MOTs, done my own repairs about as well as any old man can.      I had to get a solicitor last year for some family stuff. It cost me a fortune, but it handled my father’s inheritance. That part was rather troubling, honestly.      I can imagine. You would think these things would be straight forward, but no, you always have to pay someone who knows their way around.      Ah, well, that’s a new world entirely. Me, I lived with no worries for ages, never worked.      Yeah, go easy on the lifestyle, if you ask me. But at least I get to spend quality time with the family. Speaking of, how about we stop for some food? Rain doesn’t seem to be letting up and we’ve been driving for hours.      True, I need a break from driving over this furniture-falling-apart road.

Rather a damp day, isn't it? That window's been open ages and it's still damp in here.      Oh love, I've closed it! You don't want us catching a chill, do you? You'll be in bed with a bad cold before you know it.      That I will, then. Not that I haven't been there already — last winter, I spent half the time under the duvet! Properly wrapped up like a parcel, bless me.      You and your parcels. Still, you're a right character.      Right, I am. Mary, when did you last get the cleaner out, then? You know the one that comes round on a Saturday?      Well, I did, didn't I? Darcy, last Saturday I think. She did the hall and the downstairs loo. Made a bit of a mess in the kitchen, though. Left a puddle there and everything, you ever looked in that corner, didn’t you?      I told her about that puddle, you know. She looked guilty as anything. I said, "Now, if you were my grandchild, I’d hide the pudding tin from you!" She laughed, poor thing. Looked shocked, too – but it's got to be done!      She’s sweet enough, though. All that time taking care of other people's kids and now she’s old, she’s out there still someone depends on. Mind you, I often read about the poor treatment carers get. You’d think something’d be done by now.      That I would! Look at me — never worked a proper day in my life and here I am, talking the hind legs off you. But I suppose you and I knew it wasn’t to be. Still, it does give one time to do what one fancies. Like playing the radio for hours on end.      And the bingo papers – any chance you'll ever get it done accurate, or am I always going to find you with a pencil in hand and 12 mistakes by the first quarter?      Now, love, I do it proper, I do. It's just the numbers get away from me a little. One day I'll be famous for my bingo.      Hopefully not for losing the box, then.      Now don’t you go worrying! I’ve kitted it in two! And with ribbon, even.      Oh Darcy, you're one of a kind. Now, I’m making tea – what kind do you want?

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh? You’d think by June we’d have seen some proper sunshine in Cambridge yet.      Oh, I agree completely. I’ve been meaning to get out there and plant some sunflowers in the patch behind the house, but it’s like the forecast’s against it eeny time I plan!           Aye, well, if I’ve learned anything from my flat’s small pot of basil, it’s that you don’t wait for the rain to do the watering. You just crack on when you can. Did I tell you about how I nearly killed it by overwatering it when I first got it?      You did, but that’s you being typical. Still, you managed to nurse it back to life, didn’t you? D’you think it’s worth trying the same techniques with the roses in the garden? They’re been a bit droopy of late.      Aye, they’d be fine if we didn’t get this wind every evening. I’ve got some stakes I can attach to them, just to give 'em a bit more stability. I read somewhere about using banana peels as fertiliser too, seems mad but might give it a go.      Banana skins? Hmm. I remember Matey talking about composting last night, swears by kitchen scraps. Maybe I’ll join him for that weekend session after all.      Matey? What, the one from the uni party in May who claimed he used to DJ in a shed?           Aye, that’s the one. Can’t believe he’s been doing it for years in about five square feet. Seems like he’s the only one of us who’s still properly into music.      Not you as well? I still listen to the playlists you used to make for us on the road trip to Exeter. I haven’t got the heart to delete the one called ‘MH’s Saddest Vibes’.           That one was  you , as well as me. Still, I figure a little sad music helps the brain regulate the stress. Even if it does make me crave chips like mad.      Aye, well if you ever need a side of chippy vinegar to go with your melancholy vibes, you’ve got the chips on the table right here. So, have you made progress with your conference paper?      I’ve had a few rewrites, but it’s still not over the line.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You've only just started your PhD and here it is, another university increasing tuition again. I often think about how lucky I was to get a grant for my postgrad.      Aw, don't I know it! I wouldn't say it was lucky exactly, more like survival, eh? I've been working part-time at the library to cover the costs most weeks.      Fair dos. Proper dedication, innit? I used to work while studying as well. Manage to balance it all somehow. Funny how things work out when you least expect ’em.      Yeah, speaking of unexpected, did you hear the news about another round of redundancies at the local university? I’ve met a few folks who’ve lost their jobs, some good mates.      I did, turned my stomach to be honest. They’ve been working their socks off, and universities seem more focused on funding streams these days than supporting people. It’s bleedin’ rough, innit?      One of my mates, Lisa, worked there ten years—personable, enthusiastic—now she can’t even land a part-time job. I tell ya, it's like they’re chuckin’ the ladder up after you when you struggle to get up.      I agree, and now it's spreading to other sectors too. I’m trying not to panic, but I hear a few teams could shake out at our place soon. Honestly, feels like the music's changed and we’re not readin' the same notes.      Just don’t let it get you down. Any weekend plans to shake all that off?      I’m actually seeing  Les Mis  next weekend! Got my missus to let me take her thanks to some good old charm and a few dishes cleaned up. You up for it? I know a ‘Revolution’ could always do with more guillotines.      Oh, I was just saying I fancy a bit of musical stuff myself. I haven’t seen a live one in over a year.  Phantom  comes to town in a couple of weeks—might have to grab a ticket. Still,  Les Mis  is a classic, proper banger go every time.      If it hits you in the feels like it hits me, you might need a box of tissues—and a stiff one after. Shawty doesn’t take flu seriously, but this? This is full-blown plague territory.      Ha, talk like that and you might get the last drink at the bar.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be hanging out with my mates.      Okay... Well, I’ll put them in the bin then.      Oh no, wait! I was being funny.      You frightened me for a minute.      I thought I’d make a joke to see your reaction.      You don’t often make jokes like that. I was worried this stuff was bothering you.      It's just embarrassment and meanness, mostly.      What happens?      Not much. They just make fun when I talk, or when the teachers ask questions.      My word, that's not nice. Do they know how much of a good job you're doing in your classes?      No.      Maybe you should talk to a teacher.      I'm alright for now.      Well, if it starts to get you down, please talk to someone.      I tell you what - I’d rather be up in the room with your DVDs. They might be a little dusty, but still better than this.      I thought you'd got left behind at school – but it's better than me watching old films again.      Yeah, better. All that “Jimmy Stewart Silly Man” stuff is getting boring after ten goes.      Well, one of these days I might read to you instead – settle down with a good book and something nice.      Fine with me. Can I pick the book though?      Of course. What would you like to read?      Not one of Grandma's old books.      I know.      Maybe the one about the boy who baked pies for dragons.      The one I told you about the other day? Billy and the Pink Pie?      Yeah, that one. It sounds funny and cool.      Well, that book is on the shelf by the window if you'd like to read it yourself.      Can you read it go me? I don't know how to pronounce some of the names.      Of course. Let’s get settled then.      Thanks. It's nice to get to hear a proper grown-up read.      You don’t say that enough, laddie.      I tend to forget. You have my permission to read to me.      Right, then, let's get on with it. Just make sure to keep the popcorn close by.      That's a good idea.      I'll go get it.      Before you do, do you want to have a cup of hot chocolate to go with it?      Please. With marshmallows.      Coming right up. Let's settle in.

Rather annoying this, innit? I’ve been tryin’ to get this leg hair ‘ere off and it’s decidin’ to play up now.      Yeah, I mean, it is June. Not quite summer yet, but it’s startin’ to warm up a bit. I don’t know  why  we still shave like it’s 1950…      Dubby. I know! Why do I even bother? If I’m gonna get a spot or a cut, no one’s even gonna see me in a skirt or anything. Probably just waste of time.      Right? I swear, the only reason I still do it is because my nan’s still around and she’d have my guts for garters if I told her I’d gone au naturel.      Ha! She’d be far more bothered than if I told her I’d gone and eloped. Honestly, I’m thinking about just not doing it anymore. Maybe just let it do its own thing.      I mean, do it, but maybe just less often. Or I don’t know, wax? But that's a whole other nightmare. Have you tried any of those de-piles ones?      Not really – I tend to just do it quick and cheap with the old cartridge thing. Yeah, somethin’ to do with the legs first, then under ‘em. Smerte.      Aww, poor luv. That stuff does a number on your legs. I tried one of them ones with aloe or something, and it didn’t help at all. Looked good, didn’t do diddly.      Oh, you lot in Cambridgeshire probably spend more on your legs than I spend on my week’s shopping.      Well, for the record, I do not! But I did buy that one fancy loofah. It was something ‘artisan’ or whatever.      I could stick to my trusty old yellow shower thing. It’s got probably 27 uses and one of ‘em happened last year.      Right? This is such a random conversation to go off on on a Tuesday afternoon. How does it go from discussing essays to leg hair?      That bloke on campus what your uni’s employin’ as a cleaner? He looked like he’s been out every night with the boys and then came in to mop up the mess or summat. Might’ve had a go at my feet. S’all my brain could think about was how hairy they were.      Okay, don’t do that! I now have visual flashbacks.

Rather annoying when a bar’s got no lager, innit? I was just trying to work through the alphabet with the lager one by one, like a proper British football game superstition. A for Adnams, B for Becks, C for… what’s that one like the posh one again?      Champion?      Ay, that's it. Reached D and couldn’t be arsed. Not like in this lot back here where we're stuck with what, a session bitter and a can of cider? Bit of a disappointment for a Cambridge pub.      Bit of a surprise even, honestly. I mean, Cambridge's the real Oxford Street when it comes to ale and whatnot, innit? I swear though, I remember this uni boy I used to know who'd get all picky: "A for Akasha, B for Barlow’s," you know, like it was a drinking version of mastering Anglo-Saxon.      And the lad never hides he’s indulging in a bit of the old fizz bomb under that sweater of his.      Yeah, but he always said if you land a punch to the gut and say "C for ... Camel Trophy", you walk away with it. Still, when it got to boxing, he – Baptiste: “E for Evander, F for Haye,” – the lad couldn't quite nail that one.      Oi, don’t talk about Haye like that. Fergal one-year wonder. And boxing, man? It just brings up sour memories. Some nut had the cheek to shout a vile slur and bottle through at a match in Sunderland last season, and it still gives me the shivers. Just shows you can't touch the beauty of the game without facing a bit of that filth.      Doesn't it just? Maybe we're the last bastion for the proper lot. To survive in beer and boxing with that lot? Well, the blood is still in the fists and the lager still tastes like victory.      As long as we can survive being sober enough to spell it with 'proper British lager' to do it justice, let’s raise a glass, even if it is cider.      To alphabets, boxing and surviving racism in stadiums. Let's get some more of this session bitter. And maybe a bag of crisps. Pass the salt, innit.      You’re on, love. And maybe next time we go to a football game we can start our own alphabet chant. C for "Cunts!" and D for "Don’t!"

Rather annoying this, isn't it, Dottie? Seems like everything we apply for ends up with a  halted pending review , or some nonsense like that. I could have had this phase of the Stag's Head alehouse project started by now, and not be knee-deep in forms.      I know, I understand the frustration, but these funders are cautious for a reason. The last thing they want is a scandal involving historic buildings and poorly managed budgets. You’d think they’d trust professionals like us a little more.      Didn’t your chums at the Heritage Preservation Trust get through to the Heritage Lottery Fund smoothly last season? I remember you mentioning a supply list that included "spitunes" and turkey vulture excrement for mortar mixing.      [laughs] That was Darcy, not me. She’s the one who convinced them she was reviving an 18th-century turd-removal method. Honestly, I’m not above a bit of embellishment when it comes to grant writing. You ever tried putting a few details from that medieval fresco into a proposal—personally, I start with the falcon with the severed head.      That’ll only get you rejected if they cross-check it. I remember when we got that grant to restore the Baptistry of St. John, and I had to confirm every footnote. One wrong historical reference and the funding vanishes quicker than a wasp in July.      True. Our problem is not the application—it’s the system. They want a five-year blueprint, a SWOT with floring, and a ten-year forecast as if it’s a cafe in London’s West End, not a crumbling Tithe Barn from 1492. How do you write a projected return on investment for a 500-year-old thatch?      You don’t—unless you dress it up like tourism development. I had an idea once about turning that old lane into a scenic heritage strip where people pay to cycle under arches of ivy. You’d think the Arts Council would rush in.      Ah, yes, but we need more than just ivy arches and a tinted glass reflection pond. We need a sustainable income stream—educational goings-on, maybe a weekend seminar or a craft market. You could even line it up with that green architect group in Oxford.      Now that’s the sort of planning I can get behind. You think we could rope those folk in?      Only if we promise them a chance to make the buildings carbon neutral again.

Rather annoying this newfit in the kettle innit? Seems like everything sticks to it, even when y’use those descalin tablets they sell in the shop down the road. I've been thinkin’ about it a lot with all that water research I've been doin’—you'd think if it een stick to metal, the chemistry’d be very neutral. But显然 it ain’t.      I don’t know if I’d call this a social experiment, love, but you're quite interesting as it is! You ever thought of presentin’ that during your next meeting? The PhD committee'd probably like to hear a bit more about application. I mean, we're talkin’ about how water reacts differently in various regions, right? I remember you talkin’ about the water in Sunderland versus the water in Cambridge. Rather different compositions I think.      Aye, that’s part o’it, but I’m more curious about why folk from certain regions absorb and retain minerals differently. Like in the Midlands, the water’s got a higher calcium content than it does here—so over time, you get more limescale build up. I’m thinkin’ that might be connected to the real reason why folks in Birmingham have a higher incidence of kidney stones. Have you read the NHS papers on that? Mate of mine at the uni, a med student, was on about it the other day.      Honestly, I haven’t. But that’s pretty interesting. It’s kind of what someone at my uni said—water's not just water, it's a cultural and chemical phenomenon all in one! Speaking of which, I’m looking forward to next month—I’ve got a colleague inviting us for a holiday about forty miles up the coast. You know the area, near Skegness. It’s supposed to be very low key. Not like some of the other research trips we went on to the Arctic, innit?      Oh, I’d forgotten that! Signals dancin’ off polar ice was quite an experience. I dunno about Skegness, but I’m not one for overpriced seaside holidays. But if it’s low cost and low stress, I'm in! We could work on your thesis a bit more while we're there, get a break goin’ on your own research. How does your supervisor feel about you slappin’ away study between holidays?      A bit touchy, but I've been planning this for a few months now.

Right, luv, let's get this sorted before you head off to school. How did you get on with the dinner money this week?      I forgot to bring it again, Mummy. I’m really sorry. I left the envelope in my backpack over the weekend.      That’s okay, I understand. But you need to make sure it’s in your bag on a Monday so that you’re not left hungry at lunchtime. I’ve topped up your school account now, so you should be fine for the next few days. Remember, if you want to eat with Mrs. Porter at lunch, you’ve got to  tell  me earlier.      Why do you have to tell you? Can’t I just go?      Because sometimes, if you’re eating in a special group, I need to sort out the arrangements with the school office. And today, for breakfast, you’re going to have eggs. They’re sunny-side up, just like you like.      Can I have a biscuit after? Or maybe a custard cream?      I want a digestive!      Right, let's not start the biscuit war again. Each of you can have one – but  only after  you finish your toast – no arguments. And I’ve got a treat for you both tonight. We’re going to Granny’s after school, and she’s promised to make us pancakes.      With honey?      With honey. And chocolate sauce, if you behave yourself.      Does Granny have a goldfish?      That’s the  fish  she got when she nearly did the circus years ago.      She said she nearly considered going for a little while. She always joked that she could be the clown who juggle oranges while wearing a sequin dress. But she decided being a guest speaker at school presentations was more her style.      I want to be in the circus.      Well, your first step to being a tightrope walker or a lion tamper is lunches sorted and money in your dinner account. Speaking of, there's a school tennis tournament next week, and if you want to play, Mummy has to sign you up by tomorrow.      Is it after school?      Yes, on Thursday afternoon. It’s at the school field, so it’s easy to manage. Just don’t forget your water bottle and your new tennis shoes I bought you. And if you win, we’ll go see a film at the cinema – something  fun , not a documentary.

Rather enjoyed the new biopic last night, didn’t you? I thought it was incredibly well-acted. It got me thinking, though—how much do you think we should rely on films to teach history?      Ah yes, the film was very moving. But you can’t put too much stock in them, my dear. They’re dramatised for effect. I read an article not long ago about that debate in Cambridge. The discussion was about whether we should be teaching history more from a local or national angle. Interesting times we’re living in for education.      Definitely. I was at the debate too, and they also touched on how much politics is influencing the national curriculum these days. From what I could tell, it feels like everything is being massaged to fit a more 'palatable' narrative, rather than the whole truth.      It is, isn’t it? I’ve been talking to a number of colleagues about it. As a teacher, it’s frustrating. We want to give students the full picture so they can think critically, but we’re walking a tightrope.      That’s the problem with short attention spans and political pressure. You remember when I was at school? We read a book, discussed it over weeks, then wrote essays. There was no denying that it was often fairly dry, but at least you  knew  the facts.      And that’s partly why I think Higher Education universities need to connect degrees better with industry. If you come in for a history degree, why not intern with a museum or a local school? Combine theory with real-world experience. It would give students something tangible to carry into the future.      I agree with Steve. I think that’s the problem now: kids are getting so much information, but they don’t know how to use it. I remember Steve here was one of my most impressive students. Always made the lesson exciting, even if I had to cut his hand off for passing a note!      Fair point, but I was just waiting for a spoon-feeding moment! Those were the days. Although, if you two want to talk about spoon-feeding, have you seen the recent changes to how GCSEs are taught?      Indeed. It’s supposed to be about more skills-based learning now. But I read an interview with a curriculum designer and he said it feels like everyone’s being asked to do more with less.

Rather a damp day we've got, isn't it? Makes me think of my youth, when the first war was on and the rain never gave us a chance. I was a lad back then, helping about the farm in Costessey with my da and the rest of the lads.      Oh dear, yes, I remember my gran telling me stories of how she had to grow up with rationing and air raids when she was your age, George. She was born in Harrow, just a bit further west from me. She always said the police never had it easy then.      That’s easy enough to believe. I can still recall as a young proprietor, only starting out, and how well the local forces helped with security and regulation. Middlesex is not far from Costessey, after all. But I digress — the world has changed quite a lot, hasn’t it? The furniture I see now in shops — none of it has the soul in it that the old stuff had.      You're dead right there, Paul. I still do a bit of reviewing here and there for some educational institutions, and I can't help but think that the same lack of soul affects education too. As a childminder, I saw how important it was to start young — beginnings of life matter. But with the pressures of today, it's all about ticking boxes.      Aye, and tickin’ boxes won't build a nation. When I was young, you had to be resourceful. We used furniture from our ancestors — old chairs, tables, trunks — each with their own stories. Now, everything comes boxed and thrown out after a few years. Waste, if you ask me.      That's such a shame, George. I remember my own family coming over from Harrow and having barely a chair to sit on, yet they managed. My father had to start from scratch, and he did it with such resilience. I always told the children I looked after — mainly those whose parents were working — that you can’t always expect your past to hand you a silver spoon.      Precisely why I think it's vital to have strong foundations. My earliest memories are of learning from my ancestors, and the importance of hard work. But I suppose life has changed. I wonder how our grandchildren will look back on the times we're living in.      I can't help but think they'll take the same pride in their lives that we do in those of our forebears.

Rather skip the new house’s garden for a bit, old man. But you’d think it'd be like... easier to decide what to bring after this last run. I mean, we've been over this a dozen times already. What goes with us, what stays?      Aye, it’s beginning to sink in, I suppose. Not many more trips like this. Almost wanted to make it a grand day out, but with your mother in this state, it’s easier said than done. I know you said she wasn’t seriously ill, but still— Didn’t your sister come over last week?      Yeah, she did—Managed to get her round the weekend before the doctors' meetings and everything. My uncle came too, from Croydon. The one you haven’t met in years who still remembers your face from when I was a kid? We had an absolute laugh about the old place. Your breakfasts— He actually said he used to dream about them in his early days, you know?      Ha! Well, I suppose once you divide your days between tea and beans, you get a reputation. Although— Don’t think I did quite as much to impress your uncle when he was that age. Good on him for coming though.      He said he wanted to see the estate before it all changed, and before it all goes to the dogs. I reckon he’s not wrong. You and I will be gone. The house’ll either be empty, sold, or just someone else’s problem. Honestly, I wish my mum wasn’t stuck in that room at the hospital. Just the thought of her in that sterile place being split from everything else—it’s upsetting.      I know. I know. And you trying to teach the language to kids now—juggling all that and the stress of the move. I’d say it’s a wonder you haven’t burned out.      Well, I’m passed out by sundown most nights anyway. You know, I was thinking— Maybe once we’re settled, I can get back into doing some regional dialect classes as part of the curriculum. Websites mentioned it’s a draw for students.      That sounds like a grand idea. I remember you trying to learn some of the old ways of speaking when I was your age. Always had me laughing. Still—better than the language of that boy you had in your last class who thought "innit" was the sum total of fluency.

Rather than going out, I thought we could have a little do at the house for your nan’s birthday. It’s been a tough year with everything, and I’d like it to be a bit of a proper treat for her. What do you think?      That sounds lovely, actually. She always says how she liked the last one with the chocolate sponge and the candles. I’ve been thinking, maybe we should do something a bit like the Great British Bake Off, but easier? Maybe she’d get a kick out of it?      Oh, that might be fun. But we have to keep it simple. She’s mostly fine, but I do forget sometimes the dementia means small changes can confuse her. We’ll need a proper table plan too. I left the one from last year in the old shed – I’ll go pick it up tomorrow.      I was about to say something about the breakfast, but I forgot what I was going to say for a second. Maybe I should start by sorting out the menu options. I’ve always wanted to try that lemon and herb fish recipe – do you think she’d like it? I can always buy two different kinds.      She loves fish. I’ll buy in a couple of different options – maybe a salmon fillet and a haddock – just in case. I’ve got a bit of time yet, thank goodness. I’ve been trying to rearrange the kitchen cupboards too – it’s getting a bit chaotic. I put the old photos someone gave her in a box in the attic. Should I bring those down?      Yeah, that’d be good. She always comes to life when she sees the old photos. Maybe we can put them out on the mantel piece again. Oh! And we had those candles from the other night, the ones you bought that smell like lavender. I think she liked them – mentioned that the smell reminded her of her mother’s garden.      Well that’s all settled then. I’ll pick up the fish tomorrow and get the table plan sorted. You can sort out the photos and candles as you’re here. Also, if you’re happy with the menu idea, I can do the lemon and herb fish, and I’ll make a nice side of roast potatoes and seasonal veg. For dessert, maybe a Victoria sponge or a couple of other options.

‘Ey luv, ain't this place swank? Cheeky croissant in ‘and an’ all, and I’m not even bickering yet. Proper France, innit?’      ‘Haha, yeah, I know what you mean. I can’t get over how eeny the rooms are here. It’s like,   everywhere   is cobbled… not just the streets. A lot o’ policy needed in this town, honestly.’      ‘Aye, and me grinding teeth like a mad woman. Me bottom right one’s binnit absobloodylutely murdering me. I’ve been tannin the doc, only they’ve said it’s probably the turkey wisdom tooth. Told me to left it a few more weeks, see if it decides to bin itself properly o’ not.’      ‘Oh no! ‘ave they told you if they’re need to drill it out or what? I lost me’s bottom one o’ver a year ago, near deaded me. One second I’m blooming fine, next me face is the size o’ a melon.’      ‘Aye, sounds deadly. I might’ve got a hole in me cheek by this point, from scrunchin so much – cheek it or not. I’m still thinkin’, though, cos me mum’s being extra cheeky and sayin’ I should’ve bin it already, cos uni starts in two weeks an’ whatnot.’      ‘Oh man, uni again. I can’t tell what I’m’d rather do: get a bit drilled in the face or sit in lectures for six hours straight. Not nearly about to make that choice any time soon.’      ‘Aye, I’m bin panikin that I shouldn’t even be up outta bed for the next two weeks, ‘cos I’m treed that I’m going to be all sodden at me first lecture. Last time was bloody stressful enough. At least this flat I’m movin into is all fixed up proper, not that hovel of a place I was in before.’      ‘Who’s with? Me an’ a couple of other tarts from the course. Room go bad? I remember your old place like it was mine. Walls were the colour of soggy prunes. Honestly, ‘ow bad could it’ve been?’      ‘Worse than that, innit. The boiler was broken for weeks, an’ I kept bin talkin to ‘em, but no nobody’d do nuttin. Now the new one’s near to brand new. My flatmate’s even done them all the floors in wood, so it’s got class now.’      ‘No you’re no shagin me, innit?

Rather than going out and doing something extravagant for Chinese New Year, I thought we could do something a bit more... meaningful, you know? Like random acts of kindness?      Oh, that's lovely, Aunty Georgia! What sort of things?      Well, we could make some nice treats, maybe lactose free if we're careful with the recipes. I found this adorable recipe for almond milk cupcakes with honey buttercream that's easy to adapt. And since we’ve got some time before it’s Chinese New Year, we could bake a few batches and leave them with the neighbours.      Can I make the cupcakes? I love baking!      Of course you can, Mycroft! I’d be glad to help you. And you know what, to make it even more fun, we could use the Chess and Draughts pieces in the drawer as pretend ‘coins’ when we go out to give the treats. Maybe a bit of roleplay helps us be more creative in how we present them!      That would be so funny! I want to dress up like a knight or a princess too!      Why not? It’ll make the act of kindness feel a bit like an adventure—and it'll definitely make our neighbours smile. I remember when my nan used to do the same, and it made her seem like some magical messenger of goodwill. It was brilliant.      I could ‘trade’ the pieces for hugs and thank yous. Like in a game!      Perfect! That’s the spirit. Now, while we're at it, maybe we can talk a bit about what Chinese New Year means. Did you know it’s about starting over, cleaning away the old, and bringing good fortune?      My teacher said the year is of the dragon! I really like dragons—they're so cool.      Exactly! And if you’re lucky enough to celebrate with red pockets or maybe even a dragon parade where you live, it's very special. But even if we can't do all that, acts as small as a cupcake or a game piece traded for a smile can mean just as much.      Can we also do something with our hair? I saw a video of someone with rainbow stripes!      Maybe one day, Mycroft—but let’s see how we like the box braid look first. Maybe after we finish our baking mission, I’ll help you both pick one hair colour you’d like to try.

So do you remember the time we went to see Alice in Wonderland on the stage in Brighton, Mummy? I got to dress up in all the costumes afterwards, and I wore a crown like the Red Queen! It made me feel like a real princess, even if it was just for ten minutes.      Oh, I remember that so well, love. I think it was about five years ago? You were so tiny then, but you stormed that stage like a star. Oh, and you were quite upset when it poured and we had to run to the car. Do you remember the seagulls diving at us like we had popcorn in our pockets?      Yes, yes, I do! They made that one turkey look really silly, too. Funniest thing ever. But I was sad because I had already planned to pick daisies afterwards and make a crown with them for my bear. Then it rained, and I lost them!      Aww, that’s such a typical Alice in Wonderland day, isn’t it? Real and magical at the same time. I was thinking the other day about how I listen to the soundtrack every time we drive past that theatre. It brings back such good memories. You’ve always loved watching shows, haven’t you?      Yeah! My drama teacher at school says I should consider doing it for a career. I’ve even started making my own stage out of the living room. I borrowed one of your scarves for a cape the other day. It was red and sparkly!      That one came from a car accident I had years ago. It was the only thing that wasn’t ruined – I had it in the back seat. I was lucky, really. Just a few scratches to the car and a bruised elbow. The police were so kind, giving me that scarf and telling me it helped save me from the cold. I found it over the years hiding in my wardrobe.      Wow, I didn’t know that. You got all those fancy presents and ended up with a waiting scar on your arm. Do you ever show it off to people at the garage?      Only the funny ones. Some people still laugh when I say I got a red scarf from a man in an ambulance. But really, it wasn’t that dramatic. Anyhow, have you read the latest book you borrowed from the library?

Rather annoying, the entire situation really. You remember what we told that group last night—the wind turbines in Halberton, I mean? Just a beautiful expanse of green, and now they think they’ll chuck three hulking £200k things in the middle of it.      Yes, yes, I remember. It was fascinating really, the way they presented all their points—they knew the law, knew when to file the objections too. But it was quite naive, really. They trusted the local planners! You and I both know what that means.      You’re probably right, Horace. Though I’ll say this much: the ones last night had heart. That kind of organisation—drawing on social media, petitions—you don’t often see much of that anymore.      Oh, I think the world has changed. It used to be that you’d have village meetings, leaflets passed out by hand. Now it’s all digital. And I have to say, we gave them the run-down. We showed them where to find the Land Use Waterfowl Report, and told them to listen for the impacts of noise, land degradation. They asked about solar farms too, since they were dealing with another application for panels in the valley.      Yes, that’s been another fairly recent phenomenon. Small solar array proposals everywhere. Some of them quite acceptable, others questionable. But the real problem is the lack of foresight in our planning principles. Local politicians just want to look ‘green’ without understanding the consequences.      And the worst part? The money. You know as well as I do that the government gives  billions  in subsidies for wind and solar, yet barely a fraction of that goes into proper research—especially for things like storage technologies. We could be developing better battery solutions or even hydrogen tech if the money went in that direction.      Absolutely. And while we’re chasing the weather and pretending we can rely on these unreliable sources, the scientists are left with crumbs. I read recently that research budgets for energy storage are down over 40% compared to five years ago.      That’s staggering. And no wonder things move so slowly. You’d think if the government believed in the long-term vision for renewable energy, they’d invest properly. But no—if you tick the ‘green’ box in the box, that’s deemed sufficient.      Politics, politics. You know, while we’re arguing over windmills and solar panels, there’s a bigger one going on over in Scotland.

Rather annoying this, having to go through all that driving lot. I've had my car for thirty years and never got nought for a test. Still, more power to you, Hermione.      I know, Dad. It seems like a big deal at first, but once you get the hang of it, it’s not so bad. I actually really enjoy learning.      Oh aye, I remember when your Dad got his test all those years ago. He drove into a parked dump truck because he wasn't watching the mirrors. Still doesn't chase when he's talking about it.      That was mostly  your  doing, Moira. You had the radio blaring and made me think you'd seen a bird you wanted to chase. It was just a bin lorry, as it turned out.      Oh no! So I was about to ask — what do I need to look out for this week? I'm starting in two weeks and I'm a bit nervous.      Well first, the insurance. Your Uncle Charlie said he's getting a few quotes for you this week. Might be best if we spread a bit to family to get the best rates.      Sounds good, luv. And then the lessons. Moira, can’t you vouch for me, still? I’ve driven this car for the best part of forty years and never done wrong.      No, Frank. Times have changed. Our Hermione here has to go through the system like the rest of them. Besides, we can’t let her floring the law now, can we?      Aye, aye, Prime Minister. I do like the idea of a weekend trip, though. Maybe we take Hermione out to Stratford once you've got your licence. Not too far, and it's a nice change.      That would be brilliant! I've never been to Stratford. I've read a lot of Shakespeare for school, but I've never actually visited his birthplace.      There's a bit of a player centre there now, very grand. Bits of the old town are still there, too. You’d like it, luv.      Oh, go on then. But let’s see about booking it properly first, and once you’ve passed that test. We don’t want you driving off a cliff your first weekend out.      I won’t Father, I’ll be careful! I’ve got all the manuals to read, and I’ve already downloaded this app that helps with the theory part.

Rather annoying the new Facebook app, isn't it, Dad? Keeps sending me notifications for every like and comment... got to my head one day after I received 200 in an hour      Aye, computers do try and take over sometimes! I wouldn't know where to start with eeny of it, I don't use it much these days      You should give it another go though, I reckon you'd find a few old school friends from around the area      Nonsense, I got more than enough people in my life, what with you and your lot. I prefer my chats over a nice cuppa with someone face to face      That's true, I haven't met anyone new recently. It'd be nice if I had someone to talk with, apart from the usual suspects      Well, there's always the weekend breakfasts at Bucks Hill... I used to go there for the morning betting and a bit of lunch      I've never been, why not take me along one time? Might be interesting      Might be! You might even fancy a quick flutter, like I did back in the 50s      Well, I'd only bet on Lady – Mate though      Careful, betting on long shots is a sure-fire way to go broke      I already am broke! Though not from betting, from this student life      That's just a phase, love. I remember when I first had to move out of the house to live in Brighton. That was a right struggle in the beginning, trying to get on my feet      And the parking there is an absolute nightmare! I remember arriving at the cab rank and then barely finding a spot near the front      I've thought about moving there too. Though I'm not sure if I could live with the sirens going off every hour      Aye, madhouse. We had to rush for everything. Though being self-employed also meant trying to find work sometimes and it was hard with various working patterns. I remember you used to help around with the errands sometimes      I remember! I used to cook for you at times as well. I was quite the chef back then      You were! Reckon I have never made a decent dinner in my life after that      You gave me a right laugh though. Feeding you was part of the entertainment      I reckoned I got quite a rise out of people with my comments on politicians, always getting me tea and biscuits from the local baker      You did, you were as bad as a weather reporter with your daily updates      Wasn't me!

So, I swear I haven't seen anything so pretentious since I tried to quote Shakespeare at a golf tournament... and the guy next to me just stared at me like I'd asked for caviar with a side of mayonnaise.      Lmao. You serious? What were you quoting? Macbeth?      Yeah, something like "Out, out, brief candle," only I messed up the next line because I got stage fright under a tree. It wasn’t even that dramatic! Just a bunker near the 9th hole.      That’s gold. You should’ve won  Best Dramatic Reading  instead of the hole-in-one. On second thought, maybe you still did.      Well, I did win the nickname "The Bard on the Fairway" from the guy who called me "desperate to be interesting." Based on breakfast, no less.      That's honestly criminal. I pity the man who hides behind his Bridgestone irons and still claps sarcasm out like it's Tuesday.      Honestly, I don’t get sarcasm as much as I should. For a smart uni grad, I’m sometimes like,  Wait, did that just happen?       True. I once tried to act all  woke  while studying Renaissance history and failed to catch my roommate when he said, “Oh yeah, universities are  great  places for people just starting out in life.” I thanked him. He was a prat, but oddly proud.      Bro, I think sarcasm comes with overcoming a fear of  actually  being funny. Kinda like how I’m finally learning to be “skillfully bad” at golf. Not great, but entertaining.      That's the spirit. You're not in it to be a  winner —you're in it to make others feel like they just won by comparison.      Exactly. Same with surnames, am I right? We’re from such straightforward places that our full names are like, “Taylor Smith, a new idea from the 17th century.”      You're like a man with a surname as noble as my nan's hat collection. I’m Taylor Smith, and I once started a bet that I could be the most forgettable Taylor Smith at a family gathering. Lost to my cousin Tassie.      Tassie? Is that even a name or a brand of biscuits from the 1990s?      Fair. But honestly, forgettableness is kind of a skill, right? Nicknames are distractions, surnames are burdens, and we’re stuck with them like an old job you can’t quit without a reference from your nan.

Rather annoying I’ve got to be honest innit, me event’s tomorrow and I haven’t even seen half the bits yet. Someone at the marquee firm sorted the wrong tables again, sure I’d scream! Got to pop into town to track ‘em down in the rain.      Got eeny plans for the weekend then? I was just thinking I reckon me and Jess wanted to lift a tent up in Ake by the coast, got this mate got a van we can tag along in, dump the gear. Know you lot was doing the London pop-up gig though, don’t forget to send pictures later like, I like get united.      Oh, I’d rather stay in and contemplate my MyFavio list, you know me. I’m trying to cut down on carbs like crazy, can’t handle bread anymore. Ate a sandwich for lunch and now I’ve got gigantiss breakfasts—like, I just happened to have a drive-thru at the Tesco five o’clock, ate the lot before eleven.     Sounds like you need a Yorkshire pie—proper one, with all the gravy and shortcrust. Here innit, I tell ya, my nan’s recipe would save you. Doesn’t work if it ain’t got onion in it mind ya?      Nah, I swanny eat carbs either but the van trip’s gonna be fried chicken and loaded chips for everyone, so no worries there! Though if we carry on in this weather, the campin’ll be a blearly mess. Raining like mad at seven—looked like the sky was crying and I thought it wasn’t even a sad day.      Camp about nowhere! I’m not living off bangers and chips all weekend. Gonna document a no-carb failsAFE. Proper smoothie shakes and boiled egg breakfasts, like, to the max.      Envy. All I had for tea was a packet of Leanins biscuits and a cuppa, can’t get nuthin decent on when I’m working all the time. Like, I’m in constant work mode always trying to catch up innit.      Yeah, work, work, work—told ya like two years ago I wouldn go to uni, didn life if you ask me. Just wanted to go out and chuck in a builders’ barrow of concrete, or something.      But at least you get lives to build, eh? Whereas I’m stuck with spreadsheets and deadlines, life’s like a tightrope.

Rather annoying this new TV licence regime, isn't it, George? I had to fill in a form like I were still in school.      Blimey, I've nearly dropped me cup twice trying to figure it all out. Look like the children've picked the lock on me independence. Got eeny weeny passive-aggressive messages on the screen. 'Would you like to continue…'      Spare me. I've got too much on me plate with this new painting programme on Antiques Roadshow! Put me in the present and I'm more interested in the pot I made at the weekend. It's a rather fetching shade of sage.      Aye, do you have that on the turkey table? I saw you skimming the surface with this potting business the other day.      I do! A little basil started in it, but the cat's taken an interest, no doubt. I've been thinking of putting in a owl box. Our planting seems to attract every feline in the county.      Speaking o’ which, I do tell you—there is this cat that takes occasional interest in me fence.      And how's that fancy bamboo growing on the back fence? You'd think it was from the moon it's so tall?      That was actually from the Haye, Bert. I planted it in the spring as a bit of a filler. Bless ‘im, it's been growing up like it was someone's full-time job!
