Walker, just imagine we had a black hole in the garden and it sucks in the bamboo and comes through as a patent-leather fence post, eh? Not a flamin’ far off.      George, don’t get carried away with what you've been watching on that Cosmos programme! I mean it is bloody fascinating, but black holes bein’ over here—that lot’d be screaming!      I have been trying to keep up a bit too, love. We watched that eclipse too, bless. I did stick the glasses on as tight as a safety pin, but bless me, I couldn't tell what was going on half the time. Too far for proper view.      Still, the sky goin' on like it was sufficin’ or something—it made me feel a little out of it. Like the box set had gone silent and your cat was licking the PSU.      Oh, moving in next month mind you, dear. You might find your cat on the ceiling or somethin’ when we get them modern remoteness blocks.

Rather than going the usual route, I thought I’d take us through the back roads—the traffic’s been piling up again on the A1. Bit more scenic down this way, anyway.      Aye, we can’t have you driving as fast as you like again, can we? I saw the state of the bridge last time you took that corner at thirty. Almost threw me out the window!      That one was a bit tight, I’ll give you that, but you said you wasn’t scared anyway. Bit of a rush, innit?      Right, because it’s brilliant to be dead before we get our dinner. Still, if we’re taking the scenic route, then I hope you’re not passing up The Ivy this time. I ain’t eating sandwiches again.      Oh, no—Donna said they’ve got something better than breakfast, and cheaper if you ask early. Some place off in Bishop’s Stortford.      Bishop’s Stortford? That’s like halfway to—      Yeah, I know, but I don’t fancy going back into Harpenden and getting stuck on that road again. It was a nightmare last week.      Fair point. Even buses are held up there sometimes, and I take the number 4 almost every day. Still don’t get how you can live in a place that big and don’t even know which road the supermarkets are on.      That’s just a bit of bad planning, innit? I mean, who builds a church and then doesn’t make sure the roads around it are clear? Prime spot for a cathedral and they left it surrounded by potholes!      You said you were going to ask her about that. I mean, it is a cathedral, but if the roads are like that, someone should’ve put up signs warning people about the terrain. Not me, driving it like a rally car all day trying to weave around bikes.      I’ll tell her. I’ll also say we’re not trying the lunches there anymore if it’s going to cost us an hour in delays just trying to get around.      Exactly. Look, I don’t know what our plans are for tomorrow, but I do know I’m not driving. If it’s blooming something with roads and directions, you pick.      Oh, come on, you can’t just hand me all that responsibility. I had to look up where the bloody bus stop is at my end half the time.

Rather annoying this newfit alarm clock, innit? It goes off with this birdsong, real muzak if yer ask me. I’ve tried switching it to a proper bell, but the bleedin’ thing won’t let me.      Aye, I had one o’ them eeny-time.  Sings a trill tune.  Dunno what bird that is… not a wren, I’m sure. Got t’be a chaffinch or a goldcrest. Mind, I once mistook a tree sparrow for a tit. Looks a right mess with that squinty little face, but it don’t  sound  like much, no.      You like that sort of thing, don’t you? Terry left me a note last week, said I’d missed the barred cuckoo and the black redstart by the garden fence. Course, when I went out, I see nothin’ but this pair of magpies playing in his ornamental grass.      Ah, Terry. Still got that knack for seein’ birds while I’m still seein’ shadows, eh? Got one in my own garden yesterday as well. A long-tailed tit, fancy that. Real tiny little thing, proper workin’ up from the feeders. I feed them black sunflower seeds, mind. My old man’s got a fit, says somethin’ about “rat bait.”      You should talk to him about the benefits, someone at the dentists told me they’d read that feeding birds helps them come around at meal times. Though, mind, my nose wants to come with ‘em at the same time. Had a good one at the surgery last week, nosebleed brought it on. She said it were stress.      Aye, that’s a right worrying lark. My cousin in Manchester had throat cancer ‘cos she smoked like a chimney. Now she’s all cut up and worried about gargling. She told me yesterday, said Terry used to meet her for a little lunch, but he hasn’t turned up since.      Poor Terry. He’s not the only one with health worries, is he? Still, I’m more concerned by these feeders. I reckon goin’ on them is about more than food.      Oh?      Y’see, when I were younger, you could sum up a bird by its call and its looks. Now, you’ve got to choose what they eat to win ‘em in, where they sit, when they sing. Seems like we’re the ones trainin’ them now, not the other way ‘round.      Right enough, luv. ‘Course, isn’t that what we do with ourselves?

Rather skip the new book, eh? You've done a proper about-turn on life, haven't you? I remember you were working at the local council office, and now you're talking about publishing a memoir and doing yoga every morning. Charming!       [laughs]  Oh, it’s not half! I thought I’d die of boredom if I kept on that council path for another five years. I’ve been through a proper change—IVF didn’t work out, and I’m now a single parent of two. But you know what? It’s also the best thing that’s ever happened to me. I’ve had to juggle school runs, admin jobs, and personal projects, and somehow, it all managed to come together.      Oh my goodness. That takes real grit, doesn’t it? I can only imagine how emotionally draining it must be. I did feel for you when you posted about it on social media—though I noticed you’ve been a bit less visible lately. I missed the updates! What's going on?      Ah, yes, that—social media’s a bit of a double-edged sword for me these days. A few years ago, I loved the idea of having a platform, of sharing my journey, getting support. But then people got way too nosy—commenting on my choices, my body, even the way I parented. I’ve set boundaries now. It’s all about protecting my kids’ privacy and keeping the negativity at bay.      Oh, I completely get that. I’ve noticed it too. I left a school job last year, moved out of the house I’d been in for 15 years, and now I’m trying my hand at teaching adults. I’ve kept it to the bare minimum online because I didn’t want to be judged. Going into that new area of teaching adult literacy is a bit daunting, to be honest.      That’s brave of you! Adult education is such a rewarding field. I used to do some work with it as a social worker too. You must be doing some amazing things. Have you thought about writing a blog or even contributing to a book? It’s a good way to reflect and also reach people who might be where you once were.      Actually, I have! I’m working on a book—that’s the next big project in the making.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun is just beginning to warm up the garden properly. Mind you, I’m not one for basking like a lizard, but a few rays after such a long grey winter are quite welcome.      You bet. Just like the weather, we’ve waited all year for a decent weekend. It was beginning to feel like this spring had gone on holiday with a friend and forgot to come back! Got the kettle on, incidentally. If you’ve a moment, you're welcome to join me inside for a cuppa.      That's very kind of you, I'd be delighted. I've been meaning to pop over anyway, actually. You know, now that the turkey still hasn’t quite settled in my left leg, I suppose I need to start reintegrating into the community and stop hiding in the classroom all day!      Good choice. I've been mostly nursing the garden myself. Not a bad thing — keeps the mind off the news! Speaking of, didn’t you say the other day you had a new bunch of students starting?      I did, and I can tell you quite a few of them were early arrivals for their placement today — some of them watching the clock like it owed them money. Mind you, most of the young ones are bright enough, even if they take the journey to learning a little like an obstacle course.      You know what it's like. I used to teach biology back in the day — full house of teenagers suspicious of everything from DNA to detention. One lad once asked me what made something a law instead of a fact. It took me an hour to untangle that curiosity without giving him a headache about quantum physics!      Oh good lord — teenagers and philosophy. I had one last week asking if “all that school stuff” really mattered if machines could do all the work. Had quite the little existential crisis, poor boy.      Aye, well, it's a time when all those big questions come crashing in. I remember my daughter having one while painting her room. Declared to me out of nowhere: “If no one sees it, is the painting real?” Sounded far too much like something I once read in a philosophy course I never go back to!      If I didn’t respect kids more, I’d be tempted to teach mindfulness along with verbs!

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh? You’d think in Cambridge we’d know if it’s ‘ere first... got the cow parsley growing in the dining room more than I’ve seen on the fells round Leeds.      No, I mean—get in, James—it’s April in Yorkshire een! You lot  breathe  rain! We haven’t even got cabbages that stubborn back in Tyne and Wear. Though I’ll admit I never thought I’d eat a stew and call it 'artisan’!      Oh come off it, don’t be squinting at the cow parsley like it owes you tax. I much prefer the idea of sitting here arguing about whether  The Social Network  is a drama or a documentary-style script. Marc Zuckerberg’s more real to me now than Oliver from next door. I think he turned me down for a date once by mistake.      He turned you down  on purpose . I remember he said he’s allergic to oversized desktop hides, which are clearly for the discerning. Good for you, Oliver—vastly overqualified and under-employed in a place like Cambridge. Anyway, speaking of films, I’ve been watching that  Drive  again—every time I do, it feels like a Beethoven symphony dressed as a knife fight.      Yeah, well, if you lot fancy film nights, don’t forget to invite the cat. If I understand one more line of that American grunge soundtrack in this damp flat, I’m considering retirement to a seaside shelter. It just sounds like sour milk wrapped in flannel!      Hey, you know what I fancy more than films? Some actual food that about daft university cafeteria wouldn't consider a 'contents may separate' joke. I'm cooking lasagne tonight—traditional, no frosting or fondant. Just lasagne. You’re all welcome, ‘cos I baked treacle sponges at 5am. I’m told they go nicely with a surf ‘n’ turf of relapse and regret.      As long as it's not the one with edible flowers from the 'vegan meets dystopia’ edition. Some of us work with road networks, not wheat alternatives. Still, the sponges go straight on my list—fine recipe or not, you're a national treasure once you voluntarily bake that early.      And what your cat’s opinion on all this? I seriously think it’s starting to understand more than those of us who choose not to sleep to listen to talk shows about ‘authentic pronunciations’.

Rather annoying the gym's closed today. You know, that one by the station in Cambridge, they said it’d be open by now after renovations. I’m more than a bit out of shape after over a year of doing bug fixes and no time to hit the weights.      Honestly, if it’s all the same, I don’t think I’d bother with the gym. I’ve been trying these online workouts. A lot of them are free, too. I’ve even started incorporating some into what I teach the kids at primary school. They love the dance warm-ups — it’s called  Groove and Grow , like, literally, it’s just shaking and bouncing, but the children love it.      That’s cute, definitely. I’m more of a solo gym person, but I do like the idea of getting some sort of routine in. Oh, actually—my editor was at a writing retreat in Austria earlier, and she suggested I take a break for a week in the summer. I might do it! Maybe even ski in the Alps. I mean, why not, right?      Haha, yeah, sounds good. I mean if you land a week to yourself, I say do it. I might go on a cycling holiday with my sister. West Country, maybe. She loves kids – works part-time at a summer camp – and it’s a perk of her job that her staff gets discounted trips as well. Maybe we can all go together?      That would be lovely. I miss just being in the fresh air. Speaking of, it’s oddly sour weather here—looks like it might rain later. I can’t be the only one who’s had enough of this endless drizzle.      I don’t know, I kind of miss this weather. I just got back from a holiday in Barcelona, you know, and it was unseasonably hot—40 degrees. Burgers baked on the beach. All I can think is that I need better fans in my flat. But on the upside, I finished a new level for the game I’m working on while I was over there. The landscape there is so different, it inspired a new desert aesthetic.      That's brilliant, I love that. I was just reading a piece about gothic architecture on the coast, and it had me thinking of atmospheric settings. You in the games industry really do get的好处 of imagination!

Rather annoying that the ref’s still not given a card for that foul – you’d think it’s red. I swear, the lads on the pitch are more level-headed than the bloke in the middle!      I know, I know—some ref wouldn’t have let it happen in een-a if they  seen  it with their 'ead on straight! But c’mon, don’t you think Man City are starting to knuckle down now? They’ve got a few records to break, ain’t they?      Oh aye, if they keep passing like that they’ll polish the whole league out! Not like United, mebbe—still kickin’ it up the park like it’s turkey day an’ they’re playin’ for a leg of it!      Roight, I think I’ve had enough of watching them for now. Minging! Wait, you fancy a film? I happened to lend a DVD in me bag the other day from uni—can’t remember the name now. Something with dinosaurs, I reckon.      Aye, we can put it on after this half. Right, as long as it’s not one of them fancy arthouse ones… I reckon I’d rather watch a domestic services advert.      Don't be stingy with me, eh? It’s a proper film— Jurassic Park , if you must know. Bit iconic, eh? Still, been a good few years since someone first cast an eye on it.      That’s not a bad idea, actually—there’s a fair stretch between this being tea-time and us needing to head in for Easter lunch at Nana’s later.      Oh, speaking of which—did they say what time they want us there? Not that I mind staying up, but we should probably make the effort, ‘cos they baked the lot o’ Easter eggs already, an’ I reckon me mum’s tryin’ to memorise all the recipes again!      Aye, my Nan mentioned she’ll have to call me nan to help with lunches, or she’ll ruin the scones again. I swear you could hear the smoke shootin’ out the back of the gothic oven on Number One if she overcooks them.      Haha, don’t go boxin’ her ears, your nan’s a good woman. She made me a picture frame with one of them digital printers last year—me belly in a toga on it.      C’mon! That’s a classic! You lot should be at the Channel Five awards, with all them flash dinners an’ things.

Rather skip to the front of the book, isn’t it? A few hurrahs for when the first one got the diploma, same with the second one more recently. Not a bad show himself, that boy. I was chuffed to bits when the photos came back from Iceland.      Got eeny weeny, yeah? I think they took me on holiday when I was five years old? I remember that car fair by Sligo where they had all the funny-looking donkeys and penny-farthings or something. We had to ride the donkey. Didn’t even want to.      Oh, I had photos taken at Wimbledon once. That was when the boys were small, before the marathon made everyone think you had to be in top form to have any fun. Ten thousand, twenty thousand, thirty thousand steps, and then you think, "What for?" But I was proud of them running it. I still have the medals up here.      And don’t forget the cinema trips! Used to take them to see the smashem-up chasem ones, like Waterworld or whatever, and we used to end up upchanging in the aisles.      It took me ages to get used to changing nappies in a cinema. Be all proud parents one minute and then trying to figure out whether I’d still got it on the right way. Let’s see… What about that birthday party when Silas was seven? There was a juggler, a bouncy castle, someone got stuck in a cake. And Kevin didn’t like the cake at all.      Also, he didn’t like the fair being crowded. That was a right panic in the middle of it.      I think you had the good sense to take it to the one in Limerick. Going anywhere that wasn’t crowded sounded worrying to me. Still, I’ll have to say, for all the hassle, it was grand to see them growing up and getting into their ways. Even if it was all jackets and sandwiches.      I always thought they would come back as barristers or accountants or something grand like that. Never imagined the one with the lopsided grin would want to be a vet.      Maybe he just wants go out walking on the mud, like our dog Roxy. I’d rather do that than work in some office.      And what your dad used to dream about was planning big IT projects. Thought he’d be out making those big, swooping belly-laugh jokes like on the telly.

Rather lovely to have you both over. You know, ever since we moved into this house, it's felt... proper, rather than just a place to crash. Blows me how something like a kitchen table can make it feel like “a real home,” don’t you agree?      Oh, I'm with you there, Liesel. I was just saying to Janet yesterday how all the little choices—like that soft grey paint on your walls—make all the difference. Oh, and what was it you said about the herbs you planted in the window?      Rosemary and thyme. I like to think of them as little green friends. Now, we’ve been talking about decor, but have you had the turkey soup? I’ve been playing about with it all week. I put a little cumin in for some warmth and I think it turned out rather nicely!      Oh! Cumin, really? You always surprise me. I suppose I’m used to the old tray-bakes and stews, to be truthful. Cooking was always more of my mother’s domain.      Now, I can tell you I put two spoons of cumin once and grief of my life followed. My sister was allergic to everything—and it wasn't a light allergy either. She turned purple and ran down the road fairly badly, I think it was the lime in the same curry, not the cumin, but you never know. Still, no harm in a little cumin now!      That’s a story! God, Janet, you’ve never told us that one—what were you, about ten or eleven?      Aye, that’s right! We were in about 1958. I remember the doctor coming all the way from St. John’s. My father nearly fainted when he told us she was okay. Still, I never quite got over the way she took off like that. All I saw was a flash of blue duster and then silence for hours.      That’s terrifying! You must have been so worried—      Nonsense, we always were with lunches to keep the whole street fed. Now, the toys… do you remember those little wooden animals we carved with the old church set go? They were scratchy if you swallowed them, but I think I still have one in the attic somewhere. Sue’s box might have it.      Wood carvings? Oh, I had a set too, my mother made it herself with friends in her youth group.

Rather fine day today, isn't it? That sun feels gentle on the skin. Mind, it does like to cheat and hide behind a cloud every now and then. I’ve been sitting by the window with a cup of tea, watching the garden. That bird in the hawthorn—it’s a proper old eeny-meeny, if you ask me.      Oh aye, I’ve noticed that one too. Proper cheeky, isn’t it? It thinks it’s got the place to itself. I reckon the cat doesn’t chase it because it’s well aware the bird can out-talk it! Still, it’s nice to have a bit of bird song now and again, and not that of a dustbin lid clattering down the street. It’s just us, the sandwiches, and the peace, bless it.      Aye, it’s a rare thing peace and quiet, isn’t it? I used to fancy a bit of noise in my day, the clatter of shopping, the rumble of the bus. But now, I find I rather enjoy the stillness—don’t get me wrong, I don’t mean to sound as if I’ve taken to reading poetry by the hour or anything like that. Just... a rhythm in the day gives one a sense of purpose?      You’re not the only one, love. All these years, and now it’s just the two of us at home. It’s strange, feels like the house has gotten a bit more generous with its silences, don’t you think? Some folks talk of filling it with plants and pictures and radio chatter, but I’ve found that silence, when it comes, about dares you to hear the rest of the world beyond it. You get to hear a whole new sort of life going on.      Aye, I quite like the idea of ‘hearing the world’ that way. I remember when I were younger, me mum used to say a quiet afternoon was just the moment to hear your thoughts properly. I always thought she was tooting her own horn for being deep, but now I do find there’s more to it—more to thinking when there’s less noise trying to distract one.      Oh, go on then, what do you think about now, then? You can’t very well go on like that, blooming modest.      Well, perhaps I think about the garden, the tea, the bird—or not, perhaps I don’t think about much at all.

Rather annoying I had to take the train in to work this mornin’, me car’s ‘ad a spot of trouble again. I’m startin’t think it’s got a vendetta against me!      Aw, don’t I know it! Mine wouldn’t start two morns ago and I was runnin’ late for a lesson. I nearly got onto the wrong train because of it.      Honestly, that sounds like a top way to start the week. I wouldn’t wanna be one of your pupils if you’re running late chase after them!      Right, but enough of that. How’ve you been, Jess? I heard you got yourself a pet recently? My turkey, Elsie, seems to despise the new cat next door, so I reckon you might have some company for her.      Yeah, I’ve got a rescue cat called George—reluctant to cuddle, but brilliant in every other way. And no, he hides, he doesn’t cuddle—and I mean he hides like he’s evad’n the SAS, luv.      Honestly, your cats both sound like my grief when I’m trying to meet a deadline… invisible, elusive, and generally a little too proud of themselves.      I feel you, Mollie. Work’s been the same—book reports, staff meetings, and now trying to figure out how we’re going to fit in those ‘emotional resilience lessons’ the new policy expects.      That’s so me! Some days I’d swear half my job is just psyching myself up to speak in front of people, let alone trying to get them excited about algebra!      Well, I envy you for it. My work as a copywriter is like trying to get a toddler to write a novel—ridiculous.      Aw, I remember when you were just at uni, trying to get internships and all that. Now look at you, scheming mad ideas for advertisements while you sip your overpriced coffee.      Ha! It’s just been the same path but with more deadlines and fewer friends who come with birthday presents! Anyone get any good goody bags on your last birthday? I had a friend give me socks once.      Honestly, socks might be better than what your mum gave you. I once got a live gerbil and a note that said, “Teaches responsibility!”      Oh my gosh, I nearly bought food at the party like I was goin’ to feed it at a zoo! Totally forgot where I was!

Rather lovely to be here in this part o’ L8. A bit more lively 'an usual, if y’ask me. I teach at the uni, down near Edge Hill, so I see me a lot o’ change in the area. Look at this garden! Y’know, it’s got that eeny weeny bit more charm 'an the 'ouses where I live. Almost like Harry Potter world a bit. A lot o’ character in this place.      Oh, aye, 'tis nice 'n all, but I’m tellin’ yeh, it ain’t as safe as it was thirty years back. I work at a school round the corner, and sommates been talkin’ 'bout strange lads hangin’ about the high school. Not the lads from the school, them from the o’ther side o’ the city, if y’know what I mean. I've heard talk 'bout this ISIS lot still creepin’ around in the back streets. Proper spooky, m'arse.      Oi, don’t go terrifyin’ the lads, Laurie. Y’know I work at the school as well, and I dunno, I fancy we’ve got more to worry 'bout with students skipping then from them “dangerous” characters?      Yeah, Ma, they’re not gonna be the ones sommatin’ to me. I mean, I've got my own problems at school — homework and all 'at. Though, one o’ the teachers said readin' Harry Potter was good practice for schoolwork. Though, is it a fantasy novel or a proper book? Can I get housepoints in it or is it just about daft boys and a snake?      Oh, luv, it’s all about the mechanics of language and narrative! I mean, it does have a lot to do with imagination, but 'tis allegorical. All that tragedy, friendship, and moral choice — the whole business is probably got as much heft in it as you’d find in Dickens or Tolstoy. Though not as much as Chaucer, mind.      Aye, well, I don’t know where y’all get these fancy ideas. I started with a set go every mornin’ if I don’t get properly fed, I’m off in the loo. Never could go three bloomin’ minutes without a cup o’ tea. Me doctor says it's stress, though I think 'tis just the way I’m wired.      Stress ‘n' all’s not helped by this work I’m doin’ down near Calderstones. Proper hustle. My boss says I’m to be always cheery, but you try being cheery when some bloke’s flippin’ you a scribbled-out invoice in the hand.

Rather exciting to be thinking of Nepal, isn't it, Mary? I've never been further east than Israel when I was younger, but I dream of those mountains and villages! Mind, I nearly dropped my coffee this morning—Mark had to ask if the beans were as strong as motor oil again!      Oh, Mary, we do miss you down at the school displays. I’ve taken over most of your old tasks now, but I must admit, I don’t have your flair for the dramatic. We’re trying to include gluten-free options for the children's lunches more often, but the parents complain either too much or not enough—it's a balancing act.      I heard only yesterday that the local Farm Shop has turkey sausages that are gluten-free now. It’s about time, isn’t it? Darcy, bless her, eats nothing but salads now—nut allergies, poor thing. I still remember breakfasts with my mother during the war; no sausages, just posh porridge and stale hides, ha!      That reminds me, Nancy, I was recalling the time you told me your mother-in-law escaped from Siberia with your husband as a child. I only wish we could still get those kinds of stories now—and not have to rely on the village shop's loo for tales of wartime survival!      Ha, yes, but the war-time rations were nothing compared to the current free school meals system. Mark’s at that school, and he's just starting to help in the kitchen. He’s a man of many talents—cooking, school duties, and managing the Tour of Britain marshals next month!      The Tour of Britain? I nearly about blocked the road last week trying to wave the riders past my garden. It brought back memories of when my husband ran the local Iron Man! I’m so proud of Darcy now—she just trained for her first one. She got her route passed near Gloucs and all, bless the girl.      Oh, I tried to follow her training on the TV once. Feels as if I'm being asked to run a marathon with lunches to keep up with the pace! Now, about our Nepal trip—should I start bringing my travel books from the attic? Or go straight online?      If you go online, make sure to mention the gluten-free meals. I tried a trip last year where the ‘vegetarian’ dish at 13,000 feet turned out to be chicken with masala and bellyache included!

Rather annoying I had to cancel last minute innit, me an’ the conference organiser had a right pother last nigh’. Organising the poetry festival at the university, y’know, and me boss was hankering for a spreadsheet o’ the delegate accommodation! Gah. But it was my mum’s birthday and she  wasn’t  havin’ no excuse.      Oh aye, family before work. Fair dos. Proper show-off, Miss Doncaster, hah! But you said you were coming to Leeds for the weekend. Didn’t even get to the M1 last Tuesday?      Lakin, I was  supposed to . I’d have driven up in me Renault Mytyke if I didn’t skid left on the A1 over the motorway junction and end up in Wakefield instead of Leeds. Turns out I’m in the North, and forgetin’ breakfast, no less. I just happened upon this café and spent two hours eavesdroppin’ on a group of lads arguing about Man Utd. Real culture shock—vast.      I can imagine! I mean, we all live in Cambridge and yet I only started drivin’ this year. Me folks live in West Sussex, and when I got “stuck” – that’s what I called it, leastways – on Haywards Heath roundabout, I nearly had a heart attack. Someone at work was  laughin’ at me  for havin’ a sat nav in one hand and two steering wheels in the other. Rude.      Yeah, but it’s fair, innit? Beginners make mistakes. I had a colleague, Laura, once nearly about to fall off the M25 round the area where it’s like 20 lanes. She was panikin’ and then barely noticed the lorry unloading bobblehead toys alongside her. Proper mental. But hey, at least she wasn’t cuttin’ lane-changers open. Unlucky buggers.      Aye, I could stick to my spreadsheets and speaker line-ups. Websites and contracts are one thing, but the A-road system in this country is a proper labyrinth for a Yorkshire lass.      Don’t go badmouthing your roots! It’s got real quirks—like me in-laws living between two train lines, and the main A24 just outside their window. They’ve made peace with the noise and the occasional pothole so deep I had to borrow money to buy a spare wheel for the car.      Well, I’m not entirely surprised—second to collision damage for our warehouse, the next thing we repair is always flats from potholes. Me job now?

Rather annoying that the council’s thinking of knocking down the old library. I was just in there last week—what with the kids needing quiet space after school.      Yeah, I heard about it too. Mind you, I’ve seen the kind of things they get up to in there. Got eeny weeny books stacked haphazardly and teenagers on the computers doing goodness knows what. But a clean space is all I ask for, so this isn’t helping.      Exactly. That place is part of the community. You can’t chase progress if you lose what made the community what it is. I think we need to start a petition, get the people who still value it on our side. My turkey and noodle casserole is left cold, this is more important to me right now.      Fair enough. But how many of us are going to do better than breakfast, no doubt. I’ve been thinking about this for a while. When’s the last time we both saw you not working those evening transcription hours? You bleed that job, like you need mnemonics to remember what day it is next.      It pays the rent. And yes, I might’ve got a bit… what's the word… domesticated by routine. Though I remember all the faces, all the people I’ve worked with—does that count as brain training or just brain rut?      Both probably. You should talk to the town hall people too. As an administrator, I’m used to knowing which ones have ears for local folks. Mary—yes, the one with a red pencil habit and a tea addiction—she’s more your colleague than most because she understands about community binding.      Oh, she’s the one who gave out free sandwiches during the local fete last year. I remember it. Mary, theཀ red penciled, sandwich distributing local Gazette queen. Got her down.      Exactly. You need to show strength in numbers, and talking to someone within the council can help bridge the gap. As for you and that shift of yours, cut it down a couple of hours and join the cause. Not all the working class can be expected to live off brain cells and desire, but we can go for a middle path.      I’ll ask my line manager, but only if they give me a bean bag to lay on your suggestion. It’s all happening right here, isn’t it?

Rather fine day today, isn't it? That sun gracin’ the table just right for a spot of lunch. You've brought some of that cake from the village shop, Eunice? That lemon type they make in the shop near the church, I s’pose?      Aye, it is a fine day, Thomas. Not as good as the one last week, though—that’s a truth. A shame too; I’d have liked to take a stroll by the field path and see if that little wren’s still nesting near the hawthorn tree. The birds seem more chirpy these days, as if they've forgotten the harsh winter.      That’s a rum lot of talk about birds, Eunice! The only thing I’ve seen about them lately is the seagulls stealing pastry from the bins in the High Street. Blighters, they are. Made quite the breakfast, no doubt about that!      Aye, well, you ever looked at one, Ken, and thought they was elegant? No, I didn’t think so. Though tell me—personally, I’ve been meaning to ask—what d’you make of them Jehovah’s Witnesses who still turn up on the door now and then? Still getting their leaflets left in the letterbox?      Oh, heavens, they were here the other day, trying to tell me that “the world is about to end” and that I should be joining their meetings. Like I've got time for that!      Thomas, you remember when we first moved out here? That man with a red beard used to be their rep—Mr. Williams, I think his name was. Always polite, always quiet. He used to bring such nice brownies once or twice. Strange what you miss even now.      Aye, a kind man in many ways. But ‘course, I’ve always held steady against that sort of thing. I’m no great fan of religious folks any longer, not after how it tried to shape my life back in the factory. As for politics and voting—do you reckon we've been better off not voting the last few years?      Truth be told, I’ve not voted since ’64. What good's it ever done us? Taxes keep going up, and the streets look like a dog’s dinner. Never mind the parking near the coast—good luck getting a space in Weybourne in the summer!      As for parking, I had to park two miles away on our last visit and walk back with a ice-cream cone in one hand and a bag of chips in the other.

Rather do I! The smell of fudge is delightful, isn’t it? I do wish they’d let it cool a bit, though—nearly scalded my tongue already.      You’re far too eager, love. That fudge needs at least a quarter of an hour. Got it all from that little antique shop down by the river. Still got his wife's recipe, of course. She’s been making it for nearly fifty years now.      I was going to mention the budget. We’ve been meaning to look into that new restaurant that just opened next door. You know, the one near the upholsterer’s? I heard it’s the real deal—proper brunch on the weekends.      Oh, dear! Another restaurant in this backwater village? I’d rather eat at the old bakery. The school turned into an academy last year, by the way. The headmaster, no doubt gone to ground in some Indian outsourcing firm in his old age, you know?      Now now, Eleanor—leave the schools out of it. They’ve been trying to get funding for ages. Though I must say, with all the logs they burn and the way they treat the budget, they might as well have considered it a hobby.      Speaking of logs, we really should get a proper log burner installed. The one we’ve got is ancient. It barely keeps the place warm at this time of year.      True, but it’s someone else’s problem for now. I think my mum wants to talk to you about the cats—yes, the ones with the muddy paws and the tendency to chew through cords.      Cats and dogs are both far too much trouble these days. I still remember watching over thirty kids at a time in my day. This family is small enough, and it still feels like chaos.      Oh, I rather like it. All the company, the stories, the fudge. I do miss Tokyo, though. That trip I took last year was unlike anything I could’ve imagined—      Let’s not go there. London’s fine. No speaking English to the wrong people, no overcooked mashed potato, no delays.      Oh please go back then, James. I’d rather not sit through one more plate of your “mike stew.”      Mike stew? That one time was a mistake.      You had a job in Tokyo, Gillian? I had no idea. I’ve been meaning to talk to you about your work—transcribing reports all day?

Rather annoying this new tax they’ve brought in, isn’t it? I was just reading it in the  Eastern Daily Press —something about local authorities having more power over land use, or whatever. Seems a right bureaucratic mess to me.      Oh aye, they’re after more money again, all right. I’ve got a nephew who tried to buy a house just outside Wymondham a year ago. Told me he needed ten different forms just to get permission to install a new kitchen! Ridiculous! And the pensions? They’re dragging their heels when it comes to uprating them too.      Honestly, I can’t be arsed to keep up with all this anymore. Being retired is supposed to be relaxing, not dealing with government forms and satellite navigation! I had the sat nav in my car last week and it gave me directions to the wrong village, nearly got me lost! And when I finally arrived, I just happened to pass a recycling bin, and the council had the cheek to fine us for not putting it out the right day!      Ah yes, recycling, luv. I’ve noticed the rules keep changing. One week it’s this container for food waste, the next it’s banned again—what’s it for then, the pigeons? I’m at my wits’ end trying to keep track. At my age, I should be worrying about retirement homes, not whether my banana peel will end up in the wrong bin!      Our pensions aren’t in a strong position either. All my lot are drawing from the same old state pension—piece of toast money it is, and I’d be lying if I said I wasn’t seeing more people my age in about the same boat. I don’t suppose the government really cares, though. Not when they’ve got more shiny projects to sell us on the telly.      The telly, yes! I was watching  EastEnders  last night, sods it, and the whole time I was thinking, “What have I done with my life?” I ran a childminder for years and never saved a bob. Now here I am, not a penny to my name and still trying to programme the bloody set top box.      Still, I suppose we’ve got one another, if nothing else. Mind you, I’d kill to spend a day in some remote place—somewhere far off where the government can’t reach.

Rather annoying this, the laptop's playin’ up again. Aye, it's been through the paces, and I thought she'd be sorted under warranty after I fixed it last time      What's wrong with it this time? Is it overheatin’ like the last time or is it somethin’ else?      Ay, just tryin’ not to let you fix everything yourself, but if you're this confused, maybe send it into the shop rather than pulling it to bits again.      Didn’t even want to touch it at first, but the shop near Kinvara won’t do anything for me, and the warranty’s still valid. I managed to get the boot drive replaced, but now it just goes into a blue screen. I’m beginnin’ to think it's the motherboard.       points at the table       You need to eat Brian, or I’m throwin’ the chicken nuggets in the bin, even if they are the non-battered ones      Noodles, yes please, I’m not really one for fajitas, as much as you tried to make them look fancy Sean      You callin’ out the humble fajita sauce – Mate, I got the real stuff in, it's Texas quality      It smells nice, but it's not really what I fancy tonight. Still, the chicken’s tasty, just someone got chickenpox on the recipe book.      I preferably buy what you make, but I mind the mess you make with the plastic wrap – Look at your hands, there's sauce in about five places.      Oh come on, this is part of cooking. You and failsafes be havin’ a laugh while the rest of us are tryin’ to make things edible.      I did manage to get the swimming sorted for the weekend – any chance you can drop us off at Midleton on Saturday? I don't fancy my kid catchin’ a cold from a puddle in the garden       makes choking sounds with a mouthful of fajitas       That go bad? I thought it was more of a celebratory sound      It’s not ideal but he hasn’t said "more" once all night, so I’m callin’ it a win      Regarding the computer warranty Brian, I'll sort it tomorrow. I'll get the receipt up online and see if I can send the laptop back without havin’ to get dressed.      And what about the rugby game Saturday? You didn’t mention if you want us to come      Aye, I want you to come, you're on the team for goodness sakes.

Rather lovely to be out here today, isn't it? The way the light catches the hills through the trees... It's so peaceful out in the countryside like this. I can't say I get out nearly as often as I should with all the marking and lectures.      It really is. There's something about walking like this, even just for half an hour, that just clears your head completely. I remember when I first came to Norfolk, I was just struck by how different it is from London. Everything's so open and green.      Didn’t you say your family's from the north? Yorkshire, was it?      That’s right. I spent most of my childhood in Harrogate. It was definitely hillier up there, not quite like this flat, rolling Norfolk landscape. You get a completely different kind of view—rolling waves of green instead of sharp rises and rocky outcrops.      I happened to visit Harrogate once when I was younger. Such a charming town, tucked in the hills. There was the scent of tea and hot water everywhere—very Bronte novel, in a way. Norfolk, in comparison, feels a bit like a living painting. All these old villages, the white-cobbled streets, thatched cottages... It gives you a real sense of history.      Oh, it really does. And you know, I think it's that sense of depth, of layers of history, that keeps me coming back here even when I could just as easily be in the city. Like that village a few miles down the road—Thorney, was it?—where the marshland meets the hillside. The stories they say come from there, about people living off the land for hundreds of years.      I remember visiting Thorney once for a weekend retreat. The silence you get out there is something else. No traffic, no beeping phones, no deadlines. Just the sound of birds and the wind. And at night, the sky is just something else—with all the stars.      I think your favourite part is hearing about the Danelaw or something like that—how parts of Norfolk were once under Danish control.      Oh, I did a module on that once during my MA. There's a map that shows where the Danish influence ends and the Anglo-Saxon line begins, right here between Thetford and Norwich. You can almost taste it in the dialect and the place names.      That’d make for a really interesting class next term.

Rather than going out tonight, eh? You fancy a flick? I've had enough of club nights for a while.      That’s a good shout. What’ve we got on? Up for something action-packed? I reckon that was a proper brain melt the one time I tried to watch it.      That sounds a bit arduous, to be fair. But, honestly, as long as he’s got real job security, I won’t complain. Bloke works in central London, from what I hear. Pretty much cycle heaven compared to the roads down here, if you ask me. Tell me, you remember that film with the cyclists and the man with the time goin' on in his head like a metronome? The one that left us in the car wondering if we were missing somethin'?      You're thinking The Eternal Return of Outer Space, again, aren’t you? Nah, that was a proper head scratcher.

Rather lovely this place, isn't it? I mean, I've lived in London for years, but there’s something so peaceful here in Norfolk. Look at those wildflowers by the path.      You're not wrong. Any chance of discussing football at the conference? I see you're supporting Spurs, I'm a Diehard.      If only I could focus on anything else but my next lecture.

You think you could get me in contact with him? That’d be goon. I’ll see if I can meet up or at least get the line in, yeah?      No problem. I’ll give him a bell. It’d be better than this cave, eh? An’ you can finally get outta that car without suffocatin’ in the process.      Aye, I’m not entirely sure what I did to deserve gettin’ stuck with this thing, but it can’t be far off now.

Pretty – very pretty birds, actually.      You mean the ones that hissed at you and squawked when you moved? I saw one try to grab your leg, dear. Like a someone at a Premier League game trying to chase a ball. It just thought you had a meal in your pocket!      That’s being rude, Margery. But it is a good story. I do miss the old days a bit. When the birds lit up the sky and most of us were too busy not to worry about anything. Now I hear it on the news—Celebrity A on trial for Burglary B—and it’s like the birds have flown somewhere else too.      You know, scientists say some of these geese are waiting till the temperatures drop. There’s been so much rain this year, they’re probably adjusting their timing. It’s all related to the environment, obviously. Even more than those celebrity trials.      Yeah, goenvironmental on them! I’ve seen a few go off at kids feeding the ducks, but that’s because we were wasting bread—should’ve read your book, Vicky.

So do you ever just lie awake at night and think about what’s next? Like, what’s the  plan , right?      Honestly, sometimes I can’t even plan the next two weeks. I’m just trying to keep up with the day job at the minute. But it’s weird, isn’t it? You get used to one routine and then suddenly you wonder if that’s it.      Exactly. Half of me wants to just do something gig-based, travel, maybe even teach abroad. Like, volunteer or something in South America. But the other half is like, you need to have a mortgage and security and  plans .      Oh yes, the ‘real-life adult’ version of me says property as quick as possible and a stable job with a pension contribution. The other version wants to work on a boat from the Canary Islands. Ha – but it’s so hard to split the two because they both seem huge.      I did try taking a course for digital skills. Not sure if I’m the coding type, but at least it gave me a bit of direction. You know? It just felt good to do  something  other than just going through the motions.      That’s the thing, isn’t it? I did an online course after uni too, just to fill the gaps, but I didn’t take it seriously and dropped out. I regret that now. I think it’s important to keep investing, even if it’s small stuff. Maybe not even toward a job, just for the sake of learning.      Do you think talking about this is helping or just making us feel more lost?      Honestly, a bit of both. But at least we’re talking about it. Some people just… accept where they are.      Maybe the first step is just figuring out what we  don’t  want. Like, I don’t want to be in admin for forty years, but I also don’t fancy some high-powered corporate mess.

Rather annoying me a bit, eh, love? That Tom fella keeps trying to get closer ‘n closer... got me feelin’ all kinds of skint. I mean, I know we’re just friends and all, but it’s startin’ to grate me a bit.      Oh eeny weeny, yeah? That’s sorely thick if he ain’t clear where he stands with a lass. What’s he doin’ exactly?      Well, he’s always sendin’ me private messages, like he don’t wanna chase when he’s with his lot o’ mates. It’s like he’s tryin’ to get me all to himself, only he’s got a bird already—Sarah, I think her name is. Yeah, she’s back home, works part-time at Dobbies, I think.      Blimey, that’s dodgy. Why doesn’t he sort himself out proper? He can’t be in two heads at once, can he?      Honestly, he sounds like he’s just playing games—something I know far too much about, I’m afraid. I mean, don’t get me wrong, I like Tom, but he doesn’t sound like much of a lad.      Tell me about it—he’s cheeky alright, but I wouldn’t mind swappin’ him for the lanky bloke from that uni place near Sillet Stones. Oi, Liam! He been around lately? Our group’s been missin’ him. He’s got this calm sort of edge ’bout him, y’know?      Aye, Liam’s been a bit quiet. I spoke to him at the aboutise last weekend—said he was headin’ up to Manchester for a mate’s do. Maybe he’ll be back next week.      Liam does sound quite charming. My sister had a thing for someone rather similar. All quiet and thoughtful. Though I have to say, it can be exhausting being with someone who doesn’t meet your eye for longer than a nanosecond—      Right, but if they’re with someone else, like Tom is, do you do the same? Tryna get a lass’s head mixed up?      That’s exactly it, and it’s not real. Genuineness is whike, don’t you think? I dunno, I just get so sick of lads who act like they’re the Romans and we’re the Carthaginians just because they’ve got a laugh and a look.      Or them that like stringin’ you along like I did with Alan once—six months of soft touches, promises, laughs, and then poof!

Rather skip the new pasta sauce, Joshua? That’s odd. I thought you’d like it — it has a proper kick to it, no nonsense about it.      It does, actually, but it reminded me of the spiciest chilli jam at our friend Martha’s place — we couldn’t all handle it, and we were out for the day on the lake. Almost had to lift Dan off the floor — wouldn’t stop spinning in circles.      Haha, yeah, Dan’s quite the one when he’s hit the hot stuff. Looks like he inherited the firebug gene from his aunt. I still can’t figure out how she got through three bottles of garlic chilli oil on her own that one turkey dinner.      Speaking of meals, Nicky, the boys mentioned their hockey match next Thursday. I think it’s at Alrewas ground again — do you want to pop along, or shall I sort out a picnic for after?      If the weather holds, I say go for it. We could grab Emily and Tom too, if they’re free. Might get a proper crowd in for the occasional ruck — quite a nail-biter last time. Josh, what line-up are they expecting?      Dunno yet. Coach is still picking – Mateo’s got a twisted ankle and needs a sub. I’ve been offered a slot — don’t know if I’m good enough. I mean, I’ve never played in a league before, just someone at the weekend jammers.      Nonsense, Joshua. You handled the hotter sauce, and now you’re worried about a bit of hockey? Just don’t overthink it — make a goal, and I’ll walk us all to the local for chips and green tomatoes. Not much better on a Saturday.      I’d take it. You could be the one who breaks ranks. And then we could travel up for the next match — Parents’ weekend? Maybe a weekend getaway to Milton Keynes or Newark?      That’s not half a bad idea. There’s a decent pub nearby as well, if you ignore the lunches and focus on the whiskeys. Might be a good way for us to get a bit of a stretch after all the family goings-on.      If we go, I’m booking the tickets, making the meals, and explaining the rules — someone’s got to save the world. Alright, lads, settle down and finish your greens before the tea goes cold.

Rather annoying that the GPS keeps looping us back to Highway 128, isn’t it? I was sure we turned left at that treehouse-looking maintenance building. She’s been quite mired in looking for a proper job. I overheard her saying something about temping just being a band-aid. She doesn’t want short-term anything.      It must be tough. Rob’s been trying to bail her out by texting daily, but I get the feeling Myra just doesn’t want the same kind of organisational life he does. I mean, he works in logistics and all—very structured.      And Myra? She’s all over the place at the moment. Honestly, I think she just wants time to settle down. I remember what you were saying at dinner last week about how even being an editor or a translator can be tricky when there’s a lot about contract work and flexibility.      Exactly. We were saying how much it depends on your client base. Sometimes I work barely two days a week if the contracts are thin. My sister Lucy tried freelancing like that once. All she had was sundry assignments at 60p a word. It was barely worth it.      I sort of stick out my thumb as an office temp as well. I always knew the lunches would be lukewarm and the company hierarchy fairly invisible, but you do get a slight buzz from helping people out with the day-to-day drudgery if you like that sort of thing.      It’s funny how we go from big plans about stability to just getting by with what we have right now.

Rather annoying this new bank’s gettin’ so much in tha papers about money laundering, innit? Seems everyone got to be checked out now. I’m just tryin’ to get my student finance sorted!      Yeah, it is a bit of a faff. I was in the post office the other week and they were askin’   loads   about where I wanted to send money. I just wanted to buy me mum a birthday present and I had to prove it wasn’t   dirty cash   or summat!      Didn’t it get worse after that big case in London? You know, the property developer bloke who was chuckin’ loads of cash around? It turned out that it was all from some dodgy offshore accounts. The lawyer got fined a fortune. It’s safety first now, I reckon.      But it’s a pain for regular folks. I mean, I’m just a student. I’m not in the criminal underbelly of London!      Well, I suppose once you start checking everyone, you get the innocent, and the guilty slip through as well. I know a land developer in Suffolk and he had to be arrested for false bookin’s… funny thing was, the police thought it was just him being a bit – how do I say – sneaky with profits, but it turned out he was helping sommat bigger.      If what I heard from Liam at work is right, he said this all started back in the 80s with some big crime families in the North. They’d fling the money about in pubs and buy up places through false names – all to make it look legal. Kinda about blocked up our system back then.      I had to teach a business ethics class at the uni last week. One of the lads said, “But if the system catches ‘em, then it’s not even worth it,” and I said, “That’s the whole point – it shouldn’t be worth it.” But then you’ve got these fancy lawyers who make sure it   is   worth it.      Crikey, it all sounds so grown up! I mean, you lot are talkin’ like it’s the next James Bond goings on! But it’s sufficin’ to give me anxiety just thinkin’ about that when I’m goin’ to the cashpoint.      Aye, but it’s best to keep yer noddin’ simple. You don’t need to be talkin’ ‘bout this at the bar, innit?

Rather nippy today, isn't it? I needed my cardigan the minute I stepped out the door. I swear the weather’s changed overnight.      Not a bit wrong. It’s a proper Midlands switch-up. I’d love to pick up something like that. I tried piano once—two minutes in and I was crying. It was dreadful.      We should all go for a Saturday afternoon visit to your class, Margot. It’d be something different, anyway.      That'd be so kind of you.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun is making everything feel a bit dreamier than usual. I got up rather early this morning—couldn’t sleep after I started reading this fascinating study on regional dialect shifts in rural Buckinghamshire.      Morning, Alice. And yes, it is a bit of a golden day. I think I actually   did   sleep through the sun coming up, I’ve been working late so often this week. Honestly, I’m running on coffee and guilt.      You poor thing. Guilt doesn’t run your blood pressure the same as coffee, I promise. What’ve you been working on so late, anyway?      Oh, you know—galley proofing, layout tweaks, chasing missing endnotes. Probably the same hell I’m in every month. Anyone I hand off the manuscript to ends up coming back with a million comments.      I feel that. Honestly, I spent two hours this morning untangling a manuscript that had, like,   eleven   conflicting formatting styles. One chapter was in helvetica, the next in courier.      Oh no! Does it still look human when you submit it, or does it end up looking like it got through a paper shredder?      Well, I’m not a miracle worker, but I gave it the old college try.      You know what I find interesting? I’m the editorial assistant here for just a few more weeks, and already I’m starting to notice patterns in what authors are submitting. Some are still very old school with their formats—full double spacing, underlining where bold should be, manual line breaks everywhere.      Ugh, I still cringe when I see document options like “legacy Danish” or “Arabic booklet.” Doesn’t anyone check the style sheet?      Maybe it’s less about willful ignorance and more about just not knowing where the modern tools are. I think it might have something to do with education or access. My previous research highlighted how regional and socioeconomic disparities affect digital literacy—though this is a publishing office, not a village in Buckinghamshire.      You’re not wrong. I started noticing the same kind of patterns on day one. It’s not about laziness—it’s about education in digital workflows, I think.      Anyway, all of you sound like you’ve made it to the conference seminar roles after I was hours late to my team meeting this morning. Do we talk about formatting every day, or do we at least try to enjoy a lunch where we all sit down at the same time?

Rather dozy the lot of them, if I'm honest. A few too many crumpets with custard, and I’ll not be moping about it. I’ve had words with the cousin about the noise, mind. Not proper decorum for a fiftieth anniversary. But it was nice to see the grandkids, eh? Kept twitching about on the settee.      Aye, it wasn’t terrible, but too much telly blaring in the corner. I couldn’t get a word in edgeways. But when me nana came in with the Victoria sponge, that was something else! Still, I reckon Aunty Diane got the best of it, didn’t she? Everyone pinching a bit o’ cake off her plate. She tried to throw a napkin at their heads, but I thought I saw Aunty Sharon take a bite for about a minute.      Sharon’s always been a bit tipsy early in the day. I expect the sherry went straight to her puffin. Still, the toffee sauce on that custard was the business, don’t you think? My old Nan used to make it every Boxing Day. Proper sticky, real Malton syllabub in a cup. I asked her where she’d put the tin of preserves, and she said: “Eh, stillsomewheres in the back of the larder.” Mind you, the phone’s been going all night with photos! I’m off for my tea and to make sense of this bloody phone.

Rather annoying when a water bottle freezes up in a car, innit? Me an’ nan ‘ad to chisel the ice off one time. Like, proper propered!      Aw, that’s right. When I was a lad, we used to take thermos flasks full of eeny cocoa. Keeps the drink warm, an’ puts a big grin on yer face in the wintertime. A lot o’ folk nowadays have this obsession wi’ iced drinks, even in wintery weather.      Nah, me n’ friends always keep it cold. Freezing like, even! One o’ ma classmate’s got IBS, so she cannae have hot tea at turkey time. You’ve gotta be careful what’s in ‘em. I read once about this bloke, he used to think he could drink ‘Oolland an’ Barrett’ herbal tea an’ breakfast, but then he spent a fortune in hospital after getting food poisoning.      That sounds right dodgy. Ma old nan used to bleed me eyes out if I drank iced tea—she used to say it'd freeze me bowels up! Still, I s’pose times change. Tell me, have you ever thought about living in a manor house? You’d have all the space in the world. I wouldn’t mind that myself—just me an’ a couple o’ black cats wanderin’ the halls.      That’d be mental! Like outta a storybook. Although I reckon cats can be a nightmare to look after. I once tried to paint the cat flap with red and gold and it ended up green because I mucked it up!      Ah, I bet you fancied it lit up like a manor. I remember when I moved house, that was right messy. I nearly lost a leg runnin’ round with a delivery for the washing machine. To this day I don’t know how I managed not to knock it over.      I dunno how people manage to sort out all the boxes when you un-pack. I’d prob’ly end up eating all the chocolate by accident! Me nan took ages sorting out her irises, an’ she’d like a man with a pick goin’ on in her living room. If I was moving, I’d just chuck the lot in Amazon. Quick an’ nappy.      You could say that again! Me mum was obsessed wi’ Latin—she used to think every exam was life or death. I still remember ‘dulce et decorum est’ like it was yesterday!

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh?      Aye, it's been damp as a cellar in Edinburgh in winter. I used to dread those afternoons in the school cloakroom — a whole pile of wet uniform to dry before the next day.      I was lucky at school, we had passive solar dryers. Not many schools would think about that now — sustainability was a bit of a buzzword back then, before it became a social media tag.      Hah! If only we had solar dryers for the sawdust, or the paint fumes. I like to keep it traditional mostly. My tools don't need Wi-Fi, thank you very much.      Just keep the sawdust away from the dining room rug! I had to clean that last week, and it’s not the sort of thing that comes off easily — unlike old school slogans, I suppose.      Ah, yes — in my day the boys would graffiti oversized 4s on the back wall of the cloakroom. I still don’t know why.      Maybe it was a code. I remember we used a similar system for passing messages during fire drills. Nothing too cheeky, but enough to keep the prefects scrambling.      You lot sound like you had it easy. My school days were all about survival. I didn’t want to be a headmistress’s shadow or hide messages in physics class — I just wanted to finish woodshop on time and get a paycheck.      That's oddly enviable. Some of us are still trying to get through admin and being told to smile more while analysing ballet competition transcripts.      I know the type. I do it for different areas, but let’s be honest, “gradually implementing digital data transition platforms” really just means unstacking folders that have bin bags for covers.      Oh, I did all that when I taught. You learn to keep any folder with a rubber band and a smile. It’s the only way to stay sane when you’re trying to track 320 sixth form lunches and a new student with digestive allergies.      Still, I bet you had it better than the rest of us go-getters on day jobs. At least there was a building full of posters to cover up the mildew. I just have sawdust and the ghost of my dad’s lathes.      Must be tough starting up your own trade. But it gives you more freedom — like, you can call in when the ceiling leaks or the floor boards go wobbly.

Right, luv, what do you two think about painting some cards for your mums tomorrow? It's Mother’s Day on Sunday, you know.      Can we do it in the kitchen? I don’t wanna go into my room and sit on the floor.      Yeah, Mummy’s floor is all dusty with the puzzle pieces and the lego.      Ha! A fair point. The kitchen is fine. I’ve got some scraps of card and some glitter you can use. Just nothing messy, mind. We don’t want to be cleaning up all weekend.      What does  messy  mean, though? Like, when you do something and you  messy up ?      Well, sort of! It means making a big, sticky, or untidy situation. Think of it like making a scene at the supermarket — definitely messy.      I once  threw  a doughnut at the shop and it  landed on the floor . That was  messy .      That’s not a  messy  story — that’s a  shameful  story. And you got  told off , remember?      Well, then it got  complicated . My gran said: “When you stir up the soup, expect to end up with a mess on your blouse,” or something like that.      That’s an idiom! “When you stir up the soup, you expect to end up with a mess on your blouse.” It means if you start trouble, it’s going to come back and bite you. Although I  wouldn’t  make your gran say it unless you want a real lecture.      I had an idiom in class this week. The teacher said: “We’re all in the same boat.” I thought she meant  literally  like a waterside boat. I said: “Are we going to the lake tomorrow?” and she nearly  had a fit !      My teacher said: “Don’t put all your eggs in one basket,” and I asked if the basket was chocolate. Now he calls me “basket boy” behind the bike sheds.      That’s brilliant. I think your teacher is trying to teach you two things: one, not to bet all your weekend savings on a big Time Machine from the Roadshow, and two, to maybe  think before you speak .      I think I’m  buttering up  Gran for a gift this year. I’m going to say I’m  on my best behaviour  at Forest School this week — kind of like trying to  sweeten the pot .      I’m not used to Forest School, though. I’m used to  tiptoeing around them  in the playground, like trying not to  wake a sleeping bear .

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You know what, I've been trying to get my old mummy to come and visit, she's been off for weeks after that operation. I've been over there a few times, but with the kids and the dog, things get a bit chaotic.      That's true, I understand. It was the same with my mam. I used to go most weekends before everything changed. I still do, but these days I’m so busy with work. It's pulling double shifts as it is. How's she holding up?      Still in the same old house, which is lovely, but I can see it’s getting to her, you know? On the one hand, you don't want to move them out unless it's absolutely necessary, especially if they’re still mobile. But on the other hand, the stairs are becoming an issue for her. Cats are better than stairs, no doubt about that!      Oh, absolutely. I remember the day we thought, you know, it's not a matter of  if  but  when . She had the surgery for the lung cancer—non-small cell if I remember rightly. They said she might only live a year, but she's holding on for two and a half now, thank the good Lord. It's strange though: one day you’re planning holidays, the other day you’re choosing a coffin.      It's hard to accept. Last week, I found her sobbing in the garden. She was just looking at the roses. I asked her what it was, and she said, “These are the things I used to plant with your dad. Can I even make it to next summer?” I nearly about cried myself. That pulled the heart strings, right enough.      I know exactly what you mean. I had to take my sister to the hospital the other day—she collapsed, they said it was stress related. But after that, she started crying and said, “I can't lose any more family members. I don't know how long I can keep doing this.” It's mental and physical health being completely intertwined these days.      It really is. I took the kids out for a proper meal the other day, just to get their minds away. Mummy doesn’t see them as often now, so I think it helps to spend quality time, you know.
