Rather annoying this, innit? Traffic’s mental at this time. I was just in Chester-le-Street yesterday, and I swear they’re building a whole new motorway!      Aw, it’s probably £20 million worth o’ concrete and a motorway junction shaped liek a eeny weeny  spit  on the map. Still, better that than all them potholes in the A1, if you ask me.      Yeah, I woz pulled over by a council van the other day for going over a speed camera site with a big “pot hole like to shag yer arse” grin. I swear, the roads in the North’ve got more bounce that MySpace filters.      Haha, fair play, I’ve been lucky in Herts, o’ course. They’ve got all the cash for tarmac and shiny lights. I mean, I’m working this project now with a firm in Cambridge – posh sorts, o’ course, you know the type. All got the brightest arses on the planet.      Yeah, sounds familiar. I mean, don’t get me wrong, I like the uni vibes and everything, but in Sunderland we reckon if it rains it’s a project. “Oy, look at it rainin’! Quick, let’s slap a cover on it and call somethin’ new.”      Oi, don’t talk like that! I love what someone said in one of the reports I read the other day – “The North-East is the new frontier for innovation, if by innovation you mean pulling mouths through split zips.”      Hahaha, brilliant! Someone’s gotta speak the truth. Anyway, what’s this job in Cambridge like?      Not too bad. It’s all about updatin’ the railway crossings ‘cos they keep treed by lorry drivers who think they’ve got more power than the pantograph on the bloody train.      So you’re sort o’ the technical good Samaritan of the railway world then?      In a whack. Not as exciting as workin’ on a rocket engine with Elon Musk, but hey, got goin’s on. How about you? Corpus administrator – what the blithering is that exactly?      Well, basically what I do is make sure all the words in the database are kippin’ out o’ line, like. You know how some words come in like, “doin’”, “ain’t” or “’at” – all the little shibber that nobody writes in proper English, but it always appears in the real thing. Me job is to keep the dirty English flaked out and let the clean sliver shine through, if you catch me drift.

Rather nippy today, isn't it? That wind's nippin' right through me coat. Mind you, I've always preferred a bitta sunshine, don’t you think, Doris?      Oh, honestly, Herbert, I've had enough of this weather. One minute it’s eeny and the next, we’re trudging about in muck! My backs been killing me with all the wet winds about. At me age, this weather affects me like clockwork.      Oh dear! You poor thing, Doris. Didn’t your doctor say you should be doing more low-impact exercises, even in the weather? I remember you told me last week.      Yes, yes, Elise, I know! Me daughter’s always on about it, but I’m not getting any younger and I’m not climbing hills for the sake of it, not with this knee of mine, no!      Aye, I’ve been feeling it too. Me heart’s been acting up a bit. Should have been to the doctor weeks ago, but I pushed it aside—personally, I hate admitting I’m not quite up to it.      That’s exactly what we’re here to change, Herbert. We’re all getting older, so we’ve just got to look after ourselves a bit more, take things slow and steady. You know, regular check-ups and all that. Silly as it sounds, we don’t seem to pay attention until it’s someone else in the hospice talking to us from the other room.      That’s something we could all be a bit better at being honest about. I’ve had a colleague, Sam, who nearly had a heart attack after neglecting symptoms for far too long. We were lucky.      That’s scary to hear. I’d rather have the aches and pains to know I’m still on the go. Speaking of which, passed the shop on the way over, they’ve got these new Android phones on promotion. Rather fancy one, I must say. I could stick the weather app on it!      Heh, that’s a new one from Doris—weather apps. I’d be careful, though. Smart gadgets these days, they’re as go-faster on your life if you don’t watch out. But yes, they sure are handy, especially for managing appointments, meds, and everything else your age forgets to do.      Oh, leave it out, Derek! I never had a mobile phone to begin with and I’ve done very well so far, thank you very much.

So, I just wanted to say congratulations again to both of you. I know it's been a busy week with all the planning, but it’s so sweet to see both of you finally getting married. I feel like it was only yesterday we were at the pub in Peterborough pretending to know how to make cocktails and accidentally set the shaker on fire.      Classic. You were a menace that night, I still can’t believe this is the same girl who is now an administrator, pulling spreadsheets and paperwork all day.      Oh, come on, we all have our sides. I mean, who  would’ve  thought Lucy here would become an artworker and still be able to make an acceptable lasagne on the side?      She makes the best I’ve ever had! But anyway, back to the big day — how’s breakfast at the Bucks Head working out? I still can't believe you guys are having it there.      Honestly, the food is great, but the menu choices terrify me. I’ve had to explain to them twice now that “veal” is not a vegetarian option and that “stout” is a type of beer, not a surname.      And don’t even get me started on trying to track down that vintage Hayley wanted for the table centrepieces. I’ve been through at least four wedding suppliers already and am pretty sure one of them may have just wanted to give me a compliment so they could read my palm.      Okay, but the good news is, the venue and the flowers are still amazing. I saw the preview photo and it made about five people cry.      That’s because we’re all emotional wrecks. I think part of that is because I’ve only recently moved out of my parents', so I’m  technically  still eligible to elope with someone , but let’s not go there.      Not waiting too long, are we Lucy?      No! He’s just… not a complete disaster with my mismatched socks yet.      Then you're wasting time. From what I’ve seen of my parents’ marriage, socks  are  the pre-requisite line in the sand.      Well, if it helps, Mike’s latest joke is about flu shots and why he’s decided to avoid any tea after 3 PM. It’s not exactly thrilling material.      At least he’s avoiding caffeine. You know my cousin’s husband?

Rather annoying this newfit laptops an’ all, ay? I tried to email my granddaughter ‘Mollie’ last weekend an’ she said it was full o’ misspelled words.      Aye, we do try, don’t we! I wouldn’t know where to start wi eeny o’ that gadgetry. My ‘Annie’ comes over every now an’ again an’ teaches me ‘properly’, but I always forget. I’m still using a calculator for me bank transactions like it’s 1950.      You lot make it sound too difficult. It’s really not! I still teach m’kids at the school, only now we use laptops an’ MyMaths an’ all that. Fun to watch the young ones pick it up – I mean, they’ve barely used a pen!      Well, I can forget the tech. What I remember is when I used to take Hattie, my niece’s horse, out for a canter down the fields. Used to feel free as anything on that nag!      Oh I remember Hattie! Beautiful chestnut mare. We still had a barn for her by the garden there. Me ‘Annie’ used to gallop all round the hedges at the park estate when she was younger, like a proper wild thing!      It’s not as if you couldn’t get the kids out o’ the house if you owned a horse these days though. These mums n’ dads are always glued to their smartphones, not letting the kids out without a search party.      I know – I had to come over here because me son about blocked me off every social media! Said the photos of me old dog “Harry” were too embarrassing. That pup was gorgeous!      Aye, but that’s just kids ‘cos they don’t understand tradition. Myinnie here was once chased by a puppy too big for his boots. We had to rush her to the vet.      Family pets can be dramatic! I’ve had enough drama with class pets – remember that turtle that ‘vaped’ the classroom by cruising go-faster on pond life?      Ha ha! Better than the time I had to give the council a right bollocking about ‘proceedings’ at the planning office! Me conservation concerns and all that – they’d just handed over the old field where we kept the chickens.      We used to have a few. Served my late husband well for Sunday evenings, the odd stew. They weren’t the cruel things they are now, y’know.      Aye, but now it’s all prefabs, off-license schemes, them an’ the youths round here getting up to no goods.

Rather lovely to sit out in the garden on a Sunday afternoon, isn't it, Mr. Thompson? We haven’t had a day like this in weeks.      Oh, Joan, please! “Mr. Thompson” makes me feel like I’m being addressed by one of the footmen in an old Poirot episode. “Alf” will do just fine.      Very well, Alf. I still think “Mr. Thompson” has a certain dignity to it, though, especially given your journey from business to retirement gardening. You always insist on using your spade with more precision than a language teacher uses a red pen.      That's because I still have standards, and now that Myra’s gone, I’m the only one who can be bothered to keep the roses in line. A bit of order keeps the mind sharp, don’t you find?      I do, though I tend to keep my order with a dictionary in one hand and a tray of scones in the other. I’ve been working on compiling a lexical comparison between Old English and modern dialects—personally, it's fascinating. I never tire of the way words shift and slip over time, like ... like daffodils leaning with the wind.      Hmm. Language – it’s a curious thing, isn’t it? When I was a lad growing up in Essex, we spoke as if the Queen’s head would roll if we ever said “arse” in polite company. Now it seems one can say practically anything on television without a blush.      Some things never change, Alf. Or at least, they change in curious ways. I was in枣庄 last month for a teaching exchange—they speak such a different dialect, but the sense of community is the same. I suppose that’s the part of language that shouldn’t change: it connects us, even in translation.      Poetic stuff, Joan. I admire your work. I always told Myra I’d never have got through those long meetings I used to have if I hadn’t known who the bloody hell everyone was talking about. But what about you? Do your students keep up with your enthusiasm?      Some of them, yes. The younger ones are quite responsive to the gothic poetry I occasionally throw in. Others—especially the teenagers—roll their eyes and say things like “Miss Alley, do we  have  to?” But I keep them laughing, and I think they leave with a bit more culture than they came in with.

So did you go out for dinner on Valentine's or just do the whole Netflix and chill thing?      No way, I actually went to this Italian restaurant in the city. It was a mad rush because half the town must’ve shown up. But it was nice. We got a table eventually and had the most  embarrassing  waiter incident.      Oh come on, you’ve got to tell me!      So we're halfway into our meal and he keeps mishearing my accent. Every time he says 'pasta' I say 'No thanks, I'm good.' And he just looks so confused, like 'well, are you sure?!' and everyone at the table is laughing. Honestly, I just left extra on the table for him to be nice.      Oh my God, that’s classic Midlands for you. I swear, when I go to Bucks or something, people are like “y-you’re not posh, are you?” as if Londoners puff up their chests and walk around like royalty or something.      Oh, I’ve had the same thing in London! You walk in and someone’s like “oh, you’re from the  other  side of the river,” then immediately gives you a list of the best pubs in Bread Street.      True! Anyway, I didn’t go out to mark the occasion. Me and the girlfriend went to the cinema instead. Watched some rom-com someone said was "deep and moving." All it was, was a girl oddly souring lemonade and getting rejected by a man in a café.       Sigh , there is a conspiracy about movies being written by a single monotonous English lit major, I swear. But hey, least you got to watch it in style!      Maybe. The popcorn bin, though— oh Lord . It was like they dipped it in sand and handed me a teaspoon.      Ugh, that’s them restricting your portions, making you shop for more as  extractive asides . Next time, take your own bag and demand your rights.      Still, I’m happy with it. I mean, Valentine's go bad when it’s forced, you know?      Yeah, I’m just glad it wasn’t a bloke who forgot what your actual name was. I had that last year. Turns out "she" was my barista, not someone I was supposedly dating.      Yeah, why not? "You're my Valentine’s cup of tea." Cute.      Honestly, my plan this year was to stay in, watch some action movies, and eat cake for dinner.

Rather annoying the new tax policy, isn't it? Seems like everything's getting more expensive, especially when you're trying to save up for a place of your own. I can't even afford a deposit on a flat in this city anymore.      It's ridiculous. We're being priced out of our hometown now, of all places. I read an article the other day about how government policies are designed with wealth in mind, but policy changes that would help social housing barely see the light of day.      It's like the housing crisis is being ignored, or worse, underplayed. I went to university with people who'd already got jobs and parents who could afford to help them out. It made everyone else’s situation seem... hopeless, really.      I had the same feeling, honestly. I used to think it was just about luck or how driven you were. But then I started looking into the structure of this whole system, and it's hard not to see the connections between politics and how people are treated based on where they're from. Or what they look like.      Yeah, I remember one of my professors talking about structural racism and how it intersects with housing and employment. It was something I wasn't really aware of before then. You start to see how – even though people often say we’re in a post-racial era – the reality is far from it.      For sure. And it's not just about race, it's about someone's full identity. If you're a minority migrant or from a working-class background, the doors you're allowed to walk through in this world feel very different from the ones I get to access as someone who looks and talks like me.      That really hits home. Both my parents are from India and I’ve never been to school or university where it felt uncool to mention that. My friends don’t always get it, you know? They’re all white, and they can’t see it because they don’t live it.      You’re not alone in that. I’m mixed-race as well, and it’s only recently that I’ve started talking openly about it. It’s not that you  should  bring it up, but sometimes it's hard not to when it feels like you're always standing out or being questioned about who you are.

Rather annoying this new routine, eh? You know, since Lucas’s nursery started. Every morning it’s like I got to dress him up like a little rối, and I’m up by the crack of dawn! Used to sleep in when we were at the cottage, mind you.      Yeah, I saw the place, Mum. It’s nice, but I reckon his nursery's all better than me trying to juggle uni stuff with looking after him too much. Still, you're used to getting up early, right? You’ve been doing that since you were me working in that café.      Oh, I didn’t! Not like that. That was short days, no small child to get ready like a pin turkey. Although I must say, I left work a while back for this, and I do miss it, a bit I do. Think I may take an admin job at the Cats Protection if I get too bored.      Mum... I thought you said being with Lucas non-stop was what mums were supposed to want? But I get it, I’d like to get into a full-time course next year, maybe Marketing. I’m looking into a part-time job to get me started, though. You’ve got good tips for that, remember?      Aye, just find something stable with fairly long hours and decent rate, don’t end up like me working in shifts! You know what it’s like in the North, eh? Everything’s been shut up for ages.      Honestly, I’d rather live a bit closer to the North. Manchester’s got something going on most weekends. You should come here more often! Although I  would  miss out on most of your cooking. I know I’ve had a mammoth week of watching “Strictly” and doing nothing else.      Aye, it is a proper laugh, that. My sister ‘ates it, but I quite like watching those dancers. Lucas tries to tap-dance as it is on any bloody flat surface he can find.      He’s so cute! Like,  proper  cute. Even if it’s just random moves. I wonder what he looks like when he’s not wearing a onesie.      Oh, he’s goin’ on the weening soon. I think so at least. I just started giving him some porridge with the oats, but he’s already trying to grab the spoon! Bit messy, though.      I’m scared to touch that spoon, honest.

Rather annoying day today, really. I had to give a statement to the police for that incident at the petrol station last weekend. Never realized how tedious the whole process would be.      That's probably for the best, love. No sense in rushing things at the police station. I was in contact with them earlier too, regarding some fund-raising calls that haven't been going well as of late. One of the ladies from the committee swore she got a call but didn't log it. It was quite a puzzle to track down.      Ugh, when are the days ending with work dramas? I had a right hassle with the EE bill today. The store's phone supply only lets us change the bill date once a year, and I only realized it left me with this ridiculous overpayment on the back end of February. I might just cancel the whole contract.      Hang on, why not get it sorted online? I've been messing with mine for work purposes and the settings are actually pretty accessible once you get to the section. Also, we might actually need EE more—there's a new project starting for the company, and I might have to keep landlines as well as mobiles. It's going to be a tricky balance watching expenses.      Speak for yourself. I remember being at university when you could deal with these things in person in an afternoon. Now, you're faced with web portals and confidentiality phone lines. It's almost like they make it hard on purpose.      That’s also the way of modern business, love. But we can at least make our week ahead better. After this, let’s be clear on what we all  actually  are doing come Wednesday.      I’ve got a store inventory week. We’re doing internal audits and doing walkabouts with stock. Properly grim. I might have to cancel the Thursday night drinks. My sister’s planning on meeting someone new, though.      I’m actually on a meeting call on Thursday afternoon, so better not come anyway. I’ll be holed up in the shed with my laptop. Though I  might  pop by the lunches on Friday.      Well, let’s hope you remember to log off once in a while, shall we? I for one need to see if that police report has done anything for the petrol station. I’m still wondering if we’ll need to pay something through the charity to cover the damage.

Rather annoying that the TV’s on the blink again, isn't it?      Yeah... got to admit, I miss catching up on more than  X Factor  or whatever.      Not to worry—I’ve got the DVD of  Spartacus . You in for a bit of ancient Rome and plenty of bad choices?      Classic choice. Though I reckon that A-list Julius Caesar would’ve had a better social life than most modern celebrities.      Fair point. Though I also reckon he never had to deal with the drama of  Keeping Up With the Kardashians .      That’s true. You want a cup of tea? I’ve got enough to last the week—what with the mortar and pestle I got from a holiday I took.      Palestine? Again? Got a bit of mint and cloves stashed in there.      Yep, that’s it! Used it to make some kind of warming tea. Good for the cold, apparently. I do tell you—personally I’d rather take my chances with a strong black as opposed to messing around with leaves and spices.      Well, if it’s about convenience, I get it. Though I swear by mixing a bit of nutmeg and cinnamon in there.      All that? You must have a higher tolerance for spices than me! Though, on the topic of food, have you ever tried making hummus from chickpeas?      Some years ago—before I got into tea ceremonies and being an English tutor—I actually had a colleague from Cyprus who taught me about it. Herbs, chickpeas, tahini...      I bet that failsafe Mediterranean diet is why she probably didn’t die young, like my uncle. My grandma always said he died from stress and spicy nuts passed him around.      Oh, I assume he lived it up with intense snacks and too much waiting on the cricket field.      That’s what we always joked about. Speaking of which, you been to China?      No, but I’ve read a fair bit about it. Though I get the impression if you don’t get the herbs right, you run the risk of malarials or sea lice or something equally questionable.      I mean, I’ve never had one in my life. But I’ve had bellyache from dodgy street food in Bangkok. Still, I bought a souvenir from there—a string of prayer beads my missy wears.      Oh, she's the one who gave you those clothes from her ex's adventure, isn't she?

So did you get an email about the English test tomorrow? I was panicking for like half an hour thinking I’d missed it.      Yeah, I did! I've been revising a little, but honestly, we’ve only read  To Kill a Mockingbird  and a chunk of  1984  this term. Not sure what they’re even gonna ask.      I know right? Like, do they want us to write an essay? Because  1984 ’s so abstract, I keep losing what the whole point was. Do you remember what the hell the three slogans were again?       Big Brother is Watching You ,  War is Peace , and  Ignorance is Strength . Fun stuff. Honestly, I think I’m just going to copy some quotes and then say what I think Orwell was trying to do, even if I’m not sure. What are you going to do?      Pretty much the same. I looked up a sample essay online last night and was like, why do they expect us to write like adults? I get Bs in class, not essays written in two hours!      I know! But what am I meant to do—cry during it? I’m sure it’s not that bad. Oh wait—isn't the wind-band still meeting after school today? Anna’s trying to get us to come to the next practice.      No way! She said we could help her out with the music and get spare tickets to the concert in a month. That’s so sweet of her. Though the clarinet section still wants to rewrite the Beginners rep, so I’m dreading it.      Yeah, Anna’s trying to make the concert lit. She says it’s going to be like  La La Land , but with barely practiced wind instruments. Still, it's better than just sitting in for the whole lesson. Geo’s been passed out on the floor the entire time.      Ugh, he needs to start showing up for things. I don't get how we’re in the same year. Anyway, speaking of classes—we had a new French teacher today. Some chap from Marseilles who speaks so fast I can barely understand him.      Yeah, he threw about seven questions at me so fast I thought I was in a password recovery system. Honestly, maybe I should drop French and take art instead. The GCSE art spec looks way more fun than conjugating verbs every week.

Rather chilly for a Saturday, eh, love? Thought we’d get a bit of a break ‘ere Christmas, but nay, same old mizzle from the sky. Mind you, this café is a proper little haven in all this.      Aye, cannae argue with that een, dear. Keeps the wind out, an’ puts a bit o’ warmth in the bones. I’ve been neglectin’ this place far too long. Old habits, see? Out o’ teaching, out o’ routine.      Didn’t your mum use to say you could hear a pin drop in your class, Miss? Like nothin’ got the audacity to make a sound in there? My English teacher, Mr. Coghill, bursts in like Ten Cossacks if the photocopier stops pickin’ in A4.      Aye, better than when I was still teachin’. One lad once told me in his report his dreams were about not being late, an’ I wrote back, “ цель успешна, сын мой.” He looked like I’d told ‘im I’d killed ‘is mascot!      Did you say that in Russian, or just in… Russian-sounding English?      She most certainly did say it in Russian. I helped her with it, see? She was into learnin’ quite a few languages in ‘er days. Bit of Russian, a bit of Italian, and some old Cornish just to confuse us.      It kept them lads on their toes, did the odd bit o’ Slavic in a class. Can’t fault the lad in Newcastle for his attitude, about as mischievous as a kestrel in the wind, but mind you… a spark o’ genius if you catch ‘im.      Maybe I’ll do better at ‘ismetrical Poetic Enunciation’ if I learn a few languages. I could be the next Liam Payne, but with more sjamboks an’ fewer plastic hobbies.      Aye, just as well he mentioned sjamboks. Town’s full o’ ‘em these days, Johnny Foreigner thinkin’ ‘e’s t’undisputed king o’ the bin on a Sat night. Not while I still got a lad in line for the title, I don’t.      Pass the salt will you, love? I’ll be needing it with this afterchat. And speak o’ saints, have you seen the new Lion King announcement ‘neath this window? Cannae believe ‘em. S’all pixels an’ no soul, they said.      Makes you wish they did a version in Nads slang, and Leon backin’ it up with a saxophone. Imagine Mufasa walkin’ in, sayin’ “Blimey, ‘Mufzelf, y’alrite lads?”

Rather annoying driving up from London today. The sat nav decided to glue the car in the middle of nowhere. I got turned around at least four times before I found this road!      You probably got thrown off by all the cows in the fields—somehow they always seem to make the roads appear narrower than they are.      I reckon it's not all that different from a jigsaw puzzle, really. If you've never seen the full picture, it's easy to get lost.      I got lost when I came up to visit the bloke who runs the garage three times last year! Not because I don't know the way, but because I was stressed about needing to fix a carburetor for him.      I hear you, Dad. D’you know, I think stress has a knock-on effect in all sorts of ways. I’ve read about studies saying it contributes to obesity. Not just lack of exercise, but the chemical mess it creates in your body.      That rings a bell, love. I do notice, though, some people are just wired differently. My sister has a sweet tooth and she’s only ten pounds overweight, but I have a glass of wine and by twelve I’m already thinking “what if I just eat the whole tin of biscuits?”      Could be the genes, or maybe the hormones? Me and Silly Sally down the village—same age, we both retired two years ago. She put on fifteen pounds in a year, me? I’ve lost ten. Funny thing, the body!      It’s not surprising when you consider the differences in metabolism and even lifestyle. I mean, I walk to the lecture hall each day, you lot are sat here. I suppose lack of exercise helps her more than you!      Maybe I’ll start using a jigsaw like Silly Sally told me about. Said it calms the mind, gives the blood pressure a chance to drop. Not sure I’ve ever been so keen on a box of 1,000 pieces as I am right now!      If I do it, I’ll want almonds for glue, something nutty and sweet! But wait, almonds go straight to my sinuses if I eat too many. I think I might have started developing allergies in my 50s, bless it!      Allergies can be hereditary, though, can’t they? I remember my Uncle Brian had severe reactions to pollen and seafood, and over time, the food ones disappeared.

Rather annoying this new module integration on Moodle. I’ve been trying to upload the practical component for the software module all morning and I’m not even halfway there.      I know, right? I was doing mine earlier and honestly, I gave up and waited until our coffee break to come back. Got a bit stressed out, honestly. It’s one thing teaching theory, it’s quite another trying to get a programming simulation up online when half your brain is preoccupied with teaching Timmy how to use a mouse.      Oh, I heard from a colleague that when he tried the new Moodle version on a mobile, it crashed. I’m still using the desktop, but the interface is still clunky. You made that My_modules folder, did you? The one with the week-by-week structure?      Yes, I thought I’d be clever and label all folders with both week numbers and titles. Like "Wk01_IntroToPython" or "Wk03_Excel_Basics." That way, even if students are a bit behind, they can still find what they need.      That’s clever. I just named mine "Week 1", "Week 2", and so on. I didn’t think of including the software title. Maybe I should go back and add that. Also, I’m not sure how it will look on mobile. Did you test it?      I will today after the students login. I might set homework up for next week. Let me just ask—did you upload the tutorial files already?      Some of them—there are ten in total. I’ve split them between the lecture package and the practical section because most people do both. I’m not sure about the pdfs, though. I had to convert a few screen recordings to video because they were too large. It felt inefficient, but Moodle kept splitting the text.      Yes, I ran into that too. The audio files for the demonstrations would strip out any annotations, so I converted them to mp4s instead. I hope they don’t lag for the students. Let’s monitor the space we've left—last semester one of my quizzes got deleted because the cloud flagged it as a risk.      That is so gothic of it. Honestly, sometimes I think machines are more paranoid than college admin. Right, I need to submit the course outline by end of day today. Can you check if the file I shared with you this morning looks okay?

Rather annoying jetlag, isn't it? I mean, I've only had an hour or two in bed... What time did you manage to go to sleep last night?      Around midnight, I think. Not quite enough. Look, we’ve got that play on in two days. Got a ticket booked at  The Globe —six o'clock on Saturday. Should be easy to get most of the day out of the baby’s system so she’s back to sleep by bedtime. It was quite easy getting tickets. We’ve been lucky.      That's brilliant. I hope she hasn’t taken to waking up in the middle of the night, though. I had only another go at settling her that one night, and I was too tired to think straight. Honestly, I felt like I’d had a sleepless week and I hadn’t even managed a single hour of proper sleep.      Believe me, I've been there. Hitting the point at which I didn’t know whether we were day or night—it's so unsettling. Good news is, she’s sleeping better now, thank goodness. I’d say maybe up three or four times a night. But still, it’s nothing like what I’d go through when watching football during the European championship in France.      Mate, I often wonder if people still think it's  normal  to stay up all night watching sports when you've got a newborn. I understand the passion, but your priorities shift—well, at least mine have. Though I’m not saying my man wasn’t inspiring. He had a point—looked like he was going to pull off a double hat-trick at one point.      I mean, I get it. I binged the whole series of  The Rings of Power  while trying not to fall asleep at the steering wheel. But it does kind of make you feel... less like a parent and more like someone who can’t help chasing nostalgia.      Exactly. But I think it's something we’ll look back on when she's older and crack up about—how we were professional academicians dealing with sleep deprivation and a new baby while still trying to keep up with work and TV shows. You know, it's a weird time, but go with it.      Yeah, I think I'm just in the acceptance phase now. And the boxset binging? Fully abandoned.

Rather annoying this, having to get my cousin sorted for a visa. I know her solicitor’s handled dozens... but still, it's bloody bureaucratic, innit?      Yeah, I know what you mean. Not all that long ago I had to get a friend from Erbil sorted for a family visit. Even with the paperwork in both English and Arabic, he had to prove all sorts of things. The UK authorities love a bit of red tape these days, don't they?      Aye. Especially with the way the government's playing up the political stuff in the Mideast. Get the wrong surname, even if you're dead clean, and you're on a list sommates can't get you off. Just seen the news — some new laws about Wahabi influence over here. I reckon it's all about oil and who controls the narrative round it.      Cats and dogs. I've worked in places where this happened. Oil companies drive in like they're the bosses and then tell the local people to back off. I wonder how much of it's really about time zones, and how much of it is just about differing priorities. I’m only 33, but I can already picture what your 50s could look like—like, randomly forgetting half the people you used to speak to every weekend because your life just got so different.

[through a mouthful of food] Blimey, you’ve got it better than when I was a kid. I used to have a packet of spaghetti hoops and a banana five days a week, and didn’t moan about it. Good for you.      Come off it, Darren, you were the one who used to smuggle in crisps and grief the other kids for more pocket money. Still watching football, luv?      Every Sunday if I can. I got tickets to the local game this season—top of the league and all. It's not as fancy as the Premier League, but it's a proper shout. Ben’s coming, what about you lads? That’s brilliant news about the tennis, Tom. I thought you were going to try and convince me to coach you up for it? I do a bit for local kids on the weekends. Might earn a few extra bob and give me a bit of purpose other than proofing brochures.      I’d watch one game to be honest. I’m more of a striker than a server.      [laughing] That's you alright, Harry. You're like a man with a goal in every other game.      Any plans after school, Tom? I was thinking about getting into an apprenticeship in IT. Tom what your dad does, isn’t it marketing? Maybe there's something there?      I’ve had a few conversations with some companies about marketing apprenticeships over the last while—nothing finalised yet.

Rather annoying this train being delayed again. You’d think in 2025 it would be a bit more reliable, wouldn’t you?      I know, I've been on this line before for a conference and we were held up outside Wigan for over an hour. Honestly, if it’s not the tracks, it’s the drivers for some reason. So, are you all set for this weekend in Lancaster?      Yeah! I’m really looking forward to seeing the coast again. I did a project on the Morecambe Bay cockle pickers disaster a few years back—it feels almost like a personal visit. I had a cousin who went to Lancaster University and I visited her once for a weekend. It was lovely, really friendly atmosphere. I still remember her dorm room covered in Anglo-Saxon literature posters. You planning on applying there?      Possibly for a masters in linguistic anthropology. I was doing media studies. Though I'm still thinking of going back part-time in organisational communication—between my role at the language research centre and working as an administrator, it all lines up.      That’s great! She go back to work yet?      No, she had her line of work made redundant during lockdown. She’s actually working on starting her own business with some online language tutorials. I think she’s inspired by our career paths!

Rather annoying, innit? I’d rather be at the Forge watching the Roosters, ‘ow much I got to pay for this pint?      Nah, it’s all right, a buck fifty-five. Not bad for a bit o' town like this.      Got eeny plans after? I was thinkin’ o' bumpin' into Jess and the lads. They’ve got a gig up North, so this is a good stop-off point.      Oh, nice! Who’re they playin’ now? I remember when they used to play grunge like, y’know,  Pearl Jam  or someone like that, before they went all acoustic.      Oh, they’re chillin' now. Tenpence, if I’m not mistaken, and some sad acoustic covers. But it’s Jess, so I’ve got to go. I still miss those prime nights at the Anglo with a bit o' noise and a few dodgy bottles hides.      Yeah, them were the days. Last time I went there, the lads nearly started a rumble over who short-changed who on their rounds. I tell ya, it still ain’t got much better.      Be fair, Rob. It’s just Matey’s new shift, he still needs time to get his head round the till. Now don’t go making mortal enemies over a pint.      Ehh, maybe. But what someone said in jest, someone else might not read like a joke.      Fair point. So, what’s up with you and being down at Margrove’s house last week? I heard he nearly about blocked his kettle after he burned off a mammoth eclair?      Ron? Oh luv, that was grim! I mean, it were  meant to  be a ‘cosy baked treacle guest night’ and he tried to conjure up some sort o’ Provincial flan instead. He had to Binco his way through the kitchen with a stick while it was smoking.      Sounds like Ron with a plan! Grumbles with a plan.      Still, I did come out with a new hobby—pottery goin’ on in his studio. It’s weird, but it were fun. Finally, I’m not just sittin’ around on my arse all weekend.      Pottery? Oh gawd, you startin' to act like your grannie now? I saw her ‘bath bombs’ last time I were down at her place... they were near to explode on her!      Ehh, but it's art, right? Just not for the faint-hearted!      Bit before midnight? Maybe we can pick up some fresh cake— actual  cake, not Ron’s ‘Mammoth Oblivion’ one.

Rather annoying that the red plague is spreading so fast, isn't it? I think it's only been like... three turns and it's already in three cities. Blows my mind what happens when you don't coordinate properly.      That's the trick of the game, isn’t it? You’re all working together, but if even one of you puts the wrong card down or fails to plan efficiently, you’ve got a major outbreak on your hands. I mean, look at Chris. He was meant to be building a research station in Atlanta, but instead he tried to cure black plague.      Right, because it looked like  this  round we were going to cure all the diseases before the end of the hour, but no, Marco decided to spend his turn trying to rally more players to play the disease card on purpose. Why?      Because he thought it would be funny to make us all fail—like a bit of a dark twist on Game of Thrones. Bloke’s got principles! hides behind his mug of tea      I told you—settle down, settle down! Championship level bluffing takes skill. Anyway, your turn, Emily. Did you draw Chicago and Milan today?      I did. And I was just about to build a research station in Milan when David knocked my hand and scattered all the cards on the floor. I didn’t even know if they were disease cards or city cards anymore!      Oh dear. Our kitchen table at home has seen more suspicious disturbances. At least the floor here’s oddly clean. Now—what’s the plan? We have three cures left, and green and black are both in the ballpark of being nearly about to spread.      Let’s just focus on this—London and Paris. Move your pieces there. Don’t let the game get ahead of us again. Remember that last round, Amy tried to cure the black plague in Sydney and missed by one card. Classic Amy.      Oh, I was defending myself! I was just waiting on a teammate to hand me the card and then—"  nervously glances at Speaker_3 and Speaker_4 “      Still trying to plead ignorance with the rest of the team? That go-to excuse doesn’t work if you’re  always  waiting for someone else to pick up the slack.      Time to lay off your passive-aggressive jabs, David. You’ve been the one moving into out-of-reach areas and acting like it's a personal mission to see if we can win without you.

Rather annoyingly, I've got to do a six-hour train journey to Exeter today. I hate traveling when I don’t have a sleeper. I’m so exhausted I can barely keep my eyes open!      Why do they have to make those services so cheap yet so unpleasant? I remember once, I went from London to Edinburgh with you and fell asleep on your shoulder for most of the journey. You let me stay there too!      Well, you were far more pleasant back then. Today, you’d be the one telling me to stop drooling or touching your phone while you snored.      Haha, fair point. I’ve only become a grumpy gusset since university. You’ve still got the tolerance of a saint. Probably because you’ve been married seven years and survived my sad attempts at cooking?      And endured your morning snoring, no doubt. I do miss some things though — like when we used to travel non-stop for days, exploring the back roads of the Lake District. That was real love-struck fun.      Oh, I’ll take full credit for that. We made the grief of moving halfway across the country into an epic adventure. I still remember pacing in our tiny flat in Cumbria – trying to figure out whether I’d still love you if you forgot my birthday.      And what did you find out?      That you remembered. Despite being someone who once bought my present two days before my birthday because you thought it was cheaper. You bought me a crate of beer and a Rubik’s cube. I still have the cube.      I did that because I couldn’t be bothered to go out and get “something better.” You made me sound like a total philistine.      No, I made you sound like  you —a man who didn’t care about what was on the outside, only the challenge of working something out. Speaking of, I tried solving it the other day. Got one side done and gave up.      There’s your answer right there. You’re the same today – you want things done  your  way.      Exactly. And I get to share that nonsense with you for the rest of my very blessed life?      That’s the plan, yes. Unless you develop a sudden interest in fluency in Russian and start moving to Moscow.      Nah, I prefer my Russian studies to be over pirozhki and a very modest string of Svetlana albums.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh? You’d think by June we’d have seen some proper sunshine in Yorkshire... or even a decent cricket match.      Honestly, I've been over it! It’s thrown my camera schedule into chaos, and I’ve had to cancel three interviews. I don’t get it—climate change or just a bad summer?      I know what you mean. I’ve been huddled inside marking essays more this week than teaching. Oh, and I had to dump my carefully planned dinner party last night. Nothing like a good chase of rain to test your vegan lasagna recipe.       laughs  Well, at least the lasagna still tasted good when it rained last Saturday, didn’t it? So, what’s new with you two, apart from the weather drama?      Fair enough. I had an interesting chat about job relocations yesterday. Turned down a prime opportunity to cover tech policy in Berlin. Didn’t want to leave the UK again, especially after spending so many years in Europe. How about you, Charlie—moving over to Germany, maybe?      I considered it, honestly. There’s still work and family in both places. My wife isn’t keen on the move. She says she already got “the foreign experience” with me growing up near Heidelberg and now it's “enough.”  laughs       Honestly, Silas was thrilled to hear about you growing up in Germany. She's just someone who prefers one place and doesn’t chase adventures like a journalist does.  turns to Speaker_2  But I suppose Berlin would have been a solid next chapter for you.      It might have been. I’m not unhappy here, but it can feel a bit... insular at times. How about you, Eleanor? Still enjoying the language teacher life?      Oh, I love it. There’s something so rewarding about seeing your students progress and learn new ways to express themselves. But I do miss the idea of working something with more... direct impact. We had to talk about this the other day with a young guy trying to find his path.      Yeah, Johnny’s stuck between trying to get into teaching and feeling like the system is set against him. I tried to help him with CV formatting and got a cold shoulder. Thought I’d offered some genuinely good advice.      Maybe he’s just overwhelmed. Education can be so bureaucratic. I remember feeling that way when I first tried to choose a postgrad program myself.

Rather annoying when the book club meeting finds its way into a debate about the best Sunday roast, isn’t it? But honestly, I’m with you, Jane—the perfect one’s a blend of decent meat, a little rosemary, and proper gravy. Nothing like the one at our house.      That sounds more like the kind of roast you get handed on a plate at a posh hotel, not in a family kitchen. At our place in Peterborough, it was always a battle between me, my mother, and one of my three brothers. Someone always burned the potatoes, or the Yorkshire pudding came out deflated.      I don’t know how you people manage to cook anything without an electric whisk. I still use my grandmother’s jelly mould left over from the 1950s—probably risk of salmonella, but it turned out a perfect jelly last Sunday.      Egg boxes and jelly moulds remind me of my childhood in Boston. We’d have the oversized desktop hides, you know, those plastic ones that came in packs of four, like a red, green, blue, yellow set. My brother and I used to play hide-and-seek with them.      Oh, I had those! But I remember when we got one of those cardboard – what’s it called—those pyramid-like blocks that you had to fold together into a certain shape. All of us would be at the kitchen table, arguing over whose turn it was to put the next piece.      I had a different one. A building set with those metal bits and plastic ones that connected with a hinge. It was called “Geobits” or something close to that. I did an awful lot of origami back then, too. Actually, I still do. I made some for my sister’s wedding last year.      Maybe we’re all just rebelling against the baked Alaska and guest speaker topics at book club. Though I have to admit, it is a chance to meet up and not talk about work too much. I always feel like the outsider at these meetings.      Oh, but we all know what you do. I do too, but at least you get to meet with clients and dazzle them with charm. I deal with HR—the paperwork, the boring stuff. Not much glamour in line managers, no.      Well, I might not get to dazzle people directly, but I manage spreadsheets and tax forms with the same enthusiasm, I’ll have you know.

So did you really just take off to Majorca without anyone knowing? I had no idea you two had booked it last weekend!      Yeah, I know, we've been saving up for this for ages. Not only do we have flights and accommodation sorted for a week, but we also booked a rental car. We wanted to do some driving and explore the north part of the island.      Oh, that’s brilliant! I’ve never been to Majorca, but I’ve heard it’s a lovely place to relax. What made you choose it? Did you just fancy a different destination?      Not only that. I've got the time, and Rob here decided it’s well past our time to take a proper vacation! We’ve both been working ourselves to the ground for far too long, and Rob said jokingly the other day—“we’d be better off working from the breakfast table in Majorca than this one!”      That’s me alright! I thought, you know what? Why not? We might die of stress before we get to do something, and we need a proper break. I mean, we even convinced both of you to come along for a couple of days in the middle—it wasn't just going to be about us.      Oh come on, I wouldn’t mind that either. But really, the timing is perfect. We did have a bit of a rough time at work lately, with that whole IT failure two weeks ago.      I can vouch for that, love. I was on the phone to the IT company for hours sorting out the printer—finally got it all back to normal, but it took nearly about half the week. I swear, these modern things can be a real pain.      Tell me about it. I've only retired, Rob, so I've got time, but for someone who pays for that service, I'd be fuming. Still, I think it's a chance to give us some breathing space.      Exactly what I said! So what I’m suggesting is, once you two've booked your holiday, maybe you can come join us mid-week. We’ll set up something around day three or four, and we can go out to one of those nice coastal restaurants there. And that was the line of conversation. Hopefully, it conveys the dynamics and topics effectively. Would you like me to continue or focus on a different part of the scenario?

Rather annoying the newfit in the boiler innit? Seems like we've had her in and out every week since we moved in. I mean, I’m more than happy to explain it once, but this is getting tedious.      Oh I know what you mean, James. Honestly, if it’s not the boiler, it’s the wi-fi splitter. I reckon someone just unplugged it trying to charge their phone last night. At least the kettle still works, unlike Tim's fridge last week.      Ugh, was that the one that spewed when he tried to open the freezer? I still haven’t been able to smell like that. Honestly, someone needs to supply the flat with some kind of emergency My turkey came out undercooked last week and left it in the bottle warmer, didn’t know what the hell it was for.      Blimey, that’s a new one. I still can’t figure out this tea bag socket she installed in the kitchen. It’s like oversized USB but for Kenyan puff. Have you got it working, Alice?      To be fair, it’s a clever idea I think. puts your leaves in their own electrical grief. Kind of like fancy brewing gear in a country where people just dunk it in boiling water.      Mate, I got a gift last Christmas, it was a programmable tea kettle that steamed apple pie and sent you a text. If that weren't real, I might not live in this flat at all.      Just trying to keep afloat here. I had a proper laugh last week, this article I read about some engineer being accused of charging too much for a ballet-themed light switch. I about wet myself. Turns out the lighting just didn’t match the decor.      Maybe they should’ve gone for something less dramatic. I read yesterday about a superhero-like architect who claimed to ‘reinvent the living room’ after building it around a kebab van. Sounds like it was a disaster but everyone said it brought the kitchen to life.      Not to rain on your parade, but how are we meant to take any of this seriously when the news is full of people going viral for pouring exotic sauces on their toast and calling it the 'healthy revolution goenvironmental map of life'.      Honestly, I just wish I could afford that kind of nonsense. Paying off the mortgage and your training courses at the same time is like trying to build a rocket while wearing potholders.

Rather annoying when the satnav takes us the long way round. I blame it on the satellites. Honestly, I got lost in Liverpool last week. I’m more of a Google Maps person anyway. It updates in real-time at least.      You British people and your love for satnavs and Google Maps. I remember when we got lost in Saudi Arabia on our road trip—Reg couldn’t resist trying to take a shortcut. Got stuck in this desert, no signal, no water. It was a mess.      That sounds like me in the 80s. Had to get from Liverpool to Hebden Bridge once—no satnav, no idea where I was going. Got turned around three times before a bloke in a Ford Cortina gave me directions. Probably saved my life. You kids wouldn’t last five minutes without a smartphone now.      Yeah, well, I still can’t figure out this app. I tried to use it at work, planting the site plan, and ended up looking for the q in the database for 20 minutes. I swear, if it had a voice, it would be laughing at me.      It’s not that complicated, is it? You just follow the dots. Maybe you need a break from the heavy lifting?      Haha, yeah, maybe I do. Though I reckon the dots are moving just to tease me.      Honestly, though, I think people just get too reliant on them. I’ve seen my mum use Google Maps for going to the post office across the road. Just adds 10 minutes being confused.      You’re not wrong. I mean, I get it. I’m the project co-ordinator at work. If I don’t log everything, it doesn’t exist. So why not trust the digital? It’s the system, innit.      Aye, but technology’s only as good as the people holding it. Like me time with the lorry driver from Saudi Araby. We lost the route, and he just said, “No worry, the stars will keep us safe.” I was like, “Right… that sounds mad, but okay.”      That’s so cool. Reg, if you ever go back, maybe you could write a story? It’d be brilliant for the boxset or something.      You could have it made into a film—“Lost in Arabia with Reg.” I’ll even direct it.      You’ll be lucky. We were lucky to survive that trip. I’d be proud to see it on the screen, though.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun feels gentle. I was just admiring that orchid over there—shouldn’t they be hardy enough for a climate like this?      Honestly, I can’t believe the Swedes manage such greenery. We haven’t had real spring in Dorchester yet, and even then, it’s frosty! But I’ve been trying to keep up with our little garden. Not as grand as this, though. Oh, and how are you feeling these days? You’ve been looking healthier.      He’s switched to walking every morning like three times a week! Not because he’s afraid of dying but because, as he says, “I’m an entrepreneur, not a cactus—you grow or you die.” Tenacity, right? I’m the same, actually. I’ve been cutting out sugar—my doctor was giving me the ‘inconvenient truth’ look.      Well, if sugar was a person, it’d have told you to back off. Also, the walking? Great for the blood pressure and the mind, yes. I find it keeps the ideas flowing. Sometimes your health as an entrepreneur is like garden pruning: too much, you kill the possibility, too little and it’s all thorns.      I often tell my class that, you know—gardening is like growth. You don’t water daily and expect a redwood overnight. Same with patience in your health, and in life. Though I must say, I’m still trying to convince the kids to plant something sour. They all want something sweet and instant.      I know the feeling! We did a campaign last week around about sustainability—trying to get the coffee shops to switch to compost cups. Half the time it felt like trying to teach teenagers that frost forms when it’s cold.      That’s the thing, though. Habits. Small shifts are what stick. I’m trying to become minimal-waste. It all adds up. I tried cutting out plastic straws, which is easy, but then I got into filters and reusable cutlery. It’s a little obsession, I know.      I respect the dedication. I’ve tried the same, but go me one on cleaning routines if you don’t mind—I’ve been advised I’m not sanitising enough between students. You’re in the outdoor world, your hands are dirtier all the time, so perhaps you have a better routine?      Oh, this is a classic debate. Speaker_1, you always say, "If it's not visibly dirty, it's probably fine."

Rather annoying when new devices don't understand our accents, isn't it? I was trying to use that voice assistant last weekend and it just kept mishearing me completely. I swear it was nearly as bad as speaking to a brick wall!      Oh aye, I tried it once too when I borrowed that smart TV from me nephew. I said   "turn on BBC Two"   and next thing you know, it’s blasting some random bloody cartoon show. They should listen to how we speak, not just that posh Received Pronunciation nonsense. You lot from Kent still speak like the Queen's dog-walker, but at least it's  us !      I don’t think it's about posh or not, Bill. I swear my phone’s voice assistant just doesn't understand me at all, even when I speak slowly. I think it’s because most of the data is trained on better-educated users, and we ordinary folk just don't get a look in.      Yeah! That's what I said when I was trying to use one of those banking apps. I said "I want to transfer money," and up pops a bloody error message! It didn’t even  hear  "transfer." I’ve got a thick enough accent it'd confuse a Cockney fishmonger. Ha – Mate, you got a real shout!      Bet you were raised on flat white English, weren’t you?      No, I’m from Gillingham, just someone who speaks in full sentences. I suppose my accent is quite clear compared to some. You lot all still say   "lan’"   and   "fee"   instead of   "land"   and   "ferry,"   don't you? But it still doesn’t matter—devices just don’t adjust for that.      I grew up near Harlow, and to be honest, I don't notice it much until I go somewhere else. Once I went to Scotland on a day trip and was bloody stunned at how they spoke. It was like waiting for them to stick their finger in their ears and speak again. Even regional differences here take some getting used to.      Yeah, but that's what makes it interesting. Prouder the accent, the goonier the communication sometimes—but that's not a bad thing, innit? I say let the machines learn from the real blokes and lasses, not just the smooth-talking upper-middle classes!      Well, while we're discussing accents, has anyone seen how my son speaks since he's been in the city?

Rather skip the new kid’s party, love? Thought you said you’d give him a hand with the decorations... What was the name again—Oliver?      Yeah, Oliver. It's fine, we were just finishing up. Look, I’ve got a bit of a problem, actually. I'm stuck on a history assignment about consent laws in different eras.      Oh aye? A lot older than now, that's for sure. My grandmother used to refer to it as 'a husband and wife matter', like the law didn't chase it up or anything. Tore her heart out to talk about it, mind—those were hard times.      You know about this? My teacher said it changed after World War Two.      Changed, but not fast enough. Some of my mates in school back in the 70s would’ve died to know we’re talking about this now. Now, are you alright? That’s a bit heavy for the milkshake we promised you after supper.      Yeah, I’m okay. I just wanted to get it right. Thanks for the help. Anyway, your cooking as usual is incredible. That baked Alaska... still remembers the first time I had it.      Wasn’t that at my nan’s funeral, was it? Horrible memory, but yes, she had a recipe she swore by—egg white and Silletto, no less! And I’ve been grating the cheese just like she did. Mind you, I still can't get it quite right.      You’d better not let Nan hear you talk like that. She used to make your grandmother freeze in her tracks whenever about to make a dessert.      She did, she did. And cooking was where your father and I met, you know. I was the ungrateful graduate who burned her roast. She thought I was perfect after that.      Wow, you never told me that. You got through it by burning food?      I did all the talk, you see. Recruited her out of pure luck with a bit of charm and a broken oven.      Still, I’m happy with the way things worked out. Supper's really nice. This cheese is perfect though.      Is it? I’m not sure. I’ve been using the coarser grater. It’s all in technique, really. Grate like you're blaming the tool, and it’ll do half the work for you.      Like when we were younger and you taught me how to shred cabbage for coleslaw.

Rather lovely to have you here, my love. Thought we’d start the day right wi’ a proper Yorkshire breakfast, and I’ll not have none o’t that continental nonsense! Got the bacon sizzlin’ and the tea steepin’.      Morning, Deirdre! Can smell that eeny bit o’ smoke already. It’s like you haven’t forgotten the cobbles of Shipley even after all these years. Fair dos, this looks spot on. Oh, and refer to me as 'my love' again and I'll have to demand you chase me out wi’ a ladle.      Lakelands! I do love ye to bits, still can’t get yer Welsh posh turkey twizzle under control! So, got any plans for the day, or shall I lay out a route of rest and relaxation?      Well, I was just thinking we could walk down to the park this arfner after breakfast. Then maybe catch up on some phone calls — flight school’s looking for a bit more involvement from me, and that’s terrifyin’. Might get me wings this time, really might!      Oh, and tell me, what fancy trips have you got on the books? Been meaning to ask. Was it springtime ye were sayin’ you’d be in New York again?      Aye, April to be exact. Silly place, New York! Built a house made o’ air in this world — full skyline, but nary a soul to walk beside ye. I met a Japanese fellow there who’d moved out o’ London. Chanced tea in a little garden — he taught me how to write letters about nowhere at all. Just empty pages, the shape of thoughts. Very calming.      Aha, that’s right! You mentioned living out there for a time. My, time does fly. I always tell meself I’ll visit, but no sooner do I open my planner than something ‘appens.      You must! My friend Shunsuke would love that — he sent me a postcard with 'hope springs new' scribbled in the margin. Classy Welsh translation, mind. Said it like a man with a garden in every breath he took. I miss Japan, must admit. But I digress.      Wi’ all that letter writing, your social media must be summat else. Still postin’ pictures of breakfast poesy hours after it happened?      Oh, poetry is overrated, but I do like a good string of emojis. You know I got five hearts for that photo of the tea and loaf of bread?

Rather annoying when people are late, isn't it? I swear I've had more cringe-worthy experiences waiting for friends than I'd care to count.      Oh, I feel you! I was once thrown into a library with only the librarian for company because my friend had gone to make "quick" sausage and egg rolls instead of meeting me for revision. Still haven’t forgiven them.      Haha, I once swore I’d be on time for a friends’ housewarming, but someone mentioned a pizza delivery and I just got distracted. Didn’t even get there.      Right, because of course you'd choose pizza over a house party. I once waited two hours for someone to come over to play board games, only for them to show up in just their dressing gown and say their DPhil had "caused sleep deprivation issues."      Honestly, why do we even do it? I mean, I understand everyone has a bad day, but being reliably late makes it less of a day and more of a pattern.      It's funny how words can often get lost in translation too—some people take two hours to turn up because their idea of "half an hour" is different. It's like the circle of rhythm in Beowulf—I mean, at some point it's just verbosity without meaning.      Honestly, the English language is quite odd when you start thinking about it. Like, why is “island” spelled with an 's' when there's no 'i' in it? And “aluminium” with a 'b’? Also, have any of you ever thought about what word structure plays tricks in your head when playing Scrabble?      Absolutely. I always lay down the highest-scoring triple word score first. There was this one time I got “quintessential,” but managed to run out of letters and found myself staring blankly at the board for an hour.      Oh man, I remember a time when my sister and I fell in love with a little beetle in our copy of  The Very Hungry Caterpillar . It ended up eating the entire board game and somehow escaping to the chocolate supply cupboard. That's how childhood books live on. Rather lovely to sit down and have a proper meal together, isn't it? Time's been flying since we all got here. Never realized how much I've missed good conversation over a decent Sunday roast. Janice and I tried to do our best, but no replacing a proper train ride for the kids.      Mind you, I'm surprised about the delay. They were rambling on about line improvements, track replacements, and all that jazz. Time will tell what comes of it.

So did you watch The Lie last night? That Shakespeare remake they put out on iPlayer? I know it’s got the big names in it, but honestly, I could’ve done without the dramatic lighting and long close-ups.      Oh I saw it! I agree with you, it felt a bit overproduced, like they were trying too hard to make Shakespeare “relevant” without actually making it accessible. I crave a bit of bland takeaway food washed down with lukewarm lager more than most people about geopolitics these days.      Ha! We’re not going back there again, are we? Politics and Europe still make me feel like I’m in one of those student debates, where nobody actually remembers the actual facts.      A bit, but I think it's a natural response when you’re finishing university and trying to work out where you fit in the world. Like, how do I even vote if I don’t fully understand how the whole system works?      True. I still remember my dad talking about stag dos with his mates in the 80s, and how everyone used to just forget about politics on the weekend. I suppose we could go further than that sometimes.

So, I heard you've been living in Manchester for a few months now? How's it treating you? I remember the snow last winter was brutal up there!      Oh, yeah! He came out in about five minutes asking if he could be a tree! And you had this job at the café doing ices! You know that was you!      Maybe I did have stage potential after all. Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun is just beginning to shine through the clouds. I like to think the garden’ll take notice and finally start to grow properly. Now if the next class of recruits remember to water the shoot and not the manure, away go the roses!      If only real estate in cities followed suit. Right, I suppose I’d better box this lot up and finish your conversation with the latest sum.

Right, so basically, the whole thing hinges on how you frame your argument in the literature review. The first few chapters are supposed to show you’ve got a solid grip on what’s already been said, but then you need to carve out a space where your own research adds value. Got to be careful not to just repeat what others have done.      Yeah, that part still confuses me a bit. I’ve got all these sources, but I’m not sure which ones are actually relevant. It feels like every paper you read has something important to say, but you can’t just list them all. You gotta... like, synthesise them?      Exactly. It’s not just about summarising; you’ve got to compare, contrast, and then identify the gaps. So, for example, if five studies argue A, and one argues B, you might say—okay, there’s a trend here, but when does B actually apply? That’s where your research question comes in. You’re using the existing scholarship as a starting point, not the end point.      Right, I see what you mean. But how do you even know what the gaps are? I’ve read a few of the core reading list books, but I don’t feel confident enough to say, “Oh, no one’s looked at this yet.”      It’s not about saying “nobody’s looked at this,” it’s about saying, “Not many people have explored X within the context of Y,” or “Most people focus on this demographic, but my focus is different.” That’s a classic entry point. Just start by flagging the areas that feel underdeveloped or where the research is in conflict.      Yeah, okay, but what if the problem still feels too broad? I’m worried I’ll end up with a paper that’s barely focused at all. Like, I mentioned social mobility and education in my proposal, but that’s like an entire topic.      True. That’s where the ‘research question’ comes in handy. Instead of waiting till the end to crack it, you should be building toward it as you go. So your methodology chapter and literature review are both leading up to it. The more you read, the clearer it’ll become. For example, go from “social mobility” to something like “the role of mentorship in education-based social mobility among working-class students in the North of England.”

Rather annoying to wake up in the middle of a good dream. I had one last night where I suddenly won the lottery and bought a caravan with a dog parked up on a coastal path by the sea. You keep calling your doll Bucksy, darling. Haha. Tell Alice’s teacher I want to discuss circle time rhythm sticks when we meet next.      True. Let’s hope Bucksy makes a full recovery. As for me and that lottery win of mine... Perhaps we’ll dream of a new one tonight!      Alice tells me Bucksy is not unwell! She’s just away go-karting with her best friend.      I like go-karts! Go-karts go ‘vroomvroomvroom’ and make loud noises. I made Bucksy jump in a go-kart once.      True to life?      True! We made them!      The magic of childhood, eh? Totally transporting. Lotteries, castles, go-karts, and miraculous canine survival. It’s all starting to sound like Doctor Who before bedtime.      I’d take those dreams on any night. Irrelevant of where we park on the space hopper!

Rather annoying I had to go to A&E last nigh', love.      Oh no, what happened?      Dropped me mug on the floor, nipped me leg proper bad. Chipped ceramic, I s'pose. Just like a dagger it were.      Owch, that must’ve hurt. Did they give you anything for it?      Ay, some kind o’ painkiller, but I was waitin' 'til morning t’see if me bleedin’ stopped. But it kept on, so I thought I'd better go in.      Did you have to queue long?      Aye, hours I did. Fun left t'right backr, didn’t I? D’you know how many twats turned up after me with nose bleeds an' ‘inconveniences’?      Haha, yeah, they usually have the worst allocation system, don’t they?      You don’t say. I swear, if I had to listen to老爷爷 natter on abou’ his toerag and the hobnobs again, I would’ve lost it.      Was it really that bad?      Oh aye, they were trying t’sock me somethin’ to eat like it were tea-time and not ‘Cause you lost your leg, dear lady.’      Honestly, they need to sort the triage system out. We’re not all th’walking dead and not all are that important. I mean, it were a bleed, but I was just grateful they realized it was serious enough not t’stick me in with the rest o’ the clowns. Says there’s a chance of slight infection but if I keep it dry and go back regular I’ll be fine.      You’re lucky in a way, I suppose. Thought I were more like the ‘at home’ kind of person.      Well, you are, but things 'appen. Least y’knew when to ask for help.      Aye, better safe than sorra. I just nae want to ever have t’try that again on a Wednesday nigh'.      I don’t blame you. If that’s what typical A&E is like, I’m not looking forward t’the rest o’ my life.

Rather unusual day today, isn't it? That article in  The Times  about the new renewable energy initiative... quite the big step for the government, wouldn’t you say?      Yes, it is rather. Not quite sure how the technical side of things works, mind you, but if it’s cheaper and more sustainable, I’m all for it. Still, it depends on how it's rolled out.      Absolutely. If they had access to the right resources... Tell me, have you heard from Jack lately? He’s always been the one with a vision for sustainability projects.      Jack? Oh, yes! We had a reunion of sorts last week. He and Silvia are working on a community garden project in Lewes now. Quite ambitious. He says he’s also mentoring a few students interested in agriculture and urban farming.   Speaker__2:   That’s great to hear. I certainly will. It could be a fantastic learning experience for the kids, and for Jack and Silvia too. Synergy, if you like.      Exactly. Well said. And in the spirit of green energy and community, I might start a compost bin out back. You could have the first batch to test in your workshop garden next spring.

Rather skip the starter, don't you think? That griddled mackerel looks a touch delicate for first serving. You know, like that one you took me to back in Dorset last summer, what was it, the Glory Posthouse or some such? Made me think I turned into a piece of interior design by mistake. Box diving — I seriously question why this concept wasn't invented when those of us taller had belly flops to contend with.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh, lad? Thought we’d get a bit o’ sun tae let up tae the Borders this weekend.      Aye, we’d best not put it oan. Chances are the view from the hills’ll be like a thick peat bog eenyway. But I’ll tell ye what, I’ve been thinkin’ aboot that mountain auld Jamie Aitken used tae take us up back in school. If nae mist, there's a spot tae get somethin’ decent in the lens.      Aye, I jist took ma camera doon tae the Shore last night. Still got some lights efter closing hour, an’ the rain was skippin’ aff the pavement lyin’ like mirrors. D’ye ken how I managed tae get a wee shot o’ reflections in the puddles?      Now that’s no’ bad. I’ve been looking at some o’ yer work, to tell ye the truth. They’ve got nae mercy—there's a certain feel tae them, a wee glim o’ soul. What did ye ken aboot takin' pictures as a hobby?      I dunnae ken—I just loe the calm it brings, y’see. Ma work is all boxes an’ spreadsheets, an’ orders. It’s all very methodical, no blame oan it. But photography’s lyin’ someone else in yer head—someone creative. Ever been tae Iceland, I hear it’s out o’ this world?      Aye, I went up tae the north last year.
