It's like that for you, isn’t it? The new baby’s taking up most of your time now, isn’t it? I used to think it’d be easier with you looking after them, but you’re almost constantly on the go now.      I suppose it’s the excitement, love. There’s just so much to do. Also, the grandparents are coming over for a visit one of the weekends—my mother’s very keen to meet the little one. She’s been bragging like mad.      Oh good—maybe she can help out a little. I mean no pressure or anything?      No, none at all. But I do wish I could switch places with you now and then. You’ve got all the time in the world for naps and coffee breaks. Well, in your spare time.      That's oddly sour of you—look at the positives. You get to see the baby grow up every day. I don’t, and it makes me about crazy at times. I sometimes wonder if the little one even remembers who I am.      Aww that is sad. I’m sure it does, love. You do great, you really do. But if you’re looking for company, I’m up for a catch-up. Any chance you’re watching  Doctor Who  this evening? I haven’t seen the latest episode yet.      Is that tonight? I’d forgotten altogether. I’ve told my students I’m taking a night off for once, so I might actually manage it. That is, if the baby doesn’t see fit to stage a rebellion at exactly 8 p.m.      Haha, I can see it already. A miniature rebel with all the right ideas.      Exactly. Well, if all else fails, we’ll just pretend we’re in the ‘80s and record the episode on VHS.

Rather annoying I had to cancel last minute innit, me event’s gone a bit pear-shaped ‘n Yorkshire... got to sort it out before it all skints down. Lost a few bob if ye catch mi drift.      No worries, we’ve got plenty of food an’ more if it een’t enough. Work been that bad then?      I’m tellin’ you, work’s been a proper faff as well this week. Met a client who thought she was some sort of damn celebrity and we had to change the colour scheme four times in an hour.      Right, I’ve sorted mostly finished when I’m not chuckin’ bricks, only proper exciting job I had last week was when I dug out a cat from a hole in someone’s garden, ain’t the proudest moment of me life but it saved someone’s fluffball, at least.      Ayo, that sounds proper daft... I’d be lost diggin’ about in someone’s garden, even if I had a map. Good job though.      My flatmate had a situation too—some guy left two proposals out a week apart and she had to choose, proper fancy situation innit?      Oi, sounds like one of them reality TV tales. Bet she’s still figgin’ it out now.      Now don’t go making them all sound daft, some people like a bit of romance, even if it feels someone’s castanet!      I wish I had that problem. Gone out with a few people recently, but none of them being anything special. Like, I don’t even know what it is about people who don’t want to be picked up in the first five minutes.      Another failsafe is that lot of ‘em seem to think a sandwich is enough to do with, ‘cos they just keep eatin’ while you’re trying to speak.      Unhh, bloody typical! I’ve dyed me hair for a conference today, stickin’ with the dress code, but now me nan wants knows why I look like Grimsby’s lost chocolate supply.      That’s a nice colour, I told her the last go. Worked for me, anyway.      Bet she just said, “Cor blimey luv, that’s a bit ‘business-says-over-my-soul’ for me.”      More or less, but I’m not hearing to much of it. Know where me job is anyway.      Now that I can relate to, I done me master’s in project management and still suffering the 80-hour work week.

Rather a cold day we've had, innit? Seems like winter's gripped us for good this year.      Oh, I’m more than used to it by now. A bit of cold is nothing when you can look forward to a decent cup of tea.      That’s all we lot need, isn’t it? A good mug of tea and company to enjoy it with. I’ve just boiled the kettle—anyone want a spot?      That would be lovely, dear. Put the kettle on for me when you're about, please.      Right, I’ve some shortbread knocking about. Bit old, but not too bad if you ask me.      Oh, you’re a treasure. Shortbread and tea, the English way.      I think it’s funny how we take tea for granted, really. Back when I was teaching in Manchester, I used to have a mug in every classroom. It was part of the routine, you see. Break time was tea time, no questions asked.      Aye, we’d knock off the occasional pint in the evening, as well. But early in the day, nothing like a strong builder’s brew.      Speak for yourself. I remember my father preparing tea with the same care as he prepared for a dinner party. Milk first, no sugar—strict as ever.      Mine was the opposite! He’d put two sugars, someone else in the house would take it plain. Used to drive me mad.      Still, at least he wasn’t into the fancy tea bags now, was he? I’ve seen the most absurd varieties—oolong, jasmine, you name it. But I stick to builder’s blend myself. There’s nothing like it for concentration.      Tell me about it! When I was ‘young,’ I worked construction, steady work. Boy, did that tea hit me right. Hot, black, strong as sin.      I remember once getting distracted while making tea and putting  five  teaspoons of sugar in. Took me hours to notice.      Some people still reach for those sugar cubes, don’t they? I think it's a gothic habit, honestly.      Maybe. But I say if it’s sweet, it's good—especially when the rest of the day isn’t going to plan.      Here’s to tea then—still holding the nation together, as usual.      Here, here.      And here. Served best with friends, of course. [She takes a soft sip of tea, a satisfied look on her face.]

Rather skip the new restaurant in Norwich, love. Thought we could do something a bit more home-cooked tonight... got the lamb shank from the butcher today, and I’ve a few jars of that lovely aubergine chutney you made the other week?      Oh, excellent! I was just thinking about that chutney the moment you mentioned dinner. My goodness, that needs a glass of something, doesn’t it? Cheers to this lot, honestly. Oh, and what was it you said about the CRB check again? I thought you said it was sorted before the new semester.      It  was  sorted, but I got an email last night saying another form needs signing. It’s a university thing now, you know, extra security on top of the standard one. I’m not even starting a new role — just the same as last year!      Sounds like a British bureaucracy classic. I had a similar with a drive in London a few weeks ago. Had to prove I didn’t drink before driving, even though I had my sat nav taking me over there.      Oh, I know that one — quite a few people still assume sat navs can’t get you lost in central London. I tried to take a first-year round Soho once, and we ended up in a pub, and now he won’t stop quoting “You weren’t born in London,” as if that means something.      God, pubs in this country are someone’s full-time job, aren’t they? I swear half the population is employed by them.      Don’t forget the profits being poured into premium hotels too! We went away last weekend and nearly flaked out from the sheer opulence. Paid good money to take our boots off and be served soup in thimbles that cost more than the wine.      That’s just standard up north. I’ve been guest speaker at events where they serve kebabs with cutlery. You assume you’re at some art affair, and then someone starts passing around prosciutto and a side of something called "nigella-tra-dusted lunches."      Now, art is a far easier topic than something like circumcision, which I once had to explain in a room full of American professors. It wasn’t so much the procedure as the cultural differences they had between us and the Yoruba communities.      You could have told them it was all inspired by one too many protests in Oxford Circus.

:  [currently half-lying on the bed, phone in hand]  Ugh, it’s so good to have you home. I’ve been bugging you so much I know, but I’ve missed your cooking mad skills.       [from the kitchen]  Oh, thanks! I’ve been so eeny-minded since returning from Cornwall. It was lovely, but honestly, eating granola every morning? I’ve missed our Sunday roasts.     : No, I totally get it. I think it’s nice you had the break. How was the whole trip, anyway? Still dodging your ex like you said you would?     : God, yes, still dodging him. He turned up at the same pub as us on the last night, tried to say hi to me like nothing happened. But I was with Steph, so he just gave up in the end. Honestly, it’s weird, but I actually feel much calmer about the whole thing now. Maybe I’m finally over him?     : Well, that’s good news. It’s about time, really, seeing as he treated you like absolute rubbish. Anyway, what about work? How were you when you got back today?     : To be honest, it was a bit overwhelming. I had three new faces in the same week and one of the other nurses resigned. I’m glad I had the time off to recharge, but I’m still picking up extra shifts to make up the hours. You know how hospitals are.     : Yeah, I remember when I was working with you before the project co-ordinate role. It was like non-stop stress all the time. But how’s your mum about you working so much?     : Actually, she had a fall a couple of weeks ago. I wasn’t there when it happened, but she was in hospital for two days. I visited her the morning I was due to go on holiday. She’s better now, but it really hit me how quickly things can change.     : Oh no, that’s such a bummer. Let me know if you need a hand with anything. I’m probably free this weekend if you want to pop down for a visit.     : That would be really nice, thanks. It’s not every weekend I have off, but I’ll let you know. And in the meantime, let’s at least get this house in order. I can’t believe we left the hallway looking like a bin store.     : I’ll sort the magazines and stuff this afternoon.

Rather annoying that the new planning application for the old manor house was rejected, wasn’t it? I was really warming to the idea of them converting the stables into a community centre.      It is a shame. I do understand the need for preserving such a historic building, but it’s not like it’s being  demolished . Just renovated. Still, the village council wanted to keep most of the original features intact, which tends to double the cost of any renovation anyway.      Yes, and now we might end up with another half-renovated, half-rotten Victorian pile sitting on the edge of the village. I can see it now—half the villagers are arguing about whether the windows should be double-glazed or not! Honestly, it’s a miracle they ever get anything done around here.      Oh, don’t knock it until you’ve tried living in one! Wait until you have a dormer window installed incorrectly, or some ancient pipework that’s cost five grand to unclog, and see how you feel then. Good news is, that manor house’s sale should clear up some of the housing market here. There are quite a few buyers still waiting for the right place.      That would be nice. We both know people who have been priced out of this village completely, just trying to get on the housing ladder again. I wish there were more affordable places to rent. Anyway, enough about the building nonsense—how’s your sister, again? Our friend Georgia said she’s been in hospital again?      That’s right. They caught it early this time—breast cancer, stage one. She had a lumpectomy in November and started radiotherapy about six weeks ago. I went to visit the other week. She looked tired, but otherwise doing okay. The sister is doing better too. I think it helped a lot that she started the treatment early. Her consultant says the prognosis is good if she keeps going with the sessions.      That's such a relief. I remember hearing about her from your sister last year—actually, didn’t she end up being misdiagnosed at first? That must have been so stressful.      Defo. She went around with it for a couple of months thinking it was just a cyst or something. It wasn’t until one of her college friends started showing her the same symptoms and insisted she get checked properly.

Rather annoying when the bar’s out o’ order at six on a wednesday. Should be stocked up like... proper, yeah? And no luck now unless yer down the pub a few streets away. An’ yer tryin’ to relax after a long shift.      Aye, that een’t nice. But I’ll say one thing,   I reckon this place needs a better lift system.   I swear me arse’s done more work than I’ve done in a week just waitin’ for it. Especially when the uni’s got events on the top floors, or the blokes up north fetchin’ their parcels.      Oh, the bins, yeah.   Right nightmare they are.   Every Thursday I’ve got to double up bursts runnin’ between the flats and the bins, riskin’ o’ being late for my shift. It’d be far better if they put ‘em on the ground floor or something. Course, someone’d be throwin’ out stuff from their window instead, probably.      Good one, real nightmare that’d be.   I get patients complainin’ all the time about the smell from the bins.   It’s only ten paces from the lifts, but it’s enough to ruin a whole flat from the way it drifts – especiall’ with the wind, like, it just  hums  into the corridors. It’s enough to make you want to chuck the whole flat in the bin yourself.      Aye, smell’s gotten me a few times. It just catches ye sour at the worst possible moment, like just when ye finished your dinner.   I dun’ like the noise in the evenings, most o’ all.   That bloody music from the flat next door – blastin’ vibes th’ whole time. Like someone’s been given a barely informed bat handle.      That, I agree wi’. An’ not even anything like proper music.   Just some douchy minimal techno bloke on Spotify.   It’s like, you can’t even complain without stickin’ yer head out the window to see whose flat it comes from.        An’ the visitors.   Every night, after ten. Pissed, loud, no goin’ on ‘em if you don’t wanna end up barricated into your flat, yeah? Some of these lads, they think it’s a holiday. It’s supposed to be private lives, innit? Instead it’s like a bloody nightclub setup every night of the week.      Yeah, been on to them a few times. S’all go down the same route – they imply we're harsh or something, like it's our job to let them get plastered in the public space.

Rather annoying when you've got aching feet and nowhere to perch. I was just trying to take in the view of the seafront when some bobby came up and told me I couldn't stay where I was. I don’t blame them really, the place is jammed on a Saturday morning.      Aye, I used to bring the lads here every year before I retired. They loved the chip shops and all the little stalls that pop up at Christmas time. Oh, and those markets in Antwerp once. We took a package tour. You get the whole lot, hotel, dinner, and someone fetches you up in the morning. Bit dead if you ask me now, but back in the eighties they were the go-to.      Yeah, we tried one once, didn't I tell you, love? We went to Aachen for a weekend with a couple of the girls from the care home, and it was lovely. Such a historic place. The Christmas market was magical, and not too cold, mind you. I picked up a little wooden Christmas star for Charlie—set it on the mantelpiece, and he's still got it two years on.      And then, when you're there, you can’t help but trot out a little of the local language. My son Mateo used to be proud of his basic French, but when we went into a café in Lyon once and he tried to order a coffee and ended up sounding like a parrot, well, it was someone else in the tour group who got his order in properly. He's been sour on language lessons ever since.      I thought being abroad would be a good excuse to learn a second language at uni, but honestly, after a year of trying to conjugate French verbs, I gave up and just switched to Danish because it wasn’t as painful. Doesn’t sound too English, but I do enjoy a ‘hygge’ once in a while.      Come on, the English do a few things quite well. We don't often get the credit, but our stick-to-itiveness and ability to survive being rained on always comes with a bit of pride. At least the traffic in the city isn't too bad today.      Still, I reckon go back to Herne Bay if you want a bit of quiet action—no rush hours, no exhaust fumes.

So do you know what the "equality vote" is, like, the one in Ireland? I heard about it in school and it sounds important.      Oh yes, that was a big deal a few years back. It was about the same-sex marriage referendum — they had a vote to decide if Ireland should allow same-sex couples to get married.      Oh! So like making it a legal thing? I never thought Ireland would do that first, honestly. I mean, it was a very Catholic country, wasn't it?      Yeah, it was true. But the people saw the difference, right? They wanted to be fair and give same-sex couples the same rights. It was like everyone coming together, even if they didn’t agree.      I didn’t know you voted on it, and I think it turned out really good, like, they got a yes vote?      Oh yes! It was a shock in a way. It passed with over 60%, even in many rural areas. Young people like you were out there campaigning and spreading the word.      Yeah I wish we did stuff like that in the UK. It took ages for same-sex marriage to be legalised here. But it’s all good now, I guess.      I agree, and actually it makes me smile that you’re so interested in this sort of thing. You should use your voice more when you’re old enough — vote and all that.      Definitely. I think my mum wants me to run for mayor or something when I finish school — she’s a bit embarrassing and thinks she knows everything.      Haha, I know how that goes. My mother used to bring me into parties and ask people if they "supported my future as a politician", and then I’d just hide behind a cushion.      Oh that’s so funny! I had one birthday party where my mum wore a union flag as a dress and was giving everyone tea. I still get teased about it.      Sounds like a  proper  British themed party! Except trying to find a mate and maybe having your first vote — but let’s not skip ahead, you’re not 18 yet!      I know, I know. I’m still waiting for my GCSEs, but I really like politics in school, especially learning about what your vote can actually change.      That’s impressive, love. As long as you never lose that curiosity, you’ll be alright.

Rather fine day today, isn't it? That sun gracin’ the table just right, ‘as p’d me to fetch some more of that chicken pie from the oven.      Yes, dear, it were £2.49 at the shop yesterday — well worth the two for one deal on the cheese scones, if I say so myself. Ay, that's all gone now, I reckon. A shame too — they were so stubby but perfectly crumbly.      Stubby and crumbly? That sounds like me cousin when he tried to make scones... went to put it in the  microwave . Now, I’m not sayin’ we should test this idea — turkey, definitely not — but his new hamster, you see... I ain't responsible.      I’ll be the judge of that if I were you, James — better not breakfast, no doubt. But this chicken pie, now — in my day, cookin' it in a mason jar on the stove was a proper knack. My father, he was one clever ‘un with the tools — lathe work, that sort of thing.      Oh, Cyril! Tell us more. I’ve always fancied workin’ with wood. You ever make spoons?      Spoon and plough, both! But best of all were the apple carvers — them things that’d chip the wood ‘til you had yourself a daisy. Our garden ‘as full of ‘em. Just a simple lathe — not them flashy CNC machines now — you had to be steady with the chuck and the toolpost.      I’ve seen a few Apple about, actually... though not the carvers, the phones. We were lured in by what you could do with it. Not that I’d ever handle it uncase-up.      Oh, I’ve got one. All passed out on the sideboard — me grandkids brought it for christmas ‘n I can’t seem to stop them from waiting on me. We just talk about tutu vouchers and filters of all things.      Gracious, talk about being rendered obsolete. Me, I’m still learning to use tongs! But hey, if goin' on ‘bout Apple pies or Apple machines makes one forget about the dent in the microwave, I’m all in.      Pass the gravy, would you, Eleanor? This pie really is impressive. I’d never seen one made like this — chunks of chicken still on the bone, ‘as a certain charm.      That’s how my late mum used to do it, bless ‘er. Right, old school. She once baked a cake in a saucepan when the oven went on the blink — and it were as light as a feather, I swear.

Rather unusual this, isn't it, reading those mirror scripts they talk about on the news. I remember learning it in the transcription course—some of the older documents are written backward. But I can’t imagine ever doing it willingly. Do you do it, Denis?      Honestly, I don’t get it either. I mean, it’s one thing transcribing old ledgers backwards as part of a job, but I wouldn’t want to write that way just for fun. Oh, and speaking of, did you see the bank’s latest statement? They’re dragging me in again about the debt. You know how these institutions are— always  offering credit and then  always  reminding you to pay.      My dear, you young people and your overdrafts. Back when I was the headmistress, we didn’t worry about debt—though I did spend most of it on the school renovations. And house prices—good heavens, I can’t believe how much everything has soared. I lent the local bank quite a tidy sum back in the '80s, and now they expect me to move out of this pleasant home I’ve had for thirty years.      I read somewhere the other day that the price per square foot is now higher than any time in history. Mind you, most of us can’t afford to move anyway, least of all with these ridiculous mortgage rates. Though I do quite enjoy that little comic relief the news gives us—do you remember the story about the cat that climbed out someone’s chimney and ended up in a neighbor’s house? It had them oddly sour on the internet.      Oh yes, and it wasn’t even the cat’s fault. They found it quite content about its misadventure. Far better story than talking about crypto or this whole debate over charging for plastic bags. I know it’s necessary, but I still feel a bit cheated when I pay 5p for a bag I once got for free.      Come now, Denis. It’s for the planet, and besides, if you’re restricting your plastic, you’re being responsible. Now, that’s what I learned in the ‘70s. Though speaking of responsibility, have the two of you considered tying the knot? I’ve heard you two arguing over the crossword as long as I’ve known you.      Denis and I do spend far too much time bickering, I’ll grant you that.

Right, I just wanted to bring up something I noticed, Lucas. I know it's weekends and it's all about play and having fun, but I’m a bit concerned they're not reading much over the long weekend. They’ve spent all afternoon glued to Lego Ninjago on the tablet and then straight into Minecraft on the Nintendo.      But Mummy, it's not all day! We only turned it on after lunch. And the story mode in Ninjago is actually a bit educational, isn’t it? We’ve been learning about the different villages and weapons the Ninjas use.      Yeah! And in Minecraft, I made a castle with the dragon in front, and I have like ten Mycelium trees now! I watched a YouTube tutorial on how to make a portal to the Nether. It was cool!      It is, sweetie. Minecraft definitely has elements of creativity and problem-solving, and Lego has a story in there too. I’m not against letting you play, not at all. But I want to make sure your screen time is balanced with things like reading or drawing or even just building with actual Lego. Your reading ages have been lagging a bit, and I know there's something to be said for audio rhythm in games, but words still matter.      I know, Mummy, but reading is  so boring  compared to Minecraft. It’s like, why would I go through a whole book when I can just build a world that’s full of fire and lava and dragons?      Because a book gives you something to dream about too, and sometimes even more exciting things than a game! Look, Lego Ninjago has about forty books written about it. You could read those and then take on the game knowing exactly what you’re up against. Doesn’t that make the game even more fun? Maybe we could do something like ‘read first, play later’ for an hour or so.      Can we read something  adventurous ? Not boring stuff about waiting at the bus stop.      Absolutely. There’s that new Ninjago graphic novel I bought—loads of action and pictures. Even you’ll like it, Lucas. And if you finish the chapter, Mummy promises to let you play Minecraft  with real building blocks  for an hour, no screen.      Oh! Can we all do that together? Like, I’ll read a page and then we’ll recreate it with the blocks?

Rather lovely to have you both over. You know, since Sarah’s back from her holiday, it does feel like proper weekend fun, doesn't it? I've made my usual tea cake, if you fancied a slice later. Not quite as good as Gran’s, but I've had a few years to get on top of it, I think.      Honestly, Mum, your tea cake is a national treasure now, if you ask me! I don’t remember the last time she was back; it’s been far too long. So, Sarah, how was your holiday? Let's hear some gossip...      It was so refreshing, actually. We stayed in Cornwall, and it turned out that Myra, my roommate, met this eccentric local who runs this potter’s studio from an old farm. He showed us around in the evening and made us all feel like proper artists. Made a plate I still can’t throw away, even if it wobbled in every direction.      Oh, didn’t I say so? Young people always need culture in their lives! Though tell me—was the weather consistent, or did it change with your mood as usual?      Haha, mostly good—rain during the trotting on the beach, but somehow no one minded. We made new friends, helped ourselves to a couple of crab sandwiches while the weather held on.      You know what I found interesting? We had the same kind of coffee this morning at the shop. Strictly ground beans from this local roastery, oddly sour. Not what you’d serve at a family get-together and be proud of!      Well, most people about would make do with a cafetiere, but here we take this job seriously. I’ve switched to aeropress for better clarity and more taste. You're welcome to try it.      Sounds exciting. I’m more of a cafetiere fan, to be honest. Steady brew, no muss, no fuss. I’ve little time for fancy gadgets while my budget is tight. Though being back at uni, trying to find part-time work besides the student grants—well, let’s say it’s a balancing act.      That goenvironmental shop in Lichfield needs a few extra hands, and I do mention you when I can. Sue’s looking for friendly faces to help train some new baristas.      Oh good, we’d like that! Sarah needs some extra cash, to say the least. How ‘bout this—on Saturdays, mornings tend to be quiet.

So, I swear the sandwich shop near our school only ever has ham and cheese. How do they not get sued or something?      It's not even bad, I mean, ham and cheese are reliable classics. Not like we’re allowed to bring our own food into the common room — Mrs. eenie weenie  would  say something if we handed her a tuna sarnie with extra eyelashes.      Honestly, that woman’s got a face like a calculator. Last week, she docked three points from our house because someone called the canteen “a glorified chip truck.” Not even jokes are safe these days.      What’s worse is that we’re in Year 12 and still have to sit cross-legged around the dining hall pretending we’re in Year 7. It’s like the headteacher’s world is stuck in 1992.      Maybe that’s why they’re thinking of making some of the prefects cook lunch. I heard Mrs. Kenway’s idea is to get the Year 12s to make sandwiches for Year 7 on Wednesday afternoons — I mean, we’re not even trained chefs, we’re just deadly with highlighters.      You'd think in a town like Slough, at least one of the shops could provide something like, I don’t know, a sweet chilli chicken wrap or something? Why do we still get egg salad and soggy ham?      Maybe someone should start a petition. Let's call it  "Give us freedom, give us variety, give us something that doesn’t taste like the inside of a fridge!"       You know what would really do it? If we pulled a "das the problem" from that show [name obscured —  ed. fails to recall ], then formed a flashmob in the hall singing about crusty bread.      Speaking of shows — have you all seen that new military drama on the BBC? The one where all the soldiers look like they stepped out of a photo shoot. I swear, if one more of them says  “Orders are orders”  in a slow dramatic whispy voice, I’ll reach into the TV and slap someone.      Yeah, go for it. But let me warn you — if you slap the screen, you’ll just end up with a red handprint and an expensive electric bill due to the sparks. It’s not even live!      I miss those old war movies with belly laughs and dodgy accents. Remember that one where this guy’s “heroic” speech ends up making him trip over his own boots and get hit by a tank?

: Oi, Jess, have you seen what Mr. Thompson’s been getting up to in physics lessons lately? Like, I swear he’s half asleep at the front of the room by the time we get to electronics.     : Oh my gosh, I  know ! I was writing on my phone the other day and then he just like   "Emily! My cup is levitating?!"   and I had to delete whatever I was writing  so fast . Honestly, I thought he'd fallen asleep on his desk.     : Didn’t even look up? He just carried on... like, is it even fair to us? I mean, we're doing AQA, and some of us  actually  want to understand the syllabus! Ugh, I just can't take it anymore.     : Yeah, me too. I’m actually thinking about emailing our form tutor, Miss Gale—she seems more switched on. Maybe she can talk to Mr. Thompson for us?     : Honestly, I wouldn't mind. I mean, I try to do my English reading book in physics class—everyone does it!—but it’s like he's giving me ten deadly looks as if he knows I’m not paying attention. It’s so awkward.     : Oh wait, I loved the film  17 Again ! Remember the part where he tries to cheat on his math exam and the teacher catches him? Like, that teacher was 100% Mr. Thompson. Strict. Just not even in a helpful way.     : Yeah, but some of the teachers are actually pretty cool. Like Mr. Ellis, in drama. He actually made about five of us walk around the room trying to touch the ceiling without falling over. It was absolutely chaos and I   still   got an A in the unit. So, like, that’s dedication.     : Geo., right? I did that once and fell into a chair. It was probably the most embarrassing three seconds of my life. Also, speaking of people at school, did you hear that Lucy’s doing a short story competition with Miss Gale? I think she’s written like, five of them already.     : No! Rather annoying the wet weather isn't it? I was supposed to get the strawberries in the garden picked up first thing, and now it's all mucky underfoot. I can't say I fancy walking about in this drizzle. So, I heard you got an offer for Human Sciences at Oxford. That's massive, mate. Well done! What made you go for that over, like, Physics or Maths?      Thanks, it was pretty nerve-wracking, I'll admit! But I like the idea of studying how humans work from loads of different angles—psychology, biology, sociology. It's all kind of a mix of what I love. I just couldn’t decide on one specific route, you know?      Yeah, I get it. I’m still torn between Maths and maybe Engineering. My dad’s a structural engineer—he says it's solid, but I love the abstract side of pure Maths. Have you ever considered doing an extended project around that?      A bit, but I’m not obsessed enough to risk spending all my evenings in the library doing proofs. But I’d definitely lend you my notes if you go for it. Look, while we're on the topic, what are your plans for uni in a year or so?      I'm thinking Cambridge, if I get the grades, otherwise maybe Manchester or Bristol. Got a bit of a soft spot for their Maths societies and the social vibes. Have you ever been to a bar here before? I remember when we got “stuck” at this one with your cousin last summer and ended up ordering nachos instead of the cheapest beer on the menu.      Oh, yeah, that was a disaster. Ben’s never let us live it down. But also, seriously, my man, those nachos were legit. You out here talking about Maths and Nachos like some strange double life. Can we actually  order  something now? Not that I’m drunk or anything... yet.      Sure, but first—did you hear about the local rugby trials? My cousin mentioned they're starting a new sixth-form team. My brother plays for the club. If you’re up for it, you could train with them next month. It’d probably look nice on your uni application.      I could stick to touch rugby, but I’ll consider it. I always liked the lunches after a game more anyway—my nan taught me how to make a proper chicken curry once. Picked it up watching her in the kitchen. You ever cook anything more than pasta or toast at home?      I can make a halfway decent bean burrito if I have to. But I’d settle for something edible to call my own one day.

Rather annoying this new tax, eh, love? I’ve been looking over the statements, and they’re taking a bit more out than they used to now.      I know, Dad! I was doing some reading about it for a topic I had to cover in class. It’s part of that “eco tax” they’re pushing to disincentivise fossil fuels.      Oh aye, I read a bit about that in  The Guardian . Still, it makes me think—every time there’s a government change, the taxes shift. Didn’t your mum get chased by some tax man a few months back about her property?      That was the Inheritance Tax review, wasn’t it? They’re saying higher thresholds for families passing on their homes. Ten more years and I reckon they’ll get rid of it altogether in our area.      They’ve been saying that for decades, luv. I remember back in the 80s, when I was setting up my accounting practice, the government kept changing the tax brackets every few months. It was a nightmare.      I can imagine! I mean, with your background as an accountant, you probably saw it all as routine, but… it wasn't easy for regular folk then, was it?      Not at all. I still remember one bloke in Woburn, he nearly had a heart attack when the tax inspector came to talk about his barn conversions. He’d put all his life savings into improvements and didn’t even know it made him a higher earner.      That’d be a surprise, wouldn’t it? Anyway, I was thinking more about the overall government policy. I did a postgraduate paper on the economic impact of such policies. Have you seen how they’re pushing for more public projects now that the tax revenue is higher?      Aye, I read that they’ve allocated extra funds for rail upgrades and broadband. Though I have me doubts. I remember a few years ago they announced a huge road scheme, and when I looked into it, half the budget had already been eaten up by bureaucracy.      That’s what I was reading too! There’s this concept called “rent-seeking” by bureaucrats and lobbyists. They end up wasting money on stuff that doesn’t help everyone.      Sounds about right. I suppose it always has been, though. When I were younger, you could at least take the word of a Chancellor and think they’d follow through with something solid.

So, I just got back from my weekend trip up to Manchester. I had this team-building thing with the project team from the city office. You would not believe the amount of paperwork we've been buried with this quarter.      Oh, I bet! It must get quite hectic managing all these projects on top of the administration. I remember when I was your age and had just started as an assistant at a secondary school—they had us organizing documents before even thinking about teaching.      It is a bit overwhelming. We've had three big funding applications this month alone. Honestly, the worst part isn’t the detail—it's the deadlines! One application is due in two days and I haven't even started on the final review yet.      You should have asked one of the more experienced co-ordinators for a hand. We all started somewhere. When I was an assistant, my head of department always said, "You don’t need to do it all by yourself in one go." I remember the time I thought I could handle the entire school's exam scheduling alone over the summer break—nearly lost my mind.      Yeah, I know, I’ve been told that several times. It's just ... I want to do well. My parents work so hard, and I don’t want them to think they overspent on my degree and I’m just slacking off.      That’s sweet, and I know they're proud of you. Still, you can't expect to outwork forty hours in a week. And you know, a bit of down time doesn’t make you a slacker. I see young teachers these days being their own bosses all the time, trying to do everything at once, and honestly, they burn out quick.      I guess I just take on too much. I know that. Speaking of which, have you managed to meet up with the girls recently?      To be honest, not really. Since the exams ended, the school is holding on to all of us until August to finish grading and preparing reports. My daughter is visiting from Spain over the summer though. It’s always nice to catch up with the whole family—my nieces love going out with you and your friends.      That's brilliant news! They’re growing up so fast. If you're around in June, we could go out for a weekend trip—somewhere close—and make it your holiday too.

Rather annoying this new recycling schedule eh, love? Thought me an’ the bin was gonna be real chums... got the white one out by the gate today, and I’m blind by the time I try an’ work it out. Oy, I did ask me old friend Reg about bin buggers the other day... mind you he said what he always says - “Ain’t bin a week goes by without sending one back to the bin, ‘cos they just keep buggin’ about”      Ohhh, Reg, love. We haven’t seen them for a few weeks. We should really pop down and see them again. Got a game coming up at the weekend and I told Reg we would if the weather was any nicer.      I told Reg we’d go out for a bite to eat after the match. Maybe bring some wine? Thought I’d open that bottle of red you bought last time we went to your place. It was nice, right?      Oh, that cheap stuff, eh? You gave me a right heart attack with that ‘bottle o’ Ceylon’ you had.

: You know, I just got my schedule for the TESOL conference this year, and I’m honestly considering not going. I had such a bad experience at the one last year, you know?     : Oh no! What happened? I’ve been going since about 2015 and it’s always been interesting. I met some really good contacts at the last few—maybe not world-changing, but worthwhile all the same.     : Well, it wasn’t the sessions, as such. It’s more the stress of traveling on your own when you don’t really know many people there. I mean, I mostly just ended up sitting with a sandwich and people-watching in the speaker lounge like everyone else’s a bit busy living their best lives.     : Oh, I totally get that! I used to feel the same until I started making it a point to reach out to someone I’d met online or at a conference previously. You’d be surprised how many people you meet in Twitter or on teacher forums wind up at the same events. It makes it so much easier when you’ve got a familiar face or two to lean on.     : Hmm, I only started using that kind of stuff properly a couple of years ago. I’m a bit old-school. I remember when networking meant writing letters and waiting weeks for a reply!     : Oh, you and your nostalgia for the old days! No, I get it, though. Our jobs have changed so much. I mean, not to mention the rush of meetings we had at school with Ofsted looming and half of us just clinging on by our fingernails!     : Don’t even get me started. Rather annoying this, having the GPS play up. I remember back in the day, it was just a map... Well, and sometimes maps were wrong, too, if I'm honest.      It is a bit funny, isn’t it? I mean, I wouldn't dream of driving without it now, but when I first started teaching TEFL, I used to rely on directions from strangers in cafés in Istanbul. Half the time they were so lost they got me lost too!      That sounds a bit dangerous. I mean, for someone who’s not yet fluent.      Oh, it was! Though honestly, I think I learned more about people than I did about geography. Being lost together kind of bonded us, you know? Makes you laugh later when you hear the real names of the streets they called "That Road There."      Well, let’s forget about directions for a second—maybe I'll just ask you a bit about teaching. You went for the postgraduate course, didn’t you? How was that? I always fancied that—something practical and flexible, maybe for later in life.      It was great to be honest. It wasn’t easy, but there was something so satisfying about it. I remember when I got my first batch of students from Argentina—they were fairly motley in age, but all trying hard. One of them was quite old, like in his sixties, and he said he wanted to talk to his grandchildren in English. That got to me. It made me think why I wasn’t teaching them.      That’d be something. Being able to give people their dreams—language does open doors, doesn't it? I did some teaching years ago, but I just didn’t keep at it. It wasn’t a mission for me like it is for you.      You could still do it. My sister’s planning on retraining in her fifties—says it’s never too late to go back to a hobby and give it the attention it deserves. I mean, I see your reading. You had that mystery novel on the seat behind you. What were you reading?      “The Lake House” by Kate Morton, something a bit soppy but the kind of thing I like when I want to be immersed in a setting. Not much else to do in the evenings, between you and me, when the campervan stops and it’s just me and the T.V.

Rather than share a text-based article, I request a conversation. A few people in our circle came up on a weekend trip to Donegal. We intend to discuss anti-ageing, gerontology, and a bunch of other topics. Do you fancy coming along? We're likely to take things slow, maybe do some kayaking if the weather holds up?      Ay, that's all well and good. A change of scenery never hurt anyone, so long as I’m not juggling a toddler while trying to think about telomeres and the like. Is this the same group, or are new folk joining?      Some older faces—Finbar and Moira are in, and another couple from the village that Myra keeps saying I must meet. Fun folk. It’ll be more of a discussion group as well. We pick one topic every night and riff off it. Last time, we ended up talking for breakfast about Viking metal and how much they likely enjoyed a good dram while hammering out runes.      Ah, now that’s a thought. I reckon they’d have adored it here, all the cliffs and caves—perfect for hiding if you fancied a spot of mischief and a litre of mead. But in all seriousness, what are we rhythmically discussing from the get-go?      We’re starting with gerontology because someone’s trying to sell us a new anti-ageing cream as if it’s a miracle worker. And we’ve heard enough about telomeres in this group to rival an entire university seminar. That stuff alone deserves a focused week.      Fair point. I did read something interesting the other day about how stress actually  shortens  telomeres, about how meditative practices might play a role. Do we know if this cream promises cellular immortality, or just leaves you with smooth skin and a worrying reflection?      Let’s say ‘cosmetic immortality’ will do for now. But seriously, I’m open to the whole racket. If someone can prove immortality, I’ll be the first to question the tectonic plates holding it up. Let’s not forget, we've got to keep the conversation from collapsing entirely.      Still, I’m intrigued. This sort of thing—history, goings-on on Earth, if we’re going to go rambling about pyramids in conversation, I suppose we’d better box in the topics a bit. Otherwise we’ll be at it for decades.      Agreed. We’ll rotate themes every couple of days to keep it lively.

Rather annoying I could've got a latte at the café down the road but Maw said they’re piling in the vouchers from Thursday’s shopping now they’ve got that new coffee maker.      Aye, we wouldn’t have got the vouchers if it hadn’t been for that baby chair eeny we got online last week. It was on   50% off  , wanted to make most a the bargain. True enough, Maw, but really should’ve used the vouchers first. Now don’t go making me the villain for asking what the big plan is with that fruit tree they gave you at work party.      A cherry tree, actually. Blooming gorgeous thing with pinky-white blossoms. Should be delicious and it’s supposed to grow well in your garden, Neil. More importantly, have we discussed whose money's going on delivering the furniture with the online shopping? That baby chair goin' on your share, your share or mine?      Oh no, not this again. That bloke at the chip shop told me you could sum it all up by saying sums and marriages don’t match.      It's just like trying to count the change over a bed of marigolds! Sorted that last week, so all I got to do now is collect them vouchers next week once they’re ready, right?

Rather annoying the new neighbours, eh, love? That lot down the end of the road, they’re like... proper loud on a Thursday. Less... destructive in recent months. I think the vet gave him something, or maybe he's just got the attention span of a goldfish now.      Haha, maybe he’s tired of chewing your furniture. That sounds beautiful. And you don’t even mind the food? I was someone who found German culture fascinating once. All the beer, the music festivals, the history – what with the reunification and all. You ever want to go over there?      Maybe! Though I did crash at university while doing a module on the Renaissance, which had quite a bit of stuff on Germany and Austria. Honestly, I zoned out and started Googling nail care routines. My manicurist reckons I need to start doing more maintenance, cuticle oils, that sort of thing.      Oh, I tried that stuff for a bit – your gran sent me tubes of  Nail Butter  or something. Didn’t do much for me. More importantly, have you seen our work shifts for December? Rather skip the newfit tutorial? So rather swank, do you thinks this flat's hop? The first floor, and rather well-furnished. I’m more than a bit chuffed with the kitchen, though we’re going to need to do a bit of a shop before the weekend.      Right on! I mean, it’s very neutral, but that gives us a blank canvas, don’t you think? I’m halfway through unpacking my stuff, and I swear I’m going to get a coffee table as soon as we’re set up for the internet. Have you called the provider yet?      Still haven’t tracked them down, to be honest. I only grabbed the box and made that MySpace call, but they sent an email last week saying someone will come out to connect the lines in a week or so. Honestly, I think she’s got a second lease of life.     : She’s looking better for it, I have to say. Made me wish I had a man as good-looking as that about now. I’m not even joking. Have you still got that bloke from the project you were working with? The one that you barely mentioned again after the third week?     : Oh yeah, you mean Daniel. No, he was fun for about two weeks. It just didn’t add up.     : Yeah, that sounds familiar. I mean, it’s not the end of the world. But I think it would be nice to get out more, go on a day out or something. Rather annoying this new ad for cigarettes, innit? Still doin’ that “mood” malarkey, like it’ll sort out yer day.      Yeah, smells a bit off to be honest. Why do they have to flog it on the telly after the watershed? I saw it when I was checkin’ the time.      Know what? I reckon that bloke的声音 sounds just like that fella from them NLP training ads. “Empower yer mind” and all that.      Oh, don’t remind me of NLP. I’ve had some dodgy clients through that avenue, and the last thing I want is some pushy therapist thinkin’ they can re-wire my left foot.      I’m not sayin’ it’s not useful for some. NLP for teachin’ is one thing, NLP for sellin’ smokes is another. It’s like they’re tryin’ to sell us comfort, not products.      Yeah – but it’s got me thinkin’ ‘bout the other things we see. Maybe I’ll do the house ‘cos I’ve left it all for weeks. I did the loo floor on a weekend. It was eventful, I can tell ya. Got them new bleach ones an’ all.      Let me guess... explosion of bubbles and a shout of “hurrah!”?      No, more like a shout of “bloody hell go back to my day job!” It’s not just teachin’ kids, it’s teachin’ myself how to scrub a bloomin’ loo ‘fore it’s older than me!      Yeah, I know what you mean. I mean, I’ve used them for work, you know? Clients, needs, goals… it works for them, it should work for us.      Somewhere in that brain of yours, you should put it on paper then.

Rather annoying, though—my phone’s dictation software keeps turning everything I say into gobbledegook. I tried to write a quick note about the weather, and it turned into something like, “The reverend is a cashmere moon.” No idea what that means!      Honestly, I'm thinking about returning the thing. It was ridiculous enough when he tried to read aloud "The Cat in the Hat" from my reading list before bed!      Yeah, I get that. My kids have me using the speech-to-text when they're in the car with me. You'd think the tech would be better by now—especially for a British accent. I had it try to write directions to my parents’ house, and it sent me to a "flaming rally in Nottingham". I had to explain for ages why I couldn’t get the kids to watch an open-air pyjama gig!      I've been messing with a new BBC app at work, using it as a voice assistant, and it’s the same—half the time, it can't even differentiate between "Cumbria" and "Cumbrian". You say "Cumbria", and it writes "Combria", which is probably something else. Doesn’t work at all when people have local accents.      I agree, and it's really frustrating trying to write quickly on tight deadlines. I did an interview the other day and meant to say “the situation appears critical”, and the software just changed it to "situation appears crit: read". I had to delete half the transcript and re-record just the awkward lines. So much for advancements being helpful.      Oh, I had a similar problem at work. I was dictating the script for a local news segment and meant "cider and Danish pastries", and it somehow became "cider and Danish parsnips". My producer nearly fell off the chair laughing. Honestly, I'd switch to handwritten notes if I wasn't constantly racing a deadline.      Honestly, I'm starting to wonder if the AI is trained on American English again. Even regional British English with 'proper' enunciation gets mangled half the time. My voice sounds like a textbook version of Midlands English, and it still can go off the map.      Maybe it's deliberately adding some creative flair. I suppose it could go further and start summarising what your actual thoughts  ought  to be.      That’d be a step too far even for me. I prefer my apps to just get over the pronoun “you” without missing 70% of the time.

Rather do share a drink and bring us all up to speed. I confess I’d forgotten how long it has been since the big move down from the North.      Ah yes, that was 1963 or 4, I believe—some seven years after the war was over. I came down to take up a lecturing post at the university out on the edge of town. The job came through word of mouth; one of my old professors back in Manchester had a cousin on the interview board.      I remember that! Didn’t you get the job with a rather gruff interview panel? And then you had to find a place to live the same night?      My word, you haven’t forgotten a thing. The panel was most formal, to be sure—none of them showed much interest in the world beyond the lecture theatre, which was a bit frustrating. And when it was over, I had a letter with a starting date two weeks later, thanks to the college bursar ordering them to be efficient. So I had to camp out in a boarding house near the university for the first month—until I found a flatshare with another lecturer and his wife.      Sounds like a breeze compared to me. I was from Birmingham and landed here after my dental surgery training at King’s, and I had to find a practice almost the same day as my arrival. And then the whole problem was where to live—there were no empty houses in the area at that time. I ended up in a bungalow just a mile from the surgery, which had been a boarding house converted hastily. The kitchen sink and bath didn’t match, but I was in heaven!      I recall a different dilemma. I had come from Ramsgate to teach at what was then a small grammar school. Got the job and housing together—the headmistress arranged the flat, but it was just a single guest room above the garage. Still, I was young and the school uniform was something I lived through.      You mustn’t all outshine me as the speaker of hardship. I came here from Almondsbury with little more than my suitcase and took the job as an EFL teacher after a posting in Moscow! The accommodation was even gothic—half-timbered and required constant sourcing of builders for small fixes.      Speaking of builders—oh, what a story I could tell about postgraduate work!

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun gracing the windows just as it would through the pines in the garden at home in Somerset. It makes me miss those mornings by the old oak table with a cup of tea and a sketchbook.      Yes, the light was quite bright on the hills when I drove over. It was reminiscent of the Blue Mountains just outside Sydney, not that I’ve lived there all my life—came over from Australia a decade ago. I used to work in a clinic there as a speech and language therapist. You might say words were my world.      Oh, I like that! Art and language—both are about the expression, don’t you think? Being surrounded by words, stories, therapy—while I left bursts of life on canvas, albeit from the safety of my studio. Now I run a little gallery down in Taunton, selling old pieces I’ve collected, mostly from dear friends' estates. It’s taken on a kind of life of its own.      I can only imagine the memories stirred by those paintings—especially when the teller of the story is no longer there. I never thought about it as much with my clients. For them, the story was in their voice, how it shifted rhythm and tone from the way it was supposed to be. But with antiques, and art, the story is in the brushstroke and the dust.      You know what struck me about you at our last tea? That you came all the way from Australia—what was it like growing up there?      Oh, it was quite idyllic, honestly. My parents raised me in a house with wide, open windows and books about everywhere. My father taught English literature, and I can still remember sitting on the floor with his old Greek poetry books. I was always told I had a way with words, but I think I found my way first with playing quiet guest speaker in class discussions.      Sounds a bit like where I was raised—Somerset, that is. Not unlike country Australia, I imagine, with its wide open spaces and constant companion—silence. I spent a lot of time wandering the pasture with an old book of watercolours, sketching birds or the odd fox by the gothic details on manors I passed.      You seem to have carried that sense of wonder with you, even now.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather just get a few decent sticks and just get it over with. I got the white chocolate ones from the shop today, by the way. They've got that nutty thing in them. Not bad.      Yeah, well, you know how my mum always fancies herself a bit of a decorator. She handed me this tacky reindeer thing that’s a bit too cheerful for my flat. I tried to tell her it was going into the café as a sort of "home-made" touch, but she just beamed. Apparently, she still thinks I work in marketing.       laughs  Classic! Look, the real debate here is whether we add candy canes to the Christmas cupcakes I’m making. I’ve got this marzipan mix from Birmingham market, and they seem to say "festive". Or should I stick to the gingerbread theme?      Look, just go with the marzipan and the ginger. Everyone loves a bit of spice in their cakes. Also, I might actually need your help—my printer’s decided to play dead, and I’ve still got that shortbread recipe I stole from you to print off for my flatmates. One of them is always disappearing, and it’s Christmas. I don’t feel like explaining?      Listen, I know the printer game. I had a printer once that thought it knew what it wanted for tea. Eventually, I just handed it over to the bin in a velvet box. But yeah, if you need my printer, it’s at the café. You can pop over, but I warn you—there’s a gingerbread latte incident currently staining the counter.      Oh, come on! What did the gingerbread latte do?       chuckles  Don’t know! I mean, it didn’t run away or anything. But I tried to reheat it after sitting out all night, and it just turned into a sort of browned, brittle mess. One of the customers took it for a performance art piece and left a 10p tip as homage.      Classic. So what are the plans? We going over to yours after delivering the cookies? My flat’s not really Christmas-ready. Nor is my life, if we’re being honest.      I’ll let that slide. But yeah, I’m aiming to finish these by six. We could have dinner after? There’s this new Greek place two streets down with really solid souvlaki.

Rather annoying driving back from Cambridge on a weekend, isn't it? But I suppose it's only a couple more hours and we’ll be home.      That's right, love. I was just thinking… how are things going with your thesis? You've been studying all term, haven’t you?      It’s going alright. There are days when I actually make progress. I’ve got a good structure now, so this next week, I’m hoping to just get it pulling together properly. Once that's done, the submission doesn't seem so far away.      That’s excellent to hear! I'm so proud of you. You've worked so hard for this. And you know, university definitely changed you — you talk like a lawyer now most of the time.      [laughs] Yeah, the heavy reading and all the academic jargon eventually gets into your blood, I suppose. I've been thinking, though — in all honesty, I'm not too sure what comes after graduation. I mean, I want to do something real, like work in policy, maybe get into public law. But I’m not in a rush.      It doesn’t have to be a decision you make today, darling. I remember when you got that offer from Cambridge – it was such a proud moment, and now it's all about what’s next. But you don’t have to figure it out alone. I’m here, and so are your aunts. Family is someone you can always ask.      I know, mum. I do appreciate it. Though, is it weird to think I might be living at home for a while longer? I mean, most people about to finish university are already living independently.      Not at all. Many graduates take some time to get their feet under the table before jumping into a mortgage or rent that’s just ridiculous. And besides, you always said Oxford was more of a friend than a place you ever planned to live long-term.      That’s true. You always joked about me being a “Cambridge man.” I think I kind of am. I like how the whole university plays such a big role in the town. It’s something different from London.      I remember when I used to dream about living there. Maybe one day I’ll even rent a flat in the city again. But for now, I’m just glad we get to spend time like this.

Rather exciting to be here at Cambridge Law Faculty for Alumni Day 2, isn’t it, Sarah? I’d never imagined my job in language research would bring me to a setting like this.      I know what you mean, Claire. I mean, it's one thing to coordinate research in linguistics, and another to find yourself in a room with academics and history enthusiasts. Almost as if we're a bit out of our element.      Ah, but language is the key to understanding history, is it not? I was lecturing for nearly four decades when I retired.      That’s truly impressive. What did you specialise in, Professor?      I lectured on the crossroads between law, history, and cultural exchange, especially during the medieval Islamic Caliphates. A special interest of mine in the Arab world’s cultural and linguistic influence on European thought.      That actually connects to something very close to home in my research. I’ve been tracking dialectical shifts in Eastern English due to globalisation and emigration, but I recently became fascinated with Chinese, and how isolating it is phonologically in comparison with European languages.      Chinese, yes. A beautiful language, but linguistically it resembles little of our own. Though it's amazing – I once oversaw a lecture series in which we linked ancient Silk Road interactions with Arabic-script merchants and Eastern scholars. Fascinating how trade was the conveyor of language and culture.      I work with Claire in language data administration. That kind of integration is inspiring. I remember a talk on the connection between law and early legal texts in the Arab world. Can I ask if your time as a lecturer brought you about to any fieldwork?      Indeed. I once had the great fortune to excavate a small village that was once a Roman and later Saxon trading post in South West Shropshire. Uncovering inscriptions that had echoes of Latin, Old English and even Celtic was a humbling experience. Travel broadens the mind, but it also gives you context – your language is only part of your story.      That reminds me of a new project I’m helping co-ordinate. We’re looking at how digital records can preserve dialects and minority languages as go-to tools for both education and tourism.      That’s really timely, especially with the emphasis on heritage today. I think it might link well with Sarah’s Arabic transcription work in the 13th-century legal manuscripts she studied last year.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I get that people love a bit of drama, but when it’s got nothing to do with them—well, that’s just attention-seeking, innit?      Yeah, honestly, sometimes the things that go viral are just things that shouldn’t. Got eeny idea why  this  one took off?           It was some woman in Manchester clashing with a photographer at a bus stop. Looks like he asked for a photo and she said no, but it went wonky when he kept taking it anyway and she flipped out. Then some lad made a My Name Is song parody out of it and boom—trending. Probably gon’ be the main event on news this morning.      Blimey, that’s bonkers. Why do people feel the need to interfere in everyone else’s lives in public? People’s lives are already complicated enough without some stranger puffing nonsense onto a national stage over a photo.      Might as well talk about class, really. I mean, quite a few people jumped in and started saying, “Oh, but she was watching TikTok videos while pacing in the queue.” So she must be some kind of vapid influencer, and now it’s  her  fault the photo happened. It’s that whole thing where you assume someone’s “type” based on how they look and what they do. As if TikTokers aren’t allowed to be normal people.      Some people still equate viral with  worthless . But look at Lizzo or  any  of the actual talented people about. Yeah, they went viral, but the thing that stayed around was the vibes they brought. Not this person—you know who I mean—acting out like it’s  her  show.      I mean, I can see it both ways. I run a café and it’s a madhouse all day. People come in, you know when they’re having a cracky day, and sometimes they take it out on wait staff with no reason. It wears you out. Now imagine doing that in front of  a phone , with millions of people watching. Yeah, go viral or get your life sorted.      True. I just started my MA last month. Honestly, the academic vibe sometimes feels like your own virtual world. It’s like I live 300 roles in one day—student, helper, bit of a gossip like you lot. But I’m still trying to find time to learn about dyslexia in my reading list.

Rather annoying, though, isn't it? That tooth grinds on the side. I've booked in to see the dentist next week, but it's already costing me a fortune with these dental bills. I told them we were cashing in some savings, but it's such a tight week with the rent due again and all the holidays coming up.      I reckon it's not all that bad, love. At least it wasn't serious, and this way, maybe we can stretch the savings a bit further if it turns out we need to do a bit more. Do you want to split the cost of the treatment like we discussed, or does it still fall mostly on me since the savings are still in my name?      Well, I did mention it last week, didn't I, when I was moaning on about the whole thing in the kitchen? But to be honest, I’ve been working better hours this term—thanks to that new grant. Maybe I can pitch in a bit more than the fifty-fifty, you know, to be fair? After all, I’m the one with the broken tooth, not you!      I never thought about it that way. You know me, always trying to hide the fact I spend more time grading work than earning it. But listen, I was thinking about something else while I was watching the news last night—politics are getting a bit of a kick-up again. Seems like inflation is going to hit us hard at the universities, and the cuts are starting to come in for part-time lectures. Ever thought of applying elsewhere?      Honestly? Not at all. I like it here. The students are decent, the campus is close enough for most people, and I’m finally managing the work-life balance without the stress of London. Not saying I don’t miss the buzz of that place now and then, but it does cost a lot to live there, doesn’t it?      True enough. Still, I reckon we'll manage. If anything, this all adds to the weekly agony over what to cut on the shopping bill. Speaking of, did I mention I’ve taken to watching that new cooking show? It’s whetted my appetite, let me tell you, but after seeing what they charge for the ingredients, I go straight back on the healthy-and-cheap meal plan.

Rather lovely to have you all here for lunch, especially with such a promising bit of sunshine. I made potted shrimps with a bit of lemon and shallot. Not quite what you would find in a posh seaside town, but it'll have to do!      It’s brilliant, honestly! I never get to eat things like this back at home. You know I’ve been eating most meals from tins these days. Not that I’m complaining, it’s easier with my schedule as it is.      You’re too kind,亲爱的. Eat up before the pasties go cold. I brought some of those Laksa pasties from the shop in the High Street—thought we might have a bit of a twist today. Still, best to have a bit of variety over the festive season, yes?      Oh, the festive season—Donna, you’ve got to come for breakfast on the 26th. We still do the Boxing Day Walk. It’s five miles along the River Witham, always a bit of a challenge for my legs, but I wouldn’t miss it.      I might take you up on that! I read about it last week on the uni forum—something about watching kingfishers and red deer, right?      Exactly! Plus, the wildlife, and the walk, and best of all the mince pies and hot drinks at the end. You know what it is—tradition.      Speaking of which, I noticed you two seem fond of your screens. I remember when we used to read letters and watch the box on a Saturday night. Now you’re scanning through feeds and watching those short clips of absurdity about cosmic eggs or something.      Hah, I had to look it up too—that one about “The Planck egg”? It was trending after a lecture I attended. My boss at the publisher says we need to understand what's popular, even if it’s nonsense.      Well, I say if it brings people together, even if it’s all crackpot science, then maybe there’s something to be said for it. Provided people still learn from the real things, like our young Donna here.      She’s the one who got the job because she could explain quantum entanglement to a first-year.      Oh, don’t go on, Stuart. You’ve always been a bit of a puff about her.      I’d never consider myself that smart! But it’s nice to be appreciated in that area.

Rather than playing a new game on my phone, what are you into these days, Fergus?      I’m into Pokémon now, more than I ever was when I was younger.      You wouldn’t have even been born when I was playing Pokémon with my brother when I was a teenager, and we used to sit on the staircase for ages just trading all our cards with a paper envelope.      That’s cool, but now it’s all done through apps or games. We can even battle online.      Is that how you came to get into it again, then, online competitions?      Yeah, my friend showed me an app where you can catch digital Pokémon with an AR feature. It’s like walking around the real world and catching them, which is quite fun.      That’s brilliant. How do you get on with Patrick then? He loves playing with the soft toys while we're out for our walks.      Aye, he clings to that green elephant like it’s his best friend. I’d say he takes after you two with the soft toy obsession.      Well, there was a time when I used to love a little pink rabbit—I still have it – but it's got fairly badly mended now because Patrick’s been chewing on the ears.      You have to be quite careful when you're outside with him, huh? Like what if you come across a puddle or a puddle of mud?      Aye, and it's a wonder that the elephant stays clean at all. I had to take it in for a dry clean last week after he sat on it the day the gardener was using the hose.      That is messy! I remember when I was younger, my stepdad used to hose down the garden every Saturday, and I used to be really active and play around in the puddles.      I tried to stop him when he started doing that. There are so many things crawling in the water and faeces from pets or wildlife.      Yeah, that’s true, but I can't say I blame the kid for goin' on adventures in the garden. If it wasn’t for the elephant, I don’t think I'd be goin’ out there myself.      That sounds like it's helping you both out in more ways than one, maybe even improving your walking to some extent?      Definitely, and I tend to push a little further so I can beat him to the next tree where his next toy might be.

Rather a lot of folk taking the long weekend to get in early. I was just reading the weather forecast—bit of a freeze coming Thursday. Hope the road isn’t too bad for the drive up. Livin’ in the country, we do see the worst of things at times.      Oh, don’t worry, I’ll leave early if need be. I’ve got the car serviced not too long ago. A lot less stress now I got this old thing sorted. Oh, and bless me, I’ve made a new jumper to take up. You always say it looks right childish.      Right, but it will make the girls laugh. I swear, the last jumper you knit had a cardigan that Myra still wears. Still, enough talk of jumpers—what about the dinner? I’m thinking we go traditional and do the whole lot? Half the village is coming, after all.      Can we do something else? Not that I don’t like the turkey, but I’d quite like some options. Maybe a bit of something spicy? Or something that’s not over the top, maybe?      I second that. Like a different kind of roast or even a vegan shepherd’s pie? My friend Jade always does one. She says it’s got lentils and rosemary?      Right cheery, the pair of you. Let’s not forget tradition! You din’t expect me to forget what I learned from my mum and her mum before her. A proper Christmas dinner in my book is turkey, stuffing, a plum pudding, and a glass of something hotter than the fire.      But look at it this way, we can do both! Half turkey, half something else. I’ll ask round the area, see if anyone fancies a change. Maybe even some local cheese—I do know a farmer down the road who’d be more than happy to give us a few slices.      That sounds reasonable. And while we’re on it—has any of you heard about James? My cousin’s lad. His car broke down while visiting his girlfriend over in Lincolnshire. Got stuck in a layby, a couple of miles out the village path.      Oh no! Is he all right?      Aye, well, more or less. Just got a cold, and the car’s still being fixed. Seems his bloke isn’t what your dad would call “man enough” to get help. Mind you, it was snowing so hard by Lincoln that even the patrols couldn’t get in for hours.

Rather annoying I had to take the day off work, but Sarah’s birthday was her big one — sixty. I got her a lovely candlestick set, you know the one we saw by the river? Thought it would make a change from the usual kitchen gadgets I bring her.      That’s thoughtful of you. She deserves something more elegant. I got her a vintage scarf I found in that little shop on the high street — still got some tassels and a bit of fraying, but it looked interesting. Thought she might wear it to the birthday dinner at the pub.      You two are brilliant. I’ve only just finished work and I’m already tired. I got her a poem written in like that old English style, with rhymes and everything. I thought it’d be funny to hear her read it aloud, but I’ve not told her yet. Might make her cry — or laugh — not sure which.      Well, she did get in a bit of a state the other day when I mentioned ordering the spare wheel from the garage. I said something like, “We do need to get it sorted before we start the journey,” and she looked at me like I’d tried to speak Martian. I might’ve used a bit too much jargon without thinking about it.      Mate, you often do. I still remember that time you described the broken boiler like you were giving a staff meeting. Sarah just said, “Darling, you lost me on the word ‘thermostat’. Let’s just get a man to look at it.”      I think what you were saying is a bit unfair, Dad. You do make things complicated — but your passion for work is great. I mean, I’m a copywriter now, right? So I sort of owe you a bit of that.      Aye, it is a bit strange how that all works, isn’t it? I always tell her I passed my sixth form with just a bit of a push, and it was all I needed to get where I am. You’d think doing a degree would’ve been better, but I’ve seen colleagues with degrees and they don't always know what to do with their hands. Me, I’m a nurse — I’m helping people, and that’s good work.      Honestly, I feel like I made the opposite choice, but I suppose it all ends up in the same place.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh, Doreen? I was promising to pop down to Bury St Edmunds and pick up some new mags for the box I’ve been putting together      Aye, quite alright. Look, George, you can take mine in the meantime if it’s all the same, I’ve a full pile and I haven’t had time to sort them yet with a bit of A listing too.      Oh, well that’s alright then, thank you.      Speak for yourself, George. You don’t say a word to fetch the newspaper without mentioning it! Not like I don’t do my fair bit, only I’ve been attending this organisation My turkey shop, bless them, who are left with no one to help, they’ve been moaning on about the place I think it turned round thanks to us assembling for about a month at the weekend breakfasts.      Aha! The turkey shop! I remember the day we walked past, didn’t we say the man looked like Mr. Potato Head?      Oh, I can’t remember I don’t think quite a week goes by without supplying Turkey for something. Tell me though, did they have the proper trotters in then?      Mate, I got fairly concerned, and I had to confirm if the woman had a turkey or not!      Oh, well done! That’s your ability, huh? Our George here      Just because my tongue is long, Roger, doesn’t mean what you say is true.      Anyway, Margot called me last week, said her parents have about five ducks and they want someone to look after them for a while. Both going off on what she said was a “religious retreat”. Supposed to have gone to Cornwall for two weeks.      Aha! You can bet they did. They just want them to go.      Oh, I tried to get them when I was doing some shop visits in Torquay. They gave me a grand total of lunches to keep the ducks happy! They asked if I knew someone who knew someone, something around this idea of a man with a vast goatee beard on the coast if you know what I mean.      Oh, I don’t know, I imagine it’s what your mother used to call someone “a big lost soul,” and Father’s been blaming the sheep!      Oh right, talk about putting two over on us. We were lucky! Our parents were always open; all I remember is going for walks.

Rather than chuck a DVD in eh, innit? Thought we'd cook summat first, ‘ow like... got us a chilli recipe off the interweb. Proper fancy, innit?      Oi, alright then, I didn’t know you could cook! Thought you were just eeny event organiser chuckin’ bunting 'bout and servin’ cuppas.      Ha, well I  do  organise social events, love it or loathe it, innit. Rather chilly this morning, ain't it? That’s me remembering to draw the curtains in time ‘fore they all got nippy with draft.      I prefer it warm, gran. Keeps the radiators on full blast all day. Well, as long as you both got all set. I’ll pop out for some milk and biscuits later while the two of you are shopping for Auntie’s birthday present.
