You can go down to Cambridge at half four, collect them, and we’ll all catch the bus up together.      It’s gonna be the best day, right before the light show

Rather annoying this new red traffic light near St Austell, isn't it? You'd think they'd employ someone with a bit of sense to sort this road out. I can't say I'm surprised, though. Seems like cash is only doled out to the places that shout the loudest these days.       laughs dryly  You'd think the traffic problems were mirrored in government priorities, wouldn't you? Politicians promise policy changes one day and back down the next. I watched a debate on the road safety bill last week, and the Tories were bickering about spending.      Honestly, I'm just glad I'm not driving. All this politics is making my head spin. From what I've seen, MPs seem more interested in fighting each other than making things better for everyday people like us.      That’s the trouble. Back in the 80s, if something went wrong, there was at least a clear plan or some semblance of accountability. And the unions were strong, you know? I remember my father talking about factory strikes and how workers had a voice.      Oh, he might have known a few of my uncles back in the day, then. My father was a coal miner near Nantyglo, and the way he tells it – tales of camaraderie, hardship and strikes that lasted months. It was the heart of the community back then.      I can only imagine. We might not live in the same county, but in places like Cardiff or Swansea, the spirit of those old community ties still flickers, doesn’t it? Just a bit more under the surface now.      That it does. Though I do wonder if our young people even know such places exist beyond what's on the news. You learn to think beyond your postcode, right? I mean, climate change or housing issues aren't just local problems anymore.      That’s true, but there’s more to it than just being global-minded. My grandad used to say, ‘You can’t fight the tide if you don’t know your own shore.’ It’s about knowing your roots.      I suppose it always has been a balancing act – what your roots hold you to and what winds push you to change.

Aw, it's probably just the timer or the sensor. You frightened half the street the other night shouting at it! I thought  someone  had broken in!      Classic Ruth! Though I reckon that machine should've been chucked out a year back, like you said. It was costing a fortune to keep running!      Didn’t ask  you  what you thought, Chloe! You're still living off student loans and probably wouldn’t know the cost of an electricity bill if it bit you on the backside!      Well, I can afford to throw my old phone out and pick up a new one every six months if I want, thank you very much! You’re still using that ancient landline in the kitchen!      And the phone call we had with your Aunt Mae the other day? Good grief, she thought I was one of her grandsons for twenty minutes.      Aye, that was a proper belly laugh, that. Imagine her going on about football tactics with Tom!      And don’t even get me started on trying to explain what a meme is to her. She looked at me like I’d just offered her a tea-flavoured yoghurt!      You know what? That reminds me. Did you read about Aunt Lucy and Uncle Pete’s wedding anniversary? They had the most ridiculous scheme—something to do with flashbacks to their first date?      I did! They dressed up as they did the day they got engaged and had a little "sparkle and shine" cabaret at the pub. Doesn’t sound like  our  kind of night, personally!      All I know is, if I have to suffer through another round of karaoke, I might have to start using you for a human chair, Chloe.      Let’s not talk about New Year’s Eve  too  soon! I’m still nursing a hangover from  last  year’s telly marathon. That was one go of  Doctor Who , three series of  I May Be Wrong  and six glasses of sherry between us.      And your cat was licking the floor for three days!      Well, you try watching two people belly-laugh to a sitcom at midnight when you’re half-cut!      Now that I’ve been watching a lot more of since the cat started ignoring me!

Rather unusual to see butterfly forks on the table, Christopher. I do confess they look rather decorative, but they're not the most practical choice for supper, are they?      Oh, we found them in the kitchen box we discovered under the shelves. It says 'Tuesday' on it, so we thought—well,  Tuesday , so today was the right day to use them.      A quirky tradition? I suppose that's one way to liven up a Tuesday. Though I'd hesitate to suggest dining on anything more than salad with them. Didn’t your mother teach you how to use proper cutlery?      We were practicing, Aunt Ursula! Look, we can push the food across the plate, and sometimes it flips—it’s like a seesaw! I made the peas bounce!          Oh bother. I see you've already begun to mastering them, then. I’ll just pour the gravy and marvel at your nimble fingers, shall I?      Speaking of which, I do like the way we have this quiet time every Sunday. You don’t talk as much during the grief minute.      It’s two minutes, Christopher. The two minutes of silence. It's a mark of respect for those who’ve given and lost so much. It begins to feel like somnambulism by now—everyone’s used to it, stepping out of the kitchen, brushing past each other in silence. But it also gives me a moment to consider the weight of the world. You might think about it more now that you're growing up.      I did think about it last year when I was at school. My teacher brought it up when we were watching Remembrance Day videos.      Excellent. Understanding shouldn’t be left to memory books alone. You’re quite clever, Luke. And I rather like that you're ready to celebrate both his and your birthdays on the same day this time instead of quarreling.      I sort of forgot about my own, to be fair. But he mentioned it first with that cake I brought from the bakers.      Still, it’s thoughtful of you both. I do hope you go out of your way to be more patient with one another. And speaking of Russia, Christopher, I had a fascinating call with Professor Ivanov from the Institute about a new partnership program. He’s quite charming, and despite the political climate, he spoke earnestly about education as a bridge.

Rather annoying I had to take the marking home with me, but I need to get it done before the half-term trip to Cornwall. The kids have been talking about it non-stop ever since I mentioned Adventure Island! It’s a bit chaotic, truth be told, but children love a bit of adventure, don’t they?      Mmah, I want to go on the rollercoaster… not the wobbly one though, that’s too scary! I got a tummy ache last time we went there.      I don’t get tummy aches! I had vegan chips and a frozen drink last time. I’m allergic to dairy, so we always have to check what we can eat now. My turkey burger was brilliant, you should try it next time, Mummy.      Aww, and I bought you the little pirate hat you wanted for the park. We’re going breakfast, rides and then the museum in Falmouth for the afternoon. The Maritime Museum has an exhibition that's part of the V&A collaboration—plenty to see for all of us.      Museums are boring! I want to build a sandcastle like last time and play in the waves.      Well, we can do that too. We’ll take the buckets and spades with us. Maybe even try that seafood café again, if the menu is okay for you, Lily. I bet they’ve got vegan fish and chips!      They do have a vegan menu board now—developing restaurants are quite inspiring. I had a lovely lunch there myself the other day. So, as long as you both behave and finish your veggie wraps for lunch at home, we’ll have an excellent time.      I had my thimble sandwiches and drank my milk yesterday!      And  I  packed the binoculars for the seashell hunt. I bet we’ll see dolphins again!      If you see dolphins, we’ll take a little detour to see the lighthouse from the clifftop path. It’s always beautiful with the sea all around. But first, I do need to work on these essays for a bit. I’ll make the dinner while you go and get the snacks ready from the larder.      Can I help? I’ll be good, I promise!      Shawna can have the big spoon to help, and I can stir the pan! I don’t like helping with the chopping, though.      We’ll see! One at a time, my loves.

So did you get the History coursework back yet? I still haven’t submitted mine. Mr. Thompson is piling on the pressure with all those deadlines now that we’re in sixth form.      Yeah, mine came back last week. I got a B! I thought for sure it was a C. Do you know mine’s due on Friday?      Oh man, that’s next week already. I haven’t even got the structure sorted yet. I’m thinking of asking Jess to help me out. She aced hers and she’s really into the whole Black Death module.      Jess is decent enough. Though I still can’t get over how the teachers promote only prefects for extra help. My brother was a prefect and he got to skip assemblies all the time! I’m not obsessed with Darcy, the prefect head in our class? Dude’s so annoying, always correcting people.      He’s alright I guess. Just a bit in his own world, you know? Anyway, speaking of teachers, have you ever got the vibe Mr. Patel in Physics is over it? I swear he’s been coughing up a lung since we did the circuit diagrams last week.      Oh no, I didn’t know that. Does he have an allergy or is he just –?      No clue, but the other day he walked into a poster on the way to the whiteboard and stayed cool the whole lesson like it never happened. Like, bro, just someone said, "Are you okay?" and he just said, "Physical contact can damage surfaces."        [snorts]   That’s classic! I need to write that down for the yearbook about him. Anyway, hey, you’re going to the party at Charlie’s on Saturday, right? My cousin is going to be there and she’s bringing her uncles who both got the tickets for  Mission: Impossible 7 . You can see it for free if you come with us!      Wait, seriously? I tried to bike to the cinema last week but the security didn’t like that. They gave me a warning or something 'cause I walked in with my helmet still on.      That’s so stupid. I ride the bus to school go every day on my own bike. It’s not like anyone’s going to bike in, drop a bomb and then go, “Hey, I left your helmet behind.”      I know, right? But it’s amazing how many rules we’re given now.

Rather annoying this new road layout eh? You can’t even get past the roundabout in Chester-le-Street without feelin’ like you’re in a bloody obstacle course. I swear, someone needs to give the planners a crash course in proper layin’ out roads—get a motorbike through it an’ it’s practically a death trap!           Yeah, I heard most a the complaints came from motorcyclists and cyclists too. I had to take a detour last week; pulled over a lorry and nearly hit a bus. Didn’t even want to test my luck on the main routes. I reckon they just  think  they’re clever when the real world don’t match their blueprints.           Yeah, typical. Ten more months they’ll say it’ll be sorted, and I’ll be the one stuck in an hour’s jam every day ‘cause they’re still digging up the tarmac again. Reminds me—watched the cricket last night, you catch it?      Man, I did, and that Ashes game was  huge . Root nearly pulled it off with one of them miracles he does. But still, grief. Hales dropped that catch—absolute watery grave if I’ve ever seen one. Was Rob really playing at the same time as that? He was still talking about the Ashes today while we were out on site.      Aye, I got that email at work too, from the coffee bar someone at Spennymoor. Rob’s got this thing about cricket—half the village agrees with him, the other half moans ’bout the price of a pint and where the telly’s gone. Not that I mind—wins or loses, you can bet it’ll be lively this summer.      Speaking o’ that, you still thinking of taking the old bike for the North Pennines challenge this September? I’ve got a mate who passed it last year—he said it was a scenic hell if you don’t know the routes.      You read my mind. I’ve had a few pals offer to join me—course, they’ve all been on big whistles with fi’teen gears and suspension you could park a car on. But I’ve got the KTM.sorted up on the back if you fancied a go. G’no line in the sand, it’s just mud, stones an’ determination what your legs do.      You’ve got to be joking—I’d love that! I’ve had that new gravel bike for months and done zero ‘cause I’ve been working flat out.

Okay, I just wanted to double-check the menu before we order. I know it's late, but I really don’t want to get chicken when I ordered beef and broccoli! Any of you seen where that ends up?      No, I kind of zoned out once the garlic prawn came on the page. I mean, that’s the only good option if you ask me—everything else is a betrayal of our senses.      I don’t hate sweet and sour. It’s not like it’s a crime to like the standard options. Didn’t your mum always make sweet and sour meatloaf, Ben?      I don’t know what’s worse—my mum's meatloaf or you thinking it was Chinese food. I left that trauma behind when I was 12.      I think the real trauma is when you actually  try  something new and it doesn’t kill the taste buds. Like that duck pancakes place in Leamington, you ever go there?      Yeah! That was actually pretty good. The duck was tender and the pancakes—personally, I’d take duck over sweet and sour any day.      That’s only because there was something to dip it in. I remember when we got “stir-fried” something at that place off High Street, and the “chili paste” looked like it had been made by someone licking their own elbow and then throwing in a handful of cumin and some old wasabi paste.      That was unfortunately a very British attempt at sour-spicy-tangy-chilli fusion. Or as I like to call it, the national dish of Clacton-on-Sea about five minutes before the local health inspector stops the oven.      Okay, what are we even ordering now? I know I’m not voting for the classic sweet and sour. My tongue  remembers  trauma.      What if we just split into thirds? I’ll take something safe, you can have something adventurous, and Sarah can do whatever she normally does to torture her poor digestive system.      Oh, come on, it was digestive balm last time. That's not  my  fault.      Yeah, go ahead and pretend your life mission is to discover every sauce at the bottom of the packet, Sarah.      I will—and when I taste all of them in one mouthful, it will hurt, and I will scream, and you will never speak to me again.      Perks of being the food pioneer of this group.

Rather annoying the new folk in next door innit? Seems they’ve got a budgie squawkin like it’s the bloody apocalypse at six every mornin’. I were tryin’ to read a chapter on postcolonial theory last night and the bird just wouldn’t shut up.      Oh dear, I’ve noticed it too. Me and the lads at the surgery have been talkin' about nosy neighbours. Not the best this year, honestly. Oh but don’t get me started—my GP just told me the NHS is like a fish called a herring—it's under pressure from all sides but somehow still keeps goin’.      That’s only if we’re lucky. It’s turkey time around here, you know. Me and the department’ve been talkin’ about the D word, deliv’ry times for undergrads. It’s like they’ve dropped the ball. I mean, universities are funded this way and that, but in the end, we’re the ones stitching hides, innit?      That’s real, I mean I do ten-to-one patients some days. Y’know I were down in Finland as a student nurse and the system there? Like clockwork. The folk are healthy, the rhythm of it all gives you time to breathe. Mate of mine lives there now, and he swears by his sauna schedule.      Aye, I’ve been to Oulu once. Smashing place, and the people just walk into hospitals and get sorted. No queue-jumpers, just peace and quiet. You ever think about the housing crisis over here though? Me and me missus considered packing up and headin’ abroad for a few years. My sister lives in Manchester, but she can’t get on the property ladder there either.      Poor things. I have a cousin up in Leeds; she just found a flat after four years of lookin’. She’s rentin’ and worried about eviction. I tell her to take my sister’s advice and start lookin’ in Arbroath or Inverness—cheap as chips and beautiful out there.      Aye, the kids do miss playin’ in proper green space around here, course Liverpool's got the docks goin’ on but it’s more of a buzz for the tourists than the kids in the estate. You got any of ‘em yourself?      Two at secondary school, both lucky enough to have roles in the drama department—grateful for that, gives ’em a bit of stability ‘mid this madhouse we call the modern world.

Rather do a day's work than rely on handouts, innit?      Oh, lass go on, Harold. Times are different now. Not everyone can afford to work, especially with health thrown into the mix.      Health, eh? I was in good een when I was younger, and I got an 'rogy bill now just for having a desk job.      Ay, that's the lot for you. If you live long enough, you'll get one arse end of the stick. Didn’t your wife get the new tablet last week?       laughs  She did, and the thing’s still got her stressed trying to figure it out. She blames me for not setting it up properly. Ten minutes, and I’m out the door, and she’s in there for an hour.      Blimey, I couldn’t teach that thing a thing. Haha. Though at my age, the phone call centre told me to “press button one” and I had to ask, “Button one with the big blob on or the one with the written bit?”       laughs  Hah! Tell 'em they're watching the future generation trot off in their chairs. So what about the new chap down the road? He got a van, and he’s always stopping the traffic trying to make a go of it.      Mark? Oh, he's alright. Family man. Takes in odd jobs—removals mostly. Poor lad, his missus is on some kind of waiting list for a specialist and can’t be seen for ages.      That’s a about everywhere. My cousin sent a screenshot round the family the other day—she lives near Barnsley and had to travel an hour to get a basic screening.      My sister ‘ad the same. She was screaming down the phone about it. Said it was a bit much after a few too many glasses of wine. Guess they just played it on the news again.      Police doing a round-up by the docks last night. They told me someone spotted some lad with no papers trying to sneak something around. Course, it's all the usual goings on, but it worries me.      I just worry for the kids. Never had it easy, but now it’s a lottery. My latest neighbor said her daughter lives with six others in one flat and still can’t afford to visit her nan.      It's a mad world we've inherited. I mean, the conversations my students have about paying rent...

Rather nippy today, innit? You’d think for June we’d have more of a real summer. I got nowitz from me flat to this place, and I were nearly superstoked I’d gotta jacket on.      No, I mean—get in, it’s freezing! I always take a sweatshirt, even if it’s the middle of summer. You never know in Cambridge. Though I reckon that Aylesbury summer tends to be a bit more dependable. Warm but not stifling, which is just about acceptable.      Oh, honestly, if I had a pound for every time I’ve forgotten a scarf in  this  weather, I'd be out of here and working on a beach in Mykonos by now. I swear, the weather in this city fluctuates more than the stock market. But hey, I’ll take the cold over the Lincoln drizzle any day.      Believe me, I know a cold! Hailing from Pennsylvania, the winters there are not messing about, you know? But this? Man, why do universities always have to be built with ancient, drafty buildings? These place are like iceboxes with a side of cobwebs. I tell ya, it's like they want us to live perpetually in flannel shirts and wool socks.      Don't I know it. My Leeds flat’s got a broken boiler and no central heating—so winter was a whole season of wearing three jumpers and calling it fashion. Still, at least someone at the printing house should sort out the heating in the archive room. I had a cold so bad I’d swear it was a frostbite and it wasn't even winter!      You know, about the archives... have any of you seen the new corpora we were meant to be compiling for the summer research projects? I got an email from the department yesterday asking  where  we were with them. And I mean, no pressure or anything.      Aye, the one about verb collocations in informal speech? I tried to start on that last week but me laptop’s such a  piss-poor —takes forever to upload the data and keeps crashing! I’m thinking of going back to the university library where they’ve got those shiny Macs that don’t sound like my nan’s washing machine.      Speaking of libraries, anyone fancy hitting the UL this afternoon? I need to grab a few reference books for the PSU project, and it might help us all rally up some steam for the data upload.

Rather annoying when the box office is sold out, ay? Still, the queue for the matinee does let you in for a spot of tea and cake at John Lewis. Not a bad plan      Aye, we do love the convenience of being able to purchase things in advance, don’t een? I always liked the idea of one-stop shopping      I’ve been trying to resist buying that coffee from Costa but they do have this voucher deal for 20% off      Ah! You mean the one where you have to chase it up the escalators with your hot chocolate frozen to your hand?      That’s the one, precisely. Still, it's like that My turkey shop doorstep madness but with jelly babies left and right      I reckon you're on to a good idea in the world of language teaching with your PhD, aren't you?      It keeps me busy enough alright. The hard part is persuading non-language people that being multilingual is kind of the new black. I reckon culture and language need one another like, y’know, gloves and knitters      It is interesting how the younger generation seems more open to language learning these days, especially with all this YouTube and Twitch paraphernalia      I agree, and I take the view that learning a language is almost an antidote to homophobia and xenophobia if we’re being honest. Still, the curriculum is stuck in this ‘big four’ mindset—French, German, Spanish, and Mandarin      I had a kid once who spent three months in Kyoto through an exchange programme and came back speaking Japanese better than most people I know who’ve been to the same countries the other way around      Exactly! Cross-cultural projects are such a plug and play for language learning. No one mentioned to the curriculum, ‘Hey, just playing Enya in the background doesn’t cut it’      No, it bloody well doesn’t      So when are you going to crack on with that Swedish speaker exchange again? Got a space in the diary for a new one?      I’d be lying if I said I haven’t considered the proposal, but go on then, make it official      Sorted! You’re on in two weeks, I’ll be in touch with the details through the proper channels. Now then, have you made it to that conference seminar on cultural competence in education yet?      I did alright. It was over in Birmingham, but at least the refreshments were homemade macarons

Rather chilly this morning, ain't it? That’s me remembering to draw the curtains in time ‘fore they all got nippy with draft.      I prefer it warm, gran. Keeps the radiators on full blast all day. Look, I’ve unpacked my things in the spare room. I left the folder with the mock papers on the bed. I reckon I’ll try to get that next round of practice done before tea.      Ah, mocks, you used to dread those when you were a lad, didn’t you, love? Didn’t your mum nearly pull her hair out over those exam books?      Aye, she were the real terror when marks weren’t up to scratch. One time, I dropped my best O-levels in ‘whatr, Arithmetic – I still remembers her face, and I’ll be the first to say, she was far harder on me than she was on no one else.      I don’t reckon GCSEs ever looked like that, Grandad. These days it’s all percentages and grade boundaries that shift like sands.      Nonsense, the world don’t change quite that fast. You’re still answering questions, ain’t you? Just shorter legs, same old trot rhythm.      Let’s see about preparing tea while we’re at it, shall we? There’s a tray in the larder with shortbread and those biscuits I mentioned. ‘Balderdash’ we’d call ‘em at North Ferriby. Strictly for emergency biscuits, like this here week.      ‘Balderdash’ or not, I’ve got a spot of hankering for a nice buttery bikkie. My lungs might not be quite the same, but my taste for sippets remains what it was.      I’ll help, if I may? I’ve got a bit ‘o energy left after shifting my luggages.      Bless you, dear. Let me stir the tea. I’ll pop a splash of milk in there. We don’t rush, not this week. ‘Tis grandkid week, after all.      Speaking of, I’d be grateful if you could shoot me a message the minute you set goin’ on your own about that bus number to go back to York. I’d rather not see you missin’ a thing.      Reckon I have it sorted, Miss North Ferriby. I’ll check the app again just to be certain. I expect it’s number ‘44’ anyway.      Now that I can corroborate. Always number 44, unless it’s been renumbered in me absence.

So did you go out last night?      Aye, me and the lasses went to this naff little bar in the city. It was properly packed, by the way. I think it was hen do season or somethin'. Did you end up going anywhere?      Yeah, went out with my mates from the uni. We hit this little watering hole near campus — a bit of a dive, but we got in a few pints. Oh, and watched a football match on the telly while we were there. It was me cousin’s birthday or somethin'.      Oh nice! Did you end up goin' to the pub only or stay for the night? My turkey came around with me, an’ left at like midnight. Probably goin’ back to the same boring office tomorrow sad face.      Nuh, we just stayed out for a couple of hours then came back. I'm a bit in two minds about going out too often these days, you know? With school and all. I'm trying to keep up with the work, you know? But I’ve got this one friend who puts pressure on me to go out and enjoy.      Aww, that's proper crap. I was like you last year. Back then I had a dog called Milo, and I barely had time to take him out, let alone go out with friends. Now I've given him to my aunt, but that made me feel kind of guilty. I miss him, but I’ve got my own life to work on.      Yeah, I get that. I had a cat once — called Mr Whiskers — but I couldn't really look after him properly while I was stressing out over exams. It's funny, looking back — I remember this one time when I was trying to cook and it knocked a bottle of wine to the floor, and for like five whole minutes I didn’t even notice.      Ha! I’d have probably got all fired up about it. Honestly, I am mad at myself for being such a clumsy idiot sometimes. Let me tell you, trying to upload uni work on the laptop while the Wi-Fi's going out and you're in a room with three other people arguing over the telly is a nightmare.      Oh, I know how that goes. I remember trying to do group work with blokes who were watching a Premier League match.

Rather lovely to sit out here on this evening, ay? The garden looks nice after the rain. The peas are warming up rather well in the pot, I think. I can already smell the chips.      Aye, Ma, I got those chips frozen fresh. We'll make do with cheese and gravy if you fancy it. It was lovely of Gran to offer to come up for the weekend. She’s been hankering to see the place since I mentioned it in our last letter.      Aye, and she’s very spry for her age. Let's just hope she can handle the stairs! Still, it’ll be good to have someone to talk to besides herself and the cat.      I’ve met her once before. She’s quite the character. I reckon she remembers every pastry recipe and every football match the old man ever took in, by the look of it. I still can’t figure out how she’s still got all those names and dates remembered.      Grandmother’s always had a prodigious memory. I remember her taking me over to her village once for Championship Day. She showed me how to keep score properly. We still play it by numbers, old-school style.      You remember that West Ham match she swore was robbed at the 94th minute? She still calls it the  Hand of God  despite her age. All that time spent watching the telly and poring over match reports.      Haha, yeah. She also insisted Liverpool won the title a year too late because of a referee’s mistake. Also, I think she blames the government for bad drainage at Anfield after that midsummer downpour in '82. She’s not the kind to lay blame lightly.      I suppose that’s why you know that she shouldn’t be left alone near a FIFA World Cup finals table. She once tried to reassign goals to her grandkids during a virtual match and nearly dethroned the actual teams’ rankings.      I miss waiting for those Saturday afternoons when you and I would watch the live games. There was something to be said for the old ways—tea-break, no replays, no streaming. Just telly and the team on the go.      Aye, and now I have kids who think football’s all about transfers and pixels on a screen. Hard to impress your 12-year-old with a flukey 30th-minute goal against a mid-table side.

Rather annoying this, having my laptop play up again — anyone fancy a cuppa while it reboots? I got the kids from Brighton today, and they left their muddy football boots by the door. Annoying, really. Not to mention they forgot their dinner things at the hostel.      That is so  not  the first time, mate. They always seem to forget their socks, a clean shirt, and half their provisions before they go anywhere social. Still, it gives you a chance to introduce them to one of the local chip shops. Oh, by the way, the bin strike isn’t getting any better. The heap under the stairs is becoming a bit of an issue, don’t you think?      Honestly, I’m just left wondering how much water companies charge to provide clean water, only for us to be in a world of muck most of the time. I’d quite like to see a proper debate on this while everyone has a nice cup of tea. I’ve also been meaning to ask, have you ever tried the filtered water from the kettle vs. the tap? Makes a big difference for tea, in my opinion.      Ah, water and bins — two things I tried not to think about for 40 years. When I got married in the 1970s, I didn’t think I’d see the day we were worrying about the same old problems as my dad did in his time. And don’t even get me started on the SAT NAV. I still rely on a good map and my memory of the old town roads. I remember walking all over Brighton when I was young and never needing a navigational device. Far more fun in a way, if I do say so myself.      That’s something I’d love to take up again. Maybe start walking there weekly with friends. It’s not too far, and I do need to get out of the flat more. Although I passed out last night on the floor with the TV on after a few too many glasses of wine. Guess I need to invest in a proper SAT NAV to navigate my way home after a few pints.      At least your eyesight’s good. I’ve lost my glasses twice now this week. I swear they vanish into the sofa or get swallowed by the cat. And setting up my brother’s Blackberry is turning out to be harder than explaining the differences between "mate" and "chum" to foreign students.

Proper moved me, watching her fight for extra portions in a war-torn café. Made me think though: with all this advance in computers these days, imagine if she had a device she could just plug into and it sorted her portion sizes or calculated the caloric needs for a whole village in five seconds flat. That’d be revolutionary.      Technically speaking, we  do  have that now. It's just not practical in conflict zones. The energy required to power it or the infrastructure to support it is... absent. And you can't exactly slap a USB port on most kitchens in a civil-war scenario.      Fair point. But does any o’ that lot take account o’ local culture anyway? Like, if you’re a mulher on the outskirts of Kathmandu, you probably don’t want some camera-toting robot shouting about your macronutrient intake to the rest o’ the village. Websites and gadgets are one thing, mate, but whack the wrong code into a folk's day and you might as well throw a grenade the size of a go-kart on your own computer.      True, very true. Technology without understanding context is like a box of chocolates without labels. Some are virtual, some are just virtual in the wrong sense. You ever tried out that app with the step-by-step photos of your meals?

Rather annoying to be honest. He’s not bad looking, but he thinks he's the centre of the universe... Like, I don’t have time for that sort of nonsense!      Aw, don’t be harsh. You only went out once—maybe he’s not the biggest jerk in real life? I mean, I don’t think you'd   seriously   date someone as self-obsessed as that, right?      I’m with Evie on this one. He needs to do a bit more   learning to listen   before he even thinks about talking about himself every five minutes. You know, even I’m not that arrogant and I once made a documentary about my own cat!      Fair point, Aaron—but not all of us want to hear about someone who refers to themself in the third person. Honestly, I spend most of my time arguing with clients about structural integrity, and then I go home and have to put up with his “I’m the future of dating” vibe? No thanks.      So what’s the plan? Another one, maybe? Try and avoid him next time?      I don’t know. Maybe. I might go on something proper for a change. You know, like a website that doesn’t just have photos of people posing with Tesco value meals and self-help book shelves.      Ugh, yeah. If I could blame dating apps for everything, I would. Like, someone at some point said “Let’s design a platform where algorithmic ghosts try to match people with hotter photos than their profile”, and I’m here being told I match with someone  literally only because we both have about five tattoos .      Oh come on, Charlie—your profile said you enjoyed “the socialist manifesto and drinking too much cider in the park”, how many people are you going to match with like that?      A lot, apparently. I got a message from a woman in Plymouth last night talking about coercive capitalism. You mad?      Anyway… moving on. Websites aside, are we still on for the weekend trip to London? Some of our Manchester-based mates are coming down, right?      Yeah, I think so. I’ve heard there are a few people from London coming in, too. Some architect from the boxset house on Thames Embankment. Shawna or something? I might’ve been obsessed with her Twitter during lockdown.      True, Shawna’s designs are insane—love the raw concrete and the natural light.

Rather exciting to have your parents over for the first time, Sarah. I hope they like the flat — we’ve got the essentials sorted out with the kitchen and everything. I’ve asked their previous address where we should borrow anything we need. Charming kitchen, I think!      Yeah, my mum’s bound to be curious about the spices on the counter. I reckon she might try to "tidy" them. A lot of this tends to happen when my parents visit. Oh, and she always insists on using plastic bags! It gets a bit much for me.      Plastic bags, really? I used to fill those with nuts when the fridge supply ran out. Never managed to stop the turkey on Christmas Day, though. Fun anecdotes. And you mentioned benefits earlier — is the flat covered on them?      Benefits? Hmm, I’m not entirely sure — better for breakfast, really. My agreement says I pay for utility bills in advance. Nothing’s too heavy as long as I’m ordering online spare parts when I need to. Speaking of which, I should do a bit of reading on senescence — I keep seeing words about centenarians and how they manage cholesterol and such. Rather fascinating, really.      Oh, from what I’ve studied at my master’s degree level, it seems like avoiding gambling and other bad habits are the keys. Nothing quite tests that as much as Brighton’s restaurants and travel spots! And I might be wrong, but I’ve heard premonitions are also suspiciously often associated with a rush of bad habits.      Ah, Brighton! I used to live near there in my youth — had a colleague who taught in a school about window cleaning secrets. Oddly helpful when the landlords didn’t take care of things. I suppose you could say he was an expert on friends who didn’t pay their share for things like that.      That’s quite the anecdote! On a tangent, have you managed the pronunciation of scones yet, Dad? I tried to teach him when he visited last time. It didn’t go well — "scones" comes with a cream tea and not with "skoan."      I plead ignorance with the pronunciation! But the cream tea go-to is my best bet if you ask me. Just don’t ask me to distinguish diverticulitis from any other ailment — I stopped at your mother’s GP. It was enough flu and all!

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh? You’d think in Cambridge we’d know if it’s ‘goin’ to stop or not by now. I’m more used to the blasts of wind we get in Sunderland, but this… this is just soggy and boring as anything.      Yeah, I saw the forecast, and it said “sun and cloud” at 10 am… not a single cloud in sight now. At least the rain helps keep the plants alive round here. It was a dump of a place to grow up in Pembury for a while during the drought season.      Right, I’ve heard talk of that. My nan’s got a garden in Seaham and she says she had to turkey out all the veg last summer—it left her in bits. Probably why I’ve been cookin’ up more and more in the flat now. Curry dishes, you know, something warmin’ when it’s bone-achin’ cold outside.      I hear you. I’ve been dabblin’ in German stews too, since I’ve been thinking over the move to Berlin for work. My place up near Cambridge City puts me a fair way from the uni when I’m workin’ on campus… plus, the house prices round here are laughin’ in my face.      I know, I know. We were up seein’ somethin’ in Milton and the rents were higher than some ‘ouses in Newcastle. And I’ve never even thought ‘bout settlin’ down. Just trying to keep afloat with my job sourcin’ out all them digital speeches for corpus linguistics projects. Bit dry at times, but I like it, y’know.      That does sound quite the niche gig. Whereas I’m out thumpin’ concrete and steel for clients that think they’re the housing kings of the South East. Jokes on ‘em. I’ve been lookin’ into freelancin’ and maybe openin’ my own small practice ‘stead of working with the big contractors.      That’s bold! Like, I know being academicky is one thing but creatin’ your own business must have risks?      Oh aye, but if you’ve got the technical go-to-it on your own, you don’t get so stuck in the corporate line of, “No, because we done it this way before.” Anyway, what do you think about the internet fluency now? Like, gen Z kids using those slang bits?      Oh, it’s wild. My job is effectively codin’ that stuff up.

Rather chilly this morning, wasn't it? I needed three cups of coffee just to get out of the house.      Oh, I’m more of a one-cup-and-go kind of person these days. Too much to do before the day even starts! How’s things at the hospital been?      Ugh, it’s been   mad  , love. Two of the nurses called in with sickness, and I’ve just been doing this and doing that. You’d think staffing was easier in a general practice!      Funny you say that, because the care home’s been hell too. We’ve even lost two staff to self-isolation. It’s taken its toll. I miss my breaks more than anything. You’ve got enough to deal with without having to cover everyone else’s shifts.      I hear you. I work with an elderly couple about a mile from here. I see them every morning and I’m dreading it some days, just because I know the day will stretch on, and I’ll be so knackered by the end that I won’t even feel like cooking.      I can relate — even as a copywriter, I’ve started feeling like I’m just going through the motions. You work from home, so you don’t get much of a break from it all. I still think it’s easier than yours, though.      It’s all different pressures, I reckon. You don’t get the grime of wet nappies in an office!      Laughs, imagine that! I remember working in a cafe at uni and the mess customers left being bad enough. I don’t even want to know what it’s like with seniors needing help eating all day.      You get used to it, though. The good days are better than anything. I had this one resident last week who hadn’t smiled in weeks. I just sat with her while she watched a film — and at the end, she looked at me and said, “Thank you for being you.” You can’t put a price on hearing that.      That’s beautiful. I think I miss that from my younger days — the little smiles, the thank yous. You know, I started this job because I wanted to help others, but sometimes it does get monotonous.      I suppose it always does, in any career. But your work matters. So do you — I seriously think the world would be in more trouble without you all.
